This is a promise to the believers and a warning to the disbelievers. ﴿We fulfilled for them the promise﴾ is of the pattern of "ikhtara" (to choose), where the verb transitive to one object and to another by a preposition, and it is permissible to omit that preposition, i.e., in "al-wa'd" (the promise). This is a pattern that is not regular according to the majority, and only a few verbs of this kind are preserved, which are mentioned in the grammatical works. Similar to ﴿We fulfilled for them the promise﴾ is the saying: "They were true to them in fighting," "He was true to me regarding the age of his camel," and "I was true to Zayd in the report." ﴿Whom We willed﴾ [al-An'am: 83] are the believers, and the transgressors are the disbelievers who exceed in their misguidance and disbelief; and everyone who abandons faith is an excessive transgressor. Their deliverance is from the evil of their enemies and from the punishment that descended upon their enemies.

When He threatened them in this verse, He followed that with the promise of His blessing upon them, saying: ﴿We have certainly sent down to you a Book in which is your Reminder.﴾ The Book is the Qur'an. From Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿your Reminder﴾ means your honor; the genitive was omitted and the genitive-attached word was put in its place. From al-Hasan: the Reminder of your religion. From Mujahid: in it is your news. From Sufyan: the noble characteristics of your morals and the excellence of your deeds. It was also said: a reminder so that you avoid what is not permissible and desire what is obligatory. The author of al-Tahrir said: What the context of the verses requires is that the meaning in it is the mention of your faults and your failings and what the prophets of Allah were treated with, of denial and obstinacy. On this view, the verse is a censure of them and not from the enumeration of blessings upon them, and the speech stays within its context, and the meaning of His saying ﴿Is this anything but a human like yourselves?﴾ [al-Anbiya: 3] ... ﴿Will you not then use reason?﴾ [al-Anbiya: 10] is a rebuke against them for their neglect of reflection and contemplation, which lead to heedlessness. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It may be that it means in it your nobility and your remembrance until the end of time, as we mention the greatness of great affairs, and in this is encouragement. Then he reinforced the encouragement with His saying ﴿Will you not then use reason?﴾ and stirred them thereby to reflection. Al-Zamakhshari said similarly, saying: ﴿your Reminder﴾ means your nobility and your renown, as He said: ﴿And indeed it is a Reminder for you and your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44]; or your admonition; or in it are the noble characteristics by which you sought praise, and good repute is like good neighborliness, fulfilling covenants, truthfulness in speech, returning trusts, generosity, and what resembles that.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 1–10 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿The reckoning of the people has drawn near, while they are heedless and turn away.﴾ ﴿No fresh reminder comes to them from their Lord but they listen to it while playing.﴾ ﴿Their hearts are distracted. And those who did wrong conspire in secret: "Is this not just a man like you? Will you then submit to magic while you see it?"﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord knows every word in the heavens and the earth, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing."﴾ ﴿Rather, they said: "A confusion of dreams! Rather, he has invented it! Rather, he is a poet! Let him bring us a sign, as the earlier messengers were sent."﴾ ﴿No town that We destroyed before them believed. Will they then believe?﴾ ﴿We sent before you only men to whom We revealed. So ask the people of the Reminder (ahl al-dhikr), if you do not know.﴾ ﴿We did not make them bodies that do not eat food, nor were they immortal.﴾ ﴿Then We fulfilled the promise to them, and We saved them and whom We willed, and We destroyed the transgressors.﴾ ﴿Indeed We have sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder. Will you not then understand?﴾

[p. 295] This surah is Meccan without disagreement. From Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud): al-Kahf, Maryam, Ta-Ha and al-Anbiya' are among the first of the "ancient" (al-'ita q al-ula), and they are of my "tilad," that is, of the earliest of what I memorized and acquired of the Qur'an, like the inherited wealth (al-mal al-tilad).

The connection of this surah to what precedes it: when He mentioned ﴿Say: "Each is waiting, so wait"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 135], the Meccan polytheists said: "Muhammad threatens us with the Return and with recompense for deeds, and this is not true; and if it were true, it would be far off." So God sent down ﴿The reckoning of the people has drawn near﴾. The word ﴿اقْتَرَبَ﴾ (iqtaraba, "has drawn near") is of the form ifta'ala, with the meaning of the bare verb qaraba, just as you say irtaqaba and raqaba. It was said: it is more emphatic than qaraba because of the additional letters in its form. The "people" (al-nas) here are the polytheists of Mecca. It was also said: it is general, covering those who deny the Resurrection. The "drawing near of the reckoning" means the drawing near of its time. In linguistic usage, "hisab" (reckoning) is the extraction of a quantity from the total of a count, and it may also be applied to the thing counted. It is called "drawing near" because whatever is coming is near, however long the wait for it may be; what is truly distant is what has passed away. Or it is near in God's reckoning, as in His saying ﴿And indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ [al-Hajj: 47]. Or it is relative to what remains of the world, which is shorter and less than what has passed. In a hadith: "I was sent, and the Hour is like these two (fingers)." The poet said:

*"Whoever he loves never ceases to be nearer than tomorrow,
and whoever he fears never ceases to be farther than yesterday."*

The word ﴿لِلنّاسِ﴾ (lil-nas, "for the people") is connected to ﴿اقْتَرَبَ﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: this lam must be either a complement (silah) of iqtaraba, or an emphasis [p. 296] on the attribution of the reckoning to them, as you say "azuffu lil-hayy rahilahum" (I hasten the departure of the tribe). The original is "azuffu rahil al-hayy," then "azuffu lil-hayy rahilahum." Similar to it is what Sibawayh cited in the chapter on what the stable element may be repeated in for emphasis: "ʿalayka Zaydun harisun ʿalayk," and "fika Zaydun raghibun fik." From the same is the saying "la aba laka," because the lam reinforces the meaning of the idafa (annexation). This second view is stranger than the first. End of quote. By his phrase "a complement" he means that it is connected to iqtaraba. As for his making the lam an emphasis for the annexation of the reckoning to them, despite the lam coming first and entering upon a noun, we know of no one who says this. Also, it would need something it is connected to, and it cannot be connected to "hisabihim" (their reckoning), since it is a verbal noun (masdar) with a complement, and its complement cannot precede it. Also, emphasis comes after what it emphasizes. Furthermore, if it were postponed in this structure, it would not be correct. As for his comparison with what Sibawayh cited, the difference is clear: ʿalayka is a complement of harisun, and the second ʿalayka is a later emphasis; likewise in fika Zaydun raghibun fik, fika is connected to raghibun, and the second fik is an emphasis. What misled him is the correctness of the structure "hisab al-nas." Likewise, "azafa rahilu al-hayy" (the departure of the tribe drew near): he believed that when the noun is fronted with a lam-prepositional phrase and the verbal noun is annexed to its pronoun, it falls under the category of "fika Zaydun raghibun fik," but it is not like it. As for "la aba laka," it is a problematic question with disagreement, and it is possible to say it is so there because the lam is adjacent to the annexation, but other cases cannot be measured on it because of its irregularity and its departure from the general rules. We have discussed it at length in our commentary on al-Tashil. The waw in ﴿وهم﴾ (wa-hum, "while they") is the waw of circumstance (al-hal).

He informed about them with two predicates whose apparent meanings are contradictory, since heedlessness of a thing and turning away from it are incompatible. But they are reconciled by a difference of states. He first informed that they do not reflect on the outcome, but are heedless of what their affair will come to. Then He informed that when they are roused from the slumber of heedlessness and reminded of what the affair of the doer of good and the doer of evil will come to, they turn away from it and pay no heed. Here the "reminder" (dhikr) means what descends of the Qur'an piece by piece. It was said that the intended meaning of "dhikr" is the sayings of the Prophet ﷺ concerning the law, his admonition and his reminding, and describing it as "muhdath" (fresh, newly arrived) is because the Qur'an came down at times, one time after another. One of the Companions was asked about this verse and said: "Fresh in its descent, fresh in its speech." Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: the intended meaning of "dhikr" here is the Prophet ﷺ, by the evidence of ﴿Is this not just a man like you?﴾ and His saying ﴿God has sent down to you a reminder, a Messenger﴾ [al-Talaq: 10]. The Mu'tazilites used the word ﴿muhdath﴾ as an argument for the createdness of the Qur'an, and this is a question discussed in the science of kalam (theology). The majority read ﴿مُحْدَثٍ﴾ (muhdathin) in the genitive as an adjective of "dhikr" according to its form (lafz). Ibn Abi ʿAbla read it in the nominative as an adjective of "dhikr" according to its position (mahall). Zayd ibn ʿAli read it in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from "dhikr," since it has been described by ﴿from their Lord﴾. It is permissible for ﴿مِن رَبِّهِمْ﴾ (from their Lord) to be connected to ﴿يَأْتِيهِمْ﴾ (comes to them). ﴿اسْتَمَعُوهُ﴾ (they listen to it) is a circumstantial clause, and its circumstantial element (dhu al-hal) is the object in ﴿ما يَأْتِيهِمْ﴾. ﴿وهم يَلْعَبُونَ﴾ (while they play) is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَمَعُوهُ﴾. ﴿لاهِيَةً﴾ (distracted) is a state from the pronoun in ﴿يَلْعَبُونَ﴾, or from the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَمَعُوهُ﴾, in which case it is a state after a state. The word "lahiyah" comes from the Arab saying "lahiya ʿanhu" when one is distracted and heedless: yalha lahyan and lihyanan. That is, even if they perceive, this does not benefit them, because heedlessness and bewilderment have taken over and their hearts lack insight. Ibn Abi ʿAbla and ʿIsa read ﴿لاهِيَةً﴾ in the nominative as a predicate following the predicate ("wa-hum"). 

"Al-najwa" (secret conference) comes from "tanajji," and it occurs only in secret. So the meaning of ﴿وأسَرُّوا﴾ (and they conspired) is that they went to great lengths to conceal it, or made it such that no one would notice their secret talk or know that they were conferring in private. Abu ʿUbayd said: ﴿أسَرُّوا﴾ here is among the words with contrary meanings (al-addad): it may mean they concealed their speech, and it may mean they revealed it. From it is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

*"When al-Hajjaj saw that he had drawn his sword,
the Kharijite who had been concealing (his intent) revealed what he had hidden."*

Al-Tibrizi said: in common usage it is used only for concealment. They "conspired" the speech because it took place by way of consultation, and it is the custom of those consulting to hide their secret from their enemies. They conspired it so that they might say to the Messenger ﷺ and the believers: "If what you call to is true, then inform us of what we have concealed." They allowed several possibilities in the parsing of ﴿الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾ (those who did wrong): [p. 297] the nominative, the accusative, and the genitive. The nominative as an apposition (badal) from the pronoun in ﴿وأسَرُّوا﴾, indicating that they are the ones branded with gross wrongdoing in what they concealed; this was said by al-Mubarrad, and Ibn ʿAtiyyah attributed it to Sibawayh. Or as the subject (fa'il). The waw in ﴿أسَرُّوا﴾ is the sign of the plural according to the dialect of "akaluni al-baraghith" (the fleas ate me), as said by Abu ʿUbayda, al-Akhfash, and others. It was said: this is an anomalous dialect. It was also said: the correct view is that it is a good dialect, and it belongs to the dialect of the Azd Shanu'ah. On it is based His saying ﴿Then they became blind and deaf, many of them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 71], and their poet said:

*"They blame me for buying palm trees,
my family, and they all blame me."*

Or the view that ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ is the subject (mubtada') and ﴿وأسَرُّوا النَّجْوى﴾ is its predicate; this was said by al-Kisa'i, who fronted it. The meaning: "And these conspired the secret conference," so the explicit noun was placed in the position of the pronoun, to record their act as wrongdoing. Or it is the subject of an implied verb of saying, and the verb "say" (qala) is often elided. Al-Nahhas preferred this and said: what supports the correctness of this is that after it comes ﴿Is this not just a man like you?﴾. It was also said: the sense is "those who did wrong conspired it." It was said: ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ is the predicate of an elided subject, meaning "they are those who did wrong," and the accusative is for censure; this was said by al-Zajjaj, or by implying "I mean"; some said this. The genitive is that it be an adjective of "the people" or an apposition in His saying ﴿The reckoning of the people has drawn near﴾; this was said by al-Farra', and it is the most remote of the views.

﴿Is this not just a man like you?﴾ This is an interrogative whose meaning is amazement: how could he be singled out for prophethood over you, when he is similar to you in humanity? Their denial and amazement arose from their view that God sends none but an angel. ﴿Will you then submit to magic﴾ is an interrogative whose meaning is rebuke. By "magic" (al-sihr) they meant the miracles that appeared at his hands, the greatest of which is the Qur'an, and the Reminder recited to them. That is: "Will you bring in magic while you see that it is magic and that the one who brought it is a man like you? How then can you accept what he brought, when it is magic?" They believed that a messenger from God would be none but an angel, and that anyone among humans who claimed prophethood and brought a miracle was a sorcerer, and his miracle was magic. These two interrogative clauses are apparently connected to His saying ﴿and they conspired the secret conference﴾, and they are reported by the word "najwa," since it carries the sense of a hidden speech. So they stand in the accusative position as objects of "najwa."

Al-Zamakhshari said: they are in the accusative position as a substitute (badal) for "al-najwa," meaning "and they conspired this speech." It is also permissible for it to be connected to an implied "qalu" (they said). End of quote.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, al-A'mash, Talhah, Ibn Abi Layla, Ayyub, Khalaf, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, and Ibn Jarir read ﴿قالَ رَبِّي﴾ (He said: "My Lord...") as a report about His Prophet, peace be upon him. The rest of the seven read ﴿قُلْ﴾ (Say) as a command to His Prophet ﷺ: "[God] knows your sayings, and He will recompense you for them." The word "qawl" (word) is general, encompassing the secret and the open, so informing of His knowledge of the "qawl" includes the knowledge of the secret and more, and it was more emphatic in indicating awareness of their private conference than saying "He knows their secret." Then He clarified that with His saying ﴿and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾: the All-Hearing of your words, the All-Knowing of what your hearts conceal.

When He mentioned that they said what he brought was magic, He mentioned their confusion in their statements: that they turned away from attributing magic to him, and "they said" that what he brings is none but ﴿a confusion of dreams﴾. Its explanation was already given in the surah of Yusuf, peace be upon him. Then they turned away from this and said ﴿Rather, he has invented it﴾, that is, he fabricated it, and it is not from God. Then they turned away from this and said ﴿Rather, he is a poet﴾. Thus is the one in falsehood: he does not hold to one statement but remains bewildered. The apparent sense is that these statements came from speakers in agreement who moved from one statement to another, or from differing speakers, each of whom said a saying. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also possible that it is a description by God of their statements in a descending scale of corruption, and that their second statement is more corrupt than the first, the third more corrupt than the second, and so is the fourth than the third. End of quote.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: then he related the view of those who said he is a poet, and that is the saying of a vulgar faction, because the daughters of poetry among the Arabs would not have been hidden from them at once, and the structures of the Qur'an are not the structures of poetry. Abu ʿAbdullah al-Razi said: God related from them these five statements, and the order of their speech is: that his being a man is an obstacle to his being a messenger of God. Granting that it is not an obstacle, but we do not grant that this Qur'an, [if it is] either supporting the claim that the eloquence of the Qur'an is beyond the measure of humans, then why is it not possible that it is magic? And if it does not support that, then if we claim that it is in the utmost weakness, we say it is a confusion of dreams. If we claim that it is intermediate between weakness and eloquence, we say it is fabrication. If we claim that it is eloquent speech, we say it is of the same kind as the eloquence of all poetry. And under all these assumptions, its being a miracle is not established.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verse 1–10 (part 2 of 2):

When they had finished considering these possibilities, they said: ﴿So let him bring us a sign, as the earlier messengers were sent.﴾ They proposed signs of the kind after which there is no respite, like the signs in His saying: ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth.﴾ [al-Isra: 90] Al-Zamakhshari said: The correctness of the comparison in His saying ﴿as the earlier messengers were sent﴾ lies in the fact that it has the sense of "as the earlier ones brought signs," because the sending of messengers entails bringing signs. Do you not see that there is no difference between your saying "Muhammad brought a miracle" and your saying "Muhammad was sent with a miracle"? End of quote.

The kaf in ﴿as﴾ may be in the position of a qualifier (na't) for "a sign," and "what was sent" is in the sense of a verbal noun, meaning: a sign like the sign of the sending of the earlier ones (al-Awwalin). It may also be a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a bringing like the sending of the earlier ones (al-Awwalin), i.e., like their bringing of signs. This sign which they asked for was in the manner of their proposal, and Allah did not bring a proposed sign except that the punishment came after it. Allah, may He be exalted, intended to delay these people. And in their saying ﴿as the earlier messengers were sent﴾ there is an indication that they knew of the coming of the messengers.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, answered their saying ﴿So let him bring us a sign﴾ with His saying: ﴿No town did We destroy before them that believed. Will they then believe?﴾ By them is meant the people of Salih, the people of Pharaoh, and others. The meaning of "We destroyed it" is: We decreed its destruction on account of the signs they proposed. ﴿Will they then believe?﴾ is a question of disbelief and denial, meaning: these, I mean those who proposed signs to their prophets and pledged that they would believe when they came, then when they came they broke their pledge, and Allah destroyed them. So if We gave these people what they proposed, they would be even more prone to breaking their word than those, and their annihilation would take place. But the judgment of Allah, may He be exalted, is to spare them, so that whoever is to believe may believe, and that He may bring forth from among them believers.

When their saying ﴿Is this anything but a human like yourselves?﴾ had preceded, and [their view] that the messenger can only be from Allah and of the species of humankind, Allah, may He be exalted, said, refuting them: ﴿And We sent not before you except men﴾, i.e., humans, and they were not angels as they believed. Then He referred them to ﴿the people of the Reminder﴾, for they, although they were supporters of the disbelievers and striving to extinguish the light of Allah, cannot deny the sending of humans. His saying ﴿if you do not know﴾ [is addressed to them] in view of the fact that the Quraysh had no prior scripture nor any remnant of knowledge. It is apparent that ﴿the people of the Reminder﴾ are the scholars of the two Scriptures, and their testimony establishes the proof regarding Allah's sending of humans. This is in spite of the agreement of the Quraysh in abandoning belief in the Messenger ﷺ, so their testimony is beyond reproach. ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam said: I am among the people of the Reminder. It was also said: they are the people of the Qur'an. ʿAli said: I am among the people of the Reminder. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is not fitting that those asked be the people of the Qur'an at that time, because they were their adversaries. End of quote.

It was said: ﴿the people of the Reminder﴾ are the people of the Torah. It was said: they are the people knowledgeable in history and the stories of extinct nations and past generations, for they used to investigate these matters. And if ﴿the people of the Reminder﴾ is taken to mean the Jews and Christians, then since their report reached the level of mass transmission (tawatur), it is permissible to ask them, and their being disbelievers does not detract from this.

Al-Jumhur read yuha (passive). Talha and Hafs read nuhi with the nun and a kasra on the ha. The word "jasad" (body) applies to what does not eat among inanimate things. It was said: it applies to what eats and what does not, so on the first view the negation falls upon "jasad," and on the second it is affirmative, and the negation falls only upon its attribute. He used the singular "jasad" to mean the genus, as if he said: beings of a kind of bodies. This is a refutation of their saying "What is wrong with this messenger that he eats food?" This sentence is part of the completion of the answer to the polytheists who said ﴿Is this anything but a human like yourselves?﴾, because humanness entails animal corporeality, and this must have a substance in which it subsists. They had excluded this in their saying ﴿Is this anything but a human like yourselves who eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink?﴾ And when He established that they were bodies that eat food, He made clear that their end is extinction and perishing, and He denied them eternity, which is everlasting endurance, or endurance for a long duration. That is: these messengers are humans, bodies who are fed and die like other humans. What made them messengers is the manifestation of a miracle at their hands and their being protected from attributes that would impair the conveying of the message and other things.

﴿Then We fulfilled for them the promise﴾: Allah, may He be exalted, mentioned His conduct with His prophets, and so likewise He fulfills for His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his companions what He promised them of victory and the elevation of the word. This is a promise to the believers and a warning to the disbelievers. ﴿We fulfilled for them the promise﴾ is of the pattern of "ikhtara" (to choose), where the verb transitive to one object and to another by a preposition, and it is permissible to omit that preposition, i.e., in "al-wa'd" (the promise). This is a pattern that is not regular according to the majority, and only a few verbs of this kind are preserved, which are mentioned in the grammatical works. Similar to ﴿We fulfilled for them the promise﴾ is the saying: "They were true to them in fighting," "He was true to me regarding the age of his camel," and "I was true to Zayd in the report." ﴿Whom We willed﴾ [al-An'am: 83] are the believers, and the transgressors are the disbelievers who exceed in their misguidance and disbelief; and everyone who abandons faith is an excessive transgressor. Their deliverance is from the evil of their enemies and from the punishment that descended upon their enemies.

When He threatened them in this verse, He followed that with the promise of His blessing upon them, saying: ﴿We have certainly sent down to you a Book in which is your Reminder.﴾ The Book is the Qur'an. From Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿your Reminder﴾ means your honor; the genitive was omitted and the genitive-attached word was put in its place. From al-Hasan: the Reminder of your religion. From Mujahid: in it is your news. From Sufyan: the noble characteristics of your morals and the excellence of your deeds. It was also said: a reminder so that you avoid what is not permissible and desire what is obligatory. The author of al-Tahrir said: What the context of the verses requires is that the meaning in it is the mention of your faults and your failings and what the prophets of Allah were treated with, of denial and obstinacy. On this view, the verse is a censure of them and not from the enumeration of blessings upon them, and the speech stays within its context, and the meaning of His saying ﴿Is this anything but a human like yourselves?﴾ [al-Anbiya: 3] ... ﴿Will you not then use reason?﴾ [al-Anbiya: 10] is a rebuke against them for their neglect of reflection and contemplation, which lead to heedlessness. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It may be that it means in it your nobility and your remembrance until the end of time, as we mention the greatness of great affairs, and in this is encouragement. Then he reinforced the encouragement with His saying ﴿Will you not then use reason?﴾ and stirred them thereby to reflection. Al-Zamakhshari said similarly, saying: ﴿your Reminder﴾ means your nobility and your renown, as He said: ﴿And indeed it is a Reminder for you and your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44]; or your admonition; or in it are the noble characteristics by which you sought praise, and good repute is like good neighborliness, fulfilling covenants, truthfulness in speech, returning trusts, generosity, and what resembles that.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 1–10 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿The reckoning of the people has drawn near, while they are heedless and turn away.﴾ ﴿No fresh reminder comes to them from their Lord but they listen to it while playing.﴾ ﴿Their hearts are distracted. And those who did wrong conspire in secret: "Is this not just a man like you? Will you then submit to magic while you see it?"﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord knows every word in the heavens and the earth, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing."﴾ ﴿Rather, they said: "A confusion of dreams! Rather, he has invented it! Rather, he is a poet! Let him bring us a sign, as the earlier messengers were sent."﴾ ﴿No town that We destroyed before them believed. Will they then believe?﴾ ﴿We sent before you only men to whom We revealed. So ask the people of the Reminder (ahl al-dhikr), if you do not know.﴾ ﴿We did not make them bodies that do not eat food, nor were they immortal.﴾ ﴿Then We fulfilled the promise to them, and We saved them and whom We willed, and We destroyed the transgressors.﴾ ﴿Indeed We have sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder. Will you not then understand?﴾

and whoever he fears never ceases to be farther than yesterday."*

He informed about them with two predicates whose apparent meanings are contradictory, since heedlessness of a thing and turning away from it are incompatible. But they are reconciled by a difference of states. He first informed that they do not reflect on the outcome, but are heedless of what their affair will come to. Then He informed that when they are roused from the slumber of heedlessness and reminded of what the affair of the doer of good and the doer of evil will come to, they turn away from it and pay no heed. Here the "reminder" (dhikr) means what descends of the Qur'an piece by piece. It was said that the intended meaning of "dhikr" is the sayings of the Prophet ﷺ concerning the law, his admonition and his reminding, and describing it as "muhdath" (fresh, newly arrived) is because the Qur'an came down at times, one time after another. One of the Companions was asked about this verse and said: "Fresh in its descent, fresh in its speech." Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: the intended meaning of "dhikr" here is the Prophet ﷺ, by the evidence of ﴿Is this not just a man like you?﴾ and His saying ﴿God has sent down to you a reminder, a Messenger﴾ [al-Talaq: 10]. The Mu'tazilites used the word ﴿muhdath﴾ as an argument for the createdness of the Qur'an, and this is a question discussed in the science of kalam (theology). The majority read ﴿مُحْدَثٍ﴾ (muhdathin) in the genitive as an adjective of "dhikr" according to its form (lafz). Ibn Abi ʿAbla read it in the nominative as an adjective of "dhikr" according to its position (mahall). Zayd ibn ʿAli read it in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from "dhikr," since it has been described by ﴿from their Lord﴾. It is permissible for ﴿مِن رَبِّهِمْ﴾ (from their Lord) to be connected to ﴿يَأْتِيهِمْ﴾ (comes to them). ﴿اسْتَمَعُوهُ﴾ (they listen to it) is a circumstantial clause, and its circumstantial element (dhu al-hal) is the object in ﴿ما يَأْتِيهِمْ﴾. ﴿وهم يَلْعَبُونَ﴾ (while they play) is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَمَعُوهُ﴾. ﴿لاهِيَةً﴾ (distracted) is a state from the pronoun in ﴿يَلْعَبُونَ﴾, or from the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَمَعُوهُ﴾, in which case it is a state after a state. The word "lahiyah" comes from the Arab saying "lahiya ʿanhu" when one is distracted and heedless: yalha lahyan and lihyanan. That is, even if they perceive, this does not benefit them, because heedlessness and bewilderment have taken over and their hearts lack insight. Ibn Abi ʿAbla and ʿIsa read ﴿لاهِيَةً﴾ in the nominative as a predicate following the predicate ("wa-hum"). 

"Al-najwa" (secret conference) comes from "tanajji," and it occurs only in secret. So the meaning of ﴿وأسَرُّوا﴾ (and they conspired) is that they went to great lengths to conceal it, or made it such that no one would notice their secret talk or know that they were conferring in private. Abu ʿUbayd said: ﴿أسَرُّوا﴾ here is among the words with contrary meanings (al-addad): it may mean they concealed their speech, and it may mean they revealed it. From it is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

*"When al-Hajjaj saw that he had drawn his sword,
the Kharijite who had been concealing (his intent) revealed what he had hidden."*

Al-Tibrizi said: in common usage it is used only for concealment. They "conspired" the speech because it took place by way of consultation, and it is the custom of those consulting to hide their secret from their enemies. They conspired it so that they might say to the Messenger ﷺ and the believers: "If what you call to is true, then inform us of what we have concealed." They allowed several possibilities in the parsing of ﴿الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾ (those who did wrong): [p. 297] the nominative, the accusative, and the genitive. The nominative as an apposition (badal) from the pronoun in ﴿وأسَرُّوا﴾, indicating that they are the ones branded with gross wrongdoing in what they concealed; this was said by al-Mubarrad, and Ibn ʿAtiyyah attributed it to Sibawayh. Or as the subject (fa'il). The waw in ﴿أسَرُّوا﴾ is the sign of the plural according to the dialect of "akaluni al-baraghith" (the fleas ate me), as said by Abu ʿUbayda, al-Akhfash, and others. It was said: this is an anomalous dialect. It was also said: the correct view is that it is a good dialect, and it belongs to the dialect of the Azd Shanu'ah. On it is based His saying ﴿Then they became blind and deaf, many of them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 71], and their poet said:

*"They blame me for buying palm trees,
my family, and they all blame me."*

Or the view that ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ is the subject (mubtada') and ﴿وأسَرُّوا النَّجْوى﴾ is its predicate; this was said by al-Kisa'i, who fronted it. The meaning: "And these conspired the secret conference," so the explicit noun was placed in the position of the pronoun, to record their act as wrongdoing. Or it is the subject of an implied verb of saying, and the verb "say" (qala) is often elided. Al-Nahhas preferred this and said: what supports the correctness of this is that after it comes ﴿Is this not just a man like you?﴾. It was also said: the sense is "those who did wrong conspired it." It was said: ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ is the predicate of an elided subject, meaning "they are those who did wrong," and the accusative is for censure; this was said by al-Zajjaj, or by implying "I mean"; some said this. The genitive is that it be an adjective of "the people" or an apposition in His saying ﴿The reckoning of the people has drawn near﴾; this was said by al-Farra', and it is the most remote of the views.

﴿Is this not just a man like you?﴾ This is an interrogative whose meaning is amazement: how could he be singled out for prophethood over you, when he is similar to you in humanity? Their denial and amazement arose from their view that God sends none but an angel. ﴿Will you then submit to magic﴾ is an interrogative whose meaning is rebuke. By "magic" (al-sihr) they meant the miracles that appeared at his hands, the greatest of which is the Qur'an, and the Reminder recited to them. That is: "Will you bring in magic while you see that it is magic and that the one who brought it is a man like you? How then can you accept what he brought, when it is magic?" They believed that a messenger from God would be none but an angel, and that anyone among humans who claimed prophethood and brought a miracle was a sorcerer, and his miracle was magic. These two interrogative clauses are apparently connected to His saying ﴿and they conspired the secret conference﴾, and they are reported by the word "najwa," since it carries the sense of a hidden speech. So they stand in the accusative position as objects of "najwa."

Al-Zamakhshari said: they are in the accusative position as a substitute (badal) for "al-najwa," meaning "and they conspired this speech." It is also permissible for it to be connected to an implied "qalu" (they said). End of quote.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, al-A'mash, Talhah, Ibn Abi Layla, Ayyub, Khalaf, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, and Ibn Jarir read ﴿قالَ رَبِّي﴾ (He said: "My Lord...") as a report about His Prophet, peace be upon him. The rest of the seven read ﴿قُلْ﴾ (Say) as a command to His Prophet ﷺ: "[God] knows your sayings, and He will recompense you for them." The word "qawl" (word) is general, encompassing the secret and the open, so informing of His knowledge of the "qawl" includes the knowledge of the secret and more, and it was more emphatic in indicating awareness of their private conference than saying "He knows their secret." Then He clarified that with His saying ﴿and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾: the All-Hearing of your words, the All-Knowing of what your hearts conceal.

When He mentioned that they said what he brought was magic, He mentioned their confusion in their statements: that they turned away from attributing magic to him, and "they said" that what he brings is none but ﴿a confusion of dreams﴾. Its explanation was already given in the surah of Yusuf, peace be upon him. Then they turned away from this and said ﴿Rather, he has invented it﴾, that is, he fabricated it, and it is not from God. Then they turned away from this and said ﴿Rather, he is a poet﴾. Thus is the one in falsehood: he does not hold to one statement but remains bewildered. The apparent sense is that these statements came from speakers in agreement who moved from one statement to another, or from differing speakers, each of whom said a saying. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also possible that it is a description by God of their statements in a descending scale of corruption, and that their second statement is more corrupt than the first, the third more corrupt than the second, and so is the fourth than the third. End of quote.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: then he related the view of those who said he is a poet, and that is the saying of a vulgar faction, because the daughters of poetry among the Arabs would not have been hidden from them at once, and the structures of the Qur'an are not the structures of poetry. Abu ʿAbdullah al-Razi said: God related from them these five statements, and the order of their speech is: that his being a man is an obstacle to his being a messenger of God. Granting that it is not an obstacle, but we do not grant that this Qur'an, [if it is] either supporting the claim that the eloquence of the Qur'an is beyond the measure of humans, then why is it not possible that it is magic? And if it does not support that, then if we claim that it is in the utmost weakness, we say it is a confusion of dreams. If we claim that it is intermediate between weakness and eloquence, we say it is fabrication. If we claim that it is eloquent speech, we say it is of the same kind as the eloquence of all poetry. And under all these assumptions, its being a miracle is not established.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verse 1–10 (part 2 of 2):

When they had finished considering these possibilities, they said: ﴿So let him bring us a sign, as the earlier messengers were sent.﴾ They proposed signs of the kind after which there is no respite, like the signs in His saying: ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth.﴾ [al-Isra: 90] Al-Zamakhshari said: The correctness of the comparison in His saying ﴿as the earlier messengers were sent﴾ lies in the fact that it has the sense of "as the earlier ones brought signs," because the sending of messengers entails bringing signs. Do you not see that there is no difference between your saying "Muhammad brought a miracle" and your saying "Muhammad was sent with a miracle"? End of quote.

The kaf in ﴿as﴾ may be in the position of a qualifier (na't) for "a sign," and "what was sent" is in the sense of a verbal noun, meaning: a sign like the sign of the sending of the earlier ones (al-Awwalin). It may also be a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a bringing like the sending of the earlier ones (al-Awwalin), i.e., like their bringing of signs. This sign which they asked for was in the manner of their proposal, and Allah did not bring a proposed sign except that the punishment came after it. Allah, may He be exalted, intended to delay these people. And in their saying ﴿as the earlier messengers were sent﴾ there is an indication that they knew of the coming of the messengers.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, answered their saying ﴿So let him bring us a sign﴾ with His saying: ﴿No town did We destroy before them that believed. Will they then believe?﴾ By them is meant the people of Salih, the people of Pharaoh, and others. The meaning of "We destroyed it" is: We decreed its destruction on account of the signs they proposed. ﴿Will they then believe?﴾ is a question of disbelief and denial, meaning: these, I mean those who proposed signs to their prophets and pledged that they would believe when they came, then when they came they broke their pledge, and Allah destroyed them. So if We gave these people what they proposed, they would be even more prone to breaking their word than those, and their annihilation would take place. But the judgment of Allah, may He be exalted, is to spare them, so that whoever is to believe may believe, and that He may bring forth from among them believers.

When their saying ﴿Is this anything but a human like yourselves?﴾ had preceded, and [their view] that the messenger can only be from Allah and of the species of humankind, Allah, may He be exalted, said, refuting them: ﴿And We sent not before you except men﴾, i.e., humans, and they were not angels as they believed. Then He referred them to ﴿the people of the Reminder﴾, for they, although they were supporters of the disbelievers and striving to extinguish the light of Allah, cannot deny the sending of humans. His saying ﴿if you do not know﴾ [is addressed to them] in view of the fact that the Quraysh had no prior scripture nor any remnant of knowledge. It is apparent that ﴿the people of the Reminder﴾ are the scholars of the two Scriptures, and their testimony establishes the proof regarding Allah's sending of humans. This is in spite of the agreement of the Quraysh in abandoning belief in the Messenger ﷺ, so their testimony is beyond reproach. ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam said: I am among the people of the Reminder. It was also said: they are the people of the Qur'an. ʿAli said: I am among the people of the Reminder. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is not fitting that those asked be the people of the Qur'an at that time, because they were their adversaries. End of quote.

It was said: ﴿the people of the Reminder﴾ are the people of the Torah. It was said: they are the people knowledgeable in history and the stories of extinct nations and past generations, for they used to investigate these matters. And if ﴿the people of the Reminder﴾ is taken to mean the Jews and Christians, then since their report reached the level of mass transmission (tawatur), it is permissible to ask them, and their being disbelievers does not detract from this.

Al-Jumhur read yuha (passive). Talha and Hafs read nuhi with the nun and a kasra on the ha. The word "jasad" (body) applies to what does not eat among inanimate things. It was said: it applies to what eats and what does not, so on the first view the negation falls upon "jasad," and on the second it is affirmative, and the negation falls only upon its attribute. He used the singular "jasad" to mean the genus, as if he said: beings of a kind of bodies. This is a refutation of their saying "What is wrong with this messenger that he eats food?" This sentence is part of the completion of the answer to the polytheists who said ﴿Is this anything but a human like yourselves?﴾, because humanness entails animal corporeality, and this must have a substance in which it subsists. They had excluded this in their saying ﴿Is this anything but a human like yourselves who eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink?﴾ And when He established that they were bodies that eat food, He made clear that their end is extinction and perishing, and He denied them eternity, which is everlasting endurance, or endurance for a long duration. That is: these messengers are humans, bodies who are fed and die like other humans. What made them messengers is the manifestation of a miracle at their hands and their being protected from attributes that would impair the conveying of the message and other things.

﴿Then We fulfilled for them the promise﴾: Allah, may He be exalted, mentioned His conduct with His prophets, and so likewise He fulfills for His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his companions what He promised them of victory and the elevation of the word. This is a promise to the believers and a warning to the disbelievers. ﴿We fulfilled for them the promise﴾ is of the pattern of "ikhtara" (to choose), where the verb transitive to one object and to another by a preposition, and it is permissible to omit that preposition, i.e., in "al-wa'd" (the promise). This is a pattern that is not regular according to the majority, and only a few verbs of this kind are preserved, which are mentioned in the grammatical works. Similar to ﴿We fulfilled for them the promise﴾ is the saying: "They were true to them in fighting," "He was true to me regarding the age of his camel," and "I was true to Zayd in the report." ﴿Whom We willed﴾ [al-An'am: 83] are the believers, and the transgressors are the disbelievers who exceed in their misguidance and disbelief; and everyone who abandons faith is an excessive transgressor. Their deliverance is from the evil of their enemies and from the punishment that descended upon their enemies.

When He threatened them in this verse, He followed that with the promise of His blessing upon them, saying: ﴿We have certainly sent down to you a Book in which is your Reminder.﴾ The Book is the Qur'an. From Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿your Reminder﴾ means your honor; the genitive was omitted and the genitive-attached word was put in its place. From al-Hasan: the Reminder of your religion. From Mujahid: in it is your news. From Sufyan: the noble characteristics of your morals and the excellence of your deeds. It was also said: a reminder so that you avoid what is not permissible and desire what is obligatory. The author of al-Tahrir said: What the context of the verses requires is that the meaning in it is the mention of your faults and your failings and what the prophets of Allah were treated with, of denial and obstinacy. On this view, the verse is a censure of them and not from the enumeration of blessings upon them, and the speech stays within its context, and the meaning of His saying ﴿Is this anything but a human like yourselves?﴾ [al-Anbiya: 3] ... ﴿Will you not then use reason?﴾ [al-Anbiya: 10] is a rebuke against them for their neglect of reflection and contemplation, which lead to heedlessness. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It may be that it means in it your nobility and your remembrance until the end of time, as we mention the greatness of great affairs, and in this is encouragement. Then he reinforced the encouragement with His saying ﴿Will you not then use reason?﴾ and stirred them thereby to reflection. Al-Zamakhshari said similarly, saying: ﴿your Reminder﴾ means your nobility and your renown, as He said: ﴿And indeed it is a Reminder for you and your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44]; or your admonition; or in it are the noble characteristics by which you sought praise, and good repute is like good neighborliness, fulfilling covenants, truthfulness in speech, returning trusts, generosity, and what resembles that.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 1–10 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿The reckoning of the people has drawn near, while they are heedless and turn away.﴾ ﴿No fresh reminder comes to them from their Lord but they listen to it while playing.﴾ ﴿Their hearts are distracted. And those who did wrong conspire in secret: "Is this not just a man like you? Will you then submit to magic while you see it?"﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord knows every word in the heavens and the earth, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing."﴾ ﴿Rather, they said: "A confusion of dreams! Rather, he has invented it! Rather, he is a poet! Let him bring us a sign, as the earlier messengers were sent."﴾ ﴿No town that We destroyed before them believed. Will they then believe?﴾ ﴿We sent before you only men to whom We revealed. So ask the people of the Reminder (ahl al-dhikr), if you do not know.﴾ ﴿We did not make them bodies that do not eat food, nor were they immortal.﴾ ﴿Then We fulfilled the promise to them, and We saved them and whom We willed, and We destroyed the transgressors.﴾ ﴿Indeed We have sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder. Will you not then understand?﴾

[p. 295] This surah is Meccan without disagreement. From Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud): al-Kahf, Maryam, Ta-Ha and al-Anbiya' are among the first of the "ancient" (al-'ita q al-ula), and they are of my "tilad," that is, of the earliest of what I memorized and acquired of the Qur'an, like the inherited wealth (al-mal al-tilad).

The connection of this surah to what precedes it: when He mentioned ﴿Say: "Each is waiting, so wait"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 135], the Meccan polytheists said: "Muhammad threatens us with the Return and with recompense for deeds, and this is not true; and if it were true, it would be far off." So God sent down ﴿The reckoning of the people has drawn near﴾. The word ﴿اقْتَرَبَ﴾ (iqtaraba, "has drawn near") is of the form ifta'ala, with the meaning of the bare verb qaraba, just as you say irtaqaba and raqaba. It was said: it is more emphatic than qaraba because of the additional letters in its form. The "people" (al-nas) here are the polytheists of Mecca. It was also said: it is general, covering those who deny the Resurrection. The "drawing near of the reckoning" means the drawing near of its time. In linguistic usage, "hisab" (reckoning) is the extraction of a quantity from the total of a count, and it may also be applied to the thing counted. It is called "drawing near" because whatever is coming is near, however long the wait for it may be; what is truly distant is what has passed away. Or it is near in God's reckoning, as in His saying ﴿And indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ [al-Hajj: 47]. Or it is relative to what remains of the world, which is shorter and less than what has passed. In a hadith: "I was sent, and the Hour is like these two (fingers)." The poet said:

*"Whoever he loves never ceases to be nearer than tomorrow,
and whoever he fears never ceases to be farther than yesterday."*

The word ﴿لِلنّاسِ﴾ (lil-nas, "for the people") is connected to ﴿اقْتَرَبَ﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: this lam must be either a complement (silah) of iqtaraba, or an emphasis [p. 296] on the attribution of the reckoning to them, as you say "azuffu lil-hayy rahilahum" (I hasten the departure of the tribe). The original is "azuffu rahil al-hayy," then "azuffu lil-hayy rahilahum." Similar to it is what Sibawayh cited in the chapter on what the stable element may be repeated in for emphasis: "ʿalayka Zaydun harisun ʿalayk," and "fika Zaydun raghibun fik." From the same is the saying "la aba laka," because the lam reinforces the meaning of the idafa (annexation). This second view is stranger than the first. End of quote. By his phrase "a complement" he means that it is connected to iqtaraba. As for his making the lam an emphasis for the annexation of the reckoning to them, despite the lam coming first and entering upon a noun, we know of no one who says this. Also, it would need something it is connected to, and it cannot be connected to "hisabihim" (their reckoning), since it is a verbal noun (masdar) with a complement, and its complement cannot precede it. Also, emphasis comes after what it emphasizes. Furthermore, if it were postponed in this structure, it would not be correct. As for his comparison with what Sibawayh cited, the difference is clear: ʿalayka is a complement of harisun, and the second ʿalayka is a later emphasis; likewise in fika Zaydun raghibun fik, fika is connected to raghibun, and the second fik is an emphasis. What misled him is the correctness of the structure "hisab al-nas." Likewise, "azafa rahilu al-hayy" (the departure of the tribe drew near): he believed that when the noun is fronted with a lam-prepositional phrase and the verbal noun is annexed to its pronoun, it falls under the category of "fika Zaydun raghibun fik," but it is not like it. As for "la aba laka," it is a problematic question with disagreement, and it is possible to say it is so there because the lam is adjacent to the annexation, but other cases cannot be measured on it because of its irregularity and its departure from the general rules. We have discussed it at length in our commentary on al-Tashil. The waw in ﴿وهم﴾ (wa-hum, "while they") is the waw of circumstance (al-hal).

He informed about them with two predicates whose apparent meanings are contradictory, since heedlessness of a thing and turning away from it are incompatible. But they are reconciled by a difference of states. He first informed that they do not reflect on the outcome, but are heedless of what their affair will come to. Then He informed that when they are roused from the slumber of heedlessness and reminded of what the affair of the doer of good and the doer of evil will come to, they turn away from it and pay no heed. Here the "reminder" (dhikr) means what descends of the Qur'an piece by piece. It was said that the intended meaning of "dhikr" is the sayings of the Prophet ﷺ concerning the law, his admonition and his reminding, and describing it as "muhdath" (fresh, newly arrived) is because the Qur'an came down at times, one time after another. One of the Companions was asked about this verse and said: "Fresh in its descent, fresh in its speech." Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: the intended meaning of "dhikr" here is the Prophet ﷺ, by the evidence of ﴿Is this not just a man like you?﴾ and His saying ﴿God has sent down to you a reminder, a Messenger﴾ [al-Talaq: 10]. The Mu'tazilites used the word ﴿muhdath﴾ as an argument for the createdness of the Qur'an, and this is a question discussed in the science of kalam (theology). The majority read ﴿مُحْدَثٍ﴾ (muhdathin) in the genitive as an adjective of "dhikr" according to its form (lafz). Ibn Abi ʿAbla read it in the nominative as an adjective of "dhikr" according to its position (mahall). Zayd ibn ʿAli read it in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from "dhikr," since it has been described by ﴿from their Lord﴾. It is permissible for ﴿مِن رَبِّهِمْ﴾ (from their Lord) to be connected to ﴿يَأْتِيهِمْ﴾ (comes to them). ﴿اسْتَمَعُوهُ﴾ (they listen to it) is a circumstantial clause, and its circumstantial element (dhu al-hal) is the object in ﴿ما يَأْتِيهِمْ﴾. ﴿وهم يَلْعَبُونَ﴾ (while they play) is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَمَعُوهُ﴾. ﴿لاهِيَةً﴾ (distracted) is a state from the pronoun in ﴿يَلْعَبُونَ﴾, or from the pronoun in ﴿اسْتَمَعُوهُ﴾, in which case it is a state after a state. The word "lahiyah" comes from the Arab saying "lahiya ʿanhu" when one is distracted and heedless: yalha lahyan and lihyanan. That is, even if they perceive, this does not benefit them, because heedlessness and bewilderment have taken over and their hearts lack insight. Ibn Abi ʿAbla and ʿIsa read ﴿لاهِيَةً﴾ in the nominative as a predicate following the predicate ("wa-hum"). 

"Al-najwa" (secret conference) comes from "tanajji," and it occurs only in secret. So the meaning of ﴿وأسَرُّوا﴾ (and they conspired) is that they went to great lengths to conceal it, or made it such that no one would notice their secret talk or know that they were conferring in private. Abu ʿUbayd said: ﴿أسَرُّوا﴾ here is among the words with contrary meanings (al-addad): it may mean they concealed their speech, and it may mean they revealed it. From it is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

*"When al-Hajjaj saw that he had drawn his sword,
the Kharijite who had been concealing (his intent) revealed what he had hidden."*
