Al-qasm (shattering) is the most severe kind of breaking, and it is used figuratively for severe destruction. (Kam) indicates multiplicity, so the meaning is: We destroyed many of the people of towns with a severe and emphatic destruction.

As for what is narrated from Ibn Abbas, that it is "Hadura" (Ḥaḍūrāʾ), a town in Yemen, and from Ibn Wahb, from some of his men, that they are two towns in Yemen whose people became insolent, this is to be taken as an illustration and not as a specific identification of the town, because (kam) indicates multiplicity. From the report about the people of Haḍūrāʾ: God sent a prophet to them and they killed him, so God empowered Bukhtnasr (Nebuchadnezzar) over them, just as He empowered him over the people of Jerusalem. He sent an army against them and they defeated it; then he sent another and they defeated it; then he himself went out against them and defeated them in the third encounter. When slaughter took hold of them, they fled running.

﴿So when they perceived Our might﴾, that is, they came into direct contact with it through perception. The pronoun in ﴿they perceived﴾ refers to the people implied in His saying ﴿How many a town We have shattered﴾, and it does not refer to His saying ﴿another people﴾, because no sin is mentioned for which they would be fleeing. The pronoun in (minha, from it) refers to the town. It is possible that it refers to (ba'sana, Our might), because it means severity, so it is feminine according to its meaning, and "min" (from) is for this reason. The apparent meaning is that when the vanguard of the punishment overtook them, they mounted their animals, driving them, fleeing and routed. It was said: it is also possible that in the speed of their running on foot they were likened to riders driving their animals, so they are "running" (yarkudūna) the earth with their feet, as He said: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾ [Sad: 42]. The answer to (lamma, when) is (idha, suddenly) the sudden particle and what follows it. This is one of the proofs that (lamma) in this construction is a particle and not an adverb; we have already discussed this earlier.

As for His saying: ﴿Do not flee﴾, Ibn Atiyya said: it is possible that it is the speech of the men of Bukhtnasr, according to the narration mentioned earlier. The meaning according to this is that they deceived them and mocked them, saying to those fleeing from them: "Do not flee, but return to your homes," ﴿that perhaps you may be questioned﴾ about a truce, or tribute, or a matter agreed upon. When they turned back, Bukhtnasr ordered a call to be made among them: "O vengeance for the slain prophet!" So they were killed by the sword, to the last of them. All of this is narrated. It is possible that His saying ﴿Do not flee﴾ through the end of the verse is the speech of the angels of punishment, describing the story of each town, and that He did not intend to specify Haḍūrāʾ or any other. The meaning according to this is: the people of these towns, through their delusion, thought they were held in a high position with God, and that if a punishment or a command came upon them, it would not descend upon them until they disputed and were questioned about the cause of their denial of their prophet, so that they would argue at that time with arguments that they imagined would benefit them. When the punishment descended, not in the manner they had hoped for, and they fled running, the angels called out to them in mockery.

﴿Do not flee, but return﴾ . . .

﴿that perhaps you may be questioned﴾ as you used to hope, because of the foolishness of your opinions.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is possible that he means: the speaker is some of the angels, or some of the believers from among them, or they are made deputies, by saying that to them even though it was not said, or the Lord of Might says it and makes His angels hear it, so that it benefits them in their religion, or He inspires them with it so that they speak it to their own souls.

﴿and return to what you were made to enjoy﴾ of the luxurious life and comfortable state. (Itraf) is the excess of blessing, and it is luxury (tarraf).

﴿that perhaps you may be questioned﴾ tomorrow about what befell you and what happened to your wealth and your dwellings, so that you may answer the questioner with knowledge and witness. Or (return) and sit as you were in your assemblies, and arrange yourselves in your ranks, until your servants and your retainers and those whose affairs you control, whose commands and prohibitions you enforce, ask you, and say to you: "What do you command, and what do you decree? How shall we proceed or refrain, as is the custom of the pampered and served?" Or the people will ask you in your gatherings, the helpers in the calamities of catastrophes, and consult you in important and sudden matters, seeking to be healed by your measures and enlightened by your opinions; or those who come to you and the greedy will ask you, seeking rain from the clouds of your palms and seeking the abundance of your kindness and your favours. Either because they were generous and spent their wealth to be seen by people and to seek praise, or because they were miserly, and so this was said to them mockingly, mockery upon mockery, and rebuke upon rebuke. End of quotation.

The calling of "woe" (wayl) is figurative, as if they said: "O woe, this is your time." The explanation of woe has already been mentioned in al-Baqara.

The wrongdoing here is polytheism, denying the messengers, and bringing themselves into destruction. The subject of (zalat, ceased) is the demonstrative (tilka, that), and it is a reference to the statement that was spoken, meaning: "that claim of theirs [da'wahum] did not cease." The commentators said: they kept repeating that word and it did not benefit them, as in His saying: ﴿Their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might﴾ [Ghafir: 85]. (Da'wa, claim) is the verbal noun of "da'a," one says "da'a da'wa" and "da'wa," as in His saying: ﴿and the last of their call﴾ [Yunus: 10], because the one who cries woe is as if he calls out "woe." Al-Hawfi said, and al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa followed him: (tilka) is the subject of (zalat), and (da'wahum) is the predicate; it is permissible that (da'wahum) be the subject of (zalat) and (tilka) be in the position of the predicate. End of quotation. What these men went to was said earlier by al-Zajjaj. As for our later companions (the Basran grammarians), the subject and predicate of (kana, was) are likened to the doer and the object. Just as in the construction of the doer and object, when there is ambiguity, the earlier cannot be the predicate and the later the subject, so in the construction of (kana) this is not permissible. When you say "Musa was my friend" (kana Musa sadiqi), it is not permissible for Musa to be anything but the subject of (kana) and "my friend" the predicate, as in your saying "Musa struck Isa," where Musa is the doer and Isa the object. None of our later companions disputed this except Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Ali, known as Ibn al-Hajj, who was one of the students of the master Abu Ali al-Shalawbin and among their distinguished scholars. He permitted that the earlier be the object and the later the doer, even if ambiguous. But according to what the majority of the companions established, it is necessary that (tilka) be the subject of (zalat) and (da'wahum) the predicate.

And His saying: (ḥaṣīdan, as stubble), that is, through the punishment, they were left like stubble ﴿extinguished﴾, that is, dead without spirits, likened to a fire when it is put out. (Ḥaṣīdan) is the second object. Al-Hawfi said: ﴿extinguished﴾ is an adjective of (ḥaṣīdan), on the basis that (ḥaṣīdan) means "reaped," meaning the singular form is used while the plural is intended. He said: it is also permissible to make ﴿extinguished﴾ a circumstantial state of the (ha) and (mim) pronoun. Al-Zamakhshari said: (ja'alnahum) means "made them like the stubble." He likened them in their annihilation and uprooting, as you say: "We made them ashes," meaning like ashes. The object pronoun is the one that was originally the subject (mubtada'), and the two objects after it were its two predicates. When (ja'ala) entered upon them, both were put in the accusative as objects. If you ask: how does (ja'ala) govern three objects? I answer: the rule for the other two is the rule for the one, because the meaning of your saying "I made it sweet and sour" is "I made it for the two tastes." Likewise the meaning of "We made them" here is: combining them in the resemblance to stubble and to extinction; and extinction is conjoined to the resemblance, not to the stubble. End of quotation.

When He, exalted is He, mentioned the destruction of those wrongdoing towns, He followed that with what shows that He did this in justice from Him and as recompense for what they had done, and that He created this upper world containing wonders of His making and marvels of His doing, and this lower world and what He deposited in it of the wonders of animals, plants, and minerals, and what lies between them of air, clouds, and winds, not as play, but for religious benefits that decree eternal happiness or eternal misery, and worldly benefits that cannot be counted or enumerated, as in His saying: (p. 302) ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ [Sad: 27], and His saying: ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 39].

Al-Kirmani said: play is an act to which ignorance calls; its beginning pleases but it has no permanence, whereas We created them so that We may recompense the good-doer and the evildoer, and so that they may be taken as evidence of the oneness and the power [of God]. End of quotation.

﴿Had We wished to take a pastime﴾: the root of (lahw) is that to which desire hastens and which inclination calls for; it may be used as a euphemism for intercourse. Here, however, Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi said it means a child. Al-Zajjaj said it means a child in the dialect of Hadramawt. From Ibn Abbas: this is a refutation of those who said ﴿God has taken a son﴾ [Al-Baqara: 116]. Also from him: that pastime here means play. It was said: pastime here means a woman. Qatada said: this is in the dialect of the people of Yemen, and it is a refutation of those who claimed that God has a wife. The meaning of ﴿from Ourselves﴾ is "from Us," in a way that no one would perceive it, because it is a deficiency, so concealing it is better. Al-Suddi said: from heaven, not from earth. It was said: from the dark-eyed houris (hur al-ʿin). It was said: from the side of Our power. It was said: from the angels, not from humans, refuting the divinity of Jesus and Uzayr. Al-Zamakhshari said: He made clear that the reason for abandoning taking a pastime and play, and for its absence from My acts, is that wisdom prevents it; otherwise I am able to take it, if I were to do so, because I am over all things powerful. End of quotation.

This does not fit except with the view of one who says that pastime is play. As for one who interprets it as a child or a woman, that is impossible and power does not apply to it. The apparent meaning is that (in) here is conditional, and the answer to the condition is omitted, indicated by the answer to (law, had): meaning, "if We were doers, We would have taken it, if We were of those who do such a thing; but We are not of those who do it."

Al-Hasan, Qatada and Jurayj said (in) is negative, meaning: "We were not doers."

﴿Rather, We hurl﴾: that is, We cast swiftly, ﴿the truth﴾, which is the Qur'an, ﴿against falsehood﴾, which is Satan, as Mujahid said, and he said: everything in the Qur'an concerning falsehood refers to Satan. It was also said: "the truth" means the proof against falsehood, which is their doubts and their describing God with attributes not His, such as having a son and other things. It was said: the truth is general, covering the Qur'an, the message, and the law, and falsehood likewise is general. And (bal, rather) is a turning away from taking play and pastime. The meaning is that He refutes falsehood with truth. He used the metaphor of casting and crushing to depict its annihilation, its nullification, and its erasure. He made it as if it were a solid, hard body, like a rock, cast upon a soft, hollow body, so that it crushes it, that is, strikes its brain; and that is fatal to a human; likewise the truth destroys falsehood. Isa ibn Umar read (fa-yadmaghahu) with a fatha on the ghayn. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is in the weakness of the poet's saying:

"I will leave my dwelling to the Banu Tamim and join the Hijaz and rest."

And it was read (fa-yadmughuhu) with a damma on the mim. End of quotation.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 11–20 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Woe to you﴾ is an address to the disbelievers, meaning disgrace and distress (al-khizy wa al-hamm). ﴿Because of what you describe﴾ means: because of what you describe Him as, of things unbefitting Him, such as taking consorts and offspring and attributing impossibilities to Him. It has also been said that "for you" is an address to those who held firmly to denying the messengers and attributed the Qur'an to being sorcery and confused dreams, and this is what is meant by His words ﴿what you describe﴾. Further removed is the view of the one who said that it is a shift (iltifat) from the third-person pronoun in ﴿Their claim remained so﴾ to the second-person pronoun. Then Allah, exalted is He, informed that whoever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, so that those they named as consorts and offspring are included in it. (﴿And those with Him﴾) are the angels. It is possible that it is conjoined to "whoever" (man), so they are included among the angels in a general sense, since they are included in "whoever," and in a specific sense by the explicit statement that they are "those with Him." Then ﴿They do not grow arrogant﴾ would be a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah) concerning them, or a resumptive statement of information (istithnaf ikhbar). It is also possible that ﴿those with Him﴾ is the subject (mubtada') and its predicate is ﴿they do not grow arrogant﴾. Here "with" ('inda) is not meant as a spatial location, since He is exalted above place; rather the meaning is nobility of rank and loftiness of station. The apparent meaning is that His words ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ are a resumptive statement of information that the entire world is His possession. It has been said that it may be parallel to His words ﴿Woe to you because of what you describe,﴾ as if He were dividing the matter within Himself: for those who hold this claim there is woe, and to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth. End.

The meaning is that the angels are honored and brought near, because of their honor with Allah, in the manner of those held close by kings, by way of illustration and explanation (p-303), because of their nobility and excellence. It is said: al-bai'ru hasara and istahsara, meaning he became weary and tired; and I made it weary (hasartuhu), so it is transitive and intransitive; and also ahsartuhu. The poet said:

"Therein are the carcasses of the wearied; as for their bones, they are white, and as for their hides, they are tough."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: istihsar is an intensification of husur, and the more eloquent way of describing them would be to negate from them even the slightest weariness, I say: in istihsar there is an indication that what they are engaged in necessitates the utmost and extreme weariness, and that they are deserving of those burdensome acts of worship, such that they would grow weary in what they do. End.

﴿Glorifying﴾ (yusabbihun) refers to the angels, by the consensus of the community; He described them with constant glorification. It is related from Ka'b: Allah made glorification for them like breath and the blink of an eye for humans, which proceeds from them constantly without weariness befalling them in it. And in the hadith: ("Indeed I hear the creaking (atit) of the heaven, and it has the right to creak; there is not a space of a palm's breadth in it but there is an angel prostrating or standing.")

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 11–20 (part 1 of 2):

(p. 300) ﴿How many a town We have shattered, which was wrongdoing, and We brought into being after it another people.﴾ ﴿So when they perceived Our might, behold, they were fleeing from it.﴾ ﴿Do not flee, but return to what you were made to enjoy and to your dwellings, that perhaps you may be questioned.﴾ ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿And that was their cry until We made them as harvested stubble, extinguished.﴾ ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ ﴿Had We wished to take a pastime, We would have taken it from Ourselves, if We were ever going to do so.﴾ ﴿Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes. And woe to you for what you describe.﴾ ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth. And those near Him are not too proud to worship Him, nor do they tire.﴾ ﴿They glorify Him night and day; they never slacken.﴾

When God, exalted is He, refuted what they had said, He went further in rebuking them by mentioning the towns He had destroyed. He said: ﴿How many a town We have shattered﴾. The intended meaning is its people, since a town cannot be described as wrongdoing, as in His saying: ﴿from this town whose people are wrongdoers﴾ [An-Nisa: 75]. Ibn Abbas said: al-insha' (bringing into being) is the bringing of a thing into existence without a prior cause that produced it; so "nasha'a" means he came into being, and he is "nashi'" (one who has come into being), and the plural is "nushshaʾ," like "khadam." Al-qasm (shattering) is the most severe kind of breaking, and it is used figuratively for severe destruction. (Kam) indicates multiplicity, so the meaning is: We destroyed many of the people of towns with a severe and emphatic destruction.

As for what is narrated from Ibn Abbas, that it is "Hadura" (Ḥaḍūrāʾ), a town in Yemen, and from Ibn Wahb, from some of his men, that they are two towns in Yemen whose people became insolent, this is to be taken as an illustration and not as a specific identification of the town, because (kam) indicates multiplicity. From the report about the people of Haḍūrāʾ: God sent a prophet to them and they killed him, so God empowered Bukhtnasr (Nebuchadnezzar) over them, just as He empowered him over the people of Jerusalem. He sent an army against them and they defeated it; then he sent another and they defeated it; then he himself went out against them and defeated them in the third encounter. When slaughter took hold of them, they fled running.

﴿So when they perceived Our might﴾, that is, they came into direct contact with it through perception. The pronoun in ﴿they perceived﴾ refers to the people implied in His saying ﴿How many a town We have shattered﴾, and it does not refer to His saying ﴿another people﴾, because no sin is mentioned for which they would be fleeing. The pronoun in (minha, from it) refers to the town. It is possible that it refers to (ba'sana, Our might), because it means severity, so it is feminine according to its meaning, and "min" (from) is for this reason. The apparent meaning is that when the vanguard of the punishment overtook them, they mounted their animals, driving them, fleeing and routed. It was said: it is also possible that in the speed of their running on foot they were likened to riders driving their animals, so they are "running" (yarkudūna) the earth with their feet, as He said: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾ [Sad: 42]. The answer to (lamma, when) is (idha, suddenly) the sudden particle and what follows it. This is one of the proofs that (lamma) in this construction is a particle and not an adverb; we have already discussed this earlier.

As for His saying: ﴿Do not flee﴾, Ibn Atiyya said: it is possible that it is the speech of the men of Bukhtnasr, according to the narration mentioned earlier. The meaning according to this is that they deceived them and mocked them, saying to those fleeing from them: "Do not flee, but return to your homes," ﴿that perhaps you may be questioned﴾ about a truce, or tribute, or a matter agreed upon. When they turned back, Bukhtnasr ordered a call to be made among them: "O vengeance for the slain prophet!" So they were killed by the sword, to the last of them. All of this is narrated. It is possible that His saying ﴿Do not flee﴾ through the end of the verse is the speech of the angels of punishment, describing the story of each town, and that He did not intend to specify Haḍūrāʾ or any other. The meaning according to this is: the people of these towns, through their delusion, thought they were held in a high position with God, and that if a punishment or a command came upon them, it would not descend upon them until they disputed and were questioned about the cause of their denial of their prophet, so that they would argue at that time with arguments that they imagined would benefit them. When the punishment descended, not in the manner they had hoped for, and they fled running, the angels called out to them in mockery.

﴿Do not flee, but return﴾ . . .

﴿that perhaps you may be questioned﴾ as you used to hope, because of the foolishness of your opinions.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is possible that he means: the speaker is some of the angels, or some of the believers from among them, or they are made deputies, by saying that to them even though it was not said, or the Lord of Might says it and makes His angels hear it, so that it benefits them in their religion, or He inspires them with it so that they speak it to their own souls.

﴿and return to what you were made to enjoy﴾ of the luxurious life and comfortable state. (Itraf) is the excess of blessing, and it is luxury (tarraf).

﴿that perhaps you may be questioned﴾ tomorrow about what befell you and what happened to your wealth and your dwellings, so that you may answer the questioner with knowledge and witness. Or (return) and sit as you were in your assemblies, and arrange yourselves in your ranks, until your servants and your retainers and those whose affairs you control, whose commands and prohibitions you enforce, ask you, and say to you: "What do you command, and what do you decree? How shall we proceed or refrain, as is the custom of the pampered and served?" Or the people will ask you in your gatherings, the helpers in the calamities of catastrophes, and consult you in important and sudden matters, seeking to be healed by your measures and enlightened by your opinions; or those who come to you and the greedy will ask you, seeking rain from the clouds of your palms and seeking the abundance of your kindness and your favours. Either because they were generous and spent their wealth to be seen by people and to seek praise, or because they were miserly, and so this was said to them mockingly, mockery upon mockery, and rebuke upon rebuke. End of quotation.

The calling of "woe" (wayl) is figurative, as if they said: "O woe, this is your time." The explanation of woe has already been mentioned in al-Baqara.

The wrongdoing here is polytheism, denying the messengers, and bringing themselves into destruction. The subject of (zalat, ceased) is the demonstrative (tilka, that), and it is a reference to the statement that was spoken, meaning: "that claim of theirs [da'wahum] did not cease." The commentators said: they kept repeating that word and it did not benefit them, as in His saying: ﴿Their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might﴾ [Ghafir: 85]. (Da'wa, claim) is the verbal noun of "da'a," one says "da'a da'wa" and "da'wa," as in His saying: ﴿and the last of their call﴾ [Yunus: 10], because the one who cries woe is as if he calls out "woe." Al-Hawfi said, and al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa followed him: (tilka) is the subject of (zalat), and (da'wahum) is the predicate; it is permissible that (da'wahum) be the subject of (zalat) and (tilka) be in the position of the predicate. End of quotation. What these men went to was said earlier by al-Zajjaj. As for our later companions (the Basran grammarians), the subject and predicate of (kana, was) are likened to the doer and the object. Just as in the construction of the doer and object, when there is ambiguity, the earlier cannot be the predicate and the later the subject, so in the construction of (kana) this is not permissible. When you say "Musa was my friend" (kana Musa sadiqi), it is not permissible for Musa to be anything but the subject of (kana) and "my friend" the predicate, as in your saying "Musa struck Isa," where Musa is the doer and Isa the object. None of our later companions disputed this except Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Ali, known as Ibn al-Hajj, who was one of the students of the master Abu Ali al-Shalawbin and among their distinguished scholars. He permitted that the earlier be the object and the later the doer, even if ambiguous. But according to what the majority of the companions established, it is necessary that (tilka) be the subject of (zalat) and (da'wahum) the predicate.

And His saying: (ḥaṣīdan, as stubble), that is, through the punishment, they were left like stubble ﴿extinguished﴾, that is, dead without spirits, likened to a fire when it is put out. (Ḥaṣīdan) is the second object. Al-Hawfi said: ﴿extinguished﴾ is an adjective of (ḥaṣīdan), on the basis that (ḥaṣīdan) means "reaped," meaning the singular form is used while the plural is intended. He said: it is also permissible to make ﴿extinguished﴾ a circumstantial state of the (ha) and (mim) pronoun. Al-Zamakhshari said: (ja'alnahum) means "made them like the stubble." He likened them in their annihilation and uprooting, as you say: "We made them ashes," meaning like ashes. The object pronoun is the one that was originally the subject (mubtada'), and the two objects after it were its two predicates. When (ja'ala) entered upon them, both were put in the accusative as objects. If you ask: how does (ja'ala) govern three objects? I answer: the rule for the other two is the rule for the one, because the meaning of your saying "I made it sweet and sour" is "I made it for the two tastes." Likewise the meaning of "We made them" here is: combining them in the resemblance to stubble and to extinction; and extinction is conjoined to the resemblance, not to the stubble. End of quotation.

When He, exalted is He, mentioned the destruction of those wrongdoing towns, He followed that with what shows that He did this in justice from Him and as recompense for what they had done, and that He created this upper world containing wonders of His making and marvels of His doing, and this lower world and what He deposited in it of the wonders of animals, plants, and minerals, and what lies between them of air, clouds, and winds, not as play, but for religious benefits that decree eternal happiness or eternal misery, and worldly benefits that cannot be counted or enumerated, as in His saying: (p. 302) ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ [Sad: 27], and His saying: ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 39].

Al-Kirmani said: play is an act to which ignorance calls; its beginning pleases but it has no permanence, whereas We created them so that We may recompense the good-doer and the evildoer, and so that they may be taken as evidence of the oneness and the power [of God]. End of quotation.

﴿Had We wished to take a pastime﴾: the root of (lahw) is that to which desire hastens and which inclination calls for; it may be used as a euphemism for intercourse. Here, however, Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi said it means a child. Al-Zajjaj said it means a child in the dialect of Hadramawt. From Ibn Abbas: this is a refutation of those who said ﴿God has taken a son﴾ [Al-Baqara: 116]. Also from him: that pastime here means play. It was said: pastime here means a woman. Qatada said: this is in the dialect of the people of Yemen, and it is a refutation of those who claimed that God has a wife. The meaning of ﴿from Ourselves﴾ is "from Us," in a way that no one would perceive it, because it is a deficiency, so concealing it is better. Al-Suddi said: from heaven, not from earth. It was said: from the dark-eyed houris (hur al-ʿin). It was said: from the side of Our power. It was said: from the angels, not from humans, refuting the divinity of Jesus and Uzayr. Al-Zamakhshari said: He made clear that the reason for abandoning taking a pastime and play, and for its absence from My acts, is that wisdom prevents it; otherwise I am able to take it, if I were to do so, because I am over all things powerful. End of quotation.

This does not fit except with the view of one who says that pastime is play. As for one who interprets it as a child or a woman, that is impossible and power does not apply to it. The apparent meaning is that (in) here is conditional, and the answer to the condition is omitted, indicated by the answer to (law, had): meaning, "if We were doers, We would have taken it, if We were of those who do such a thing; but We are not of those who do it."

Al-Hasan, Qatada and Jurayj said (in) is negative, meaning: "We were not doers."

﴿Rather, We hurl﴾: that is, We cast swiftly, ﴿the truth﴾, which is the Qur'an, ﴿against falsehood﴾, which is Satan, as Mujahid said, and he said: everything in the Qur'an concerning falsehood refers to Satan. It was also said: "the truth" means the proof against falsehood, which is their doubts and their describing God with attributes not His, such as having a son and other things. It was said: the truth is general, covering the Qur'an, the message, and the law, and falsehood likewise is general. And (bal, rather) is a turning away from taking play and pastime. The meaning is that He refutes falsehood with truth. He used the metaphor of casting and crushing to depict its annihilation, its nullification, and its erasure. He made it as if it were a solid, hard body, like a rock, cast upon a soft, hollow body, so that it crushes it, that is, strikes its brain; and that is fatal to a human; likewise the truth destroys falsehood. Isa ibn Umar read (fa-yadmaghahu) with a fatha on the ghayn. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is in the weakness of the poet's saying:

"I will leave my dwelling to the Banu Tamim and join the Hijaz and rest."

And it was read (fa-yadmughuhu) with a damma on the mim. End of quotation.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 11–20 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Woe to you﴾ is an address to the disbelievers, meaning disgrace and distress (al-khizy wa al-hamm). ﴿Because of what you describe﴾ means: because of what you describe Him as, of things unbefitting Him, such as taking consorts and offspring and attributing impossibilities to Him. It has also been said that "for you" is an address to those who held firmly to denying the messengers and attributed the Qur'an to being sorcery and confused dreams, and this is what is meant by His words ﴿what you describe﴾. Further removed is the view of the one who said that it is a shift (iltifat) from the third-person pronoun in ﴿Their claim remained so﴾ to the second-person pronoun. Then Allah, exalted is He, informed that whoever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, so that those they named as consorts and offspring are included in it. (﴿And those with Him﴾) are the angels. It is possible that it is conjoined to "whoever" (man), so they are included among the angels in a general sense, since they are included in "whoever," and in a specific sense by the explicit statement that they are "those with Him." Then ﴿They do not grow arrogant﴾ would be a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah) concerning them, or a resumptive statement of information (istithnaf ikhbar). It is also possible that ﴿those with Him﴾ is the subject (mubtada') and its predicate is ﴿they do not grow arrogant﴾. Here "with" ('inda) is not meant as a spatial location, since He is exalted above place; rather the meaning is nobility of rank and loftiness of station. The apparent meaning is that His words ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ are a resumptive statement of information that the entire world is His possession. It has been said that it may be parallel to His words ﴿Woe to you because of what you describe,﴾ as if He were dividing the matter within Himself: for those who hold this claim there is woe, and to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth. End.

The meaning is that the angels are honored and brought near, because of their honor with Allah, in the manner of those held close by kings, by way of illustration and explanation (p-303), because of their nobility and excellence. It is said: al-bai'ru hasara and istahsara, meaning he became weary and tired; and I made it weary (hasartuhu), so it is transitive and intransitive; and also ahsartuhu. The poet said:

"Therein are the carcasses of the wearied; as for their bones, they are white, and as for their hides, they are tough."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: istihsar is an intensification of husur, and the more eloquent way of describing them would be to negate from them even the slightest weariness, I say: in istihsar there is an indication that what they are engaged in necessitates the utmost and extreme weariness, and that they are deserving of those burdensome acts of worship, such that they would grow weary in what they do. End.

﴿Glorifying﴾ (yusabbihun) refers to the angels, by the consensus of the community; He described them with constant glorification. It is related from Ka'b: Allah made glorification for them like breath and the blink of an eye for humans, which proceeds from them constantly without weariness befalling them in it. And in the hadith: ("Indeed I hear the creaking (atit) of the heaven, and it has the right to creak; there is not a space of a palm's breadth in it but there is an angel prostrating or standing.")

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 11–20 (part 1 of 2):

(p. 300) ﴿How many a town We have shattered, which was wrongdoing, and We brought into being after it another people.﴾ ﴿So when they perceived Our might, behold, they were fleeing from it.﴾ ﴿Do not flee, but return to what you were made to enjoy and to your dwellings, that perhaps you may be questioned.﴾ ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿And that was their cry until We made them as harvested stubble, extinguished.﴾ ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ ﴿Had We wished to take a pastime, We would have taken it from Ourselves, if We were ever going to do so.﴾ ﴿Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes. And woe to you for what you describe.﴾ ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth. And those near Him are not too proud to worship Him, nor do they tire.﴾ ﴿They glorify Him night and day; they never slacken.﴾

When God, exalted is He, refuted what they had said, He went further in rebuking them by mentioning the towns He had destroyed. He said: ﴿How many a town We have shattered﴾. The intended meaning is its people, since a town cannot be described as wrongdoing, as in His saying: ﴿from this town whose people are wrongdoers﴾ [An-Nisa: 75]. Ibn Abbas said: al-insha' (bringing into being) is the bringing of a thing into existence without a prior cause that produced it; so "nasha'a" means he came into being, and he is "nashi'" (one who has come into being), and the plural is "nushshaʾ," like "khadam." Al-qasm (shattering) is the most severe kind of breaking, and it is used figuratively for severe destruction. (Kam) indicates multiplicity, so the meaning is: We destroyed many of the people of towns with a severe and emphatic destruction.

As for what is narrated from Ibn Abbas, that it is "Hadura" (Ḥaḍūrāʾ), a town in Yemen, and from Ibn Wahb, from some of his men, that they are two towns in Yemen whose people became insolent, this is to be taken as an illustration and not as a specific identification of the town, because (kam) indicates multiplicity. From the report about the people of Haḍūrāʾ: God sent a prophet to them and they killed him, so God empowered Bukhtnasr (Nebuchadnezzar) over them, just as He empowered him over the people of Jerusalem. He sent an army against them and they defeated it; then he sent another and they defeated it; then he himself went out against them and defeated them in the third encounter. When slaughter took hold of them, they fled running.

﴿So when they perceived Our might﴾, that is, they came into direct contact with it through perception. The pronoun in ﴿they perceived﴾ refers to the people implied in His saying ﴿How many a town We have shattered﴾, and it does not refer to His saying ﴿another people﴾, because no sin is mentioned for which they would be fleeing. The pronoun in (minha, from it) refers to the town. It is possible that it refers to (ba'sana, Our might), because it means severity, so it is feminine according to its meaning, and "min" (from) is for this reason. The apparent meaning is that when the vanguard of the punishment overtook them, they mounted their animals, driving them, fleeing and routed. It was said: it is also possible that in the speed of their running on foot they were likened to riders driving their animals, so they are "running" (yarkudūna) the earth with their feet, as He said: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾ [Sad: 42]. The answer to (lamma, when) is (idha, suddenly) the sudden particle and what follows it. This is one of the proofs that (lamma) in this construction is a particle and not an adverb; we have already discussed this earlier.

As for His saying: ﴿Do not flee﴾, Ibn Atiyya said: it is possible that it is the speech of the men of Bukhtnasr, according to the narration mentioned earlier. The meaning according to this is that they deceived them and mocked them, saying to those fleeing from them: "Do not flee, but return to your homes," ﴿that perhaps you may be questioned﴾ about a truce, or tribute, or a matter agreed upon. When they turned back, Bukhtnasr ordered a call to be made among them: "O vengeance for the slain prophet!" So they were killed by the sword, to the last of them. All of this is narrated. It is possible that His saying ﴿Do not flee﴾ through the end of the verse is the speech of the angels of punishment, describing the story of each town, and that He did not intend to specify Haḍūrāʾ or any other. The meaning according to this is: the people of these towns, through their delusion, thought they were held in a high position with God, and that if a punishment or a command came upon them, it would not descend upon them until they disputed and were questioned about the cause of their denial of their prophet, so that they would argue at that time with arguments that they imagined would benefit them. When the punishment descended, not in the manner they had hoped for, and they fled running, the angels called out to them in mockery.

﴿Do not flee, but return﴾ . . .

﴿that perhaps you may be questioned﴾ as you used to hope, because of the foolishness of your opinions.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is possible that he means: the speaker is some of the angels, or some of the believers from among them, or they are made deputies, by saying that to them even though it was not said, or the Lord of Might says it and makes His angels hear it, so that it benefits them in their religion, or He inspires them with it so that they speak it to their own souls.

﴿and return to what you were made to enjoy﴾ of the luxurious life and comfortable state. (Itraf) is the excess of blessing, and it is luxury (tarraf).

﴿that perhaps you may be questioned﴾ tomorrow about what befell you and what happened to your wealth and your dwellings, so that you may answer the questioner with knowledge and witness. Or (return) and sit as you were in your assemblies, and arrange yourselves in your ranks, until your servants and your retainers and those whose affairs you control, whose commands and prohibitions you enforce, ask you, and say to you: "What do you command, and what do you decree? How shall we proceed or refrain, as is the custom of the pampered and served?" Or the people will ask you in your gatherings, the helpers in the calamities of catastrophes, and consult you in important and sudden matters, seeking to be healed by your measures and enlightened by your opinions; or those who come to you and the greedy will ask you, seeking rain from the clouds of your palms and seeking the abundance of your kindness and your favours. Either because they were generous and spent their wealth to be seen by people and to seek praise, or because they were miserly, and so this was said to them mockingly, mockery upon mockery, and rebuke upon rebuke. End of quotation.

The calling of "woe" (wayl) is figurative, as if they said: "O woe, this is your time." The explanation of woe has already been mentioned in al-Baqara.

The wrongdoing here is polytheism, denying the messengers, and bringing themselves into destruction. The subject of (zalat, ceased) is the demonstrative (tilka, that), and it is a reference to the statement that was spoken, meaning: "that claim of theirs [da'wahum] did not cease." The commentators said: they kept repeating that word and it did not benefit them, as in His saying: ﴿Their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might﴾ [Ghafir: 85]. (Da'wa, claim) is the verbal noun of "da'a," one says "da'a da'wa" and "da'wa," as in His saying: ﴿and the last of their call﴾ [Yunus: 10], because the one who cries woe is as if he calls out "woe." Al-Hawfi said, and al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa followed him: (tilka) is the subject of (zalat), and (da'wahum) is the predicate; it is permissible that (da'wahum) be the subject of (zalat) and (tilka) be in the position of the predicate. End of quotation. What these men went to was said earlier by al-Zajjaj. As for our later companions (the Basran grammarians), the subject and predicate of (kana, was) are likened to the doer and the object. Just as in the construction of the doer and object, when there is ambiguity, the earlier cannot be the predicate and the later the subject, so in the construction of (kana) this is not permissible. When you say "Musa was my friend" (kana Musa sadiqi), it is not permissible for Musa to be anything but the subject of (kana) and "my friend" the predicate, as in your saying "Musa struck Isa," where Musa is the doer and Isa the object. None of our later companions disputed this except Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Ali, known as Ibn al-Hajj, who was one of the students of the master Abu Ali al-Shalawbin and among their distinguished scholars. He permitted that the earlier be the object and the later the doer, even if ambiguous. But according to what the majority of the companions established, it is necessary that (tilka) be the subject of (zalat) and (da'wahum) the predicate.

And His saying: (ḥaṣīdan, as stubble), that is, through the punishment, they were left like stubble ﴿extinguished﴾, that is, dead without spirits, likened to a fire when it is put out. (Ḥaṣīdan) is the second object. Al-Hawfi said: ﴿extinguished﴾ is an adjective of (ḥaṣīdan), on the basis that (ḥaṣīdan) means "reaped," meaning the singular form is used while the plural is intended. He said: it is also permissible to make ﴿extinguished﴾ a circumstantial state of the (ha) and (mim) pronoun. Al-Zamakhshari said: (ja'alnahum) means "made them like the stubble." He likened them in their annihilation and uprooting, as you say: "We made them ashes," meaning like ashes. The object pronoun is the one that was originally the subject (mubtada'), and the two objects after it were its two predicates. When (ja'ala) entered upon them, both were put in the accusative as objects. If you ask: how does (ja'ala) govern three objects? I answer: the rule for the other two is the rule for the one, because the meaning of your saying "I made it sweet and sour" is "I made it for the two tastes." Likewise the meaning of "We made them" here is: combining them in the resemblance to stubble and to extinction; and extinction is conjoined to the resemblance, not to the stubble. End of quotation.

When He, exalted is He, mentioned the destruction of those wrongdoing towns, He followed that with what shows that He did this in justice from Him and as recompense for what they had done, and that He created this upper world containing wonders of His making and marvels of His doing, and this lower world and what He deposited in it of the wonders of animals, plants, and minerals, and what lies between them of air, clouds, and winds, not as play, but for religious benefits that decree eternal happiness or eternal misery, and worldly benefits that cannot be counted or enumerated, as in His saying: (p. 302) ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ [Sad: 27], and His saying: ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 39].

Al-Kirmani said: play is an act to which ignorance calls; its beginning pleases but it has no permanence, whereas We created them so that We may recompense the good-doer and the evildoer, and so that they may be taken as evidence of the oneness and the power [of God]. End of quotation.

﴿Had We wished to take a pastime﴾: the root of (lahw) is that to which desire hastens and which inclination calls for; it may be used as a euphemism for intercourse. Here, however, Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi said it means a child. Al-Zajjaj said it means a child in the dialect of Hadramawt. From Ibn Abbas: this is a refutation of those who said ﴿God has taken a son﴾ [Al-Baqara: 116]. Also from him: that pastime here means play. It was said: pastime here means a woman. Qatada said: this is in the dialect of the people of Yemen, and it is a refutation of those who claimed that God has a wife. The meaning of ﴿from Ourselves﴾ is "from Us," in a way that no one would perceive it, because it is a deficiency, so concealing it is better. Al-Suddi said: from heaven, not from earth. It was said: from the dark-eyed houris (hur al-ʿin). It was said: from the side of Our power. It was said: from the angels, not from humans, refuting the divinity of Jesus and Uzayr. Al-Zamakhshari said: He made clear that the reason for abandoning taking a pastime and play, and for its absence from My acts, is that wisdom prevents it; otherwise I am able to take it, if I were to do so, because I am over all things powerful. End of quotation.

This does not fit except with the view of one who says that pastime is play. As for one who interprets it as a child or a woman, that is impossible and power does not apply to it. The apparent meaning is that (in) here is conditional, and the answer to the condition is omitted, indicated by the answer to (law, had): meaning, "if We were doers, We would have taken it, if We were of those who do such a thing; but We are not of those who do it."

Al-Hasan, Qatada and Jurayj said (in) is negative, meaning: "We were not doers."

﴿Rather, We hurl﴾: that is, We cast swiftly, ﴿the truth﴾, which is the Qur'an, ﴿against falsehood﴾, which is Satan, as Mujahid said, and he said: everything in the Qur'an concerning falsehood refers to Satan. It was also said: "the truth" means the proof against falsehood, which is their doubts and their describing God with attributes not His, such as having a son and other things. It was said: the truth is general, covering the Qur'an, the message, and the law, and falsehood likewise is general. And (bal, rather) is a turning away from taking play and pastime. The meaning is that He refutes falsehood with truth. He used the metaphor of casting and crushing to depict its annihilation, its nullification, and its erasure. He made it as if it were a solid, hard body, like a rock, cast upon a soft, hollow body, so that it crushes it, that is, strikes its brain; and that is fatal to a human; likewise the truth destroys falsehood. Isa ibn Umar read (fa-yadmaghahu) with a fatha on the ghayn. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is in the weakness of the poet's saying:

"I will leave my dwelling to the Banu Tamim and join the Hijaz and rest."

And it was read (fa-yadmughuhu) with a damma on the mim. End of quotation.

﴿Do not flee, but return﴾ . . .

The subject of (zalat, ceased) is the demonstrative (tilka, that), and it is a reference to the statement that was spoken, meaning: "that claim of theirs [da'wahum] did not cease." The commentators said: they kept repeating that word and it did not benefit them, as in His saying: ﴿Their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might﴾ [Ghafir: 85]. (Da'wa, claim) is the verbal noun of "da'a," one says "da'a da'wa" and "da'wa," as in His saying: ﴿and the last of their call﴾ [Yunus: 10], because the one who cries woe is as if he calls out "woe." Al-Hawfi said, and al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa followed him: (tilka) is the subject of (zalat), and (da'wahum) is the predicate; it is permissible that (da'wahum) be the subject of (zalat) and (tilka) be in the position of the predicate. End of quotation. What these men went to was said earlier by al-Zajjaj. As for our later companions (the Basran grammarians), the subject and predicate of (kana, was) are likened to the doer and the object. Just as in the construction of the doer and object, when there is ambiguity, the earlier cannot be the predicate and the later the subject, so in the construction of (kana) this is not permissible. When you say "Musa was my friend" (kana Musa sadiqi), it is not permissible for Musa to be anything but the subject of (kana) and "my friend" the predicate, as in your saying "Musa struck Isa," where Musa is the doer and Isa the object. None of our later companions disputed this except Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Ali, known as Ibn al-Hajj, who was one of the students of the master Abu Ali al-Shalawbin and among their distinguished scholars. He permitted that the earlier be the object and the later the doer, even if ambiguous. But according to what the majority of the companions established, it is necessary that (tilka) be the subject of (zalat) and (da'wahum) the predicate.

And His saying: (ḥaṣīdan, as stubble), that is, through the punishment, they were left like stubble ﴿extinguished﴾, that is, dead without spirits, likened to a fire when it is put out. (Ḥaṣīdan) is the second object. Al-Hawfi said: ﴿extinguished﴾ is an adjective of (ḥaṣīdan), on the basis that (ḥaṣīdan) means "reaped," meaning the singular form is used while the plural is intended. He said: it is also permissible to make ﴿extinguished﴾ a circumstantial state of the (ha) and (mim) pronoun. Al-Zamakhshari said: (ja'alnahum) means "made them like the stubble." He likened them in their annihilation and uprooting, as you say: "We made them ashes," meaning like ashes. The object pronoun is the one that was originally the subject (mubtada'), and the two objects after it were its two predicates. When (ja'ala) entered upon them, both were put in the accusative as objects. If you ask: how does (ja'ala) govern three objects? I answer: the rule for the other two is the rule for the one, because the meaning of your saying "I made it sweet and sour" is "I made it for the two tastes." Likewise the meaning of "We made them" here is: combining them in the resemblance to stubble and to extinction; and extinction is conjoined to the resemblance, not to the stubble. End of quotation.

When He, exalted is He, mentioned the destruction of those wrongdoing towns, He followed that with what shows that He did this in justice from Him and as recompense for what they had done, and that He created this upper world containing wonders of His making and marvels of His doing, and this lower world and what He deposited in it of the wonders of animals, plants, and minerals, and what lies between them of air, clouds, and winds, not as play, but for religious benefits that decree eternal happiness or eternal misery, and worldly benefits that cannot be counted or enumerated, as in His saying: (p. 302) ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ [Sad: 27], and His saying: ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 39].

Al-Kirmani said: play is an act to which ignorance calls; its beginning pleases but it has no permanence, whereas We created them so that We may recompense the good-doer and the evildoer, and so that they may be taken as evidence of the oneness and the power [of God]. End of quotation.

﴿Had We wished to take a pastime﴾: the root of (lahw) is that to which desire hastens and which inclination calls for; it may be used as a euphemism for intercourse. Here, however, Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi said it means a child. Al-Zajjaj said it means a child in the dialect of Hadramawt. From Ibn Abbas: this is a refutation of those who said ﴿God has taken a son﴾ [Al-Baqara: 116]. Also from him: that pastime here means play. It was said: pastime here means a woman. Qatada said: this is in the dialect of the people of Yemen, and it is a refutation of those who claimed that God has a wife. The meaning of ﴿from Ourselves﴾ is "from Us," in a way that no one would perceive it, because it is a deficiency, so concealing it is better. Al-Suddi said: from heaven, not from earth. It was said: from the dark-eyed houris (hur al-ʿin). It was said: from the side of Our power. It was said: from the angels, not from humans, refuting the divinity of Jesus and Uzayr. Al-Zamakhshari said: He made clear that the reason for abandoning taking a pastime and play, and for its absence from My acts, is that wisdom prevents it; otherwise I am able to take it, if I were to do so, because I am over all things powerful. End of quotation.

This does not fit except with the view of one who says that pastime is play. As for one who interprets it as a child or a woman, that is impossible and power does not apply to it. The apparent meaning is that (in) here is conditional, and the answer to the condition is omitted, indicated by the answer to (law, had): meaning, "if We were doers, We would have taken it, if We were of those who do such a thing; but We are not of those who do it."

Al-Hasan, Qatada and Jurayj said (in) is negative, meaning: "We were not doers."

﴿Rather, We hurl﴾: that is, We cast swiftly, ﴿the truth﴾, which is the Qur'an, ﴿against falsehood﴾, which is Satan, as Mujahid said, and he said: everything in the Qur'an concerning falsehood refers to Satan. It was also said: "the truth" means the proof against falsehood, which is their doubts and their describing God with attributes not His, such as having a son and other things. It was said: the truth is general, covering the Qur'an, the message, and the law, and falsehood likewise is general. And (bal, rather) is a turning away from taking play and pastime. The meaning is that He refutes falsehood with truth. He used the metaphor of casting and crushing to depict its annihilation, its nullification, and its erasure. He made it as if it were a solid, hard body, like a rock, cast upon a soft, hollow body, so that it crushes it, that is, strikes its brain; and that is fatal to a human; likewise the truth destroys falsehood. Isa ibn Umar read (fa-yadmaghahu) with a fatha on the ghayn. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is in the weakness of the poet's saying:

"I will leave my dwelling to the Banu Tamim and join the Hijaz and rest."

And it was read (fa-yadmughuhu) with a damma on the mim. End of quotation.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 11–20 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Woe to you﴾ is an address to the disbelievers, meaning disgrace and distress (al-khizy wa al-hamm). ﴿Because of what you describe﴾ means: because of what you describe Him as, of things unbefitting Him, such as taking consorts and offspring and attributing impossibilities to Him. It has also been said that "for you" is an address to those who held firmly to denying the messengers and attributed the Qur'an to being sorcery and confused dreams, and this is what is meant by His words ﴿what you describe﴾. Further removed is the view of the one who said that it is a shift (iltifat) from the third-person pronoun in ﴿Their claim remained so﴾ to the second-person pronoun. Then Allah, exalted is He, informed that whoever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, so that those they named as consorts and offspring are included in it. (﴿And those with Him﴾) are the angels. It is possible that it is conjoined to "whoever" (man), so they are included among the angels in a general sense, since they are included in "whoever," and in a specific sense by the explicit statement that they are "those with Him." Then ﴿They do not grow arrogant﴾ would be a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah) concerning them, or a resumptive statement of information (istithnaf ikhbar). It is also possible that ﴿those with Him﴾ is the subject (mubtada') and its predicate is ﴿they do not grow arrogant﴾. Here "with" ('inda) is not meant as a spatial location, since He is exalted above place; rather the meaning is nobility of rank and loftiness of station. The apparent meaning is that His words ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ are a resumptive statement of information that the entire world is His possession. It has been said that it may be parallel to His words ﴿Woe to you because of what you describe,﴾ as if He were dividing the matter within Himself: for those who hold this claim there is woe, and to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth. End.

The meaning is that the angels are honored and brought near, because of their honor with Allah, in the manner of those held close by kings, by way of illustration and explanation (p-303), because of their nobility and excellence. It is said: al-bai'ru hasara and istahsara, meaning he became weary and tired; and I made it weary (hasartuhu), so it is transitive and intransitive; and also ahsartuhu. The poet said:

"Therein are the carcasses of the wearied; as for their bones, they are white, and as for their hides, they are tough."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: istihsar is an intensification of husur, and the more eloquent way of describing them would be to negate from them even the slightest weariness, I say: in istihsar there is an indication that what they are engaged in necessitates the utmost and extreme weariness, and that they are deserving of those burdensome acts of worship, such that they would grow weary in what they do. End.

﴿Glorifying﴾ (yusabbihun) refers to the angels, by the consensus of the community; He described them with constant glorification. It is related from Ka'b: Allah made glorification for them like breath and the blink of an eye for humans, which proceeds from them constantly without weariness befalling them in it. And in the hadith: ("Indeed I hear the creaking (atit) of the heaven, and it has the right to creak; there is not a space of a palm's breadth in it but there is an angel prostrating or standing.")

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 11–20 (part 1 of 2):

(p. 300) ﴿How many a town We have shattered, which was wrongdoing, and We brought into being after it another people.﴾ ﴿So when they perceived Our might, behold, they were fleeing from it.﴾ ﴿Do not flee, but return to what you were made to enjoy and to your dwellings, that perhaps you may be questioned.﴾ ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿And that was their cry until We made them as harvested stubble, extinguished.﴾ ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ ﴿Had We wished to take a pastime, We would have taken it from Ourselves, if We were ever going to do so.﴾ ﴿Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes. And woe to you for what you describe.﴾ ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth. And those near Him are not too proud to worship Him, nor do they tire.﴾ ﴿They glorify Him night and day; they never slacken.﴾

When God, exalted is He, refuted what they had said, He went further in rebuking them by mentioning the towns He had destroyed. He said: ﴿How many a town We have shattered﴾. The intended meaning is its people, since a town cannot be described as wrongdoing, as in His saying: ﴿from this town whose people are wrongdoers﴾ [An-Nisa: 75]. Ibn Abbas said: al-insha' (bringing into being) is the bringing of a thing into existence without a prior cause that produced it; so "nasha'a" means he came into being, and he is "nashi'" (one who has come into being), and the plural is "nushshaʾ," like "khadam." Al-qasm (shattering) is the most severe kind of breaking, and it is used figuratively for severe destruction. (Kam) indicates multiplicity, so the meaning is: We destroyed many of the people of towns with a severe and emphatic destruction.

As for what is narrated from Ibn Abbas, that it is "Hadura" (Ḥaḍūrāʾ), a town in Yemen, and from Ibn Wahb, from some of his men, that they are two towns in Yemen whose people became insolent, this is to be taken as an illustration and not as a specific identification of the town, because (kam) indicates multiplicity. From the report about the people of Haḍūrāʾ: God sent a prophet to them and they killed him, so God empowered Bukhtnasr (Nebuchadnezzar) over them, just as He empowered him over the people of Jerusalem. He sent an army against them and they defeated it; then he sent another and they defeated it; then he himself went out against them and defeated them in the third encounter. When slaughter took hold of them, they fled running.

﴿So when they perceived Our might﴾, that is, they came into direct contact with it through perception. The pronoun in ﴿they perceived﴾ refers to the people implied in His saying ﴿How many a town We have shattered﴾, and it does not refer to His saying ﴿another people﴾, because no sin is mentioned for which they would be fleeing. The pronoun in (minha, from it) refers to the town. It is possible that it refers to (ba'sana, Our might), because it means severity, so it is feminine according to its meaning, and "min" (from) is for this reason. The apparent meaning is that when the vanguard of the punishment overtook them, they mounted their animals, driving them, fleeing and routed. It was said: it is also possible that in the speed of their running on foot they were likened to riders driving their animals, so they are "running" (yarkudūna) the earth with their feet, as He said: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾ [Sad: 42]. The answer to (lamma, when) is (idha, suddenly) the sudden particle and what follows it. This is one of the proofs that (lamma) in this construction is a particle and not an adverb; we have already discussed this earlier.

As for His saying: ﴿Do not flee﴾, Ibn Atiyya said: it is possible that it is the speech of the men of Bukhtnasr, according to the narration mentioned earlier. The meaning according to this is that they deceived them and mocked them, saying to those fleeing from them: "Do not flee, but return to your homes," ﴿that perhaps you may be questioned﴾ about a truce, or tribute, or a matter agreed upon. When they turned back, Bukhtnasr ordered a call to be made among them: "O vengeance for the slain prophet!" So they were killed by the sword, to the last of them. All of this is narrated. It is possible that His saying ﴿Do not flee﴾ through the end of the verse is the speech of the angels of punishment, describing the story of each town, and that He did not intend to specify Haḍūrāʾ or any other. The meaning according to this is: the people of these towns, through their delusion, thought they were held in a high position with God, and that if a punishment or a command came upon them, it would not descend upon them until they disputed and were questioned about the cause of their denial of their prophet, so that they would argue at that time with arguments that they imagined would benefit them. When the punishment descended, not in the manner they had hoped for, and they fled running, the angels called out to them in mockery.

﴿Do not flee, but return﴾ . . .

﴿that perhaps you may be questioned﴾ as you used to hope, because of the foolishness of your opinions.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is possible that he means: the speaker is some of the angels, or some of the believers from among them, or they are made deputies, by saying that to them even though it was not said, or the Lord of Might says it and makes His angels hear it, so that it benefits them in their religion, or He inspires them with it so that they speak it to their own souls.

﴿and return to what you were made to enjoy﴾ of the luxurious life and comfortable state. (Itraf) is the excess of blessing, and it is luxury (tarraf).

﴿that perhaps you may be questioned﴾ tomorrow about what befell you and what happened to your wealth and your dwellings, so that you may answer the questioner with knowledge and witness. Or (return) and sit as you were in your assemblies, and arrange yourselves in your ranks, until your servants and your retainers and those whose affairs you control, whose commands and prohibitions you enforce, ask you, and say to you: "What do you command, and what do you decree? How shall we proceed or refrain, as is the custom of the pampered and served?" Or the people will ask you in your gatherings, the helpers in the calamities of catastrophes, and consult you in important and sudden matters, seeking to be healed by your measures and enlightened by your opinions; or those who come to you and the greedy will ask you, seeking rain from the clouds of your palms and seeking the abundance of your kindness and your favours. Either because they were generous and spent their wealth to be seen by people and to seek praise, or because they were miserly, and so this was said to them mockingly, mockery upon mockery, and rebuke upon rebuke. End of quotation.

The calling of "woe" (wayl) is figurative, as if they said: "O woe, this is your time." The explanation of woe has already been mentioned in al-Baqara.

The wrongdoing here is polytheism, denying the messengers, and bringing themselves into destruction. The subject of (zalat, ceased) is the demonstrative (tilka, that), and it is a reference to the statement that was spoken, meaning: "that claim of theirs [da'wahum] did not cease." The commentators said: they kept repeating that word and it did not benefit them, as in His saying: ﴿Their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might﴾ [Ghafir: 85]. (Da'wa, claim) is the verbal noun of "da'a," one says "da'a da'wa" and "da'wa," as in His saying: ﴿and the last of their call﴾ [Yunus: 10], because the one who cries woe is as if he calls out "woe." Al-Hawfi said, and al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa followed him: (tilka) is the subject of (zalat), and (da'wahum) is the predicate; it is permissible that (da'wahum) be the subject of (zalat) and (tilka) be in the position of the predicate. End of quotation. What these men went to was said earlier by al-Zajjaj. As for our later companions (the Basran grammarians), the subject and predicate of (kana, was) are likened to the doer and the object. Just as in the construction of the doer and object, when there is ambiguity, the earlier cannot be the predicate and the later the subject, so in the construction of (kana) this is not permissible. When you say "Musa was my friend" (kana Musa sadiqi), it is not permissible for Musa to be anything but the subject of (kana) and "my friend" the predicate, as in your saying "Musa struck Isa," where Musa is the doer and Isa the object. None of our later companions disputed this except Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Ali, known as Ibn al-Hajj, who was one of the students of the master Abu Ali al-Shalawbin and among their distinguished scholars. He permitted that the earlier be the object and the later the doer, even if ambiguous. But according to what the majority of the companions established, it is necessary that (tilka) be the subject of (zalat) and (da'wahum) the predicate.

And His saying: (ḥaṣīdan, as stubble), that is, through the punishment, they were left like stubble ﴿extinguished﴾, that is, dead without spirits, likened to a fire when it is put out. (Ḥaṣīdan) is the second object. Al-Hawfi said: ﴿extinguished﴾ is an adjective of (ḥaṣīdan), on the basis that (ḥaṣīdan) means "reaped," meaning the singular form is used while the plural is intended. He said: it is also permissible to make ﴿extinguished﴾ a circumstantial state of the (ha) and (mim) pronoun. Al-Zamakhshari said: (ja'alnahum) means "made them like the stubble." He likened them in their annihilation and uprooting, as you say: "We made them ashes," meaning like ashes. The object pronoun is the one that was originally the subject (mubtada'), and the two objects after it were its two predicates. When (ja'ala) entered upon them, both were put in the accusative as objects. If you ask: how does (ja'ala) govern three objects? I answer: the rule for the other two is the rule for the one, because the meaning of your saying "I made it sweet and sour" is "I made it for the two tastes." Likewise the meaning of "We made them" here is: combining them in the resemblance to stubble and to extinction; and extinction is conjoined to the resemblance, not to the stubble. End of quotation.

When He, exalted is He, mentioned the destruction of those wrongdoing towns, He followed that with what shows that He did this in justice from Him and as recompense for what they had done, and that He created this upper world containing wonders of His making and marvels of His doing, and this lower world and what He deposited in it of the wonders of animals, plants, and minerals, and what lies between them of air, clouds, and winds, not as play, but for religious benefits that decree eternal happiness or eternal misery, and worldly benefits that cannot be counted or enumerated, as in His saying: (p. 302) ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ [Sad: 27], and His saying: ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 39].

Al-Kirmani said: play is an act to which ignorance calls; its beginning pleases but it has no permanence, whereas We created them so that We may recompense the good-doer and the evildoer, and so that they may be taken as evidence of the oneness and the power [of God]. End of quotation.

﴿Had We wished to take a pastime﴾: the root of (lahw) is that to which desire hastens and which inclination calls for; it may be used as a euphemism for intercourse. Here, however, Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi said it means a child. Al-Zajjaj said it means a child in the dialect of Hadramawt. From Ibn Abbas: this is a refutation of those who said ﴿God has taken a son﴾ [Al-Baqara: 116]. Also from him: that pastime here means play. It was said: pastime here means a woman. Qatada said: this is in the dialect of the people of Yemen, and it is a refutation of those who claimed that God has a wife. The meaning of ﴿from Ourselves﴾ is "from Us," in a way that no one would perceive it, because it is a deficiency, so concealing it is better. Al-Suddi said: from heaven, not from earth. It was said: from the dark-eyed houris (hur al-ʿin). It was said: from the side of Our power. It was said: from the angels, not from humans, refuting the divinity of Jesus and Uzayr. Al-Zamakhshari said: He made clear that the reason for abandoning taking a pastime and play, and for its absence from My acts, is that wisdom prevents it; otherwise I am able to take it, if I were to do so, because I am over all things powerful. End of quotation.

This does not fit except with the view of one who says that pastime is play. As for one who interprets it as a child or a woman, that is impossible and power does not apply to it. The apparent meaning is that (in) here is conditional, and the answer to the condition is omitted, indicated by the answer to (law, had): meaning, "if We were doers, We would have taken it, if We were of those who do such a thing; but We are not of those who do it."

Al-Hasan, Qatada and Jurayj said (in) is negative, meaning: "We were not doers."

﴿Rather, We hurl﴾: that is, We cast swiftly, ﴿the truth﴾, which is the Qur'an, ﴿against falsehood﴾, which is Satan, as Mujahid said, and he said: everything in the Qur'an concerning falsehood refers to Satan. It was also said: "the truth" means the proof against falsehood, which is their doubts and their describing God with attributes not His, such as having a son and other things. It was said: the truth is general, covering the Qur'an, the message, and the law, and falsehood likewise is general. And (bal, rather) is a turning away from taking play and pastime. The meaning is that He refutes falsehood with truth. He used the metaphor of casting and crushing to depict its annihilation, its nullification, and its erasure. He made it as if it were a solid, hard body, like a rock, cast upon a soft, hollow body, so that it crushes it, that is, strikes its brain; and that is fatal to a human; likewise the truth destroys falsehood. Isa ibn Umar read (fa-yadmaghahu) with a fatha on the ghayn. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is in the weakness of the poet's saying:

"I will leave my dwelling to the Banu Tamim and join the Hijaz and rest."

And it was read (fa-yadmughuhu) with a damma on the mim. End of quotation.
