Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 11–20 (part 1 of 2):

(p. 300) ﴿How many a town We have shattered, which was wrongdoing, and We brought into being after it another people.﴾ ﴿So when they perceived Our might, behold, they were fleeing from it.﴾ ﴿Do not flee, but return to what you were made to enjoy and to your dwellings, that perhaps you may be questioned.﴾ ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿And that was their cry until We made them as harvested stubble, extinguished.﴾ ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ ﴿Had We wished to take a pastime, We would have taken it from Ourselves, if We were ever going to do so.﴾ ﴿Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes. And woe to you for what you describe.﴾ ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth. And those near Him are not too proud to worship Him, nor do they tire.﴾ ﴿They glorify Him night and day; they never slacken.﴾

When God, exalted is He, refuted what they had said, He went further in rebuking them by mentioning the towns He had destroyed. He said: ﴿How many a town We have shattered﴾. The intended meaning is its people, since a town cannot be described as wrongdoing, as in His saying: ﴿from this town whose people are wrongdoers﴾ [An-Nisa: 75]. Ibn Abbas said: al-insha' (bringing into being) is the bringing of a thing into existence without a prior cause that produced it; so "nasha'a" means he came into being, and he is "nashi'" (one who has come into being), and the plural is "nushshaʾ," like "khadam." Al-qasm (shattering) is the most severe kind of breaking, and it is used figuratively for severe destruction. (Kam) indicates multiplicity, so the meaning is: We destroyed many of the people of towns with a severe and emphatic destruction.

As for what is narrated from Ibn Abbas, that it is "Hadura" (Ḥaḍūrāʾ), a town in Yemen, and from Ibn Wahb, from some of his men, that they are two towns in Yemen whose people became insolent, this is to be taken as an illustration and not as a specific identification of the town, because (kam) indicates multiplicity. From the report about the people of Haḍūrāʾ: God sent a prophet to them and they killed him, so God empowered Bukhtnasr (Nebuchadnezzar) over them, just as He empowered him over the people of Jerusalem. He sent an army against them and they defeated it; then he sent another and they defeated it; then he himself went out against them and defeated them in the third encounter. When slaughter took hold of them, they fled running.

﴿So when they perceived Our might﴾, that is, they came into direct contact with it through perception. The pronoun in ﴿they perceived﴾ refers to the people implied in His saying ﴿How many a town We have shattered﴾, and it does not refer to His saying ﴿another people﴾, because no sin is mentioned for which they would be fleeing. The pronoun in (minha, from it) refers to the town. It is possible that it refers to (ba'sana, Our might), because it means severity, so it is feminine according to its meaning, and "min" (from) is for this reason. The apparent meaning is that when the vanguard of the punishment overtook them, they mounted their animals, driving them, fleeing and routed. It was said: it is also possible that in the speed of their running on foot they were likened to riders driving their animals, so they are "running" (yarkudūna) the earth with their feet, as He said: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾ [Sad: 42]. The answer to (lamma, when) is (idha, suddenly) the sudden particle and what follows it. This is one of the proofs that (lamma) in this construction is a particle and not an adverb; we have already discussed this earlier.

As for His saying: ﴿Do not flee﴾, Ibn Atiyya said: it is possible that it is the speech of the men of Bukhtnasr, according to the narration mentioned earlier. The meaning according to this is that they deceived them and mocked them, saying to those fleeing from them: "Do not flee, but return to your homes," ﴿that perhaps you may be questioned﴾ about a truce, or tribute, or a matter agreed upon. When they turned back, Bukhtnasr ordered a call to be made among them: "O vengeance for the slain prophet!" So they were killed by the sword, to the last of them. All of this is narrated. It is possible that His saying ﴿Do not flee﴾ through the end of the verse is the speech of the angels of punishment, describing the story of each town, and that He did not intend to specify Haḍūrāʾ or any other. The meaning according to this is: the people of these towns, through their delusion, thought they were held in a high position with God, and that if a punishment or a command came upon them, it would not descend upon them until they disputed and were questioned about the cause of their denial of their prophet, so that they would argue at that time with arguments that they imagined would benefit them. When the punishment descended, not in the manner they had hoped for, and they fled running, the angels called out to them in mockery.

﴿Do not flee, but return﴾ . . .

﴿that perhaps you may be questioned﴾ as you used to hope, because of the foolishness of your opinions.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is possible that he means: the speaker is some of the angels, or some of the believers from among them, or they are made deputies, by saying that to them even though it was not said, or the Lord of Might says it and makes His angels hear it, so that it benefits them in their religion, or He inspires them with it so that they speak it to their own souls.

﴿and return to what you were made to enjoy﴾ of the luxurious life and comfortable state. (Itraf) is the excess of blessing, and it is luxury (tarraf).

﴿that perhaps you may be questioned﴾ tomorrow about what befell you and what happened to your wealth and your dwellings, so that you may answer the questioner with knowledge and witness. Or (return) and sit as you were in your assemblies, and arrange yourselves in your ranks, until your servants and your retainers and those whose affairs you control, whose commands and prohibitions you enforce, ask you, and say to you: "What do you command, and what do you decree? How shall we proceed or refrain, as is the custom of the pampered and served?" Or the people will ask you in your gatherings, the helpers in the calamities of catastrophes, and consult you in important and sudden matters, seeking to be healed by your measures and enlightened by your opinions; or those who come to you and the greedy will ask you, seeking rain from the clouds of your palms and seeking the abundance of your kindness and your favours. Either because they were generous and spent their wealth to be seen by people and to seek praise, or because they were miserly, and so this was said to them mockingly, mockery upon mockery, and rebuke upon rebuke. End of quotation.

The calling of "woe" (wayl) is figurative, as if they said: "O woe, this is your time." The explanation of woe has already been mentioned in al-Baqara.

The wrongdoing here is polytheism, denying the messengers, and bringing themselves into destruction. The subject of (zalat, ceased) is the demonstrative (tilka, that), and it is a reference to the statement that was spoken, meaning: "that claim of theirs [da'wahum] did not cease." The commentators said: they kept repeating that word and it did not benefit them, as in His saying: ﴿Their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might﴾ [Ghafir: 85]. (Da'wa, claim) is the verbal noun of "da'a," one says "da'a da'wa" and "da'wa," as in His saying: ﴿and the last of their call﴾ [Yunus: 10], because the one who cries woe is as if he calls out "woe." Al-Hawfi said, and al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa followed him: (tilka) is the subject of (zalat), and (da'wahum) is the predicate; it is permissible that (da'wahum) be the subject of (zalat) and (tilka) be in the position of the predicate. End of quotation. What these men went to was said earlier by al-Zajjaj. As for our later companions (the Basran grammarians), the subject and predicate of (kana, was) are likened to the doer and the object. Just as in the construction of the doer and object, when there is ambiguity, the earlier cannot be the predicate and the later the subject, so in the construction of (kana) this is not permissible. When you say "Musa was my friend" (kana Musa sadiqi), it is not permissible for Musa to be anything but the subject of (kana) and "my friend" the predicate, as in your saying "Musa struck Isa," where Musa is the doer and Isa the object. None of our later companions disputed this except Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Ali, known as Ibn al-Hajj, who was one of the students of the master Abu Ali al-Shalawbin and among their distinguished scholars. He permitted that the earlier be the object and the later the doer, even if ambiguous. But according to what the majority of the companions established, it is necessary that (tilka) be the subject of (zalat) and (da'wahum) the predicate.

And His saying: (ḥaṣīdan, as stubble), that is, through the punishment, they were left like stubble ﴿extinguished﴾, that is, dead without spirits, likened to a fire when it is put out. (Ḥaṣīdan) is the second object. Al-Hawfi said: ﴿extinguished﴾ is an adjective of (ḥaṣīdan), on the basis that (ḥaṣīdan) means "reaped," meaning the singular form is used while the plural is intended. He said: it is also permissible to make ﴿extinguished﴾ a circumstantial state of the (ha) and (mim) pronoun. Al-Zamakhshari said: (ja'alnahum) means "made them like the stubble." He likened them in their annihilation and uprooting, as you say: "We made them ashes," meaning like ashes. The object pronoun is the one that was originally the subject (mubtada'), and the two objects after it were its two predicates. When (ja'ala) entered upon them, both were put in the accusative as objects. If you ask: how does (ja'ala) govern three objects? I answer: the rule for the other two is the rule for the one, because the meaning of your saying "I made it sweet and sour" is "I made it for the two tastes." Likewise the meaning of "We made them" here is: combining them in the resemblance to stubble and to extinction; and extinction is conjoined to the resemblance, not to the stubble. End of quotation.

When He, exalted is He, mentioned the destruction of those wrongdoing towns, He followed that with what shows that He did this in justice from Him and as recompense for what they had done, and that He created this upper world containing wonders of His making and marvels of His doing, and this lower world and what He deposited in it of the wonders of animals, plants, and minerals, and what lies between them of air, clouds, and winds, not as play, but for religious benefits that decree eternal happiness or eternal misery, and worldly benefits that cannot be counted or enumerated, as in His saying: (p. 302) ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ [Sad: 27], and His saying: ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 39].

Al-Kirmani said: play is an act to which ignorance calls; its beginning pleases but it has no permanence, whereas We created them so that We may recompense the good-doer and the evildoer, and so that they may be taken as evidence of the oneness and the power [of God]. End of quotation.

﴿Had We wished to take a pastime﴾: the root of (lahw) is that to which desire hastens and which inclination calls for; it may be used as a euphemism for intercourse. Here, however, Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi said it means a child. Al-Zajjaj said it means a child in the dialect of Hadramawt. From Ibn Abbas: this is a refutation of those who said ﴿God has taken a son﴾ [Al-Baqara: 116]. Also from him: that pastime here means play. It was said: pastime here means a woman. Qatada said: this is in the dialect of the people of Yemen, and it is a refutation of those who claimed that God has a wife. The meaning of ﴿from Ourselves﴾ is "from Us," in a way that no one would perceive it, because it is a deficiency, so concealing it is better. Al-Suddi said: from heaven, not from earth. It was said: from the dark-eyed houris (hur al-ʿin). It was said: from the side of Our power. It was said: from the angels, not from humans, refuting the divinity of Jesus and Uzayr. Al-Zamakhshari said: He made clear that the reason for abandoning taking a pastime and play, and for its absence from My acts, is that wisdom prevents it; otherwise I am able to take it, if I were to do so, because I am over all things powerful. End of quotation.

This does not fit except with the view of one who says that pastime is play. As for one who interprets it as a child or a woman, that is impossible and power does not apply to it. The apparent meaning is that (in) here is conditional, and the answer to the condition is omitted, indicated by the answer to (law, had): meaning, "if We were doers, We would have taken it, if We were of those who do such a thing; but We are not of those who do it."

Al-Hasan, Qatada and Jurayj said (in) is negative, meaning: "We were not doers."

﴿Rather, We hurl﴾: that is, We cast swiftly, ﴿the truth﴾, which is the Qur'an, ﴿against falsehood﴾, which is Satan, as Mujahid said, and he said: everything in the Qur'an concerning falsehood refers to Satan. It was also said: "the truth" means the proof against falsehood, which is their doubts and their describing God with attributes not His, such as having a son and other things. It was said: the truth is general, covering the Qur'an, the message, and the law, and falsehood likewise is general. And (bal, rather) is a turning away from taking play and pastime. The meaning is that He refutes falsehood with truth. He used the metaphor of casting and crushing to depict its annihilation, its nullification, and its erasure. He made it as if it were a solid, hard body, like a rock, cast upon a soft, hollow body, so that it crushes it, that is, strikes its brain; and that is fatal to a human; likewise the truth destroys falsehood. Isa ibn Umar read (fa-yadmaghahu) with a fatha on the ghayn. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is in the weakness of the poet's saying:

"I will leave my dwelling to the Banu Tamim and join the Hijaz and rest."

And it was read (fa-yadmughuhu) with a damma on the mim. End of quotation.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 11–20 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Woe to you﴾ is an address to the disbelievers, meaning disgrace and distress (al-khizy wa al-hamm). ﴿Because of what you describe﴾ means: because of what you describe Him as, of things unbefitting Him, such as taking consorts and offspring and attributing impossibilities to Him. It has also been said that "for you" is an address to those who held firmly to denying the messengers and attributed the Qur'an to being sorcery and confused dreams, and this is what is meant by His words ﴿what you describe﴾. Further removed is the view of the one who said that it is a shift (iltifat) from the third-person pronoun in ﴿Their claim remained so﴾ to the second-person pronoun. Then Allah, exalted is He, informed that whoever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, so that those they named as consorts and offspring are included in it. (﴿And those with Him﴾) are the angels. It is possible that it is conjoined to "whoever" (man), so they are included among the angels in a general sense, since they are included in "whoever," and in a specific sense by the explicit statement that they are "those with Him." Then ﴿They do not grow arrogant﴾ would be a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah) concerning them, or a resumptive statement of information (istithnaf ikhbar). It is also possible that ﴿those with Him﴾ is the subject (mubtada') and its predicate is ﴿they do not grow arrogant﴾. Here "with" ('inda) is not meant as a spatial location, since He is exalted above place; rather the meaning is nobility of rank and loftiness of station. The apparent meaning is that His words ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ are a resumptive statement of information that the entire world is His possession. It has been said that it may be parallel to His words ﴿Woe to you because of what you describe,﴾ as if He were dividing the matter within Himself: for those who hold this claim there is woe, and to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth. End.

The meaning is that the angels are honored and brought near, because of their honor with Allah, in the manner of those held close by kings, by way of illustration and explanation (p-303), because of their nobility and excellence. It is said: al-bai'ru hasara and istahsara, meaning he became weary and tired; and I made it weary (hasartuhu), so it is transitive and intransitive; and also ahsartuhu. The poet said:

"Therein are the carcasses of the wearied; as for their bones, they are white, and as for their hides, they are tough."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: istihsar is an intensification of husur, and the more eloquent way of describing them would be to negate from them even the slightest weariness, I say: in istihsar there is an indication that what they are engaged in necessitates the utmost and extreme weariness, and that they are deserving of those burdensome acts of worship, such that they would grow weary in what they do. End.

﴿Glorifying﴾ (yusabbihun) refers to the angels, by the consensus of the community; He described them with constant glorification. It is related from Ka'b: Allah made glorification for them like breath and the blink of an eye for humans, which proceeds from them constantly without weariness befalling them in it. And in the hadith: ("Indeed I hear the creaking (atit) of the heaven, and it has the right to creak; there is not a space of a palm's breadth in it but there is an angel prostrating or standing.")

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 21–29 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth, which can raise the dead?﴾ ﴿Had there been in them (the heavens and the earth) gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted. Glory be to Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned.﴾ ﴿Or have they taken gods besides Him? Say: "Bring your proof. This is the reminder of those with me and the reminder of those before me." But most of them do not know the truth, so they turn away.﴾ ﴿We did not send any messenger before you except that We revealed to him: there is no god but Me, so worship Me.﴾ ﴿And they say: "The Most Merciful has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honoured servants.﴾ ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command.﴾ ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they do not intercede except for those whom He approves, and they are fearful of His awe.﴾ ﴿Whoever among them says, "I am a god besides Him," We will repay him with Hell. Thus do We repay the wrongdoers.﴾.

(p-304) When the Exalted One mentioned the proofs of His oneness, and that all who are in the heavens and the earth belong to Him, and that the honoured angels are in His service, never slackening in His glorification and worship, He returned to what preceded: the rebuke of the polytheists, their censure, and the ridicule of their intellects. Here the particle (am) (or) is disjunctive (munqati'a), and it is to be read as (bal) (rather) together with the interrogative hamza (alif of question). It therefore carries a turning away (idrab) and a shift from one statement to another, and an interrogation whose meaning is wonder and denial. The sense is: ﴿they have taken gods from the earth﴾ that are characterised by giving life and having power over it, and over causing death. That is, they have not taken gods with this attribute; rather, they have taken gods that are lifeless matter, not characterised by power over anything, so they are not gods, because it is an attribute of a god to have power to give life and to cause death.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "How did He deny them taking gods that raise the dead, when they did not claim that for their gods, and they were furthest from this claim? For, while acknowledging that Allah is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, and that He is capable of all things, and of the first creation, they denied resurrection. And it was among them an impossibility, beyond the power of the Capable. So how could they claim it for lifeless matter that is not described as having power?" I say: The matter is as you have mentioned, but by their claim of divinity it is necessary for them to claim for those gods the power of creating, because only one who has power over every thing deserves this name, and creating is among the things that can be done. In this there is a kind of mockery of them, rebuke, and ascription of ignorance, and an indication that what they deemed far-fetched from Allah is not to be deemed far-fetched, because when divinity is valid, the power to originate and to restore is valid with it. As for His saying (from the earth), it is like your saying, "So-and-so is from Mecca or from Medina," meaning a Meccan or a Medinan. The meaning of attributing them to the earth is the announcement that they are the idols worshipped on earth, not that gods are of earthly or heavenly kinds. Of this is the hadith of the slave-girl to whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "Where is your Lord?" She pointed to the sky. He said, "She is a believer," because he understood from her that her intention was the negation of earthly gods, which are the idols, not the affirmation of the sky as a place for Allah, the Exalted.

It is also permissible that what is meant is gods of the kind of the earth, because they are either carved from some stones or made from some of the earth's substances.

If you say, "There must be a point in His saying (they)," I say: the point in it is conveying the meaning of exclusivity, as if it were said: "Or have they taken gods which are not able to give life except they alone?" End of quotation.

Here (they took) (ittakhadhu) may mean "they made and fashioned," and (from the earth) is connected to (they took). It may also mean "they made the gods into idols from the earth," as in His saying: ﴿Do you take idols as gods?﴾ [al-An'am: 74] and His saying: ﴿And Allah took Abraham as a close friend﴾ [al-Nisa': 125], in which there is the sense of choosing and selecting.

The majority of readers recited (yunshiruna), the present tense of (anshara), meaning "they give life." Qutrub said it means "they create," as in His saying: ﴿Is one who creates like one who does not create?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17]. Al-Hasan and Mujahid recited (yanshuruna), the present tense of (nashara). These are two dialects: nashara and anshara are both transitive, and nashara also comes intransitive. You say: "Allah revived the dead, so they lived again" (anshara Allahu al-mawta fa-nashharu), meaning they came to life.

The pronoun in (fihima) (in them) refers to the heavens and the earth, and the two together are a metonymy for the world. (Illa) (other than) is an attribute of (gods), meaning: gods other than Allah. That (illa) may be described by an attribute is well known in the Arabic language. Of this is what Sibawayh, may God have mercy on him, recited:

"Every brother will be parted from by his brother, by the life of your father, except the two Farqads."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "What prevented you from the nominative on the basis of substitution (badal)?" I say: because (law) (if) is like (inna) (indeed) in that the speech that follows it is affirmative, and substitution is only permissible in non-affirmative speech, as in His saying: ﴿None of you shall look back, except your wife﴾ [Hud: 81]. That is because the most general of the general can be negated but cannot be affirmed. The meaning is: if there were gods besides the One who originates them, managing them and administering their affairs, ﴿they would both be corrupted.﴾ This indicates two matters. The first: it is necessary that there be only one manager of them. The second: that one must be none other than Him alone, as in His saying: (except Allah).

If you say, "Why were both matters necessary?" I say: because we know that the subjects are corrupted by the management of two kings, due to what arises between them of contention, mutual repudiation and disagreement.

It is related of Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, when he killed Amr ibn Sa'id al-Ashdaq: "By Allah, he was dearer to me than the blood of my own two eyes, but two stallions do not gather in one herd (shawl)," and this is clear. As for the method of mutual prevention (tamani'), the theologians have much dispute and argument about it, and because these acts require that essence distinguished by those attributes in order to be established and stable.

Ibn Atiyya said: That is because each would seek to overcome the other and would take away what was created. The summary of this: if we suppose two gods in whom there is disagreement over moving a body or not moving it, it is impossible that both wills be executed, and impossible that neither be executed. If one is executed, then the other is powerless, and such a one is not a god. The possibility of disagreement between them is like its occurrence. There is also another consideration: every part that comes out from non-existence into existence cannot be subject to two powers. If one of them is the power that brings it into existence, then in the other there is an excess with no meaning concerning that part. The consideration continues in this way, part after part.

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: If we suppose two existents that are necessary in existence by their essence, then they must share in existence, and each must be distinguished from the other by its own particularity. What makes them share is other than what makes them distinct. So each shares with the other, and every composite is in need of another, being possible in its essence. Therefore, the necessarily existent is only one, and everything other than it is originated. This can be taken as an explanation of this verse, because when we have shown that from supposing two necessary existents it follows that neither of them is necessary, and if the necessary does not exist, none of these possible things exists. Then corruption necessarily follows throughout the whole world.

Abu al-Baqa' said: It is not permissible for it to be a substitute (badal), because the meaning becomes: ﴿If there were in them﴾ Allah ﴿they would both be corrupted.﴾ Do you not see that if you said, "My people did not come to me except Zayd" as a substitute, the meaning would be "Zayd alone came to me." It has been said: substitution is prohibited because what precedes it is affirmative, and the accusative (naṣb) on the basis of exception is also impermissible for two reasons. The first is that it is corrupt in meaning: if you say, "If the people had come to me except Zayd, I would have killed them," its meaning is that killing was prevented because Zayd was with the people. So if it were put in the accusative in the verse, the meaning would be that the corruption of the heavens and the earth was prevented because Allah existed alongside the gods, and in that is an affirmation of a god with Allah. But if it is put in the nominative as an attribute, such a thing does not follow, because the meaning is: "If there were in them something other than Allah, they would both be corrupted." The second reason is that (gods) here is indefinite, and a plural that is indefinite is not taken as the subject of an exception according to a group of the verifiers, because it has no generality such that what is excepted would be included in it were it not for the exception. End of quotation.

Abu al-Abbas al-Mubarrad permitted that (illa Allah) be a substitute, because what follows (law) is not affirmative in meaning, and the substitute in non-affirmative speech is better than the attribute. We have discussed this question at length in the explanation of al-Tashil (Sharh al-Tashil).

Al-Ustadh Abu Ali al-Shalawbin said, in the question of Sibawayh: "If there were with us a man except Zayd, we would have been overcome," the meaning is: "If there were with us a man in place of Zayd, we would have been overcome," so (illa) here has the meaning of (ghayr) (other than), which is the sense of the (illa) meaning "in place of."

Our shaykh, al-Ustadh Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Sa'igh, said: In my view the meaning is not sound unless (illa) has the sense of (ghayr) (other than), and the substitute is intended by it, meaning: ﴿If there were in them gods﴾ one single replacement, that is the substitute for the One who is Allah, ﴿they would both be corrupted.﴾ This is the meaning Sibawayh intended in the question he brought as a preliminary. End of quotation.

When He established the proof of His oneness and His singularity in divinity, He declared Himself free of what the people of ignorance attributed to Him, by His saying: ﴿Glory be to Allah.﴾ Then He described Himself as the Owner of this great creation, whose entire world is contained within it. Then He described Himself with perfection of power and the ultimate of wisdom, saying: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does,﴾ since He may do in His dominion whatever He wills, and His action is at the highest degree of wisdom, so there is no objection to Him and no challenge. Since it is the custom of kings that they are not questioned about what issues from their actions, even though error is possible in them, the King of kings is more worthy of not being questioned about this, given our knowledge that nothing issues from Him except what wisdom requires, free of defect and of being called to account. And the phrase ﴿what He does﴾ came because the act (fi'l) comprises the attributes of actions and encompasses all that issues from Him: creation, provision, benefit, harm, and other things. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿He is not questioned﴾ is generality across times. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, in the Hereafter, ﴿He is not questioned﴾ about His judgment concerning His servants, ﴿but they will be questioned﴾ about their deeds. Ibn Bahr said: He is not called to account, but they will be called to account. It has been said: He is not held responsible, but they will be held responsible. End of quotation.

﴿But they will be questioned﴾, because they are owned, enslaved servants, and error frequently proceeds from them, so they deserve to be told, "Why did you do such-and-such?"

Al-Hasan recited (la yusalu) and (yusalun) with a fatha on the sin (sin), transferring the vowel of the hamza to the sin and deleting the hamza.

Then the Exalted One repeated His denial and rebuke against them, saying: ﴿Or have they taken gods besides Him?﴾ as an expression of horror at their condition and of magnifying their disbelief. He added in this rebuke the phrase ﴿besides Him,﴾ as if He rebuked them for intending disbelief in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Then He called them to bring proof for what they had taken. But there is no proof that stands for Allah having a partner, neither from the side of reason nor from the side of transmitted revelation. Rather, the earlier books of Allah bear witness to His transcendence above partners and equals, as in the revelation I have brought you: ﴿This is the reminder of those with me,﴾ that is, an admonition for those who are with me, who are his community, and ﴿the reminder of those before me,﴾ who are the nations of the prophets. So "reminder" here means the divine books. It is also possible that (this) refers to the Qur'an, and the meaning in it is the reminder of the first and the last. The reminder of the last is by the call and the explanation of the law to them, and the reminder of the first is by relating their stories and the mention of the unseen matters concerning them.

According to this, the meaning is the presentation of the Qur'an as a proof, that is: ﴿Bring your proof,﴾ for this is my proof in that matter, and it is evident.

The majority recited (dhikru) with the genitive construction to (man) in both places, by the annexation of the verbal noun to its object, as in His saying: ﴿with your asking of His ewe﴾ [Sad: 24].

And it was also read with tanwin on (dhikr) in both places, with (man) as a direct object in the accusative, governed by the (dhikr), as in His saying: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger an orphan﴾ [al-Balad: 14]. Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Talhah read (dhikrun) with tanwin in both places and with a kasra on the mim of (min) in both places. The meaning of (ma'i) here is "with me" (indi, "in my presence"), and the meaning is: "This is a reminder from [min] me" and "[min qablí]," that is, "I remind you with this Qur'an that is with me, just as the prophets before me reminded their communities." The entry of (min) on (ma'a) is rare, but it is a noun that denotes companionship and association, treated as an adverb of place, so (min) entered upon it just as it entered upon (qabl), (ba'd) and (inda). Abu Hatim criticized this reading because (min) enters upon (ma'a), and he saw no justification for it. From Talhah: (dhikrun) with tanwin, (ma'iya) without (man); and (dhikrun) with tanwin, (qabli) without (man). A group read (wa-dhikri man) with the genitive construction, and (dhikrin) with tanwin, (min qabli) with a kasra on the mim of (min). The majority read (al-haqqa) in the accusative, and the apparent sense of its accusative is that it is the direct object, so (fa-hum la ya'lamuna) means: the root of their evil and corruption is ignorance and the failure to distinguish between truth and falsehood, and for this reason they turned away from it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that the accusative is, in meaning, an emphasis on the content of the preceding sentence, as when you say: 'This is the servant of Allah, the truth, not the falsehood,' thus emphasizing the attribution of the absence of knowledge to them. The apparent sense is that turning away is a consequence of the absence of knowledge: since they lost the ability to distinguish between truth and falsehood, they turned away from the truth." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Then Exalted God judged them, saying that ﴿most of them do not know the truth﴾ because of their turning away from it. The meaning is not ﴿so they are turning away﴾ because they do not know; rather the meaning is ﴿so they are turning away﴾, and therefore ﴿they do not know the truth﴾." Al-Hasan, Humayd and Ibn Muhaysin read (al-haqqu) in the nominative. The author of al-Lawami' said: it is a beginning (mubtada') with an implied predicate (khabar), or a predicate (khabar) with an implied subject (mubtada') preceding it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This statement is (al-haqqu), and the pause on this reading is at (la ya'lamuna)."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It was also read (al-haqqu) in the nominative, placing the emphasis between the cause and the effect, and the meaning is that their turning away, caused by their ignorance, is the truth and not the falsehood." End of quotation.

When He had mentioned their lack of knowledge of the truth and their turning away, He informed that He had not sent ﴿any messenger﴾ except that he came confirming the Oneness of Allah, affirming His singularity in divinity and the command to worship Him. Since ﴿any messenger﴾ is general in both wording and meaning, it was made singular in wording in His saying ﴿except that it is revealed to him﴾, then made plural in meaning in His saying (fa-'budun), and the construction did not come as (fa-'budni). It is possible that the command is addressed to him and to his community. This belief in the Oneness of Allah is one on which the prophets did not differ; disagreement arose only over certain legal rulings.

The two Akhawan (Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, or the two brothers), al-A'mash, Talhah, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Qutha'i, Ibn Ghazwan from Ayyub, Khalaf, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn 'Isa and Ibn Jarir read (nuhi) with a nun, while the rest of the seven read it with a ya' and a fatha on the ha'; and there are differing reports from 'Asim.

Then Exalted God declared Himself free of what they attributed to Him of offspring. It is said that this was revealed concerning Khuza'ah, when they said: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." The Christians said something similar about 'Isa, and the Jews about 'Uzayr. Then Exalted God turned away from attributing offspring to Himself and said: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾. This phrase includes the angels, 'Uzayr and the Messiah. It appears from al-Zamakhshari's statement that it is restricted to the angels. He said: "It was revealed concerning Khuza'ah, when they said: 'The angels are the daughters of Allah.' He declared His essence free of that, then informed about them that they are (servants), and servitude is incompatible with begetting, except that they are (honored), brought near to Me, preferred over the rest of the servants because of the states and attributes they have that others do not. That is what deceived those among them who claimed that they are My children. Exalted am I above that with a great exaltation." End of quotation.

'Ikrimah read (mukarramun) with a shaddah, while the majority read it with no shaddah. He read ﴿they do not precede Him﴾ with a kasra on the ba'. It is also read with a damma: from (sabaqani fa-sabaqtuhu, asbiquhu), and the meaning is that they follow His word and do not say anything until He says it: so their word does not precede His word. The (al-) in (bil-qawl) took the place of a pronoun, according to the view of the Kufans, meaning "by their word." Likewise al-Zamakhshari said: "The intended meaning of their word, so the 'lam' has replaced the genitive construction or the pronoun is omitted, meaning 'by the word from them,' and that is according to the view of the Basrans."

﴿And they act by His command﴾: just as their speech follows His speech, so their action is based on His command; they do no act at all unless they have been commanded to do it. This is an expression of their deep devotion to obedience and their compliance with His command.

Then Exalted God informed that He ﴿knows what is before them﴾, that is, what has preceded of their deeds and words, and the events for which they are a cause, and ﴿what is behind them﴾, and His knowledge of that serves as a cause for their obedience, because when they know that He is the Knower of all knowable things, the outward and inward things of them, that becomes a motive for them to humble themselves completely and to persist in worship. Ibn 'Abbas said: "(He knows) what they have sent ahead and what they have left behind of their deeds." 'Ammar ibn Yasir said something similar, saying: "what they have done and what they have not yet done." It is said: ﴿what is before them﴾ is the Hereafter, and ﴿what is behind them﴾ is this world; it is also said the reverse. It is said: (He knows) what was before He created them and what was after their creation.

Since they were subdued under His command and dominion, and He encompasses them, they did not dare to intercede except for one whom Allah approves and qualifies for intercession, for increase in reward and glorification. Then, despite that, ﴿they are fearful of His awe﴾, anticipating and wary, not feeling safe from the plotting of Allah. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿for whom He approves﴾ is one who says: "There is no god but Allah," and their intercession is seeking forgiveness. Mujahid said: "for whom Allah has approved that he be interceded for." It is also said: their intercession is on the Day of Resurrection, and it is authentically reported that they intercede in this world and the Hereafter.

After describing their honor before Him, praising them and attributing to them those noble deeds, He suddenly turned to a severe warning and threatened with the punishment of Hell whoever among them claimed that he is a god. This is by way of supposition and illustration, while He knows it will not happen, like His saying: ﴿And if they had associated others with Him, what they used to do would have been nullified for them﴾ [al-An'am: 88]. By this He intended to make the matter of associating partners with Allah appear monstrous and to magnify the status of Oneness. The majority read ﴿We recompense him﴾ with a fatha on the nun. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Muqri read it with a damma, meaning (nujzi'uhu), with a hamzah, from (ajza'ani kadha, kafani), then he eased the hamzah so it became a ya'. "Thus," that is, like this recompense, ﴿We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, who are the disbelievers and those who place things other than in their proper place. The conditional particle applies to both the possible and the impossible, as in His saying: ﴿If you associate [others with Him]﴾ [az-Zumar: 65].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 21–29 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth, which can raise the dead?﴾ ﴿Had there been in them (the heavens and the earth) gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted. Glory be to Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned.﴾ ﴿Or have they taken gods besides Him? Say: "Bring your proof. This is the reminder of those with me and the reminder of those before me." But most of them do not know the truth, so they turn away.﴾ ﴿We did not send any messenger before you except that We revealed to him: there is no god but Me, so worship Me.﴾ ﴿And they say: "The Most Merciful has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honoured servants.﴾ ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command.﴾ ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they do not intercede except for those whom He approves, and they are fearful of His awe.﴾ ﴿Whoever among them says, "I am a god besides Him," We will repay him with Hell. Thus do We repay the wrongdoers.﴾.

(p-304) When the Exalted One mentioned the proofs of His oneness, and that all who are in the heavens and the earth belong to Him, and that the honoured angels are in His service, never slackening in His glorification and worship, He returned to what preceded: the rebuke of the polytheists, their censure, and the ridicule of their intellects. Here the particle (am) (or) is disjunctive (munqati'a), and it is to be read as (bal) (rather) together with the interrogative hamza (alif of question). It therefore carries a turning away (idrab) and a shift from one statement to another, and an interrogation whose meaning is wonder and denial. The sense is: ﴿they have taken gods from the earth﴾ that are characterised by giving life and having power over it, and over causing death. That is, they have not taken gods with this attribute; rather, they have taken gods that are lifeless matter, not characterised by power over anything, so they are not gods, because it is an attribute of a god to have power to give life and to cause death.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "How did He deny them taking gods that raise the dead, when they did not claim that for their gods, and they were furthest from this claim? For, while acknowledging that Allah is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, and that He is capable of all things, and of the first creation, they denied resurrection. And it was among them an impossibility, beyond the power of the Capable. So how could they claim it for lifeless matter that is not described as having power?" I say: The matter is as you have mentioned, but by their claim of divinity it is necessary for them to claim for those gods the power of creating, because only one who has power over every thing deserves this name, and creating is among the things that can be done. In this there is a kind of mockery of them, rebuke, and ascription of ignorance, and an indication that what they deemed far-fetched from Allah is not to be deemed far-fetched, because when divinity is valid, the power to originate and to restore is valid with it. As for His saying (from the earth), it is like your saying, "So-and-so is from Mecca or from Medina," meaning a Meccan or a Medinan. The meaning of attributing them to the earth is the announcement that they are the idols worshipped on earth, not that gods are of earthly or heavenly kinds. Of this is the hadith of the slave-girl to whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "Where is your Lord?" She pointed to the sky. He said, "She is a believer," because he understood from her that her intention was the negation of earthly gods, which are the idols, not the affirmation of the sky as a place for Allah, the Exalted.

It is also permissible that what is meant is gods of the kind of the earth, because they are either carved from some stones or made from some of the earth's substances.

If you say, "There must be a point in His saying (they)," I say: the point in it is conveying the meaning of exclusivity, as if it were said: "Or have they taken gods which are not able to give life except they alone?" End of quotation.

Here (they took) (ittakhadhu) may mean "they made and fashioned," and (from the earth) is connected to (they took). It may also mean "they made the gods into idols from the earth," as in His saying: ﴿Do you take idols as gods?﴾ [al-An'am: 74] and His saying: ﴿And Allah took Abraham as a close friend﴾ [al-Nisa': 125], in which there is the sense of choosing and selecting.

The majority of readers recited (yunshiruna), the present tense of (anshara), meaning "they give life." Qutrub said it means "they create," as in His saying: ﴿Is one who creates like one who does not create?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17]. Al-Hasan and Mujahid recited (yanshuruna), the present tense of (nashara). These are two dialects: nashara and anshara are both transitive, and nashara also comes intransitive. You say: "Allah revived the dead, so they lived again" (anshara Allahu al-mawta fa-nashharu), meaning they came to life.

The pronoun in (fihima) (in them) refers to the heavens and the earth, and the two together are a metonymy for the world. (Illa) (other than) is an attribute of (gods), meaning: gods other than Allah. That (illa) may be described by an attribute is well known in the Arabic language. Of this is what Sibawayh, may God have mercy on him, recited:

"Every brother will be parted from by his brother, by the life of your father, except the two Farqads."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "What prevented you from the nominative on the basis of substitution (badal)?" I say: because (law) (if) is like (inna) (indeed) in that the speech that follows it is affirmative, and substitution is only permissible in non-affirmative speech, as in His saying: ﴿None of you shall look back, except your wife﴾ [Hud: 81]. That is because the most general of the general can be negated but cannot be affirmed. The meaning is: if there were gods besides the One who originates them, managing them and administering their affairs, ﴿they would both be corrupted.﴾ This indicates two matters. The first: it is necessary that there be only one manager of them. The second: that one must be none other than Him alone, as in His saying: (except Allah).

If you say, "Why were both matters necessary?" I say: because we know that the subjects are corrupted by the management of two kings, due to what arises between them of contention, mutual repudiation and disagreement.

It is related of Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, when he killed Amr ibn Sa'id al-Ashdaq: "By Allah, he was dearer to me than the blood of my own two eyes, but two stallions do not gather in one herd (shawl)," and this is clear. As for the method of mutual prevention (tamani'), the theologians have much dispute and argument about it, and because these acts require that essence distinguished by those attributes in order to be established and stable.

Ibn Atiyya said: That is because each would seek to overcome the other and would take away what was created. The summary of this: if we suppose two gods in whom there is disagreement over moving a body or not moving it, it is impossible that both wills be executed, and impossible that neither be executed. If one is executed, then the other is powerless, and such a one is not a god. The possibility of disagreement between them is like its occurrence. There is also another consideration: every part that comes out from non-existence into existence cannot be subject to two powers. If one of them is the power that brings it into existence, then in the other there is an excess with no meaning concerning that part. The consideration continues in this way, part after part.

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: If we suppose two existents that are necessary in existence by their essence, then they must share in existence, and each must be distinguished from the other by its own particularity. What makes them share is other than what makes them distinct. So each shares with the other, and every composite is in need of another, being possible in its essence. Therefore, the necessarily existent is only one, and everything other than it is originated. This can be taken as an explanation of this verse, because when we have shown that from supposing two necessary existents it follows that neither of them is necessary, and if the necessary does not exist, none of these possible things exists. Then corruption necessarily follows throughout the whole world.

Abu al-Baqa' said: It is not permissible for it to be a substitute (badal), because the meaning becomes: ﴿If there were in them﴾ Allah ﴿they would both be corrupted.﴾ Do you not see that if you said, "My people did not come to me except Zayd" as a substitute, the meaning would be "Zayd alone came to me." It has been said: substitution is prohibited because what precedes it is affirmative, and the accusative (naṣb) on the basis of exception is also impermissible for two reasons. The first is that it is corrupt in meaning: if you say, "If the people had come to me except Zayd, I would have killed them," its meaning is that killing was prevented because Zayd was with the people. So if it were put in the accusative in the verse, the meaning would be that the corruption of the heavens and the earth was prevented because Allah existed alongside the gods, and in that is an affirmation of a god with Allah. But if it is put in the nominative as an attribute, such a thing does not follow, because the meaning is: "If there were in them something other than Allah, they would both be corrupted." The second reason is that (gods) here is indefinite, and a plural that is indefinite is not taken as the subject of an exception according to a group of the verifiers, because it has no generality such that what is excepted would be included in it were it not for the exception. End of quotation.

Abu al-Abbas al-Mubarrad permitted that (illa Allah) be a substitute, because what follows (law) is not affirmative in meaning, and the substitute in non-affirmative speech is better than the attribute. We have discussed this question at length in the explanation of al-Tashil (Sharh al-Tashil).

Al-Ustadh Abu Ali al-Shalawbin said, in the question of Sibawayh: "If there were with us a man except Zayd, we would have been overcome," the meaning is: "If there were with us a man in place of Zayd, we would have been overcome," so (illa) here has the meaning of (ghayr) (other than), which is the sense of the (illa) meaning "in place of."

Our shaykh, al-Ustadh Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Sa'igh, said: In my view the meaning is not sound unless (illa) has the sense of (ghayr) (other than), and the substitute is intended by it, meaning: ﴿If there were in them gods﴾ one single replacement, that is the substitute for the One who is Allah, ﴿they would both be corrupted.﴾ This is the meaning Sibawayh intended in the question he brought as a preliminary. End of quotation.

When He established the proof of His oneness and His singularity in divinity, He declared Himself free of what the people of ignorance attributed to Him, by His saying: ﴿Glory be to Allah.﴾ Then He described Himself as the Owner of this great creation, whose entire world is contained within it. Then He described Himself with perfection of power and the ultimate of wisdom, saying: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does,﴾ since He may do in His dominion whatever He wills, and His action is at the highest degree of wisdom, so there is no objection to Him and no challenge. Since it is the custom of kings that they are not questioned about what issues from their actions, even though error is possible in them, the King of kings is more worthy of not being questioned about this, given our knowledge that nothing issues from Him except what wisdom requires, free of defect and of being called to account. And the phrase ﴿what He does﴾ came because the act (fi'l) comprises the attributes of actions and encompasses all that issues from Him: creation, provision, benefit, harm, and other things. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿He is not questioned﴾ is generality across times. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, in the Hereafter, ﴿He is not questioned﴾ about His judgment concerning His servants, ﴿but they will be questioned﴾ about their deeds. Ibn Bahr said: He is not called to account, but they will be called to account. It has been said: He is not held responsible, but they will be held responsible. End of quotation.

﴿But they will be questioned﴾, because they are owned, enslaved servants, and error frequently proceeds from them, so they deserve to be told, "Why did you do such-and-such?"

Al-Hasan recited (la yusalu) and (yusalun) with a fatha on the sin (sin), transferring the vowel of the hamza to the sin and deleting the hamza.
