If you say, "Why were both matters necessary?" I say: because we know that the subjects are corrupted by the management of two kings, due to what arises between them of contention, mutual repudiation and disagreement.

If one is executed, then the other is powerless, and such a one is not a god. The possibility of disagreement between them is like its occurrence. If one of them is the power that brings it into existence, then in the other there is an excess with no meaning concerning that part. The consideration continues in this way, part after part.

It has been said: substitution is prohibited because what precedes it is affirmative, and the accusative (naṣb) on the basis of exception is also impermissible for two reasons. The first is that it is corrupt in meaning: if you say, "If the people had come to me except Zayd, I would have killed them," its meaning is that killing was prevented because Zayd was with the people. So if it were put in the accusative in the verse, the meaning would be that the corruption of the heavens and the earth was prevented because Allah existed alongside the gods, and in that is an affirmation of a god with Allah. Abu al-Abbas al-Mubarrad permitted that (illa Allah) be a substitute, because what follows (law) is not affirmative in meaning, and the substitute in non-affirmative speech is better than the attribute. We have discussed this question at length in the explanation of al-Tashil (Sharh al-Tashil).

Al-Ustadh Abu Ali al-Shalawbin said, in the question of Sibawayh: "If there were with us a man except Zayd, we would have been overcome," the meaning is: "If there were with us a man in place of Zayd, we would have been overcome," so (illa) here has the meaning of (ghayr) (other than), which is the sense of the (illa) meaning "in place of."

Our shaykh, al-Ustadh Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Sa'igh, said: In my view the meaning is not sound unless (illa) has the sense of (ghayr) (other than), and the substitute is intended by it, meaning: ﴿If there were in them gods﴾ one single replacement, that is the substitute for the One who is Allah, ﴿they would both be corrupted.﴾ This is the meaning Sibawayh intended in the question he brought as a preliminary. End of quotation.

When He established the proof of His oneness and His singularity in divinity, He declared Himself free of what the people of ignorance attributed to Him, by His saying: ﴿Glory be to Allah.﴾ Then He described Himself as the Owner of this great creation, whose entire world is contained within it. Then He described Himself with perfection of power and the ultimate of wisdom, saying: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does,﴾ since He may do in His dominion whatever He wills, and His action is at the highest degree of wisdom, so there is no objection to Him and no challenge. Since it is the custom of kings that they are not questioned about what issues from their actions, even though error is possible in them, the King of kings is more worthy of not being questioned about this, given our knowledge that nothing issues from Him except what wisdom requires, free of defect and of being called to account. And the phrase ﴿what He does﴾ came because the act (fi'l) comprises the attributes of actions and encompasses all that issues from Him: creation, provision, benefit, harm, and other things. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿He is not questioned﴾ is generality across times. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, in the Hereafter, ﴿He is not questioned﴾ about His judgment concerning His servants, ﴿but they will be questioned﴾ about their deeds. Ibn Bahr said: He is not called to account, but they will be called to account. It has been said: He is not held responsible, but they will be held responsible. End of quotation.

﴿But they will be questioned﴾, because they are owned, enslaved servants, and error frequently proceeds from them, so they deserve to be told, "Why did you do such-and-such?"

Al-Hasan recited (la yusalu) and (yusalun) with a fatha on the sin (sin), transferring the vowel of the hamza to the sin and deleting the hamza.

Then the Exalted One repeated His denial and rebuke against them, saying: ﴿Or have they taken gods besides Him?﴾ as an expression of horror at their condition and of magnifying their disbelief. He added in this rebuke the phrase ﴿besides Him,﴾ as if He rebuked them for intending disbelief in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Then He called them to bring proof for what they had taken. But there is no proof that stands for Allah having a partner, neither from the side of reason nor from the side of transmitted revelation. Rather, the earlier books of Allah bear witness to His transcendence above partners and equals, as in the revelation I have brought you: ﴿This is the reminder of those with me,﴾ that is, an admonition for those who are with me, who are his community, and ﴿the reminder of those before me,﴾ who are the nations of the prophets. So "reminder" here means the divine books. It is also possible that (this) refers to the Qur'an, and the meaning in it is the reminder of the first and the last. The reminder of the last is by the call and the explanation of the law to them, and the reminder of the first is by relating their stories and the mention of the unseen matters concerning them.

According to this, the meaning is the presentation of the Qur'an as a proof, that is: ﴿Bring your proof,﴾ for this is my proof in that matter, and it is evident.

The majority recited (dhikru) with the genitive construction to (man) in both places, by the annexation of the verbal noun to its object, as in His saying: ﴿with your asking of His ewe﴾ [Sad: 24].

And it was also read with tanwin on (dhikr) in both places, with (man) as a direct object in the accusative, governed by the (dhikr), as in His saying: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger an orphan﴾ [al-Balad: 14]. Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Talhah read (dhikrun) with tanwin in both places and with a kasra on the mim of (min) in both places. The meaning of (ma'i) here is "with me" (indi, "in my presence"), and the meaning is: "This is a reminder from [min] me" and "[min qablí]," that is, "I remind you with this Qur'an that is with me, just as the prophets before me reminded their communities." The entry of (min) on (ma'a) is rare, but it is a noun that denotes companionship and association, treated as an adverb of place, so (min) entered upon it just as it entered upon (qabl), (ba'd) and (inda). Abu Hatim criticized this reading because (min) enters upon (ma'a), and he saw no justification for it. From Talhah: (dhikrun) with tanwin, (ma'iya) without (man); and (dhikrun) with tanwin, (qabli) without (man). A group read (wa-dhikri man) with the genitive construction, and (dhikrin) with tanwin, (min qabli) with a kasra on the mim of (min). The majority read (al-haqqa) in the accusative, and the apparent sense of its accusative is that it is the direct object, so (fa-hum la ya'lamuna) means: the root of their evil and corruption is ignorance and the failure to distinguish between truth and falsehood, and for this reason they turned away from it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that the accusative is, in meaning, an emphasis on the content of the preceding sentence, as when you say: 'This is the servant of Allah, the truth, not the falsehood,' thus emphasizing the attribution of the absence of knowledge to them. The apparent sense is that turning away is a consequence of the absence of knowledge: since they lost the ability to distinguish between truth and falsehood, they turned away from the truth." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Then Exalted God judged them, saying that ﴿most of them do not know the truth﴾ because of their turning away from it. The meaning is not ﴿so they are turning away﴾ because they do not know; rather the meaning is ﴿so they are turning away﴾, and therefore ﴿they do not know the truth﴾." Al-Hasan, Humayd and Ibn Muhaysin read (al-haqqu) in the nominative. The author of al-Lawami' said: it is a beginning (mubtada') with an implied predicate (khabar), or a predicate (khabar) with an implied subject (mubtada') preceding it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This statement is (al-haqqu), and the pause on this reading is at (la ya'lamuna)."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It was also read (al-haqqu) in the nominative, placing the emphasis between the cause and the effect, and the meaning is that their turning away, caused by their ignorance, is the truth and not the falsehood." End of quotation.

When He had mentioned their lack of knowledge of the truth and their turning away, He informed that He had not sent ﴿any messenger﴾ except that he came confirming the Oneness of Allah, affirming His singularity in divinity and the command to worship Him. Since ﴿any messenger﴾ is general in both wording and meaning, it was made singular in wording in His saying ﴿except that it is revealed to him﴾, then made plural in meaning in His saying (fa-'budun), and the construction did not come as (fa-'budni). It is possible that the command is addressed to him and to his community. This belief in the Oneness of Allah is one on which the prophets did not differ; disagreement arose only over certain legal rulings.

The two Akhawan (Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, or the two brothers), al-A'mash, Talhah, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Qutha'i, Ibn Ghazwan from Ayyub, Khalaf, Ibn Sa'dan, Ibn 'Isa and Ibn Jarir read (nuhi) with a nun, while the rest of the seven read it with a ya' and a fatha on the ha'; and there are differing reports from 'Asim.

Then Exalted God declared Himself free of what they attributed to Him of offspring. It is said that this was revealed concerning Khuza'ah, when they said: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." The Christians said something similar about 'Isa, and the Jews about 'Uzayr. Then Exalted God turned away from attributing offspring to Himself and said: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾. This phrase includes the angels, 'Uzayr and the Messiah. It appears from al-Zamakhshari's statement that it is restricted to the angels. He said: "It was revealed concerning Khuza'ah, when they said: 'The angels are the daughters of Allah.' He declared His essence free of that, then informed about them that they are (servants), and servitude is incompatible with begetting, except that they are (honored), brought near to Me, preferred over the rest of the servants because of the states and attributes they have that others do not. That is what deceived those among them who claimed that they are My children. Exalted am I above that with a great exaltation." End of quotation.

'Ikrimah read (mukarramun) with a shaddah, while the majority read it with no shaddah. He read ﴿they do not precede Him﴾ with a kasra on the ba'. It is also read with a damma: from (sabaqani fa-sabaqtuhu, asbiquhu), and the meaning is that they follow His word and do not say anything until He says it: so their word does not precede His word. The (al-) in (bil-qawl) took the place of a pronoun, according to the view of the Kufans, meaning "by their word." Likewise al-Zamakhshari said: "The intended meaning of their word, so the 'lam' has replaced the genitive construction or the pronoun is omitted, meaning 'by the word from them,' and that is according to the view of the Basrans."

﴿And they act by His command﴾: just as their speech follows His speech, so their action is based on His command; they do no act at all unless they have been commanded to do it. This is an expression of their deep devotion to obedience and their compliance with His command.

Then Exalted God informed that He ﴿knows what is before them﴾, that is, what has preceded of their deeds and words, and the events for which they are a cause, and ﴿what is behind them﴾, and His knowledge of that serves as a cause for their obedience, because when they know that He is the Knower of all knowable things, the outward and inward things of them, that becomes a motive for them to humble themselves completely and to persist in worship. Ibn 'Abbas said: "(He knows) what they have sent ahead and what they have left behind of their deeds." 'Ammar ibn Yasir said something similar, saying: "what they have done and what they have not yet done." It is said: ﴿what is before them﴾ is the Hereafter, and ﴿what is behind them﴾ is this world; it is also said the reverse. It is said: (He knows) what was before He created them and what was after their creation.

Since they were subdued under His command and dominion, and He encompasses them, they did not dare to intercede except for one whom Allah approves and qualifies for intercession, for increase in reward and glorification. Then, despite that, ﴿they are fearful of His awe﴾, anticipating and wary, not feeling safe from the plotting of Allah. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿for whom He approves﴾ is one who says: "There is no god but Allah," and their intercession is seeking forgiveness. Mujahid said: "for whom Allah has approved that he be interceded for." It is also said: their intercession is on the Day of Resurrection, and it is authentically reported that they intercede in this world and the Hereafter.

After describing their honor before Him, praising them and attributing to them those noble deeds, He suddenly turned to a severe warning and threatened with the punishment of Hell whoever among them claimed that he is a god. This is by way of supposition and illustration, while He knows it will not happen, like His saying: ﴿And if they had associated others with Him, what they used to do would have been nullified for them﴾ [al-An'am: 88]. By this He intended to make the matter of associating partners with Allah appear monstrous and to magnify the status of Oneness. The majority read ﴿We recompense him﴾ with a fatha on the nun. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Muqri read it with a damma, meaning (nujzi'uhu), with a hamzah, from (ajza'ani kadha, kafani), then he eased the hamzah so it became a ya'. "Thus," that is, like this recompense, ﴿We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, who are the disbelievers and those who place things other than in their proper place. The conditional particle applies to both the possible and the impossible, as in His saying: ﴿If you associate [others with Him]﴾ [az-Zumar: 65].

(p-308) Have those who disbelieve not considered that the heavens and the earth were a single mass, and We parted them, and We made from water every living thing? Will they not believe? ﴿Will they not believe?﴾ And We placed firm mountains in the earth lest it shake with them, and We made in it broad passages as paths, that they may be guided. And We made the sky a protected canopy, yet they turn away from its signs. He it is who created the night and the day, and the sun and the moon, each swimming in an orbit. We did not grant immortality to any human before you; so if you die, will they be immortal? Every soul will taste death. We test you with evil and with good as a trial, and to Us you will be returned. [al-Anbiya: 35]

This is a interrogative of rebuke addressed to those who claimed other gods alongside God, and it is a proof of His transcendence above any partner, and a confirmation of the proofs of monotheism mentioned earlier, and a refutation of the idol-worshippers: the God who is able to create these creatures and to dispose of them in such wondrous ways, how could it be reasonable to turn away from worshipping Him to worshipping a stone that neither harms nor benefits? The seeing here is seeing of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb). It has also been said that it is seeing of the eye, and this depends on the difference of opinion concerning the rutq (joined, closed state) and the fatq (parting). Ibn Kathir, Humayd and Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿alam yara﴾ without the conjunctive waw, whereas the majority read ﴿awa-lam﴾ with the waw.

(kanata) — al-Zajjaj said: "al-samawat" is a plural, but what is intended is the singular; for this reason He said ﴿kanata ratqan﴾, since He meant the heaven and the earth. And from this (comes the verse) that God holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease; He made the heavens one kind and the earths one kind, so He spoke of the two kinds as one speaks of two things, as you say: "I reconciled between the people," and "two black sheep passed by us belonging to two flocks of sheep." Al-Hawfi said: He said ﴿kanata ratqan﴾ while "al-samawat" is plural, because He meant the two categories. From this is the statement of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur:

"Indeed death and calamities, both of them, watch my household, one who fulfils the sacred things."

Because he meant the two kinds. Abu al-Baqa' said: the pronoun refers to the two genera. Al-Zamakhshari said: He said (kanata) rather than (kunna) because what is meant is the group of the heavens and the group of the earth. Similar to this is the saying: "two black she-camels (laqahan sawdawan)," if they mean two groups; the hidden pronoun is treated as the apparent noun is treated. Ibn 'Atiyya said: He said (kanata) in respect of their being two kinds. Similar to this is the statement of 'Amr ibn Shuyaym:

"Did it not grieve you that the mountains of Qays and Taghlib have separated in severance?"

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, 'Ata', al-Dahhak and Qatada said: they were one single thing, then God separated them by the air. Ka'b said: God created the heavens and the earth one upon the other, then He created a wind in their midst and by it parted them, and He made the heavens seven and the earths seven. Mujahid, al-Suddi and Abu Salih said: the heavens and the earth were joined together as one layer, then He parted them and made them seven heavens, and likewise the earths were closed together as one layer, then He parted them and made them seven. A group said: the heavens and the earth were closed by darkness, and God parted them by light. Another group said: the sky before rain was closed, and the earth before vegetation was closed; ﴿fa-fataqnahuma﴾ means by rain and vegetation, as He said: ﴿By the sky of the returning rain﴾ [al-Tariq: 11] ﴿and by the earth of the splitting open﴾ [al-Tariq: 12]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is a good view which combines the lesson, the enumeration of the blessing, and the evident proof, and it is consistent with His saying: ﴿and We made from water every living thing﴾, that is, from the water which the parting brought into existence. End of quotation.

On these two views, the seeing is seeing of the eye; and according to what precedes them, it is seeing of the heart. Their being addressed with this (question) comes because it is (p-309) revealed in the Qur'an, which is itself a miracle, so it takes the place of what is seen and witnessed; and because the joining of the earth and the sky and their separation are both possible in reason, so the separation rather than the joining needs a specifier, and that is God, glorified be He.

The majority read ﴿ratqan﴾ with the tā' unvocalized; it is a verbal noun (masdar) used as a descriptive, like zawr and 'adl, so it occurs as the predicate of the dual. Al-Hasan, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Abu Haywa and 'Isa read ﴿ratqan﴾ with a fatha on the tā'; it is the name of the thing closed, like qabd and naqd, so its analogy would be that it is built (in the form of the noun) to match the predicate with the subject. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is on the assumption of an omitted noun qualified, meaning (kanata) "a thing" ﴿ratqan﴾. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: In this class, most often the moving form is a noun in the sense of the passive participle and the still (sukun) form is a verbal noun; or both may be verbal nouns, but the moving form is more likely to have the sense of the passive participle; yet here the better option is that both are verbal nouns, and each of them is placed in the position of the two passive forms. Do you not see that He said ﴿kanata ratqan﴾? If you made one of them a noun, it would have to be dualised; but since He said ﴿ratqan﴾, it is in both cases like rajul 'adl, rajulayn 'adl, and qawm 'adl. End of quotation.

(wa-ja'alna) If it is transitive to one object, it means "and We created from water" every animal, that is, its material is the seminal fluid; said by Qutrub and a group. Or, since its substance is drinkable water, and since it needs it and cannot do without it, it is made to be created from it, like His saying: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ [al-Anbiya: 37]; said by al-Kalbi and others. On this view, life is literal and "every thing" is general but specified, since the angels and the jinn are excluded, for they were not created from a drop of fluid and do not need water. Qatada said: that is, We created every growing thing from water, so plants and minerals are included; and on this view life in them is metaphorical, or He used "life" for the common quality shared between them and animals, which is growth; and on this view too it is general but specified. If ﴿ja'alna﴾ is transitive to two objects, the meaning is: We made ﴿every living thing﴾ by means of something from water, which it cannot do without. The majority read (ḥayy) in the genitive as an adjective of "shay'" (thing). Humayd read ḥayyan in the accusative as a second object of ja'alna, and the prepositional phrase is superfluous (laghw), that is, it is not the second object of (ja'alna).

﴿Will they not believe?﴾ This is an interrogative of denial with the sense of wonder at the weakness of their minds. The meaning is: will they not reflect upon these proofs, act according to their requirements, and abandon the way of associating partners with God? Belief is attributed here to its cause. This verse brings together two of the proofs of monotheism, which are from the heavenly and the earthly signs.

Then He mentions another proof from the earthly signs, saying: ﴿And We placed firm mountains in the earth lest it shake with them﴾; the explanation of a parallel of this sentence has already been given in Surat al-Nahl. ﴿And We made in it broad passages as paths﴾; this is a fourth proof from the earthly signs. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (fīhā) refers to the earth; it has also been said that it refers to the firm mountains. Here (fijājan) is placed before (subulan), whereas in Surat Nuh it is ﴿that you may follow from them roads, broad paths﴾ [Nuh: 20]. Al-Zamakhshari said: (fijājan) is an adjective, but it has been made a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), as in his saying:

"For Mayya, a desolate abode."

He means that it is a circumstance of (subul), which is indefinite; had (fijājan) been placed after it, it would have been an adjective as in that verse, but since it came first it is in the accusative as a circumstance. He said: If you ask: what is the difference between them in terms of meaning? I say: there are two aspects. One is the information that He made in it wide roads; the other is that when He created it, He created it with that attribute, so it is an explanation of what was left ambiguous there. End of quotation. By ambiguity he means that a description does not require that the described thing be characterised by it at the time of the report about it, although most often it is characterised by it at the time of the report; do you not see that one says: "I passed by a savage slayer of Hamza," where at the time of passing the slaying of Hamza was not a present attribute of him? As for the circumstance, it is the state of what you report about at the time of reporting. ﴿So that they may be guided﴾ in their paths and their conduct.

Whatever is raised and elevated over something is called a canopy (saqf). Qatada said: a protection from decay and change over the length of time. It has been said: a protection from falling, since it holds itself up without a support or pillar. It has been said: a protection from polytheism and sins. Al-Farra' said: a protection from the devils by meteors. From Ibn 'Abbas: the Messenger of God ﷺ looked at the sky and said: "Indeed the sky is a raised canopy and a restrained wave, flowing as an arrow flows, guarded from the devils." If this ḥadīth is sound, it is an explicit text on the meaning of the verse.

(p-310) ﴿And they turn away from its signs﴾, that is, from what God placed in it of proofs and lessons: the sun, the moon, and the rest of the luminaries and their courses, their rising and setting according to a straight reckoning and a wondrous order, which indicate profound wisdom and overwhelming power. The majority read ﴿ 'an āyātihā ﴾ in the plural. Mujahid and Humayd read ʿan āyatihā in the singular; this may mean that He made the making, or the canopy, or the creating, that is, the creation of the sky, one single sign comprising all the signs; or it may mean by it the plural, and He made it a noun of the genus, and the abundance of signs in the sky indicates this. The meaning is: ﴿and they﴾ from taking heed of its signs ﴿turn away﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: They are aware of what reaches them from the sky of worldly benefits, such as being illuminated by its two moons, guidance by its stars, and the life of the earth and of animals through its rains; ﴿and they﴾ turn away from its being a clear sign of the Creator.

The tanwīn in (kullun) is a substitute (ʿiwaḍ) for the genitive noun that was omitted, and al-falak is a body that revolves in the course of a day and night. From Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi: al-falak is the sky. Most of the exegetes said: al-falak is a restrained wave beneath the sky in which the sun and moon flow. Qatada said: al-falak is a rotation between the sky and the earth that turns with the stars while the sky remains fixed. It has been said: al-falak is the pole upon which the stars revolve, and it is the north pole. It has been said: each of the wandering bodies has a falak, and the falak of the falaks moves them all in one motion from east to west. Al-Dahhak said: al-falak is not a body; it is only the orbit of these stars. The apparent view is that it is a body, and the difference mentioned above concerns it. The apparent view is that each swims in one falak. It has been said: each has a falak specific to it, as in the saying: "The governor clothed them with a robe," meaning he clothed each one. (yasbahūn) comes with the plural waw for rational beings. As for the plural: it has been said that there is an elided conjoined noun there, namely the stars, and that is why the pronoun came in the plural; had there not been an elided conjoined noun, it would have been (yasbahān) in the dual.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The pronoun refers to the sun and the moon, and what is meant by them is the class of risings, each day and night, which they made numerous because of the multiplicity of their risings; this is the reason for their being pluralised as "suns" and "moons"; otherwise the sun is one and the moon is one. End of quotation. What made this acceptable is that it came as the ending of a verse. As for its being the pronoun of rational beings when the construction would not be (yasbaḥna): al-Farra' said: Since swimming is one of the actions of human beings, what is ascribed to them (the sun and moon) came in the plural form for rational beings, as in His saying: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4]. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: According to the view of Abu 'Ali ibn Sina, the reason for this is that they, in his view, have intellect. End of quotation. This sentence may be a new report, with no place in the sentence; or its place is accusative as a circumstance of ﴿the sun and the moon﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2], because (the night and the day) are not described as flowing ﴿in an orbit﴾; so it is like your saying: "I saw Zayd and Hind unveiled." Swimming is floating. The apparent meaning is that the sun and the moon are the two that flow in the orbit, and that the orbit does not flow.

﴿And We did not grant﴾ the verse. It has been said: some Muslims said: "Muhammad will never die; he is immortal," so the Messenger denied that, and this verse was revealed. It has been said: the disbelievers of Mecca reproached him, saying: "He is a human who eats food and dies; how can his being sent as messenger be valid?" Al-Zamakhshari said: They expected that he would die, and they would gloat over his death; so God negated gloating from him by this, meaning: God decreed that no human be made immortal in this world; neither you nor they are but subject to death. If you die, will these remain? In the same sense is the statement of Imam al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him:

"Men wish that I die, and if I die, that is a path I am not the only one to walk."

**The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 30–34 (part 2 of 2)**

Abu Hayyan quotes the verse of the poet:

*"Say to the one who seeks the opposite of what has passed: 'Provide for yourself for another [life] like it, as if it were already [here].'"*

And the verse of the other poet:

*"Say to those who gloat over us: 'Wake up! The gloaters will meet what we have met.'"*

The fa' (الفاء) in ﴿أفَإنْ مِتَّ﴾ is the conjunctive fa' (فاءُ العَطْفِ). The interrogative hamza (هَمْزَةُ الِاسْتِفْهامِ) has been placed before it, because interrogation (الِاسْتِفْهامُ) has the front position in the sentence. It enters upon the conditional particle in (إنِ الشَّرْطِيَّةِ) (p. 311), and the clause after it is the response of the condition (جَوابٌ لِلشَّرْطِ). That clause is not the target of the interrogation (مَصَبَّ الِاسْتِفْهامِ), so the hamza does not enter directly upon it. The condition is inserted between the two, and its response is elided. This is the view of Sibawayh.

Yunus claimed that this clause is in fact the target of the interrogation, with the condition inserted between them and its response elided.

Ibn Atiyya said: "The hamza of interrogation enters, in meaning, upon the response of the condition." End of quotation.

This verse is evidence for the view of Sibawayh. If the matter were as Yunus claimed, the construction would have been ﴿أفَإنْ مِتَّ﴾ ﴿هُمُ الخالِدُونَ﴾ without the fa'. Both views are discussed in detail in the science of grammar (عِلْمُ النَّحْوِ).

(p-308) Have those who disbelieve not considered that the heavens and the earth were a single mass, and We parted them, and We made from water every living thing? Will they not believe? ﴿Will they not believe?﴾ And We placed firm mountains in the earth lest it shake with them, and We made in it broad passages as paths, that they may be guided. And We made the sky a protected canopy, yet they turn away from its signs. He it is who created the night and the day, and the sun and the moon, each swimming in an orbit. We did not grant immortality to any human before you; so if you die, will they be immortal? Every soul will taste death. We test you with evil and with good as a trial, and to Us you will be returned. [al-Anbiya: 35]

This is a interrogative of rebuke addressed to those who claimed other gods alongside God, and it is a proof of His transcendence above any partner, and a confirmation of the proofs of monotheism mentioned earlier, and a refutation of the idol-worshippers: the God who is able to create these creatures and to dispose of them in such wondrous ways, how could it be reasonable to turn away from worshipping Him to worshipping a stone that neither harms nor benefits? It has also been said that it is seeing of the eye, and this depends on the difference of opinion concerning the rutq (joined, closed state) and the fatq (parting). Ibn Kathir, Humayd and Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿alam yara﴾ without the conjunctive waw, whereas the majority read ﴿awa-lam﴾ with the waw.

(kanata) — al-Zajjaj said: "al-samawat" is a plural, but what is intended is the singular; for this reason He said ﴿kanata ratqan﴾, since He meant the heaven and the earth. And from this (comes the verse) that God holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease; He made the heavens one kind and the earths one kind, so He spoke of the two kinds as one speaks of two things, as you say: "I reconciled between the people," and "two black sheep passed by us belonging to two flocks of sheep." Al-Hawfi said: He said ﴿kanata ratqan﴾ while "al-samawat" is plural, because He meant the two categories. From this is the statement of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur:

"Indeed death and calamities, both of them, watch my household, one who fulfils the sacred things."

Because he meant the two kinds. Abu al-Baqa' said: the pronoun refers to the two genera. Al-Zamakhshari said: He said (kanata) rather than (kunna) because what is meant is the group of the heavens and the group of the earth. Similar to this is the saying: "two black she-camels (laqahan sawdawan)," if they mean two groups; the hidden pronoun is treated as the apparent noun is treated. Ibn 'Atiyya said: He said (kanata) in respect of their being two kinds. Similar to this is the statement of 'Amr ibn Shuyaym:

"Did it not grieve you that the mountains of Qays and Taghlib have separated in severance?"

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, 'Ata', al-Dahhak and Qatada said: they were one single thing, then God separated them by the air. Ka'b said: God created the heavens and the earth one upon the other, then He created a wind in their midst and by it parted them, and He made the heavens seven and the earths seven. Mujahid, al-Suddi and Abu Salih said: the heavens and the earth were joined together as one layer, then He parted them and made them seven heavens, and likewise the earths were closed together as one layer, then He parted them and made them seven. A group said: the heavens and the earth were closed by darkness, and God parted them by light. Another group said: the sky before rain was closed, and the earth before vegetation was closed; ﴿fa-fataqnahuma﴾ means by rain and vegetation, as He said: ﴿By the sky of the returning rain﴾ [al-Tariq: 11] ﴿and by the earth of the splitting open﴾ [al-Tariq: 12]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is a good view which combines the lesson, the enumeration of the blessing, and the evident proof, and it is consistent with His saying: ﴿and We made from water every living thing﴾, that is, from the water which the parting brought into existence. End of quotation.

On these two views, the seeing is seeing of the eye; and according to what precedes them, it is seeing of the heart. Their being addressed with this (question) comes because it is (p-309) revealed in the Qur'an, which is itself a miracle, so it takes the place of what is seen and witnessed; and because the joining of the earth and the sky and their separation are both possible in reason, so the separation rather than the joining needs a specifier, and that is God, glorified be He.

The majority read ﴿ratqan﴾ with the tā' unvocalized; it is a verbal noun (masdar) used as a descriptive, like zawr and 'adl, so it occurs as the predicate of the dual. Al-Hasan, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Abu Haywa and 'Isa read ﴿ratqan﴾ with a fatha on the tā'; it is the name of the thing closed, like qabd and naqd, so its analogy would be that it is built (in the form of the noun) to match the predicate with the subject. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is on the assumption of an omitted noun qualified, meaning (kanata) "a thing" ﴿ratqan﴾. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: In this class, most often the moving form is a noun in the sense of the passive participle and the still (sukun) form is a verbal noun; or both may be verbal nouns, but the moving form is more likely to have the sense of the passive participle; yet here the better option is that both are verbal nouns, and each of them is placed in the position of the two passive forms. Do you not see that He said ﴿kanata ratqan﴾? If you made one of them a noun, it would have to be dualised; but since He said ﴿ratqan﴾, it is in both cases like rajul 'adl, rajulayn 'adl, and qawm 'adl. End of quotation.

(wa-ja'alna) If it is transitive to one object, it means "and We created from water" every animal, that is, its material is the seminal fluid; said by Qutrub and a group. Or, since its substance is drinkable water, and since it needs it and cannot do without it, it is made to be created from it, like His saying: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ [al-Anbiya: 37]; said by al-Kalbi and others. On this view, life is literal and "every thing" is general but specified, since the angels and the jinn are excluded, for they were not created from a drop of fluid and do not need water. Qatada said: that is, We created every growing thing from water, so plants and minerals are included; and on this view life in them is metaphorical, or He used "life" for the common quality shared between them and animals, which is growth; and on this view too it is general but specified. If ﴿ja'alna﴾ is transitive to two objects, the meaning is: We made ﴿every living thing﴾ by means of something from water, which it cannot do without. The majority read (ḥayy) in the genitive as an adjective of "shay'" (thing). Humayd read ḥayyan in the accusative as a second object of ja'alna, and the prepositional phrase is superfluous (laghw), that is, it is not the second object of (ja'alna).

﴿Will they not believe?﴾ This is an interrogative of denial with the sense of wonder at the weakness of their minds. The meaning is: will they not reflect upon these proofs, act according to their requirements, and abandon the way of associating partners with God? Belief is attributed here to its cause. This verse brings together two of the proofs of monotheism, which are from the heavenly and the earthly signs.

Then He mentions another proof from the earthly signs, saying: ﴿And We placed firm mountains in the earth lest it shake with them﴾; the explanation of a parallel of this sentence has already been given in Surat al-Nahl. ﴿And We made in it broad passages as paths﴾; this is a fourth proof from the earthly signs. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (fīhā) refers to the earth; it has also been said that it refers to the firm mountains. Here (fijājan) is placed before (subulan), whereas in Surat Nuh it is ﴿that you may follow from them roads, broad paths﴾ [Nuh: 20]. Al-Zamakhshari said: (fijājan) is an adjective, but it has been made a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), as in his saying:

"For Mayya, a desolate abode."

He means that it is a circumstance of (subul), which is indefinite; had (fijājan) been placed after it, it would have been an adjective as in that verse, but since it came first it is in the accusative as a circumstance. He said: If you ask: what is the difference between them in terms of meaning? I say: there are two aspects. One is the information that He made in it wide roads; the other is that when He created it, He created it with that attribute, so it is an explanation of what was left ambiguous there. End of quotation. By ambiguity he means that a description does not require that the described thing be characterised by it at the time of the report about it, although most often it is characterised by it at the time of the report; do you not see that one says: "I passed by a savage slayer of Hamza," where at the time of passing the slaying of Hamza was not a present attribute of him? As for the circumstance, it is the state of what you report about at the time of reporting. ﴿So that they may be guided﴾ in their paths and their conduct.

Whatever is raised and elevated over something is called a canopy (saqf). Qatada said: a protection from decay and change over the length of time. It has been said: a protection from falling, since it holds itself up without a support or pillar. It has been said: a protection from polytheism and sins. Al-Farra' said: a protection from the devils by meteors. From Ibn 'Abbas: the Messenger of God ﷺ looked at the sky and said: "Indeed the sky is a raised canopy and a restrained wave, flowing as an arrow flows, guarded from the devils." If this ḥadīth is sound, it is an explicit text on the meaning of the verse.

(p-310) ﴿And they turn away from its signs﴾, that is, from what God placed in it of proofs and lessons: the sun, the moon, and the rest of the luminaries and their courses, their rising and setting according to a straight reckoning and a wondrous order, which indicate profound wisdom and overwhelming power. The majority read ﴿ 'an āyātihā ﴾ in the plural. Mujahid and Humayd read ʿan āyatihā in the singular; this may mean that He made the making, or the canopy, or the creating, that is, the creation of the sky, one single sign comprising all the signs; or it may mean by it the plural, and He made it a noun of the genus, and the abundance of signs in the sky indicates this. The meaning is: ﴿and they﴾ from taking heed of its signs ﴿turn away﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: They are aware of what reaches them from the sky of worldly benefits, such as being illuminated by its two moons, guidance by its stars, and the life of the earth and of animals through its rains; ﴿and they﴾ turn away from its being a clear sign of the Creator.

The tanwīn in (kullun) is a substitute (ʿiwaḍ) for the genitive noun that was omitted, and al-falak is a body that revolves in the course of a day and night. From Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi: al-falak is the sky. Most of the exegetes said: al-falak is a restrained wave beneath the sky in which the sun and moon flow. Qatada said: al-falak is a rotation between the sky and the earth that turns with the stars while the sky remains fixed. It has been said: al-falak is the pole upon which the stars revolve, and it is the north pole. It has been said: each of the wandering bodies has a falak, and the falak of the falaks moves them all in one motion from east to west. Al-Dahhak said: al-falak is not a body; it is only the orbit of these stars. The apparent view is that it is a body, and the difference mentioned above concerns it. The apparent view is that each swims in one falak. It has been said: each has a falak specific to it, as in the saying: "The governor clothed them with a robe," meaning he clothed each one. (yasbahūn) comes with the plural waw for rational beings. As for the plural: it has been said that there is an elided conjoined noun there, namely the stars, and that is why the pronoun came in the plural; had there not been an elided conjoined noun, it would have been (yasbahān) in the dual.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The pronoun refers to the sun and the moon, and what is meant by them is the class of risings, each day and night, which they made numerous because of the multiplicity of their risings; this is the reason for their being pluralised as "suns" and "moons"; otherwise the sun is one and the moon is one. End of quotation. What made this acceptable is that it came as the ending of a verse. As for its being the pronoun of rational beings when the construction would not be (yasbaḥna): al-Farra' said: Since swimming is one of the actions of human beings, what is ascribed to them (the sun and moon) came in the plural form for rational beings, as in His saying: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4]. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: According to the view of Abu 'Ali ibn Sina, the reason for this is that they, in his view, have intellect. End of quotation. This sentence may be a new report, with no place in the sentence; or its place is accusative as a circumstance of ﴿the sun and the moon﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2], because (the night and the day) are not described as flowing ﴿in an orbit﴾; so it is like your saying: "I saw Zayd and Hind unveiled." Swimming is floating. The apparent meaning is that the sun and the moon are the two that flow in the orbit, and that the orbit does not flow.

﴿And We did not grant﴾ the verse. It has been said: some Muslims said: "Muhammad will never die; he is immortal," so the Messenger denied that, and this verse was revealed. It has been said: the disbelievers of Mecca reproached him, saying: "He is a human who eats food and dies; how can his being sent as messenger be valid?" Al-Zamakhshari said: They expected that he would die, and they would gloat over his death; so God negated gloating from him by this, meaning: God decreed that no human be made immortal in this world; neither you nor they are but subject to death. If you die, will these remain? In the same sense is the statement of Imam al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him:

"Men wish that I die, and if I die, that is a path I am not the only one to walk."

**The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 30–34 (part 2 of 2)**

Abu Hayyan quotes the verse of the poet:

*"Say to the one who seeks the opposite of what has passed: 'Provide for yourself for another [life] like it, as if it were already [here].'"*

And the verse of the other poet:

*"Say to those who gloat over us: 'Wake up! The gloaters will meet what we have met.'"*

The fa' (الفاء) in ﴿أفَإنْ مِتَّ﴾ is the conjunctive fa' (فاءُ العَطْفِ). The interrogative hamza (هَمْزَةُ الِاسْتِفْهامِ) has been placed before it, because interrogation (الِاسْتِفْهامُ) has the front position in the sentence. It enters upon the conditional particle in (إنِ الشَّرْطِيَّةِ) (p. 311), and the clause after it is the response of the condition (جَوابٌ لِلشَّرْطِ). That clause is not the target of the interrogation (مَصَبَّ الِاسْتِفْهامِ), so the hamza does not enter directly upon it. The condition is inserted between the two, and its response is elided. This is the view of Sibawayh.

Yunus claimed that this clause is in fact the target of the interrogation, with the condition inserted between them and its response elided.

Ibn Atiyya said: "The hamza of interrogation enters, in meaning, upon the response of the condition." End of quotation.

This verse is evidence for the view of Sibawayh. If the matter were as Yunus claimed, the construction would have been ﴿أفَإنْ مِتَّ﴾ ﴿هُمُ الخالِدُونَ﴾ without the fa'. Both views are discussed in detail in the science of grammar (عِلْمُ النَّحْوِ).

It has been said: a protection from falling, since it holds itself up without a support or pillar. It has been said: a protection from polytheism and sins. Al-Farra' said: a protection from the devils by meteors. From Ibn 'Abbas: the Messenger of God ﷺ looked at the sky and said: "Indeed the sky is a raised canopy and a restrained wave, flowing as an arrow flows, guarded from the devils." If this ḥadīth is sound, it is an explicit text on the meaning of the verse.

(p-310) ﴿And they turn away from its signs﴾, that is, from what God placed in it of proofs and lessons: the sun, the moon, and the rest of the luminaries and their courses, their rising and setting according to a straight reckoning and a wondrous order, which indicate profound wisdom and overwhelming power. The majority read ﴿ 'an āyātihā ﴾ in the plural. Mujahid and Humayd read ʿan āyatihā in the singular; this may mean that He made the making, or the canopy, or the creating, that is, the creation of the sky, one single sign comprising all the signs; or it may mean by it the plural, and He made it a noun of the genus, and the abundance of signs in the sky indicates this. The meaning is: ﴿and they﴾ from taking heed of its signs ﴿turn away﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: They are aware of what reaches them from the sky of worldly benefits, such as being illuminated by its two moons, guidance by its stars, and the life of the earth and of animals through its rains; ﴿and they﴾ turn away from its being a clear sign of the Creator.

The tanwīn in (kullun) is a substitute (ʿiwaḍ) for the genitive noun that was omitted, and al-falak is a body that revolves in the course of a day and night. From Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi: al-falak is the sky. Most of the exegetes said: al-falak is a restrained wave beneath the sky in which the sun and moon flow. Qatada said: al-falak is a rotation between the sky and the earth that turns with the stars while the sky remains fixed. It has been said: al-falak is the pole upon which the stars revolve, and it is the north pole. It has been said: each of the wandering bodies has a falak, and the falak of the falaks moves them all in one motion from east to west. Al-Dahhak said: al-falak is not a body; it is only the orbit of these stars. The apparent view is that it is a body, and the difference mentioned above concerns it. The apparent view is that each swims in one falak. It has been said: each has a falak specific to it, as in the saying: "The governor clothed them with a robe," meaning he clothed each one. (yasbahūn) comes with the plural waw for rational beings. As for the plural: it has been said that there is an elided conjoined noun there, namely the stars, and that is why the pronoun came in the plural; had there not been an elided conjoined noun, it would have been (yasbahān) in the dual.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The pronoun refers to the sun and the moon, and what is meant by them is the class of risings, each day and night, which they made numerous because of the multiplicity of their risings; this is the reason for their being pluralised as "suns" and "moons"; otherwise the sun is one and the moon is one. End of quotation. What made this acceptable is that it came as the ending of a verse. As for its being the pronoun of rational beings when the construction would not be (yasbaḥna): al-Farra' said: Since swimming is one of the actions of human beings, what is ascribed to them (the sun and moon) came in the plural form for rational beings, as in His saying: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4]. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: According to the view of Abu 'Ali ibn Sina, the reason for this is that they, in his view, have intellect. End of quotation. This sentence may be a new report, with no place in the sentence; or its place is accusative as a circumstance of ﴿the sun and the moon﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2], because (the night and the day) are not described as flowing ﴿in an orbit﴾; so it is like your saying: "I saw Zayd and Hind unveiled." Swimming is floating. The apparent meaning is that the sun and the moon are the two that flow in the orbit, and that the orbit does not flow.

﴿And We did not grant﴾ the verse. It has been said: some Muslims said: "Muhammad will never die; he is immortal," so the Messenger denied that, and this verse was revealed. It has been said: the disbelievers of Mecca reproached him, saying: "He is a human who eats food and dies; how can his being sent as messenger be valid?" Al-Zamakhshari said: They expected that he would die, and they would gloat over his death; so God negated gloating from him by this, meaning: God decreed that no human be made immortal in this world; neither you nor they are but subject to death. If you die, will these remain? In the same sense is the statement of Imam al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him:

"Men wish that I die, and if I die, that is a path I am not the only one to walk."

**The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 30–34 (part 2 of 2)**

Abu Hayyan quotes the verse of the poet:

*"Say to the one who seeks the opposite of what has passed: 'Provide for yourself for another [life] like it, as if it were already [here].'"*

And the verse of the other poet:

*"Say to those who gloat over us: 'Wake up! The gloaters will meet what we have met.'"*

The fa' (الفاء) in ﴿أفَإنْ مِتَّ﴾ is the conjunctive fa' (فاءُ العَطْفِ). The interrogative hamza (هَمْزَةُ الِاسْتِفْهامِ) has been placed before it, because interrogation (الِاسْتِفْهامُ) has the front position in the sentence. It enters upon the conditional particle in (إنِ الشَّرْطِيَّةِ) (p. 311), and the clause after it is the response of the condition (جَوابٌ لِلشَّرْطِ). That clause is not the target of the interrogation (مَصَبَّ الِاسْتِفْهامِ), so the hamza does not enter directly upon it. The condition is inserted between the two, and its response is elided. This is the view of Sibawayh.

Yunus claimed that this clause is in fact the target of the interrogation, with the condition inserted between them and its response elided.

Ibn Atiyya said: "The hamza of interrogation enters, in meaning, upon the response of the condition." End of quotation.

This verse is evidence for the view of Sibawayh. If the matter were as Yunus claimed, the construction would have been ﴿أفَإنْ مِتَّ﴾ ﴿هُمُ الخالِدُونَ﴾ without the fa'. Both views are discussed in detail in the science of grammar (عِلْمُ النَّحْوِ).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verse 35:

﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾. The explanation of this clause has already been given. ﴿And We test you﴾, i.e., We try you (nabluukum, nakhtabirukum), and He mentioned the evil first because being tested by it is more frequent, and because the Arabs mention the lesser and the worse first. From this is His saying: ﴿It leaves nothing small or great﴾ [18:49]. Among you are those who wrong themselves, among you are those who are moderate, and among you are those who race to good deeds [35:32].

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Good and evil here are general, covering wealth and poverty, health and sickness, obedience and disobedience, and guidance and misguidance."

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "These last two are not included in this, because one who is guided, his guidance is not by choice, nor is one who obeys. Rather, his goodness has become clear. The apparent meaning is that what is intended by good and evil here is everything that may be a trial and a test." End of quotation.

It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas: "By hardship and ease: will you be patient in hardship and thankful in ease, or not?"

al-Dahhak said: "Poverty and sickness, and wealth and health."

Ibn Zayd said: "What is loved and what is hated."

﴿Fitnah﴾ is in the accusative either as an object of purpose (maf'ul lah), or as a verbal noun (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial state (hal), or as a verbal noun derived from the sense of (nabluukum).

﴿And to Us you will be returned﴾: We will then recompense you for what came from you in the state of testing, of patience and thankfulness, and in other than testing.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿turja'un﴾ with a ta' of address and in the passive voice. One group read it with an open ta' in the active voice. Another group read it with a damma on the ya' (third person), in the passive voice, by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verse 36–43 (part 1 of 2):

(p-312) ﴿When those who disbelieve see you, they take you only in mockery: "Is this the one who mentions your gods?" And yet they are the ones who disbelieve in the mention of the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿Man was created of haste. I will show you My signs, so do not seek to hasten them.﴾ ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿If only those who disbelieve knew the time when they will not be able to ward off the Fire from their faces nor from their backs, nor will they be helped.﴾ ﴿Rather, it will come upon them suddenly and confound them, and they will not be able to repel it, nor will they be given respite.﴾ ﴿And messengers before you were certainly mocked, but those who mocked them were encompassed by what they used to mock.﴾ ﴿Say: "Who protects you by night and by day from the Most Merciful?" Rather, they are turning away from the remembrance of their Lord.﴾ ﴿Or do they have gods that defend them from beside Us? They cannot help themselves, nor will they be companioned by Us.﴾:

al-Suddi and Muqatil said: The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, passed by Abu Jahl and Abu Sufyan. Abu Jahl said: "This is the Prophet of Abd Manaf." Abu Sufyan said: "What do you find objectionable in him being a prophet among the Banu Abd Manaf?" The Messenger ﷺ heard them both and said to Abu Jahl: "You will not cease until there befalls you what befell your paternal uncle al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. As for you, Abu Sufyan, you only said what you said out of partisanship (hamiyyah)." Then this was revealed.

When the disbelievers were distressed by the mention of their gods in a bad light, they began to mock and belittle whoever mentioned them, as a form of retaliation. The (in) here is negating, with the meaning of (ma). The apparent view is that the answer to (idha) is ﴿in yattakhidhunaka﴾, and the answer to (idha) with the negating (in) does not occur in the Qur'an except in this verse and in His saying in the Qur'an ﴿When they see you, they take you only in mockery﴾ [al-Furqan: 41]. It did not need the (fa) in the answer, just as (ma) did not need it when it occurred as an answer, as in His saying: ﴿And when Our clear signs are recited to them, their argument is nothing﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 25]. This is unlike the particles of condition, for when the answer begins with the negating (ma), the (fa) is necessary, as in: "If you visit us, then we do not wrong you." In the answer of (idha) with the negating (in) and (ma) there is clear evidence that (idha) is not governed by the answer, but rather the verb that follows it is what governs it, and it is not a genitive construction attached to the clause, contrary to most grammarians. We have argued for this with other evidence in the commentary on al-Tashil.

It was also said: the answer to (idha) is omitted, and it is "they say," the quoted speech being their saying ﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods?﴾, and His saying ﴿in yattakhidhunaka illa huzuwan﴾ is an interposed clause between (idha) and its answer. ﴿Yattakhidhunaka﴾ takes two objects, and the second, (huzuwan), means "a thing mocked at." This is an interrogative expressing denial and wonder. Remembrance (dhikr) can be by good or by evil; when its object is not mentioned, the context indicates it. If it comes from a friend it is praise, and if from others it is blame. Among its uses is ﴿We heard a youth mention them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 60], meaning with evil. Likewise here: ﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods?﴾

Then He censured their denial of his mention of their gods by this circumstantial clause: ﴿And yet they are the ones who disbelieve in the mention of the Most Merciful﴾, meaning they deny. This is their condition: they disbelieve in the mention of the Most Merciful, which is what was sent down of the Qur'an. Whoever is in this condition should not object to one who disparages their gods. The apparent view is that this clause is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿yaqulun﴾, which is omitted.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause, i.e., (they take you as a mockery) while they are in a state which is the root of mockery and derision, which is disbelief in God. End of quote. So he made the circumstantial clause's governing element (they take you as a mockery), omitted, and repeated them for emphasis. It is narrated that it was revealed when they denied the word "al-Rahman" and said: "We do not know al-Rahman except in Yamamah." The meaning of al-Rahman here is God, as if it was said: "and they, with the mention of God."

Since they were hastening God's punishment and His signs that compel acknowledgment and knowledge, God, exalted is He, forbade them from haste. He first mentioned the blame of man for excessive haste, and that he is naturally disposed to it. The apparent view is that "al-insan" here refers to the genus, and his being "created of haste" is by way of hyperbole, because it proceeds from him frequently, as one says to someone who plays a lot, "You are made of play." In a hadith: "I am not of the frivolous, nor is the frivolous of me." The poet said:

"Indeed we, when we strike the ram a blow on its head, the tongue flies out of its mouth."

Since they were people of striking skulls and constant war, he said that they are "of striking." With this interpretation the meaning of the verse is complete, and what follows from it is His saying: ﴿I will show you My signs﴾, i.e., the signs of threat, ﴿so do not seek to hasten them﴾ in seeing the punishment you hasten for.

As for one who claims there is inversion (qalb) in it, namely Abu Amr, and that the original is "the creation of haste from man," and likewise the reading of Abd Allah, in the sense that it was made a nature of his natures and a part of his character, this view is not good, because inversion in sound speech is not proper, and its domain is poetry. It was said: among what occurs in speech of this kind is the Arab saying: "When Sirius rises, the wood is level over the chameleon." And they said: "The she-camel was presented to the pool." And in poetry his saying:

"I stripped my hand from the garment, taking hold of it."

Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrimah, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said that "al-insan" here is Adam. Mujahid said: When the spirit entered his head and eyes, he saw the sun approaching sunset, and said: "My Lord, hasten the completion of my creation before the sun sets." Sa'id said: When the spirit reached his knees, he nearly stood up, and God said: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾. Ibn Zayd said: God created him on Friday with haste in his creation. Al-Akhfash said: ﴿of haste﴾ because God said to him "Be," and he was. Al-Hasan said: ﴿of haste﴾ means weak, meaning the drop of semen. It was said: he was created swiftly and hastily, not in the order of the sons of Adam from drop, clot and lump; this returns to al-Akhfash's view. It was said: ﴿of haste﴾ means of clay, and "ajal" in the dialect of Himyar means clay. Abu Ubaydah recited for one of the Himyarites:

"The wood in the hard rock, its place of growth; and the palm, its place of growth is in water and clay."

It was said: "al-insan" here is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. The view that the verse should be understood as referring to him is the first view, which is the one that suits its ending. As for "the signs" here, it was said: the swift destruction in this world and the punishment in the Hereafter, i.e., it will come to you at its time. It was said: the proofs of monotheism and the truthfulness of the Messenger. It was said: the traces of past generations in al-Sham and Yemen. The first view is most fitting, i.e., what will distress you will come if you persist in your disbelief, as if he means the Day of Badr and other things in this world and in the Hereafter.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why did He forbid them from hastening when He said ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ and ﴿And man has been ever hasty﴾ [al-Isra': 11]? Is this not imposing what cannot be borne? I say: this is like the desire that was placed in him, and He commanded him to overcome it, because He gave him the power by which he can suppress desire and abandon haste. End of quote. This is in the way of the Mu'tazilah.

Mujahid, Humayd and Ibn Miqsam read (khalaqa) in the active voice, with (al-insana) in the accusative, meaning God created man. His saying ﴿When is this promise?﴾ is an interrogative in the manner of mockery, and the Muslims used to threaten them on the tongue of the Law. (Mata) is in the position of a genitive for this, so its position is nominative. It is reported from some Kufans that the position of (mata) is accusative as an adverb of time, governed by an implied verb whose estimate is "it will be" or "it will come." The answer of (law) is omitted, for the context indicates it, and omitting it is more eloquent and awe-inspiring than stating it. Ibn Atiyyah estimated it as "when they hasten and the like," and al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "when they were in that state of disbelief, mockery and hastening." It was also said: "they would have known the truth of resurrection." It was said: "they would have known the truth of the promised thing." Al-Hawfi said: "they would have hastened to faith." Al-Kisa'i said: it is an alert to the certainty of the occurrence of the Hour, and (hin), when it is meant as the time of the Hour, indicates this, in ﴿but it will come upon them suddenly﴾. End of quote.

(Hin) — al-Zamakhshari said: it is an object of (ya'lamu), i.e., "if they knew the time which they hasten about by their saying ﴿When is this promise?﴾, which is a time hard and severe, the fire encompassing them from behind and in front, but their ignorance of it is what made it light in their estimation." He said: It is also possible that (ya'lamu) is left without an object, meaning "if they had knowledge and were not ignorant, they would not have been hasty," and (hin) is governed by an implied verb, i.e., ﴿when they will not ward off from their faces the Fire﴾ they will know that they were upon falsehood, and this great ignorance will be removed from them, i.e., they will not ward it off. End of quote. What appears to be the case is that the object of (ya'lamu) is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, i.e., "if those who disbelieve knew the coming of the promised thing which they asked about and sought to deduce." (Hin) is governed by the object, which is "coming," and it is possible that it is of the type of the "working" (i'mal) construction with an omitted modifier, and the second is made to work, the meaning being "if they knew the direct contact of the Fire when they will not ward it off from their faces." He mentioned the faces because they are the noblest part of man and the seat of his senses, and man is most eager to defend them among his limbs. Then he joined to them the backs. The meaning is the generality of the Fire over all their bodies, and no one will prevent them from the punishment. ﴿Rather, it will come upon them suddenly﴾, i.e., it will startle them. Ibn Atiyyah said: ﴿Rather, it will come upon them﴾ is a transition (istidrak) preceded by an implied negation, its estimate being: "Indeed the signs do not come according to their demands." End of quote. The apparent view is that the pronoun in (ta'tihim) refers to the Fire. It was said: it refers to the Hour that will bring them to punishment. It was said: to the punishment. Al-Zamakhshari said: regarding the return of the pronoun to the Fire, or to the promise, because it means the Fire which they promised, or on the interpretation of the promise and the pledge, or to the (hin), because it means the Hour, or to the sending of the Messenger. End of quote.

Al-A'mash read (bal ya'tihim) with the yā', (baghtatan) with fatha on the ghayn, (fayabhutuhum) with the yā', and the pronoun refers to the promise or the (hin), as al-Zamakhshari said. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: perhaps he made the Fire mean the punishment, so he mentioned it, then returned the pronoun (radduha) to the apparent wording. ﴿And they will not be given respite﴾, i.e., they will not be delayed from what has befallen them.

When His saying ﴿When they take you only in mockery﴾ preceded, God consoled him that those who came before him among the messengers were also mocked by their peoples, and that the fruit of their mockery was ripe destruction and punishment in this world and the Hereafter; so likewise is the state of these mockers. The explanation of a verse like this has preceded in al-An'am.

Then God commanded him to ask them: who protects you at your times from the might of God, i.e., no one protects you from it. This is an interrogative of rebuke and reproach. At the end of the speech there is an omitted estimate, as if they had no preventer and no guardian. On this negation is the construction of (bal) in His saying ﴿Rather, they are turning away from the remembrance of their Lord﴾, as Ibn Atiyyah said. Al-Zamakhshari said: Rather, they are turning away from His remembrance, not bringing it to mind, let alone fearing His might, until when they are granted protection from Him they recognize who the guardian is and become fit to be asked about Him. The meaning is that He commanded His Messenger to ask them about the guardian, then He made clear that they are not fit for that, because of their turning away from the remembrance of the One who guards them. End of quote.

Abu Ja'far, al-Zuhri and Shaybah read (yaklukum) with a light damma and without hamza. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' recounted (yaklawkum) with fatha on the lam and sukun on the waw.

﴿Or do they have gods﴾, with the meaning of "rather", and the interrogative hamzah, as if it were said: "Rather, do they have gods...?" He turned away from the first statement and then asked a question. ﴿That can prevent them﴾ from the punishment. Al-Hawfi said: ﴿besides Us﴾ is connected to ﴿can prevent them﴾. End of quote. It was said: the meaning is, "Do they have gods that make them secure and protected from anything disagreeable reaching them from Our side?"

Ibn ʿAbbas said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech. Its implied sense is: "Or do they have, besides Us, gods that can prevent them?" One says: "I prevented harm from him" (mana'tu dunahu), meaning, "I warded off his harm." So ﴿besides Us﴾ is connected either to ﴿gods﴾, meaning, "Or do they have gods other than Us?", or to ﴿can prevent them﴾, meaning, "Or do they have a protector other than Us?" Then he began a new statement about their gods, clarifying that what is not able to help itself or prevent harm, and is not accompanied by God with support and aid, how could it prevent and help others?

Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿they will be accompanied﴾ means "they will be prevented." Mujahid said: "they will be helped." Qatadah said: "they will not be accompanied by any good from God." The poet said:

He calls out with the highest of his voice, seeking refuge,
so that he may be accompanied by us, while the spears are hostile.

Mujahid said: "they will be guarded." Al-Suddi said: "none of the angels will accompany them to repel [harm] from them."

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿their protector﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142] refers to the idols, and this is the view of Qatadah. It was also said that it refers to the disbelievers, and this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. In al-Tahrir, the discussion of this word, namely ﴿yusḥabūn﴾, depends on two meanings. One is that it derives from ṣaḥiba, yaṣḥabu. The second is from al-iṣhāb: aṣḥaba al-rajul, meaning he protected the man from calamities.
