"And how many a day have I spent in pleasure, and a night, with a maiden whose slender form was like the line of a statue."

Al-Jadhdh: cutting off. The poet said:

"The sons of al-Muhallab, may Allah cut off their root, have become ashes, leaving neither root nor branch."

Al-Naks: turning a thing over so that its top becomes its bottom. "Nakkasa ra'sahu," with shadda or without, means he lowered his head until its top became its bottom. Al-Bard: the verbal noun of barada. It is said, "barrada al-ma' harārat al-jawf yubarriduha" (water cools the heat of the stomach). The poet said:

(p. 319) "He left my she-camel idle among the saddle-camels, and she will cool hearts and make the weepers weep."

Al-Nafsh: the grazing of livestock at night without a shepherd, and the wandering of them by day without a shepherd. Al-Ghawṣ: entering under water to extract what is in it. The poet said:

"Or a Sadafite pearl whose diver is joyful; whenever he sees it, he cries out and prostrates."

Al-Nūn: the fish, plural "ninan." It is also narrated that "al-ninan" precedes it, "al-humr." Al-Farj: it is applied to the free (the front), the male as opposed to the female, and to the rear. The poet said:

"And you, when you turned your back on him, he tightened his rear, raised above the ground and not weak."

Al-Hadab: a raised part of the ground, like a mountain, a mound, a grave, and the like. Al-Nasalan: quick walking with haste. The poet said:

"The wolf's swift pace has become near, when the night grew cold upon it, so it hastened."

Al-Haṣab: firewood in the Abyssinian language. When it is thrown into the fire, before it is thrown it is not called haṣab. It is said: the haṣab is what fire is kindled with. Al-Sijill: the record, the document.

﴿And We had certainly given Abraham his right guidance before, and We were fully aware of him.﴾ ﴿When he said to his father and his people, "What are these statues to which you are devoted?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We found our fathers worshipping them."﴾ ﴿He said, "You and your fathers have certainly been in manifest error."﴾ ﴿They said, "Have you brought us the truth, or are you one of the jesters?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who originated them, and I am a witness to that.﴾ ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols after you have turned away and gone.﴾ ﴿So he reduced them to fragments, except for a large one among them, that they might turn back to it.﴾.

When the discourse had preceded regarding the proofs of Tawhid (the oneness of God), prophethood, and the return (ma'ad), He followed that with thirteen prophets, without observing chronological order in mentioning them. He also mentioned some of the trials that many of them endured, all of this as consolation to the Messenger ﷺ, and so that he might take them as an example regarding what befell him from his people.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) recited ﴿rushdahu﴾ with a damma on the ra' and a sukun on the shin. 'Isa al-Thaqafi recited "rashadahu" with a fatha on the ra' and the shin, and he attributed the rushd to Ibrahim, meaning it is the rushd of one like him, which is the rushd of the prophets, and it has a great status. Rushd means prophethood and guidance to the ways of righteousness in religion and worldly affairs. Or both are included under rushd. Or the Sahifah and wisdom, or receiving success in good from childhood. There are five opinions. The object of the preposition is from a deleted antecedent, and it is definite, which is why "qabl" is indeclinable: that is, from before Musa and Harun. This was said by al-Dahhak, like His saying in al-An'am: ﴿And Noah, We guided before﴾ [al-An'am: 84], meaning before Ibrahim, Isaac, and Jacob. He who went to the view that the implied meaning is "before his reaching puberty," or "before his prophethood," meaning when he was in the loins of Adam and the covenant of the prophets was taken, is a far-fetched view. Or before Muhammad ﷺ, because these are deleted elements with no evidence indicating their deletion, unlike "from before" Musa and Harun, since they were mentioned previously. And its nearness. The pronoun in "bihi" most apparently refers to Ibrahim. It was said: it refers to rushd. Allah, exalted is He, informed that He knew from him wondrous states and marvelous secrets, so He qualified him for His intimate friendship (khullah), like His saying: "Allah knows best where to place His messages." This is one of the greatest and most eloquent praises, since Allah, exalted is He, informed that He gave him rushd and that He knew what He had given him, upon him be peace.

Then he digressed from that to explaining rushd, which is calling to the oneness of Allah and rejecting what is worshipped besides Him. "Idh" is governed either by "ataynā" or by "rushdahu" and "ʿālimīn," or by a deleted element, meaning: mention the time of his rushd, this moment. He began first with mentioning his father, because he was the most important in his advice and in rescuing him from error. Then he joined "his people" to it, like His saying: ﴿And warn your closest kindred﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 214]. In His saying ﴿What are these statues﴾ there is a belittling of them, a diminishing of their status, and a feigned ignorance about them, despite his knowledge of them and of their veneration by them. In his address to them with "antum" (you) there is contempt for them and a reproach over their wicked conduct. "ʿAkafa" is transitive with "ʿalā," like His saying: ﴿They cling to idols they have﴾ [al-A'raf: 138]. So it was said that "la-hā" here means "ʿalay-hā," as it was said in His saying: ﴿And if you do evil, it is to yourselves﴾ [al-Isra': 7]. The apparent meaning is that the lam in "la-hā" is the lam of causation, meaning "for its veneration," and the complement of ﴿ʿākifūn﴾ is deleted, meaning "upon its worship." It was said: ʿākifūn has been made to imply the meaning of ʿābidūn, so it takes the lam.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He did not intend a deleted object for "al-ʿākifīn," and he treated it as an intransitive verb, like His saying "fāʿilūn al-ʿukūf lahā" (doers of the devotion to it), or "wāqifūn lahā" (standing before it). End of quote.

When he questioned them, they answered with mere **taqlid** (blind imitation, *taqlid* being the uncritical following of others) and said that it was the practice of their fathers, so they followed it without any proof. How ugly is this taqlid, which led them to worship wood, stone and metal. Their obstinacy in this matter, and their defence of their imitation, is also clear. His question about worshipping the images had the aim that they would mention some doubt about it, so that he could refute it. When they answered him with something in which they had no doubt-based justification, and their misguidance became evident, ﴿He said: "You and your fathers have certainly been in clear error."﴾ That is, in obvious bewilderment with no ambiguity in it. He judged that both the imitators and those imitated were in error, and he made the error settled for them. The word "you" (*antum*) is an emphatic pronoun for the pronoun that is the subject of "were" (*kana*).

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Antum* belongs to the kind of emphasis without which the sentence is not sound, because coordinating (*'atf*) upon the pronoun in *huwa* is, in the judgement of the grammarians, like part of the verb, and is therefore impermissible, and similar to it is ﴿Dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35]." End of quote.

This is not a unanimously agreed ruling, so the sentence is not invalid without it, because the Kufans permit coordinating upon the attached nominative pronoun without emphasis by a detached nominative pronoun and without a separating element. His comparison of this with ﴿Dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾ contradicts his own position on ﴿Dwell, you and your wife﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35], since he claims that "and your wife" is not coordinated upon the concealed pronoun in "dwell" but rather that "and your wife" is nominative by an implied element, meaning "let [your wife] dwell". Thus, according to him, it is a coordination of sentences. This claim contradicts the school of Sibawayh.

When this question and answer had occurred, they were astonished at his misleading them, since he had grown up among them, and they allowed that what he had said was in the manner of jest and not seriousness. So they asked him: ﴿Have you come to us with the truth, or are you among the players?﴾ The pronoun in "they said" refers to his father and his people. "With the truth" is connected to their words "Have you come to us". They did not mean the literal act of coming, because he had not been absent from them and then come to them. This is like ﴿He said: "Even if I bring you something clear?"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 30]. Here "truth" is the opposite of falsehood, meaning seriousness. For this reason they set it against play. The sentence came in nominal form because it is more emphatic, as though they had judged him to be a player and a joker in what he said to them, and also for the sake of the closing rhyme (*fasila*).

Then he turned away from their words and informed them of the seriousness: that the owner of them and the one deserving worship is their Lord, and the Lord of this upper world and this lower world which includes you and your idols. He drew attention to what requires worship, which is the One who originated this world and brought it into existence from pure non-existence. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿who originated them﴾ refers to the heavens and the earth. Since the heavens and the earth do not reach a large number, the pronoun used is the pronoun of few (*damir al-qilla*). It has also been said that the pronoun in ﴿who originated them﴾ refers to the images. Al-Zamakhshari said: "That it refers to the images is more effective for misleading them and more firm for arguing against them." End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "﴿Who originated them﴾ is an expression for them as if they understood, in that they have obedience and submission, and they have been described in several places with what is described of those who understand." Another said: "﴿Who originated them﴾ refers back with the pronoun of those who understand, because of the states that proceed from them which indicate that they belong to the category of those who understand. Indeed God said: ﴿They said: We come obediently﴾ [Fussilat: 11], and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'The heaven creaked, and it has a right to creak.'" End of quote.

It seems that Ibn 'Atiyya and this speaker imagined that *hunna* is among the pronouns specific to feminine things that understand, but this is not so. Rather it is a shared term between those that understand and feminine plural things that do not understand. An example is His saying: ﴿So do not wrong yourselves therein﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36], where the pronoun refers to the four sacred months.

The indication in ﴿That is your [Lord]﴾ refers to His lordship and His being described as the Originator of this world. The word "from" (*min*) is partitive: that is, of those who testify to lordship there are many, and I am one of them. That is, what I have said is a settled matter upon which there are many witnesses, so it is a statement validated by witnesses. The phrase ﴿upon that﴾ is connected to an omitted element, its estimate being "and I am a witness" ﴿upon that, among the witnesses﴾. Or it is in the sense of explanation, that is, "I mean upon that". Or it is by the active participle, even though it is within the relative clause of *al* (the definite article), because of the breadth in their use of the adverbial and prepositional phrase. There are views on this that were already mentioned under ﴿Indeed I am to you both among the sincere advisers﴾ [al-A'raf: 21].

He first hastened to them with a statement that alerts to the indication of reason, but they did not benefit from the statement. So he moved on to a statement that indicates action, which ends in a complete indication of the lack of benefit in the expression of what is subjected to breaking and cutting. It neither repels nor harms nor benefits, and it does not perceive what has happened to it of the dismantling of its parts. So he said: ﴿And by God, I will surely plot against your idols﴾.

The majority read ﴿And by God﴾ with *ta'* (the letter ت). Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Ahmad ibn Hanbal read *bi-Allah* with a single *ba'* (ب) below. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the difference between *ta'* and *ba'*? I answer: *ba'* is the origin, and *ta'* is a substitute for the *waw* which was itself substituted for it. The *ta'* carries an extra meaning, which is wonder, as though he wondered at how easily the plot was accomplished at his hand and by his effort, because that was considered something hopeless due to its difficulty and impossibility. By my life, the like of it is difficult and impossible in every age, especially in the time of Nimrod, with his arrogance, his haughtiness, the strength of his authority, and his zeal in defending his religion. But—"

*"When God ties together a matter's knot, it is made easy."*

End of quote. As for his statement that *ba'* is the origin: it was an origin because it is the broadest of the particles of oath, since it enters upon both nouns and pronouns, is used with the explicit verb of swearing, and may be omitted [p. 322]. As for the claim that *ta'* is a substitute for the *waw* of oath, which itself was substituted for the *ba'* of oath, this is something many grammarians have said, but no evidence supports it. Al-Suhayli advanced this view. What analysis requires is that none of them is the origin of another. As for his statement that *ta'* carries an extra meaning, which is wonder, the explicit statements of the grammarians hold that *ta'* may be accompanied by wonder and may not; the *lam* is what necessarily carries wonder in oaths.

Plotting (*kayd*) is scheming to bring harm upon the target. The apparent reading is that he addressed this sentence to his father and his people, and that it falls under the "he said" in His words ﴿He said: "Rather, your Lord..."﴾. It has been said that he said this secretly from his people, and that one man heard it. It has also been said that a group of their weaker members heard it, those who were walking at the back of the people on the day they went out to the festival. The idols were seventy, and it has been said seventy-two.

The majority read ﴿they turned away, retreating﴾ as the imperfect of *wallā* (to turn away). 'Isa ibn 'Umar read *tuwallu* by dropping one of the two *ta'*s, the second one according to the school of the Basrans, and the first one according to the school of Hisham. This is the imperfect of *tawallā* (to turn oneself away), and it agrees with His saying ﴿so they turned away from him, retreating﴾ [al-Saffat: 90]. The object of "they turned away" is omitted, its meaning being "to your festival".

It is narrated that Azar took him out on one of their festival days. They began with the house of the idols, entered it, prostrated to them, and placed food between them which they had brought with them. They said: "The blessing of the gods will not return to our food." Then they left. When he was on the road, he turned his intention away from going with them, sat down, and said: "I am sick." Al-Kalbi said: Ibrahim was from a household that studied the stars, and when they went out to their festival, they would leave none behind except the sick. So Ibrahim came to them with what they were in, and he looked at the sky before the day of the festival and said to his companions: "I am ailing tomorrow." He woke up with his head bound. So they went out and none remained behind except him. He said ﴿And by God, I will surely plot...﴾ to the end. A man heard him, remembered it, and then reported it, and so it spread. End of quote.

There is an omission in the speech, its estimate being: "they turned away to their festival, and Ibrahim came to the idols." ﴿So he made them into fragments﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Debris." Al-Dahhak said: "He took from each pair a limb." It has also been said: the idols were arranged in rows, and among them there was a great idol facing the door, made of gold, with two shining jewels in its eyes. He broke them all with an axe except that great idol, and he hung the axe around its neck. It has been said that he hung it in its hand.

The majority read *judhadhan* (فجُذاذًا) with a *damma* on the *jim*. Al-Kisa'i, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Miqsam, Abu Haywa, Humayd, and al-A'mash in one narration read it with a *kasra*. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Nahik and Abu al-Sammak read it with a *fatha*. These are dialects, the best of which is the *damma*, like *hutham* and *rufat* (debris and crumbs), as Abu Hatim said. Al-Yazidi said: *judhadhan* with a *damma* is the plural of *judhadha*, like *zujaj* and *zujaja* (glass). It has been said that with a *kasra* it is the plural of *jadhid*, like *karim* and *kiram*. It has been said that the *fatha* is a verbal noun, like *al-hasad* (the harvest) in the sense of "the harvested", so the meaning is "cut to pieces". Qutrub said, regarding its three dialects, that it is a verbal noun which is not dualised or pluralised. Yahya ibn Wathhab read *judhadha* with two *damma*s, the plural of *jadhid*, like *jadid* and *judud*. It was also read *judhadhan* with a *damma* on the *jim* and a *fatha* on the *dhal*, lightened, from a verb like *sururun* in *sururun* (the plural of *sarir*, bed), which is a dialect of the tribe of Kalb. Or it is the plural of *juddha*, like *qubba* and *qubab* (dome and domes).

He used the pronoun for those who understand in His saying ﴿so He made them﴾, since they were worshipped. His saying ﴿except a great one among them﴾ is an exception from the pronoun in ﴿so He made them﴾, meaning he did not break it. The pronoun in "among them" may refer to the idols, or to their worshippers. "Great" here means its huge body, or that it was great in standing among them, since they had made it of gold and placed in its eyes two jewels that shine at night. The pronoun in "to it" refers to Ibrahim, meaning he did this with the hope that they would return to him and to his law. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He spared the great one only because it was most likely in his estimation that they would not return except to it, given what they had heard of his denial of their religion and his reviling of their gods, so he would rebuke them with the answer he gave, ﴿Rather, their great one did it; so ask them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 63]." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible that it refers to the great one who was left, but the hope expressed in the sentence weakens this." End of quote.

This is the view of al-Kalbi. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The meaning of this is: perhaps they will return to it, as one returns to a scholar to resolve problems, so they would say, 'What is wrong with these, broken, and with you, intact, with the axe on your shoulder?'" He said: "This is built on his assumption about them, because of what he had tested and experienced of their obstinacy against their reason, their belief in their idols, and their veneration of them; or he said it knowing that they would not return to him, mocking them and calling them fools. The standard for one who is prostrated to and made eligible for worship is that one should be returned to in resolving difficulties." "If you ask: if they returned to the idol through their obstinacy against their reason and the entrenchment of polytheism in their roots, then what religious benefit is there in their returning to it, such that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, would make it his aim?" I answer: "If they returned to it, it would become clear that it is powerless, neither benefiting nor harming, and it would be evident that they were in a great matter in worshipping it."

[p. 323]

In the speech there is an omitted element, whose implied sense is: when they returned from their festival to their gods and saw what had been done to them, they asked, as a matter of investigation and denunciation, saying: ﴿Who has done this?﴾ That is, the smashing and the shattering. ﴿Indeed, he is surely one of the wrongdoers﴾ in his audacity against gods who deserve glorification and honour. (﴿They said﴾) That is, those who heard his statement said, ﴿"And by God, I will surely scheme against your idols"﴾ [al-Anbiya: 57]. ﴿Who mentions them﴾, that is, with evil. Al-Farra' said: a man says to another, "If you mention me, you will surely regret it," meaning, with evil. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the status of the two verbs after ﴿"We heard a youth"﴾, and what is the difference between them? I say: they are two descriptions of ﴿a youth﴾, except that the first, namely ﴿who mentions them﴾, is necessary for ﴿heard﴾, because you do not say "I heard Zayd" and stop until you mention something of what is heard; but the second is not like that. End of quote.

As for his statement that they are two descriptions, that is not definitively settled, for the following reason. As for ﴿heard﴾ (sami'a): either it governs something heard or something other than that. If it governs something heard, there is no disagreement that it transitively takes one object, as in "I heard the speech of Zayd" and "the saying of Khalid." If it governs something other than something heard, there is disagreement about it. It is said that it transitively takes two objects, which is the view of al-Farisi, and the second must indicate a sound, so one does not say "I heard Zayd riding." The view of others is that sami'a transitively takes one object, and the verb after it, if definite, is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of it, or if indefinite, in the position of a descriptive qualifier (ṣifa). Both views have arguments in the science of grammar. According to this other view, al-Zamakhshari's statement that it is a qualifier of ﴿a youth﴾ holds. But according to the view of Abu 'Ali, it can only be in the position of the second object of sami'a.

As for ﴿who is called Abraham﴾: it is possible that it is an answer to an implied question, since they said ﴿"We heard a youth who mentions them"﴾ and brought him indefinite, so it was said: "Who is he who is called?" and it was said to him: "Abraham." ﴿Abraham﴾ is in the nominative because it is implicitly governed by a sentence reported with "said": either as a vocative, that is, "he is called" when he is summoned: "O Abraham"; or as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is, "he is Abraham"; or as a singular noun, the object of what has no named agent, and it is then from attribution to the word, not to its referent, that is, this word is applied to him. This last is the choice of al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya, and its permissibility is disputed. Al-Zajjaji, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kharuf and Ibn Malik held that the speech verb (qala) may govern a single noun in the accusative, provided it is not an excerpt from a sentence, as in the verse:

*"When you taste her mouth, you say: 'The taste of wine!'"*

nor a singular noun whose meaning is that of a sentence, as in "I said: a sermon," nor a verbal noun, as in "I said a saying," nor a qualifier of it, as in "I said truly," but for the mere word itself, as in "I said Zayd." Some grammarians prohibited this, and this is the correct view, since it is not transmitted from their speech that one says "So-and-so said Zayd," nor "He said [the verb] daraba," nor "He said laita." The speech verb occurs in Arabic only to quote sentences. Al-A'lam held that Abraham is in the nominative by being left unanalysed (ihmal), because no governing element preceded it that affects its form, since the speech verb affects only a singular noun that includes the meaning of a sentence. So it remained unanalysed, and an unanalysed element, when joined to another, takes the nominative, as in the Arabs' saying "one and two" when counting, when they did not introduce any governor either in form or in implication, and they coordinated some number-names with others. The discussion of al-A'lam's view and its refutation is mentioned in the grammar books.

﴿They said, "Then bring him"﴾, that is, bring him here, ﴿before the eyes of the people﴾, that is, visibly, in their sight. So ﴿before the eyes of the people﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier, and (ʿalā) has the figurative sense of elevation, as if, because of their staring at him and the raising of their gazes to see him, he is elevated above their sight. ﴿That perhaps they may bear witness﴾ against him with what was heard from him, or with what proceeded from him of smashing their idols, or that they may witness what will befall him of Our punishment or Our victory over him, which leads to his punishment. It was said: "the people" here means the king's elite and his close associates, and the implied sense of the speech is: ﴿bring him﴾ in that state, under the people's gaze upon him.

﴿They said, "Did you do this to our gods, Abraham?"﴾, that is, the breaking and the smashing. As for the nominative status of (you): the preferred view is that it is governed by an omitted verb which the word (did you do) explains; and since the verb is omitted, the pronoun becomes detached. It is also permissible that it is a subject (mubtada'). When the noun precedes the verb in this kind of construction, the verb is taken as performed, and the question concerns its agent, which is the doubtful element. When the verb precedes, the verb itself is doubtful, so one asks about it: did it occur or not? The apparent view is that ﴿but﴾ (bal) is for turning away from an omitted sentence, that is: he said, "I did not do it; rather, the real agent is God." ﴿Rather, it was done by their chief this one﴾. The verb is attributed to ﴿their chief﴾ metaphorically, because the cause of breaking these idols was their veneration and worship of him and of what was less than him among the idols. This motivated them to smash and break them, so the verb was attributed to the chief, since their veneration of him was greater than their veneration of what was below him. Al-Zamakhshari said something close to this. It is also possible that the chief's act is conditional, so that it is hung on an impossibility, meaning: if these idols ﴿could speak﴾ and inform [you] who did this to them, then the chief is the one who did it. Ibn Qutayba alluded to something of this kind.

Al-Zamakhshari said: This is among the indirect expressions (ta'arid) of speech and the subtleties of this type, which only the minds of the trained scholars of rhetoric penetrate. The matter is that Abraham, may God's blessings be upon him, did not intend to attribute the act he had performed to the idol. He intended rather to establish it for himself and to affirm it for it in an allusive manner, by which he attained his aim of silencing them and rebuking them. This is like what your companion says to you when you have written him a letter in an elegant hand, and you are famous for beautiful penmanship: "Did you write this when your companion is illiterate, unable to write well, or able only to scribble corrupt scrawls?" You reply to him: "Rather, you wrote it." Your intention in this answer was to affirm it for him with mockery of him, not to deny it of you nor to affirm it for the illiterate or the scribbler, because the affirmation of it, when the matter lies between you two, is for the one who is incapable of it, as mockery, and an affirmation for the capable one. It is also possible that this is a report of what their doctrine allows, as if he said to them: "What do you deny of his doing this, since it is due to one who is worshipped and claimed as a god to be able to do this and worse?"

It is related that he said: ﴿Their chief did it﴾ — "this, out of anger, that these little ones are worshipped alongside him while he is greater than them." End of quote. As for whoever makes the subject of the verb a pronoun referring to the word "youth" or to Abraham, or to another, in disagreement with the sense, for a religious purpose, and supports this by what is narrated in a hadith (or stops at ﴿Rather, he did it﴾, meaning: he who did it did it), and makes ﴿their chief this one﴾ a subject and predicate, as al-Kisa'i did; or whose original is ﴿fa'alahu﴾ in the sense of la'allahu ("perhaps he") with the lām lightened, as al-Farra' did, supported by the reading of Ibn al-Sumayfa' ﴿fa'alahu﴾ in the sense of la'allahu with the lām doubled: they are far from the path of eloquence.

﴿Then they turned to themselves﴾, that is, to their minds, when there became evident to them what Abraham, peace be upon him, had said: that the idols to which they had given worship should be asked and interrogated first. It is possible that ﴿they turned﴾ means: some of them turned to others. ﴿And said, "Indeed, you are the wrongdoers"﴾ in your questioning Abraham when you questioned him and did not question them. This was mentioned by Ibn Jarir; or when you worshipped what does not speak, said by Ibn 'Abbas; or when you did not protect your gods, said by Wahb; or in worshipping the lesser ones alongside this great one, also said by Wahb; or when Abraham baffled them with the axe on the neck of the chief, said by Muqatil and Ibn Ishaq; or ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ in actuality, in that you ascribed wrongdoing to Abraham when you said ﴿"Indeed, he is surely one of the wrongdoers"﴾, since these idols deserve what was done to them.

﴿Then they were turned upside down upon their heads﴾, that is, they were confused in their error, and they knew that the idols do not speak. This grieved them when he pointed out that the proof had been established against them. It is a metaphor for one who plunges into his error, as if he were upside down on his head, and this is the most ugly form for a human being. So his intellect was inverted, that is, reversed, because his form had been reversed, and he made his top his bottom. Their ''turning to themselves'' is thus a metonym for the straightness of their thinking, and their ''turning upside down'' is a metonym for their disputing and obstinacy. It is also possible that ﴿they were turned upside down upon their heads﴾ is a metonym for the lowering and bowing of their heads to the ground, in a manner of shame and humiliation, because of what Abraham had struck them with of the truth and crushed them with, so they could not bear an answer.

﴿And you certainly know﴾ [al-Saffat: 158] is the answer to an omitted oath, governed by an omitted speech verb in the position of a circumstantial qualifier, meaning: saying, ﴿"You certainly know that these do not speak"﴾. So how do you tell us ﴿"ask them"﴾? You intended by that only rebuke. It is possible that the turning upside down is of thought regarding what they would answer. Mujahid said: ﴿they were turned upside down upon their heads﴾, meaning: the lowly ones responded to the leaders. Here ﴿you know﴾ is suspended (mu'allaqa), and the negated sentence is in the position of the two objects of ''you know'' if it transitively takes two, or in the position of one object if it takes one. Abu Hayya, Ibn Abi 'Abla, Ibn Miqsam, Ibn al-Jarud and al-Bakrawi, both from Hisham, read ﴿nukkisū﴾ with the kaf doubled. Ridwan ibn al-Ma'bud read ﴿nakasū﴾ with the kaf lightened, in the active voice, meaning: they turned themselves upside down.

The lām in ﴿for you﴾ indicates the one at whom the expression of disgust is aimed: that is, for you and for your gods, this expression of disgust. Then he alerted them to that by which the realities of things are perceived, which is reason, and said: ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾, that is, the ugliness of what you are upon. It is a question of rebuke and denunciation.

In the speech there is an omitted element, whose implied sense is: when they returned from their festival to their gods and saw what had been done to them, they asked, as a matter of investigation and denunciation, saying: ﴿Who has done this?﴾ That is, the smashing and the shattering. ﴿Indeed, he is surely one of the wrongdoers﴾ in his audacity against gods who deserve glorification and honour. I say: they are two descriptions of ﴿a youth﴾, except that the first, namely ﴿who mentions them﴾, is necessary for ﴿heard﴾, because you do not say "I heard Zayd" and stop until you mention something of what is heard; but the second is not like that. The discussion of al-A'lam's view and its refutation is mentioned in the grammar books.

It was said: "the people" here means the king's elite and his close associates, and the implied sense of the speech is: ﴿bring him﴾ in that state, under the people's gaze upon him.

﴿They said, "Did you do this to our gods, Abraham?"﴾, that is, the breaking and the smashing. As for the nominative status of (you): the preferred view is that it is governed by an omitted verb which the word (did you do) explains; and since the verb is omitted, the pronoun becomes detached. It is also permissible that it is a subject (mubtada'). When the noun precedes the verb in this kind of construction, the verb is taken as performed, and the question concerns its agent, which is the doubtful element. When the verb precedes, the verb itself is doubtful, so one asks about it: did it occur or not? The apparent view is that ﴿but﴾ (bal) is for turning away from an omitted sentence, that is: he said, "I did not do it; rather, the real agent is God." ﴿Rather, it was done by their chief this one﴾. The verb is attributed to ﴿their chief﴾ metaphorically, because the cause of breaking these idols was their veneration and worship of him and of what was less than him among the idols. This motivated them to smash and break them, so the verb was attributed to the chief, since their veneration of him was greater than their veneration of what was below him. Al-Zamakhshari said something close to this. It is also possible that the chief's act is conditional, so that it is hung on an impossibility, meaning: if these idols ﴿could speak﴾ and inform [you] who did this to them, then the chief is the one who did it. Ibn Qutayba alluded to something of this kind.

Al-Zamakhshari said: This is among the indirect expressions (ta'arid) of speech and the subtleties of this type, which only the minds of the trained scholars of rhetoric penetrate. The matter is that Abraham, may God's blessings be upon him, did not intend to attribute the act he had performed to the idol. He intended rather to establish it for himself and to affirm it for it in an allusive manner, by which he attained his aim of silencing them and rebuking them. This is like what your companion says to you when you have written him a letter in an elegant hand, and you are famous for beautiful penmanship: "Did you write this when your companion is illiterate, unable to write well, or able only to scribble corrupt scrawls?" You reply to him: "Rather, you wrote it." Your intention in this answer was to affirm it for him with mockery of him, not to deny it of you nor to affirm it for the illiterate or the scribbler, because the affirmation of it, when the matter lies between you two, is for the one who is incapable of it, as mockery, and an affirmation for the capable one. It is also possible that this is a report of what their doctrine allows, as if he said to them: "What do you deny of his doing this, since it is due to one who is worshipped and claimed as a god to be able to do this and worse?"

It is possible that ﴿they turned﴾ means: some of them turned to others. ﴿And said, "Indeed, you are the wrongdoers"﴾ in your questioning Abraham when you questioned him and did not question them. This was mentioned by Ibn Jarir; or when you worshipped what does not speak, said by Ibn 'Abbas; or when you did not protect your gods, said by Wahb; or in worshipping the lesser ones alongside this great one, also said by Wahb; or when Abraham baffled them with the axe on the neck of the chief, said by Muqatil and Ibn Ishaq; or ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ in actuality, in that you ascribed wrongdoing to Abraham when you said ﴿"Indeed, he is surely one of the wrongdoers"﴾, since these idols deserve what was done to them.

﴿Then they were turned upside down upon their heads﴾, that is, they were confused in their error, and they knew that the idols do not speak. It is also possible that ﴿they were turned upside down upon their heads﴾ is a metonym for the lowering and bowing of their heads to the ground, in a manner of shame and humiliation, because of what Abraham had struck them with of the truth and crushed them with, so they could not bear an answer.

﴿They said, "Burn him and support your gods, if you are going to act."﴾ ﴿We said, "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham."﴾ ﴿They intended a plot against him, but We made them the greatest losers.﴾ ﴿And We delivered him and Lot to the land which We had blessed for all the worlds.﴾ ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift, and We made each of them righteous.﴾ ﴿And We made them leaders guiding by Our command, and We revealed to them the doing of good deeds, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakah, and they were worshippers of Us.﴾ ﴿And to Lot We gave judgment and knowledge, and We delivered him from the town that was committing abominations. Indeed, they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿And We admitted him into Our mercy. So will you be grateful?﴾ [21:81] ﴿And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind, violent, running by his command to the land which We had blessed. And We are Knower of all things.﴾ [21:82] ﴿And among the devils were those who dived for him and did work other than that, and We were their guardians.﴾

[p. 328]

When he admonished them about the ugliness of their deed and overcame them by establishing the proof against them, they resorted to harming him and to zeal for their gods, and chose the most severe punishment, which is burning with fire. Fire is the cause of utter annihilation and complete destruction. Likewise, everyone against whom the proof has been established and who has the power resorts to hostility and extermination, just as the Quraysh did with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he silenced them with the proof and they were unable to oppose what he brought them. They turned to vengeance and preferred assassination, but Allah protected him.

The apparent meaning of ﴿They said, "Burn him"﴾ is that some of them said to others. It has also been said that Nimrod proposed burning him. From Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both): "[He was] a man from the bedouin of the non-Arabs." Al-Zamakhshari said: "He means the Kurds." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "It has been narrated that he was a man from the Kurds, from the bedouin of Persia, that is, its desert dwellers. So Allah caused the earth to swallow him, and he keeps sinking into it until the Day of Resurrection." They mentioned a name for this speaker about which there is disagreement, and no certain truth can be reached concerning it, because it is not vocalized or dotted. Thus many non-Arabic names occur in tafsir books that cannot be established as accurate words, because they lack vocalization and diacritical dots; therefore it is appropriate to abandon transmitting them.

It has been narrated that when they resolved to burn him, they imprisoned him, then built a structure like an enclosure (ḥaẓīrah) at Kuthā, and they differed concerning the length of his imprisonment, the width and length of the enclosure, the duration of gathering firewood, the duration of kindling, his age at that time, the duration of his stay in the fire, and the manner in which the places of the fire were set. These are conflicting differences, and we have left their mention. They also made a catapult (manjanīq). It was said: it was taught to them by Iblis, since it had not been made before. Abraham was bound with ropes, placed in the pan of the catapult, and hurled, so he fell into the fire.

It has been narrated that Gabriel (peace be upon him) came to him while he was in the air and said: "Do you have any need?" He said: "As for you, no." The exegetes mentioned things that issued from the gecko, the mule, the swallow, the frog, and the ʿuḍrufūṭ (a small creature), but Allah knows best about that.

[Nimrod] said: "I will draw near to your god," and he slaughtered four thousand cows. Then he held back from Abraham. Abraham was at that time sixteen years old. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 80–82 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We gave him victory over the people﴾ [21:77]. He transitive-linked it with *min* because it implies the meaning of "We delivered him" (*najjaynāhu*) with "We gave him victory" (*naṣarnā*), "from the people," or "We protected him and guarded him," that is, from the harm of the people, in accordance with His saying: ﴿Who will defend us from the might of God if it comes upon us?﴾ [40:29]. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is the *naṣr* whose reflexive form is *intaṣara*. I heard a Hudhali man invoking against a thief: "O God, give them victory over him" (*unṣurhum minhu*), meaning: "make them avengers against him." This is a meaning of *naṣara* that does not readily come to mind. Abu 'Ubayda said: *min* here means *'alā* (against), so that "and We gave him victory against the people" and "so We drowned them" means: We destroyed them by drowning. *Ajma'īn* is an emphasis of the pronoun in the accusative. Emphasis with *ajma'īn* not following *kullihim* has occurred frequently in the Qur'an, and this is a proof against Ibn Malik in his claim that emphasis with *ajma'īn* is rare and that its common usage is as a follower of *kullihim*.

﴿And Dawud and Sulayman﴾ [21:78] is coordinated with "Nuh" (*nūḥan*). Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Idh*" (when) is a substitute (*badal*) for both of them. End of quote. The better view is that the implied construction is: "Remember Dawud, the mountains..." [21:79], meaning their story and their situation, "when the two of them judged" [21:78]. Ibn 'Atiyya made "and Dawud and Sulayman" coordinated with "Nuh," which is coordinated with "Lut," so that the governing verb is the same: *ātaynā* (We gave), which is understood and governs Lut, explained by *ātaynā*. Thus the sense is "and We gave Nuh, Dawud and Sulayman," meaning We gave them "judgment and knowledge" [21:79]. This is not far-fetched, and the implied "remember" was stated by a group of scholars. Dawud was a king and prophet who judged among the people. This incident occurred when his son had grown up, and he would sit at the door through which the disputants exited, while they used to enter to Dawud through another door. A man who had a field (*ḥarth*), some said a vineyard (*karm*), came to him in dispute, and *ḥarth* is used for both, though it is more common for crops and is further from metaphor. A man's sheep had entered his field and damaged it. Dawud ruled that the sheep be handed over to the owner of the field. If it was a vineyard, he judged that the sheep should compensate for what they had damaged of the produce; if it was a crop, he judged that they should compensate for the field and its produce. The two went out, and when the owner of the sheep complained, Sulayman came and said: "O Prophet of God, I see a ruling that is gentler on all: let the owner of the sheep take the field, tend it and restore it until it returns to what it was, and let the owner of the field take the sheep during that period, benefiting from their uses of milk, wool and offspring. When the field returns to its state, each owner's property is returned to him." The sheep returned to their owner and the field to its owner. Dawud said: "You have been granted success, my son," and he decided between them accordingly. The apparent meaning is that each of Dawud and Sulayman judged by what appeared to him, and that was correct in his view. Their judgment was therefore by *ijtihad* (independent reasoning), which is the view of the majority, and this verse is cited as evidence for the permissibility of *ijtihad*.

It has also been said: each of them judged by a revelation from God, and the ruling of Dawud was abrogated (*nusikha*) by the ruling of Sulayman. The meaning of ﴿We gave understanding of it to Sulayman﴾ [21:79] is: We gave him the decisive judgment, which abrogates, that God willed to be established in that case. 'Ikrima read *fa-af-hamnāhā*, transitive by the *hamza*, just as the majority's reading is transitive by doubling. The pronoun in ﴿fa-fahhamnāhā﴾ refers to the judgment or the verdict. The pronoun in ﴿for their judgment﴾ [21:78] refers to the two judges and to those judged for and against them. The verbal noun here is not annexed to an agent or an object, nor does it govern anything in the implied construction, so it cannot be resolved into a verb with a verbal particle. Rather, it is a figure of speech: "the cleverness of the clever and the mind of the intelligent," and the meaning is "and We were witnesses to the judgment that was issued in this matter." The verbal noun here is not intended as treatment but as the existence of the reality. Ibn 'Abbas read *li-ḥukmihimā* (for their two judgments), so the pronoun refers to Dawud and Sulayman. The meaning of "witnesses" is that nothing is hidden from Us, and nothing escapes Us. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask what is the basis of each of the two rulings, I say: as for Dawud's ruling, since the harm was caused by the sheep, they were handed over to the injured party for their offence, just as Abu Hanifa said regarding a slave who commits a crime against a person: the master hands him over for that or ransoms him; according to al-Shafi'i, he sells him for that or ransoms him. Perhaps the value of the sheep equalled the loss to the field. As for the basis of Sulayman's ruling, he made the benefit from the sheep correspond to what was lost of the benefit from the field, without the owner's ownership of the sheep ceasing, and he required the owner of the sheep to work on the field until the harm and loss disappeared." End of quote.

"Then if you ask: if this incident had occurred in our law, what would its ruling be? I say: Abu Hanifa and his companions do not consider the owner liable for damage by night or by day unless the animal has a driver or a leader, while al-Shafi'i requires liability." End of quote.

The apparent view is that each of the two rulings is correct, according to His saying: ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾ [21:79]. The apparent reading is that ﴿glorifying﴾ (*yusabbiḥna*) is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from "the mountains," meaning "glorifying." It has also been said that it is a resumptive clause (*isti'nāf*), as if someone asked: "How did He subjugate them?" and it was answered: ﴿glorifying﴾. It was said: Dawud would pass by the mountains glorifying God, and they would respond to him. It was also said: they would travel with him wherever he went. The apparent view is that their glorification was by speech, God creating speech in them, just as the pebbles glorified God in the palm of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the people heard it. Dawud alone heard it, as Yahya ibn Salam said. It was also said: each of them glorified God. Qatada said: "glorifying" means praying. It was also said: moving, from swimming. Al-Zamakhshari said: just as He created it, meaning the speech in the tree when He spoke to Musa. End of quote. This is the view of the Mu'tazila, who deny that the attribute of speech is literally true of God Most High. It was also said: the attribution of glorification to them is metaphorical; since they moved by God's motion, they evoked glorification in those who saw them, so it was attributed to them. Most scholars hold that their glorification is the saying "Glory be to God" (*subḥān Allāh*).

*Wa-al-ṭayr* (and the birds) is in the accusative, coordinated with "the mountains," and coordination does not necessarily mean that it falls under the scope of the glorification. It was also said that it is an object of accompaniment (*maf'ūl ma'ahu*), meaning "they glorify together with the birds." It was read *wa-al-ṭayru* in the nominative, on the basis of the inceptive (*mubtada'*), with an omitted predicate, meaning "subjugated," indicated by "We subjugated," or on the basis of the pronoun in *yusabbiḥna* according to the view of the Kufans. This is the justification of an irregular reading.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why were "the mountains" mentioned before "the birds"? I say: because their subjugation and glorification are more wondrous and more indicative of power, and more included in the miraculous, since the mountains are inanimate, while the birds are living, speaking beings. End of quote. His saying "speaking" (*nāṭiq*): if he means that it has a rational soul, as they say in the definition of the human being that he is a speaking animal, then the bird would have to be a human; and if he means that it speaks as a human speaks, then that is not correct. He meant only that it makes a sound, that it has a voice. Describing the bird as "speaking" is metaphorical, since in reality it has no speech.

His saying ﴿And We were doers﴾ [21:79] means: We were doers of these marvels, the subjugation of the mountains, their glorification, and the birds, for whomever We single out with Our honour.

﴿And We taught him the craft of making armour for you﴾ [21:80]. *Labūs* is that which is worn, a form of the pattern *fa'ūl* in the sense of the passive participle, like *rakūb* in the sense of *marko ub* (that which is ridden). Here it means the coat of mail. *Labūs* is that which is worn. The poet said:

*On them are lions, fierce, their armour is flowing white (coats) that the arrow cannot pierce.*

Qatada said: they were plates, and the first to link and ring them was Dawud, so they combined lightness and protection. It was also said: *labūs* is every instrument of weapons, a sword, spear, coat of mail, helmet, and what is similar to these; Dawud was the first to make the coats of mail called *zarad* (chain mail). It is said: two angels descended from heaven and passed by Dawud. One said to the other: "What a fine man, except that he eats from the public treasury." So he asked God to provide him from his own earnings, and He softened iron for him, and he made from it coats of mail. God Most High favoured him by granting him judgment and knowledge, subjugating the mountains and birds with him, and teaching him the craft of armour. In this is the excellence of this craft, since God attributed its teaching to Himself.

Then He favoured us with it, saying: ﴿so that it may protect you from your violence﴾ [21:80], meaning: so that it might be a shield for you in your warfare and a cause of deliverance from your enemy. *Labūs* was read with a *ḍamma* on the *lām*, but the majority read it with a *fatḥa*. The majority read *li-yuḥṣinakum* with the third-person masculine (*yā' al-ghayba*), meaning God, which is an *iltifāt* (shift of person), since it came after the first-person pronoun in *'allamnāhu*. This is supported by the reading of Abu Bakr from 'Asim with the first-person plural *nūn*, which is the reading of Abu Hanifa, Mas'ud ibn Salih, Ruways, al-Ju'fi, Harun, Yunus and al-Munaqqar, all of them from Abu 'Amr: *li-yuḥṣinakum* with Dawud as subject. *Labūs* is said to be the subject, or the teaching. Ibn 'Amir, Hafs, al-Hasan, Salam, Abu Ja'far, Shayba and Zayd ibn 'Ali read with the *tā'*, meaning "so that the craft (or the armour) may protect you," the armour being feminine in the sense of "coat of mail," and the coat of iron is feminine. All three of these readings are with a sukun on the *ḥā'* and light doubling. al-Fuqaymi from Abu 'Amr and Ibn Abi Hammad from Abu Bakr read with the *yā'* below and *fatḥa* on the *ḥā'* and doubled *ṣād*. Ibn Wassab and al-A'mash read with the *tā'* above and doubling.

The *lām* in "for you" (*lakum*) may be causal, attaching to "We taught him," meaning "for your sake"; and "so that it may protect you" would be in the position of an appositive substitute, with the *lām* of the genitive repeated with it, since the verb is in the subjunctive by the implied *an*, so it is resolved into a verbal noun, meaning "for your protection from your violence." It may also be that "for you" is an attribute of *labūs*, attaching to an omitted word, meaning "belonging to you." It is also possible that "so that it may protect you" is a causal clause for the teaching, attaching to "We taught him," and that it is a causal clause for the omitted state attached to "for you."

﴿So will you be grateful?﴾ [21:80] is an interrogative that implies a command, meaning: "Be grateful to God for what He has bestowed upon you," like His saying: ﴿So will you desist?﴾ [5:91], meaning: "desist from what God has forbidden."

When He mentioned what He had singled out for His prophet Dawud, peace be upon him, He mentioned what He had singled out for his son Sulayman, peace be upon him, saying: ﴿And to Sulayman, the wind﴾ [21:81]. The construction came here with the *lām* when mentioning the subjugation of the wind to Sulayman, and when mentioning the subjugation of the mountains it came with the word *ma'a* (with), saying: ﴿And We subjugated the mountains with Dawud﴾ [21:79]. Likewise: ﴿O mountains, echo with him﴾ [34:10], and He said: ﴿So We subjugated to him the wind, running by his command﴾ [38:36]. This is because when the two of them shared in the glorification, the mention of *ma'a* indicating companionship was appropriate; and since the wind was made to serve Sulayman, it was attributed to him with the *lām* of possession, because it was in his obedience and under his command.

The majority read *al-rīḥa* (the wind) in the singular with the accusative. Ibn Hurmuz and Abu Bakr in one transmission read it in the singular with the nominative. al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read *al-riyāḥa* in the plural with the accusative. Abu Haywa read it in the plural with the nominative. The accusative is based on an implied *sakh-kharnā* (We subjugated), and the nominative is based on the inceptive. *'Āṣifatan* (violently driving) is a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*), governed by *sakh-kharnā* in the reading of the one who put "the wind" in the accusative, and by what the prepositional phrase depends on in the reading of the one who put it in the nominative. It is said: "the wind blew violently" (*'aṣafat al-rīḥ*), so it is *'āṣif* and *'āṣifa*; in the dialect of Asad it is *a'ṣafat*, so it is *mu'ṣif* and *mu'ṣifa*. This wind was described as violent (*'aṣf*) and as gentle (*rakhā'*). *'Aṣf* is intensity in motion, and *rakhā'* is gentleness. It was said: this was in relation to the time in which Sulayman wanted one of the two qualities, so the time did not conflict. It was also said: the combination of the two qualities is that it was gentle in itself, pleasant like the breeze, but violent in its effect, covering in a short period of time, as God Most High said: ﴿Its morning course is a month's journey and its evening course a month's journey﴾ [34:12]. It was also said: the gentleness was at the beginning and the violence after that, in the manner of humans hastening toward their homeland. This view refers to the difference of the times and to its movement by His command, obedient to him, according to what he wished and commanded.

*Commentary continues in part 2.*

The land (al-Ard) is the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria), which was his dwelling place and the seat of his kingdom. It is also said to be Palestine, and it is also said to be Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Al-Kalbi said: he would ride upon it from Istakhr to al-Sham. It is said that it is possible the land to which Sulayman was travelling was whatever land it was, and it was described as blessed because he came to a land that he improved by killing its disbelievers, establishing faith in it, and spreading justice, and there is no greater blessing than this. The apparent meaning is that ﴿which We blessed﴾ is a qualifier of the land. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: the sentence is complete at His saying "to the land," and ﴿which We blessed therein﴾ is a qualifier of the wind. So there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the verse, meaning that the original structure is: "And for Sulayman [We subjected] the wind (p. 333) ﴿which We blessed therein﴾, violent, running by his command, to the land."

From Wahb: when Sulayman went out to his assembly, the birds would gather around him, and the jinn and humans would stand for him until he sat on his throne. He would not stay back from campaigning: he would order a wooden platform to be extended, with the people, the animals and the instruments of war upon it. Then he would order the violent wind, and it would lift it. Then he would order the gentle wind, and it would carry him for a month in its journey out and a month in its journey back.

From Muqatil: the devils wove for him a carpet of gold and silk, a farsakh by a farsakh (about 6 km by 6 km). In its centre they placed a pulpit of gold on which he sat, and around it were golden chairs on which the prophets sat, and silver chairs on which the scholars sat, and around them were the people, and around the people were the jinn and the devils. The birds shaded him from the sun, and the east wind (rih al-Saba) lifted the carpet a distance of a month's journey, from morning to afternoon and from afternoon to morning. The historians (al-akhbariyyun, the transmitters of reports) have said much about the kingdom of Sulayman, but one should rely only on what Allah has related in His Book and in the hadith of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Since these special privileges are extremely strange by ordinary standards, Allah the Exalted informed us that His knowledge encompasses all things, and He directs them according to what His knowledge has preceded. When the Exalted mentioned the subjugation of the wind to him, the wind being a transparent body that is not perceived and cannot be seen, He then mentioned the subjugation of the devils to him, and they are subtle bodies that possess understanding. What unites the two is also the speed of movement. Do you not see His saying: ﴿An ifrit (a powerful jinn) of the jinn said: "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place"﴾ [al-Naml: 39].

(Man) is in a position of accusative (nasb), meaning: "And We subjected [to him] ﴿and of the devils, those who dive for him﴾," or it is in a position of nominative (raf') as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), with the predicate being the prepositional phrase preceding it. The apparent reading is that (man) is a relative pronoun (mawsulah). Abu al-Baqa said: it is an indefinite qualified noun (nakirah mawsufah). The pronoun in (yaghwusuna, they dive) is plural, taking into account the meaning of (man). What made this acceptable is that a plural noun preceded it, as the poet said:

"Indeed, among women there is one who is a garden, whose meadows bloom before her and wither."

Since the word "women" (al-niswan) preceded, it was treated according to the meaning of "min" (some), so it was made feminine, and he did not say "who is a garden" (man huwa rawdah) [in the masculine]. The meaning is that they dive for him into the seas to extract pearls. Diving implies both the diver and what is dived for, namely the jewel. That is why it was not mentioned. Or he said "for him," meaning for Sulayman, because the diver may dive for himself or for others. So He mentioned that the diving was not for their own sakes; it was for the sake of Sulayman and in obedience to his command. The reference with this is to the diving, that is, apart from diving, such as building cities and palaces, as He said: ﴿They make for him whatever he wishes: sanctuaries (mihrab), statues...﴾ [Saba': 13], to the end of the verse. It is also said that the bathhouse (hammam), the depilatory paste (nawrah), the mill (tahun), glassware (qawarir), and soap (sabun) were among what they extracted.

﴿And We were guardians over them﴾, meaning: lest they deviate from his command, or alter, or change, or lest any corruption be found among them in what they were subjugated to. It is also said: "guardians" means that they would not stir up anyone during the time of Sulayman. It is also said: "guardians" means so that they would not flee. It is said: He subjected them to a task that does not need guarding, because they would not corrupt what they made. The subjugation of the densest bodies was to Dawud, and this was the stone, when He made it speak in glorification, and the iron, when He placed in his fingers the power of fire until the iron became soft for him, and he made from it chainmail (zarad). The subjugation of the most subtle bodies was to Sulayman, and these were the wind and the devils, who are of fire. They used to dive into water, and water extinguishes fire, yet it did not harm them. This is a clear proof of His overwhelming power, and of the bringing forth of opposites from opposites, and of the possibility of reviving the decayed bone, and of making dry dust into a living creature. When the truthful one (al-Sadiq, the Prophet) reports it, it becomes obligatory to accept it and to believe in its existence. End.(p. 334)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 80–82 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We gave him victory over the people﴾ [21:77]. He transitive-linked it with *min* because it implies the meaning of "We delivered him" (*najjaynāhu*) with "We gave him victory" (*naṣarnā*), "from the people," or "We protected him and guarded him," that is, from the harm of the people, in accordance with His saying: ﴿Who will defend us from the might of God if it comes upon us?﴾ [40:29]. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is the *naṣr* whose reflexive form is *intaṣara*. I heard a Hudhali man invoking against a thief: "O God, give them victory over him" (*unṣurhum minhu*), meaning: "make them avengers against him." This is a meaning of *naṣara* that does not readily come to mind. Abu 'Ubayda said: *min* here means *'alā* (against), so that "and We gave him victory against the people" and "so We drowned them" means: We destroyed them by drowning. *Ajma'īn* is an emphasis of the pronoun in the accusative. Emphasis with *ajma'īn* not following *kullihim* has occurred frequently in the Qur'an, and this is a proof against Ibn Malik in his claim that emphasis with *ajma'īn* is rare and that its common usage is as a follower of *kullihim*.

﴿And Dawud and Sulayman﴾ [21:78] is coordinated with "Nuh" (*nūḥan*). Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Idh*" (when) is a substitute (*badal*) for both of them. End of quote. The better view is that the implied construction is: "Remember Dawud, the mountains..." [21:79], meaning their story and their situation, "when the two of them judged" [21:78]. Ibn 'Atiyya made "and Dawud and Sulayman" coordinated with "Nuh," which is coordinated with "Lut," so that the governing verb is the same: *ātaynā* (We gave), which is understood and governs Lut, explained by *ātaynā*. Thus the sense is "and We gave Nuh, Dawud and Sulayman," meaning We gave them "judgment and knowledge" [21:79]. This is not far-fetched, and the implied "remember" was stated by a group of scholars. This incident occurred when his son had grown up, and he would sit at the door through which the disputants exited, while they used to enter to Dawud through another door. The meaning of "witnesses" is that nothing is hidden from Us, and nothing escapes Us. As for the basis of Sulayman's ruling, he made the benefit from the sheep correspond to what was lost of the benefit from the field, without the owner's ownership of the sheep ceasing, and he required the owner of the sheep to work on the field until the harm and loss disappeared." End of quote.

Here it means the coat of mail. *Labūs* is that which is worn. The poet said:

*On them are lions, fierce, their armour is flowing white (coats) that the arrow cannot pierce.*
