So he asked God to provide him from his own earnings, and He softened iron for him, and he made from it coats of mail. God Most High favoured him by granting him judgment and knowledge, subjugating the mountains and birds with him, and teaching him the craft of armour. In this is the excellence of this craft, since God attributed its teaching to Himself.

Then He favoured us with it, saying: ﴿so that it may protect you from your violence﴾ [21:80], meaning: so that it might be a shield for you in your warfare and a cause of deliverance from your enemy. *Labūs* was read with a *ḍamma* on the *lām*, but the majority read it with a *fatḥa*. The majority read *li-yuḥṣinakum* with the third-person masculine (*yā' al-ghayba*), meaning God, which is an *iltifāt* (shift of person), since it came after the first-person pronoun in *'allamnāhu*. This is supported by the reading of Abu Bakr from 'Asim with the first-person plural *nūn*, which is the reading of Abu Hanifa, Mas'ud ibn Salih, Ruways, al-Ju'fi, Harun, Yunus and al-Munaqqar, all of them from Abu 'Amr: *li-yuḥṣinakum* with Dawud as subject. *Labūs* is said to be the subject, or the teaching. Ibn 'Amir, Hafs, al-Hasan, Salam, Abu Ja'far, Shayba and Zayd ibn 'Ali read with the *tā'*, meaning "so that the craft (or the armour) may protect you," the armour being feminine in the sense of "coat of mail," and the coat of iron is feminine. All three of these readings are with a sukun on the *ḥā'* and light doubling. al-Fuqaymi from Abu 'Amr and Ibn Abi Hammad from Abu Bakr read with the *yā'* below and *fatḥa* on the *ḥā'* and doubled *ṣād*. Ibn Wassab and al-A'mash read with the *tā'* above and doubling.

The *lām* in "for you" (*lakum*) may be causal, attaching to "We taught him," meaning "for your sake"; and "so that it may protect you" would be in the position of an appositive substitute, with the *lām* of the genitive repeated with it, since the verb is in the subjunctive by the implied *an*, so it is resolved into a verbal noun, meaning "for your protection from your violence." It may also be that "for you" is an attribute of *labūs*, attaching to an omitted word, meaning "belonging to you." It is also possible that "so that it may protect you" is a causal clause for the teaching, attaching to "We taught him," and that it is a causal clause for the omitted state attached to "for you."

﴿So will you be grateful?﴾ [21:80] is an interrogative that implies a command, meaning: "Be grateful to God for what He has bestowed upon you," like His saying: ﴿So will you desist?﴾ [5:91], meaning: "desist from what God has forbidden."

When He mentioned what He had singled out for His prophet Dawud, peace be upon him, He mentioned what He had singled out for his son Sulayman, peace be upon him, saying: ﴿And to Sulayman, the wind﴾ [21:81]. The construction came here with the *lām* when mentioning the subjugation of the wind to Sulayman, and when mentioning the subjugation of the mountains it came with the word *ma'a* (with), saying: ﴿And We subjugated the mountains with Dawud﴾ [21:79]. Likewise: ﴿O mountains, echo with him﴾ [34:10], and He said: ﴿So We subjugated to him the wind, running by his command﴾ [38:36]. This is because when the two of them shared in the glorification, the mention of *ma'a* indicating companionship was appropriate; and since the wind was made to serve Sulayman, it was attributed to him with the *lām* of possession, because it was in his obedience and under his command.

The majority read *al-rīḥa* (the wind) in the singular with the accusative. Ibn Hurmuz and Abu Bakr in one transmission read it in the singular with the nominative. al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read *al-riyāḥa* in the plural with the accusative. Abu Haywa read it in the plural with the nominative. The accusative is based on an implied *sakh-kharnā* (We subjugated), and the nominative is based on the inceptive. *'Āṣifatan* (violently driving) is a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*), governed by *sakh-kharnā* in the reading of the one who put "the wind" in the accusative, and by what the prepositional phrase depends on in the reading of the one who put it in the nominative. It is said: "the wind blew violently" (*'aṣafat al-rīḥ*), so it is *'āṣif* and *'āṣifa*; in the dialect of Asad it is *a'ṣafat*, so it is *mu'ṣif* and *mu'ṣifa*. This wind was described as violent (*'aṣf*) and as gentle (*rakhā'*). *'Aṣf* is intensity in motion, and *rakhā'* is gentleness. It was said: this was in relation to the time in which Sulayman wanted one of the two qualities, so the time did not conflict. It was also said: the combination of the two qualities is that it was gentle in itself, pleasant like the breeze, but violent in its effect, covering in a short period of time, as God Most High said: ﴿Its morning course is a month's journey and its evening course a month's journey﴾ [34:12]. It was also said: the gentleness was at the beginning and the violence after that, in the manner of humans hastening toward their homeland. This view refers to the difference of the times and to its movement by His command, obedient to him, according to what he wished and commanded.

*Commentary continues in part 2.*

The land (al-Ard) is the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria), which was his dwelling place and the seat of his kingdom. It is also said to be Palestine, and it is also said to be Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Al-Kalbi said: he would ride upon it from Istakhr to al-Sham. It is said that it is possible the land to which Sulayman was travelling was whatever land it was, and it was described as blessed because he came to a land that he improved by killing its disbelievers, establishing faith in it, and spreading justice, and there is no greater blessing than this. The apparent meaning is that ﴿which We blessed﴾ is a qualifier of the land. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: the sentence is complete at His saying "to the land," and ﴿which We blessed therein﴾ is a qualifier of the wind. So there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the verse, meaning that the original structure is: "And for Sulayman [We subjected] the wind (p. 333) ﴿which We blessed therein﴾, violent, running by his command, to the land."

From Wahb: when Sulayman went out to his assembly, the birds would gather around him, and the jinn and humans would stand for him until he sat on his throne. He would not stay back from campaigning: he would order a wooden platform to be extended, with the people, the animals and the instruments of war upon it. Then he would order the violent wind, and it would lift it. Then he would order the gentle wind, and it would carry him for a month in its journey out and a month in its journey back.

From Muqatil: the devils wove for him a carpet of gold and silk, a farsakh by a farsakh (about 6 km by 6 km). In its centre they placed a pulpit of gold on which he sat, and around it were golden chairs on which the prophets sat, and silver chairs on which the scholars sat, and around them were the people, and around the people were the jinn and the devils. The birds shaded him from the sun, and the east wind (rih al-Saba) lifted the carpet a distance of a month's journey, from morning to afternoon and from afternoon to morning. The historians (al-akhbariyyun, the transmitters of reports) have said much about the kingdom of Sulayman, but one should rely only on what Allah has related in His Book and in the hadith of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Since these special privileges are extremely strange by ordinary standards, Allah the Exalted informed us that His knowledge encompasses all things, and He directs them according to what His knowledge has preceded. When the Exalted mentioned the subjugation of the wind to him, the wind being a transparent body that is not perceived and cannot be seen, He then mentioned the subjugation of the devils to him, and they are subtle bodies that possess understanding. What unites the two is also the speed of movement. Do you not see His saying: ﴿An ifrit (a powerful jinn) of the jinn said: "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place"﴾ [al-Naml: 39].

(Man) is in a position of accusative (nasb), meaning: "And We subjected [to him] ﴿and of the devils, those who dive for him﴾," or it is in a position of nominative (raf') as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), with the predicate being the prepositional phrase preceding it. The apparent reading is that (man) is a relative pronoun (mawsulah). Abu al-Baqa said: it is an indefinite qualified noun (nakirah mawsufah). The pronoun in (yaghwusuna, they dive) is plural, taking into account the meaning of (man). What made this acceptable is that a plural noun preceded it, as the poet said:

"Indeed, among women there is one who is a garden, whose meadows bloom before her and wither."

Since the word "women" (al-niswan) preceded, it was treated according to the meaning of "min" (some), so it was made feminine, and he did not say "who is a garden" (man huwa rawdah) [in the masculine]. The meaning is that they dive for him into the seas to extract pearls. Diving implies both the diver and what is dived for, namely the jewel. That is why it was not mentioned. Or he said "for him," meaning for Sulayman, because the diver may dive for himself or for others. So He mentioned that the diving was not for their own sakes; it was for the sake of Sulayman and in obedience to his command. The reference with this is to the diving, that is, apart from diving, such as building cities and palaces, as He said: ﴿They make for him whatever he wishes: sanctuaries (mihrab), statues...﴾ [Saba': 13], to the end of the verse. It is also said that the bathhouse (hammam), the depilatory paste (nawrah), the mill (tahun), glassware (qawarir), and soap (sabun) were among what they extracted.

﴿And We were guardians over them﴾, meaning: lest they deviate from his command, or alter, or change, or lest any corruption be found among them in what they were subjugated to. It is also said: "guardians" means that they would not stir up anyone during the time of Sulayman. It is also said: "guardians" means so that they would not flee. It is said: He subjected them to a task that does not need guarding, because they would not corrupt what they made. The subjugation of the densest bodies was to Dawud, and this was the stone, when He made it speak in glorification, and the iron, when He placed in his fingers the power of fire until the iron became soft for him, and he made from it chainmail (zarad). The subjugation of the most subtle bodies was to Sulayman, and these were the wind and the devils, who are of fire. They used to dive into water, and water extinguishes fire, yet it did not harm them. This is a clear proof of His overwhelming power, and of the bringing forth of opposites from opposites, and of the possibility of reviving the decayed bone, and of making dry dust into a living creature. When the truthful one (al-Sadiq, the Prophet) reports it, it becomes obligatory to accept it and to believe in its existence. End.(p. 334)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 80–82 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We gave him victory over the people﴾ [21:77]. He transitive-linked it with *min* because it implies the meaning of "We delivered him" (*najjaynāhu*) with "We gave him victory" (*naṣarnā*), "from the people," or "We protected him and guarded him," that is, from the harm of the people, in accordance with His saying: ﴿Who will defend us from the might of God if it comes upon us?﴾ [40:29]. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is the *naṣr* whose reflexive form is *intaṣara*. I heard a Hudhali man invoking against a thief: "O God, give them victory over him" (*unṣurhum minhu*), meaning: "make them avengers against him." This is a meaning of *naṣara* that does not readily come to mind. Abu 'Ubayda said: *min* here means *'alā* (against), so that "and We gave him victory against the people" and "so We drowned them" means: We destroyed them by drowning. *Ajma'īn* is an emphasis of the pronoun in the accusative. Emphasis with *ajma'īn* not following *kullihim* has occurred frequently in the Qur'an, and this is a proof against Ibn Malik in his claim that emphasis with *ajma'īn* is rare and that its common usage is as a follower of *kullihim*.

﴿And Dawud and Sulayman﴾ [21:78] is coordinated with "Nuh" (*nūḥan*). Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Idh*" (when) is a substitute (*badal*) for both of them. End of quote. The better view is that the implied construction is: "Remember Dawud, the mountains..." [21:79], meaning their story and their situation, "when the two of them judged" [21:78]. Ibn 'Atiyya made "and Dawud and Sulayman" coordinated with "Nuh," which is coordinated with "Lut," so that the governing verb is the same: *ātaynā* (We gave), which is understood and governs Lut, explained by *ātaynā*. Thus the sense is "and We gave Nuh, Dawud and Sulayman," meaning We gave them "judgment and knowledge" [21:79]. This is not far-fetched, and the implied "remember" was stated by a group of scholars. Dawud was a king and prophet who judged among the people. This incident occurred when his son had grown up, and he would sit at the door through which the disputants exited, while they used to enter to Dawud through another door. A man who had a field (*ḥarth*), some said a vineyard (*karm*), came to him in dispute, and *ḥarth* is used for both, though it is more common for crops and is further from metaphor. A man's sheep had entered his field and damaged it. Dawud ruled that the sheep be handed over to the owner of the field. If it was a vineyard, he judged that the sheep should compensate for what they had damaged of the produce; if it was a crop, he judged that they should compensate for the field and its produce. The two went out, and when the owner of the sheep complained, Sulayman came and said: "O Prophet of God, I see a ruling that is gentler on all: let the owner of the sheep take the field, tend it and restore it until it returns to what it was, and let the owner of the field take the sheep during that period, benefiting from their uses of milk, wool and offspring. When the field returns to its state, each owner's property is returned to him." The sheep returned to their owner and the field to its owner. Dawud said: "You have been granted success, my son," and he decided between them accordingly. The apparent meaning is that each of Dawud and Sulayman judged by what appeared to him, and that was correct in his view. Their judgment was therefore by *ijtihad* (independent reasoning), which is the view of the majority, and this verse is cited as evidence for the permissibility of *ijtihad*.

It has also been said: each of them judged by a revelation from God, and the ruling of Dawud was abrogated (*nusikha*) by the ruling of Sulayman. The meaning of ﴿We gave understanding of it to Sulayman﴾ [21:79] is: We gave him the decisive judgment, which abrogates, that God willed to be established in that case. 'Ikrima read *fa-af-hamnāhā*, transitive by the *hamza*, just as the majority's reading is transitive by doubling. The pronoun in ﴿fa-fahhamnāhā﴾ refers to the judgment or the verdict. The pronoun in ﴿for their judgment﴾ [21:78] refers to the two judges and to those judged for and against them. The verbal noun here is not annexed to an agent or an object, nor does it govern anything in the implied construction, so it cannot be resolved into a verb with a verbal particle. Rather, it is a figure of speech: "the cleverness of the clever and the mind of the intelligent," and the meaning is "and We were witnesses to the judgment that was issued in this matter." The verbal noun here is not intended as treatment but as the existence of the reality. Ibn 'Abbas read *li-ḥukmihimā* (for their two judgments), so the pronoun refers to Dawud and Sulayman. The meaning of "witnesses" is that nothing is hidden from Us, and nothing escapes Us. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask what is the basis of each of the two rulings, I say: as for Dawud's ruling, since the harm was caused by the sheep, they were handed over to the injured party for their offence, just as Abu Hanifa said regarding a slave who commits a crime against a person: the master hands him over for that or ransoms him; according to al-Shafi'i, he sells him for that or ransoms him. Perhaps the value of the sheep equalled the loss to the field. As for the basis of Sulayman's ruling, he made the benefit from the sheep correspond to what was lost of the benefit from the field, without the owner's ownership of the sheep ceasing, and he required the owner of the sheep to work on the field until the harm and loss disappeared." End of quote.

"Then if you ask: if this incident had occurred in our law, what would its ruling be? I say: Abu Hanifa and his companions do not consider the owner liable for damage by night or by day unless the animal has a driver or a leader, while al-Shafi'i requires liability." End of quote.

The apparent view is that each of the two rulings is correct, according to His saying: ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾ [21:79]. The apparent reading is that ﴿glorifying﴾ (*yusabbiḥna*) is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from "the mountains," meaning "glorifying." It has also been said that it is a resumptive clause (*isti'nāf*), as if someone asked: "How did He subjugate them?" and it was answered: ﴿glorifying﴾. It was said: Dawud would pass by the mountains glorifying God, and they would respond to him. It was also said: they would travel with him wherever he went. The apparent view is that their glorification was by speech, God creating speech in them, just as the pebbles glorified God in the palm of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the people heard it. Dawud alone heard it, as Yahya ibn Salam said. It was also said: each of them glorified God. Qatada said: "glorifying" means praying. It was also said: moving, from swimming. Al-Zamakhshari said: just as He created it, meaning the speech in the tree when He spoke to Musa. End of quote. This is the view of the Mu'tazila, who deny that the attribute of speech is literally true of God Most High. It was also said: the attribution of glorification to them is metaphorical; since they moved by God's motion, they evoked glorification in those who saw them, so it was attributed to them. Most scholars hold that their glorification is the saying "Glory be to God" (*subḥān Allāh*).

*Wa-al-ṭayr* (and the birds) is in the accusative, coordinated with "the mountains," and coordination does not necessarily mean that it falls under the scope of the glorification. It was also said that it is an object of accompaniment (*maf'ūl ma'ahu*), meaning "they glorify together with the birds." It was read *wa-al-ṭayru* in the nominative, on the basis of the inceptive (*mubtada'*), with an omitted predicate, meaning "subjugated," indicated by "We subjugated," or on the basis of the pronoun in *yusabbiḥna* according to the view of the Kufans. This is the justification of an irregular reading.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why were "the mountains" mentioned before "the birds"? I say: because their subjugation and glorification are more wondrous and more indicative of power, and more included in the miraculous, since the mountains are inanimate, while the birds are living, speaking beings. End of quote. His saying "speaking" (*nāṭiq*): if he means that it has a rational soul, as they say in the definition of the human being that he is a speaking animal, then the bird would have to be a human; and if he means that it speaks as a human speaks, then that is not correct. He meant only that it makes a sound, that it has a voice. Describing the bird as "speaking" is metaphorical, since in reality it has no speech.

His saying ﴿And We were doers﴾ [21:79] means: We were doers of these marvels, the subjugation of the mountains, their glorification, and the birds, for whomever We single out with Our honour.

﴿And We taught him the craft of making armour for you﴾ [21:80]. *Labūs* is that which is worn, a form of the pattern *fa'ūl* in the sense of the passive participle, like *rakūb* in the sense of *marko ub* (that which is ridden). Here it means the coat of mail. *Labūs* is that which is worn. The poet said:

*On them are lions, fierce, their armour is flowing white (coats) that the arrow cannot pierce.*

Qatada said: they were plates, and the first to link and ring them was Dawud, so they combined lightness and protection. It was also said: *labūs* is every instrument of weapons, a sword, spear, coat of mail, helmet, and what is similar to these; Dawud was the first to make the coats of mail called *zarad* (chain mail). It is said: two angels descended from heaven and passed by Dawud. One said to the other: "What a fine man, except that he eats from the public treasury." So he asked God to provide him from his own earnings, and He softened iron for him, and he made from it coats of mail. God Most High favoured him by granting him judgment and knowledge, subjugating the mountains and birds with him, and teaching him the craft of armour. In this is the excellence of this craft, since God attributed its teaching to Himself.

Then He favoured us with it, saying: ﴿so that it may protect you from your violence﴾ [21:80], meaning: so that it might be a shield for you in your warfare and a cause of deliverance from your enemy. *Labūs* was read with a *ḍamma* on the *lām*, but the majority read it with a *fatḥa*. All three of these readings are with a sukun on the *ḥā'* and light doubling. al-Fuqaymi from Abu 'Amr and Ibn Abi Hammad from Abu Bakr read with the *yā'* below and *fatḥa* on the *ḥā'* and doubled *ṣād*. Ibn Wassab and al-A'mash read with the *tā'* above and doubling.

The *lām* in "for you" (*lakum*) may be causal, attaching to "We taught him," meaning "for your sake"; and "so that it may protect you" would be in the position of an appositive substitute, with the *lām* of the genitive repeated with it, since the verb is in the subjunctive by the implied *an*, so it is resolved into a verbal noun, meaning "for your protection from your violence." It may also be that "for you" is an attribute of *labūs*, attaching to an omitted word, meaning "belonging to you." It is also possible that "so that it may protect you" is a causal clause for the teaching, attaching to "We taught him," and that it is a causal clause for the omitted state attached to "for you."

﴿So will you be grateful?﴾ [21:80] is an interrogative that implies a command, meaning: "Be grateful to God for what He has bestowed upon you," like His saying: ﴿So will you desist?﴾ [5:91], meaning: "desist from what God has forbidden."

When He mentioned what He had singled out for His prophet Dawud, peace be upon him, He mentioned what He had singled out for his son Sulayman, peace be upon him, saying: ﴿And to Sulayman, the wind﴾ [21:81]. The construction came here with the *lām* when mentioning the subjugation of the wind to Sulayman, and when mentioning the subjugation of the mountains it came with the word *ma'a* (with), saying: ﴿And We subjugated the mountains with Dawud﴾ [21:79]. Likewise: ﴿O mountains, echo with him﴾ [34:10], and He said: ﴿So We subjugated to him the wind, running by his command﴾ [38:36]. This view refers to the difference of the times and to its movement by His command, obedient to him, according to what he wished and commanded.

*Commentary continues in part 2.*

(Man) is in a position of accusative (nasb), meaning: "And We subjected [to him] ﴿and of the devils, those who dive for him﴾," or it is in a position of nominative (raf') as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), with the predicate being the prepositional phrase preceding it. The apparent reading is that (man) is a relative pronoun (mawsulah). Abu al-Baqa said: it is an indefinite qualified noun (nakirah mawsufah). The pronoun in (yaghwusuna, they dive) is plural, taking into account the meaning of (man). What made this acceptable is that a plural noun preceded it, as the poet said:

"Indeed, among women there is one who is a garden, whose meadows bloom before her and wither."

Since the word "women" (al-niswan) preceded, it was treated according to the meaning of "min" (some), so it was made feminine, and he did not say "who is a garden" (man huwa rawdah) [in the masculine]. The meaning is that they dive for him into the seas to extract pearls. Diving implies both the diver and what is dived for, namely the jewel. That is why it was not mentioned. Or he said "for him," meaning for Sulayman, because the diver may dive for himself or for others. So He mentioned that the diving was not for their own sakes; it was for the sake of Sulayman and in obedience to his command. The reference with this is to the diving, that is, apart from diving, such as building cities and palaces, as He said: ﴿They make for him whatever he wishes: sanctuaries (mihrab), statues...﴾ [Saba': 13], to the end of the verse. It is also said that the bathhouse (hammam), the depilatory paste (nawrah), the mill (tahun), glassware (qawarir), and soap (sabun) were among what they extracted.

﴿And We were guardians over them﴾, meaning: lest they deviate from his command, or alter, or change, or lest any corruption be found among them in what they were subjugated to. It is also said: "guardians" means that they would not stir up anyone during the time of Sulayman. It is also said: "guardians" means so that they would not flee. It is said: He subjected them to a task that does not need guarding, because they would not corrupt what they made. The subjugation of the densest bodies was to Dawud, and this was the stone, when He made it speak in glorification, and the iron, when He placed in his fingers the power of fire until the iron became soft for him, and he made from it chainmail (zarad). The subjugation of the most subtle bodies was to Sulayman, and these were the wind and the devils, who are of fire. They used to dive into water, and water extinguishes fire, yet it did not harm them. This is a clear proof of His overwhelming power, and of the bringing forth of opposites from opposites, and of the possibility of reviving the decayed bone, and of making dry dust into a living creature. When the truthful one (al-Sadiq, the Prophet) reports it, it becomes obligatory to accept it and to believe in its existence. End.(p. 334)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 83–91 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And Job, when he called out to his Lord: "Harm has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ ﴿So We answered him and removed the harm that was upon him, and We gave him his family and the like of them with them, as a mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers.﴾ ﴿And Ishmael, and Idris, and Dhul-Kifl; each was among the patient.﴾ ﴿And We admitted them into Our mercy; indeed, they were among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And Dhul-Nun, when he went off in anger and thought that We would not decide upon him; then he called out in the darknesses: "There is no god but You; glory be to You. Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿So We answered him and saved him from distress, and thus do We save the believers.﴾ ﴿And Zachariah, when he called to his Lord: "My Lord, do not leave me alone (fardan), and You are the best of inheritors."﴾ ﴿So We answered him and gave him Yahya, and We made his wife fit for him. Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds, and they called upon Us in hope and in fear, and they were humble before Us.﴾ ﴿And she who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our spirit and made her and her son a sign for the worlds.﴾

The narrators of reports (al-akhbariyyun, i.e., the historians who relate accounts) have been lengthy regarding the story of Job. Job was a Roman, from the descendants of Isaac son of Jacob. Allah made him a prophet, spread worldly wealth over him, and multiplied his family and property. He had seven sons and seven daughters, and he owned various kinds of livestock and five hundred plows (faddan), each followed by five hundred servants, and each servant had a wife, a child, and palm trees. Then Allah tested him by the loss of his sons, when the house collapsed upon them and they perished, by the loss of his property, and by illness in his body for eighteen years. It was also said that it was less than that. One day his wife said to him: "If only you would call upon Allah." He said to her: "How long was the period of ease?" She said: "Eighty years." He said: "I am ashamed before Allah to call upon Him, for the period of my trial has not reached the period of my ease." When Allah removed the harm from him, He brought his children back to life, gave him the like of them, and gave him additional ones from among them. It is also reported that his wife afterwards bore him twenty-six sons. They also mentioned details about the loss of his property and family and about Iblis being given power over him in that matter, but Allah knows best the soundness of these reports.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (ﷺ) *annī* with a fatḥah on the hamzah. Isa ibn Umar read it with a kasrah. This is either by supposing an elided verb of speech, meaning "saying: *annī*," or by treating *nādā* (called out) as if it were *qāla* (said), and then breaking *inna* with a kasrah after it. The second is the view of the Kufans (al-Kufiyyun), and the first is the view of the Basrans (al-Basriyyun). *Al-ḍurr* with a ḍammah means harm in the self, such as from illness or emaciation. *Al-ḍarr* with a fatḥah means harm in everything. The difference between the two forms is due to the difference in meaning. Job was gentle in his request: he mentioned himself in a way that calls for mercy, described his Lord with the utmost mercy, did not state the thing he wanted explicitly, and did not specify the harm that had touched him.

The exegetes differed about this in seventeen opinions. The most sound of them is that he rose to pray, but could not stand up, and so he said: "Harm has touched me," as a report about a state, not a complaint about his trial. This was narrated from Anas, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ). The article *al* in *al-ḍurr* is generic, covering harm to the body, the family, and the property. As for the giving of his family, its apparent meaning is that whoever of his family had died, He returned to him and brought them back to life in their same persons, and He gave him the like of his family along with them, of children and followers. It was also mentioned that He gave him the like of them as a multiplied number in the Hereafter. *Raḥmatan* ("as a mercy") is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ūl min ajlih*), meaning: "because of Our mercy towards him." *Dhikrā* ("a reminder") is from Us, through the goodness shown to those who are with Us. Or *raḥmatan* is a mercy from Us to Job, and *dhikrā* means an admonition to others among the worshippers, so that they may be patient as he was patient, until they are rewarded as he was rewarded.

Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Mujahid said: Dhul-Kifl was a righteous servant, but not a prophet. Most of the scholars said: he was a prophet. It was said he was Ilyas (Elijah), and it was said he was Zachariah, and it was said he was Yushu' (Joshua). *Al-kifl* means portion and share, so Dhul-Kifl means the one with a share of Allah, bounded by reality. It was also said that he had double the deeds of the prophets of his time and double their reward. It was said that the explanations of his name Dhul-Kifl are confused and not sound. *Mughāḍiban* ("in anger") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*). It was said its meaning is *ghaḍbān* (angry). It is from the form *mufā'ala*, which does not necessarily imply mutual participation, as in: "I punished the thief (*'āqabtu al-liṣṣ*)" and "I travelled (*sāfartu*)." It was also said that *mughāḍiban* means he was angry at his people, whom he angered by leaving them, since they feared the descent of punishment, and they angered him when he invited them to Allah for a period but they did not respond to him. So he threatened them with punishment. Then he went out from among them in the manner of the prophets when punishment descends, before Allah had permitted him to leave. It was also said that *mughāḍiban* means angry at King Hizqiya when he appointed him to fight a king who had insulted the Children of Israel. Jonah said to him: "Did Allah order you to expel me?" He said: "No." He said: "Did He name me to you?" He said: "No." He said: "Here are other prophets besides me." But he insisted on him, so he went out angry at the king. As for the statement of whoever said that *mughāḍiban* means angry at his Lord, and reported various forms of anger toward his Lord, it must be rejected, since none of these forms befits the station of prophethood. Those scholars who said this, such as al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Jubayr, and others among the Successors (al-Tabi'un), and Ibn Mas'ud among the Companions, should be interpreted so that the meaning of their statement "angry at his Lord" is "for the sake of his Lord and his religion." The *lām* here is the *lām* of cause (*lām al-'illa*), not the *lām* that conveys the object. Abu Sharaf read *mughḍiban* as a passive participle (*ism maf'ūl*).

*Fa-ẓanna an lan naqdira 'alayh* ("and thought that We would not decide upon him"): that is, that We would not constrict upon him, from *qadar* (decree), not from *qudra* (power). It was also said that it means from *qudra* (power), in the sense of: "that We would not have power over him" with the trial. The majority read *naqdira* with the "We" of majesty (*nūn al-'aẓama*), lightened. Ibn Abi Layla, Abu Sharaf, al-Kalbi, Humayd ibn Qays, and Ya'qub read it with a ḍammah on the *yā'* and a fatḥah on the *dāl*, lightened. Isa and al-Hasan read it with a *yā'* with a fatḥah and a kasrah on the *dāl*. Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Yamani read it with a ḍammah on the *yā'*, a fatḥah on the *qāf* and *dāl*, doubled. Al-Zuhri read it with a *nūn* with a ḍammah, a fatḥah on the *qāf*, and a kasrah on the *dāl*, doubled.

*Fa-nādā fī al-ẓulumāt* ("then he called out in the darknesses"): in the speech there are elided sentences, which have been clarified in surah al-Saffat, and there we will mention his story, Allah willing. *Al-ẓulumāt* is in the plural because of its intense density, as if it were darkness upon darkness. It was said: the darknesses of the belly of the fish, of the sea, and of the night. It was said: another fish swallowed his fish, so he was in the darkness of the bellies of the two fish and the darkness of the sea. It is reported that Jonah prostrated inside the belly of the fish when he heard the glorification of the fish at the bottom of the sea. The *an* in *an lā ilāha illā anta* ("that there is no god but You") is explanatory (*tafsīriyya*), because *fa-nādā* came before it and has the sense of speech. It is also possible that the estimate is *bi-annahu*, so it would be the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, and the restriction of divinity to Him, may He be exalted, then glorifying Him from attributes of deficiency, then acknowledging what follows.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "No one in distress calls with this supplication except that he is answered." *Al-ghamm* ("distress") is what he suffered when the fish swallowed him, and the duration of his stay in its belly. The majority read *nunjī* as the imperfect of *anjā* (to save). Al-Jahdari read it doubled as the imperfect of *najjā*. Ibn Amir and Abu Bakr read *najjā* with a ḍammah on the *nūn*, a doubled *jīm*, and a quiescent *yā'*. It is the same in the Imam's codex (*muṣḥaf al-imām*) and the codices of the regions, with a single *nūn*. Abu Ubayd preferred it for its agreement with the codices. Al-Zajjaj and al-Farisi said it is a solecism (*laḥn*). It was said: it is an imperfect in which the *nūn* was assimilated into the *jīm*, but this was rejected, since it is not permitted to assimilate the *nūn* into the *jīm* which is the first radical of the verb, because of the meeting of two identical letters, just as it was elided in the reading of whoever read *wa-nazala al-malā'ika*, meaning *wa-nunzilu al-malā'ika*. On this basis Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) derived it. It was also said: it is a past verb in the passive voice, and the *yā'* was made quiescent just as whoever read *wa-dharū mā baqiya min al-ribā* made it quiescent. The place of the subject is occupied by the verbal noun pronoun, meaning *najjā* (He saved): it, that is the rescue, saves the believers, like the reading of Abu Ja'far, *li-yajziya qawman* (Q. 45:14), meaning *wa-li-yajziya huwa*, that is, the recompense itself. Al-Akhfash, the Kufans, and Abu Ubayd permitted placing something other than the object in the position of the subject, such as a verbal noun, an adverb of place, an adverb of time, or a prepositional phrase, even when the object is present. The poetic usage supports placing a prepositional phrase in the position of the subject even when the object is present, as in the saying:

"There was granted to me, from among my enemies, a warner, by whom I was protected from the spreading evil."

Al-Akhfash said, regarding examples: "*ḍaraba al-ḍarba al-shadīda Zaydan*" (he struck the severe blow Zayd), "*ḍaraba al-yawmāni Zaydan*" (the two days struck Zayd), "*ḍaraba makānuka Zaydan*" (your place struck Zayd), and "*u'ṭiya i'ṭā'a ḥasanin akhāka dirhaman*" (a good giving was given to your brother a dirham), and "*maḍrūban 'abduhu Zaydan*" (his slave was struck, Zayd). It was said: the pronoun of the verbal noun was placed in the position of the subject, and *al-mu'minīn* ("the believers") is in the accusative by an elided verb, meaning: "*wa-ka-dhālika nunjī*" (and thus do We save), "it" (the rescue) "*nunjī al-mu'minīn*" (saves the believers). The well-known view among the Basrans is that whenever the object is present, nothing else may be placed in the position of the subject. However, the author of al-Lubab reported the disagreement on this among the Basrans, and that some of them permitted it.

*Lā tadharnī fardan* ("do not leave me alone"): that is, solitary, without an heir. He asked his Lord to grant him a son to inherit him, then he referred his matter to Allah and said: "*wa-anta khayru al-wārithīn*" (and You are the best of inheritors), meaning: if You do not grant me one who inherits me, then You are the best inheritor. The "making fit for him" of his wife refers to her good character. She had a bad character, as said by Ata, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, and Awn ibn Abd Allah. It was said: making her fit refers to her ability to bear children after she had been barren, as said by Qatada. It was said: making her fit means restoring her youth to him. The pronoun in *innahum* refers to the prophets previously mentioned, meaning: their being answered in their requests was because of their hastening to goodness and their supplication to Us.

*Raghaban wa-rahaban* ("in hope and in fear") means at the time of hope and at the time of fear, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: "He fears the Hereafter and hopes for the mercy of his Lord" (Q. 39:9). It was said the pronoun refers to Zachariah, his wife, and their son Yahya. A group read *yad'ūnanā* with the *nūn* of the nominative elided. Talha read it with a doubled *nūn*, assimilating the *nūn* of the nominative into *nā*, the object pronoun. Ibn Thabit, al-A'mash, Wahb ibn Amr, al-Nahwi, Harun, Abu Ma'mar, al-Asma'i, al-Lu'lu'i, Yunus, Abu Zayd, and seven of them from Abu Amr (who are among those who read it this way) read *raghaban wa-rahaban* with a fatḥah and a quiescent *hā'*. The more famous reading from al-A'mash is with two ḍammahs on them. A group read with a ḍammah on the two *rā'*s and a quiescence on the *ghayn* and *hā'*. *Raghaban wa-rahaban* in the accusative, both are verbal nouns in the position of a circumstantial state, or an object of purpose.

*Wa-allatī aḥṣanat farjahā* ("and she who guarded her chastity"): she is Mary, daughter of Imran, mother of Jesus, peace be upon him. The apparent meaning is that *al-farj* here is the modesty of a woman. She guarded it, meaning she prevented it from lawful and unlawful things, as she said: "No man has touched me, and I have not been unchaste" (Q. 19:20). It was said: *al-farj* here is the slit of her shirt, which she prevented Gabriel from reaching when he came near to her to breathe, since he did not realize it. The apparent meaning of His statement *fa-nafakhnā fīhā min rūḥinā* ("so We breathed into her of Our spirit") is a metaphor for the bringing into existence of Jesus alive in her womb, and there was no literal breathing there. He attributed the spirit to Himself in the manner of honour. It was said: there was literal breathing, namely that Gabriel, peace be upon him, breathed into the opening of her garment, and the breathing was attributed to Him, may He be exalted, because it was from Gabriel by His command, as an honour. It was also said: the spirit here is Gabriel, as He said: "So We sent to her Our spirit, and it appeared to her in the form of a man" (Q. 19:17). The meaning is: *fa-nafakhnā fīhā* (so We breathed into her), from the direction of Gabriel, and Gabriel had breathed through the opening of her garment, so the breath reached her inside.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: the breathing of the spirit into the body is an expression for its revival, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: "So when I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My spirit" (Q. 15:29), meaning I gave him life; and if that is established, then His statement *fa-nafakhnā fīhā min rūḥinā* is clearly problematic, because it indicates the revival of Mary. I say: its meaning is that We breathed the spirit into Jesus within her, meaning We gave him life in her womb. Similar to this is when the piper says: "I breathed into the house of so-and-so," meaning I played the pipe in his house. End.

There is no difficulty in this, for it is by omitting a noun (mudaf): i.e., (we breathed) into her son "from Our spirit" (min ruhina). His statement "I said its meaning is: We breathed the spirit into Isa" uses nafakha (to breathe) transitively, whereas the established usage is that it is not transitive, so making it transitive requires a complement (ji'ma', i.e., sexual intercourse). And he used it intransitively in his saying: i.e., "I blew into the flute in his house." Ended. There is no difficulty in this.

He said "a sign" (ayah) in the singular because their condition together constitutes one single sign, namely her giving birth to him without a male (fahl, i.e., a father). Although there are many signs in the case of Maryam and many signs in the case of Isa, here he has focused on the matter of the birth without mentioning anything else, and that is one sign. His saying "for the worlds" (lil-'alamin) means: for those among the people of their time who take heed from it, and those who came after them. The mention of Maryam alongside the prophets in this surah indicates that she was a prophetess, since she is mentioned together with them in the remembrance. As for one who denies that women could be prophetesses, he said: she was mentioned on account of Isa, and the mention of the two of them here is fitting alongside the story of Zakariyya, his wife and Yahya, because of the kinship that is between them.

It was said: the darknesses of the belly of the fish, of the sea, and of the night. It was said: another fish swallowed his fish, so he was in the darkness of the bellies of the two fish and the darkness of the sea. It is reported that Jonah prostrated inside the belly of the fish when he heard the glorification of the fish at the bottom of the sea. The *an* in *an lā ilāha illā anta* ("that there is no god but You") is explanatory (*tafsīriyya*), because *fa-nādā* came before it and has the sense of speech. It is also possible that the estimate is *bi-annahu*, so it would be the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, and the restriction of divinity to Him, may He be exalted, then glorifying Him from attributes of deficiency, then acknowledging what follows.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "No one in distress calls with this supplication except that he is answered." *Al-ghamm* ("distress") is what he suffered when the fish swallowed him, and the duration of his stay in its belly. The majority read *nunjī* as the imperfect of *anjā* (to save). Al-Jahdari read it doubled as the imperfect of *najjā*. Ibn Amir and Abu Bakr read *najjā* with a ḍammah on the *nūn*, a doubled *jīm*, and a quiescent *yā'*. It is the same in the Imam's codex (*muṣḥaf al-imām*) and the codices of the regions, with a single *nūn*. Abu Ubayd preferred it for its agreement with the codices. Al-Zajjaj and al-Farisi said it is a solecism (*laḥn*). It was said: it is an imperfect in which the *nūn* was assimilated into the *jīm*, but this was rejected, since it is not permitted to assimilate the *nūn* into the *jīm* which is the first radical of the verb, because of the meeting of two identical letters, just as it was elided in the reading of whoever read *wa-nazala al-malā'ika*, meaning *wa-nunzilu al-malā'ika*. On this basis Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) derived it. It was also said: it is a past verb in the passive voice, and the *yā'* was made quiescent just as whoever read *wa-dharū mā baqiya min al-ribā* made it quiescent. The place of the subject is occupied by the verbal noun pronoun, meaning *najjā* (He saved): it, that is the rescue, saves the believers, like the reading of Abu Ja'far, *li-yajziya qawman* (Q. 45:14), meaning *wa-li-yajziya huwa*, that is, the recompense itself. Al-Akhfash, the Kufans, and Abu Ubayd permitted placing something other than the object in the position of the subject, such as a verbal noun, an adverb of place, an adverb of time, or a prepositional phrase, even when the object is present. The poetic usage supports placing a prepositional phrase in the position of the subject even when the object is present, as in the saying:

"There was granted to me, from among my enemies, a warner, by whom I was protected from the spreading evil."

Al-Akhfash said, regarding examples: "*ḍaraba al-ḍarba al-shadīda Zaydan*" (he struck the severe blow Zayd), "*ḍaraba al-yawmāni Zaydan*" (the two days struck Zayd), "*ḍaraba makānuka Zaydan*" (your place struck Zayd), and "*u'ṭiya i'ṭā'a ḥasanin akhāka dirhaman*" (a good giving was given to your brother a dirham), and "*maḍrūban 'abduhu Zaydan*" (his slave was struck, Zayd). It was said: the pronoun of the verbal noun was placed in the position of the subject, and *al-mu'minīn* ("the believers") is in the accusative by an elided verb, meaning: "*wa-ka-dhālika nunjī*" (and thus do We save), "it" (the rescue) "*nunjī al-mu'minīn*" (saves the believers). The well-known view among the Basrans is that whenever the object is present, nothing else may be placed in the position of the subject. However, the author of al-Lubab reported the disagreement on this among the Basrans, and that some of them permitted it.

*Lā tadharnī fardan* ("do not leave me alone"): that is, solitary, without an heir. He asked his Lord to grant him a son to inherit him, then he referred his matter to Allah and said: "*wa-anta khayru al-wārithīn*" (and You are the best of inheritors), meaning: if You do not grant me one who inherits me, then You are the best inheritor. The "making fit for him" of his wife refers to her good character. She had a bad character, as said by Ata, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, and Awn ibn Abd Allah. It was said: making her fit refers to her ability to bear children after she had been barren, as said by Qatada. It was said: making her fit means restoring her youth to him. The pronoun in *innahum* refers to the prophets previously mentioned, meaning: their being answered in their requests was because of their hastening to goodness and their supplication to Us.

*Raghaban wa-rahaban* ("in hope and in fear") means at the time of hope and at the time of fear, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: "He fears the Hereafter and hopes for the mercy of his Lord" (Q. 39:9). It was said the pronoun refers to Zachariah, his wife, and their son Yahya. A group read *yad'ūnanā* with the *nūn* of the nominative elided. Talha read it with a doubled *nūn*, assimilating the *nūn* of the nominative into *nā*, the object pronoun. Ibn Thabit, al-A'mash, Wahb ibn Amr, al-Nahwi, Harun, Abu Ma'mar, al-Asma'i, al-Lu'lu'i, Yunus, Abu Zayd, and seven of them from Abu Amr (who are among those who read it this way) read *raghaban wa-rahaban* with a fatḥah and a quiescent *hā'*. The more famous reading from al-A'mash is with two ḍammahs on them. A group read with a ḍammah on the two *rā'*s and a quiescence on the *ghayn* and *hā'*. *Raghaban wa-rahaban* in the accusative, both are verbal nouns in the position of a circumstantial state, or an object of purpose.

*Wa-allatī aḥṣanat farjahā* ("and she who guarded her chastity"): she is Mary, daughter of Imran, mother of Jesus, peace be upon him. The apparent meaning is that *al-farj* here is the modesty of a woman. She guarded it, meaning she prevented it from lawful and unlawful things, as she said: "No man has touched me, and I have not been unchaste" (Q. 19:20). It was said: *al-farj* here is the slit of her shirt, which she prevented Gabriel from reaching when he came near to her to breathe, since he did not realize it. The apparent meaning of His statement *fa-nafakhnā fīhā min rūḥinā* ("so We breathed into her of Our spirit") is a metaphor for the bringing into existence of Jesus alive in her womb, and there was no literal breathing there. He attributed the spirit to Himself in the manner of honour. It was said: there was literal breathing, namely that Gabriel, peace be upon him, breathed into the opening of her garment, and the breathing was attributed to Him, may He be exalted, because it was from Gabriel by His command, as an honour. It was also said: the spirit here is Gabriel, as He said: "So We sent to her Our spirit, and it appeared to her in the form of a man" (Q. 19:17). The meaning is: *fa-nafakhnā fīhā* (so We breathed into her), from the direction of Gabriel, and Gabriel had breathed through the opening of her garment, so the breath reached her inside.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: the breathing of the spirit into the body is an expression for its revival, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: "So when I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My spirit" (Q. 15:29), meaning I gave him life; and if that is established, then His statement *fa-nafakhnā fīhā min rūḥinā* is clearly problematic, because it indicates the revival of Mary. I say: its meaning is that We breathed the spirit into Jesus within her, meaning We gave him life in her womb. Similar to this is when the piper says: "I breathed into the house of so-and-so," meaning I played the pipe in his house. End.

There is no difficulty in this, for it is by omitting a noun (mudaf): i.e., (we breathed) into her son "from Our spirit" (min ruhina). His statement "I said its meaning is: We breathed the spirit into Isa" uses nafakha (to breathe) transitively, whereas the established usage is that it is not transitive, so making it transitive requires a complement (ji'ma', i.e., sexual intercourse). And he used it intransitively in his saying: i.e., "I blew into the flute in his house." Ended. There is no difficulty in this.

He said "a sign" (ayah) in the singular because their condition together constitutes one single sign, namely her giving birth to him without a male (fahl, i.e., a father). Although there are many signs in the case of Maryam and many signs in the case of Isa, here he has focused on the matter of the birth without mentioning anything else, and that is one sign. His saying "for the worlds" (lil-'alamin) means: for those among the people of their time who take heed from it, and those who came after them. The mention of Maryam alongside the prophets in this surah indicates that she was a prophetess, since she is mentioned together with them in the remembrance. As for one who denies that women could be prophetesses, he said: she was mentioned on account of Isa, and the mention of the two of them here is fitting alongside the story of Zakariyya, his wife and Yahya, because of the kinship that is between them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 83–91 (part 1 of 2):

Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿So We answered him and saved him from distress, and thus do We save the believers.﴾ ﴿And Zachariah, when he called to his Lord: "My Lord, do not leave me alone (fardan), and You are the best of inheritors."﴾ ﴿So We answered him and gave him Yahya, and We made his wife fit for him. Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds, and they called upon Us in hope and in fear, and they were humble before Us.﴾ ﴿And she who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our spirit and made her and her son a sign for the worlds.﴾

The narrators of reports (al-akhbariyyun, i.e., the historians who relate accounts) have been lengthy regarding the story of Job. Job was a Roman, from the descendants of Isaac son of Jacob. Allah made him a prophet, spread worldly wealth over him, and multiplied his family and property. He had seven sons and seven daughters, and he owned various kinds of livestock and five hundred plows (faddan), each followed by five hundred servants, and each servant had a wife, a child, and palm trees. Then Allah tested him by the loss of his sons, when the house collapsed upon them and they perished, by the loss of his property, and by illness in his body for eighteen years. It was also said that it was less than that. One day his wife said to him: "If only you would call upon Allah." He said to her: "How long was the period of ease?" She said: "Eighty years." He said: "I am ashamed before Allah to call upon Him, for the period of my trial has not reached the period of my ease." When Allah removed the harm from him, He brought his children back to life, gave him the like of them, and gave him additional ones from among them. It is also reported that his wife afterwards bore him twenty-six sons. They also mentioned details about the loss of his property and family and about Iblis being given power over him in that matter, but Allah knows best the soundness of these reports.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (ﷺ) *annī* with a fatḥah on the hamzah. Isa ibn Umar read it with a kasrah. This is either by supposing an elided verb of speech, meaning "saying: *annī*," or by treating *nādā* (called out) as if it were *qāla* (said), and then breaking *inna* with a kasrah after it. The second is the view of the Kufans (al-Kufiyyun), and the first is the view of the Basrans (al-Basriyyun). *Al-ḍurr* with a ḍammah means harm in the self, such as from illness or emaciation. *Al-ḍarr* with a fatḥah means harm in everything. The difference between the two forms is due to the difference in meaning. Job was gentle in his request: he mentioned himself in a way that calls for mercy, described his Lord with the utmost mercy, did not state the thing he wanted explicitly, and did not specify the harm that had touched him.

The exegetes differed about this in seventeen opinions. The most sound of them is that he rose to pray, but could not stand up, and so he said: "Harm has touched me," as a report about a state, not a complaint about his trial. This was narrated from Anas, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ). The article *al* in *al-ḍurr* is generic, covering harm to the body, the family, and the property. As for the giving of his family, its apparent meaning is that whoever of his family had died, He returned to him and brought them back to life in their same persons, and He gave him the like of his family along with them, of children and followers. It was also mentioned that He gave him the like of them as a multiplied number in the Hereafter. *Raḥmatan* ("as a mercy") is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ūl min ajlih*), meaning: "because of Our mercy towards him." *Dhikrā* ("a reminder") is from Us, through the goodness shown to those who are with Us. Or *raḥmatan* is a mercy from Us to Job, and *dhikrā* means an admonition to others among the worshippers, so that they may be patient as he was patient, until they are rewarded as he was rewarded.

Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Mujahid said: Dhul-Kifl was a righteous servant, but not a prophet. Most of the scholars said: he was a prophet. It was said he was Ilyas (Elijah), and it was said he was Zachariah, and it was said he was Yushu' (Joshua). *Al-kifl* means portion and share, so Dhul-Kifl means the one with a share of Allah, bounded by reality. It was also said that he had double the deeds of the prophets of his time and double their reward. It was said that the explanations of his name Dhul-Kifl are confused and not sound. *Mughāḍiban* ("in anger") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*). It was said its meaning is *ghaḍbān* (angry). It is from the form *mufā'ala*, which does not necessarily imply mutual participation, as in: "I punished the thief (*'āqabtu al-liṣṣ*)" and "I travelled (*sāfartu*)." It was also said that *mughāḍiban* means he was angry at his people, whom he angered by leaving them, since they feared the descent of punishment, and they angered him when he invited them to Allah for a period but they did not respond to him. So he threatened them with punishment. Then he went out from among them in the manner of the prophets when punishment descends, before Allah had permitted him to leave. It was also said that *mughāḍiban* means angry at King Hizqiya when he appointed him to fight a king who had insulted the Children of Israel. Jonah said to him: "Did Allah order you to expel me?" He said: "No." He said: "Did He name me to you?" He said: "No." He said: "Here are other prophets besides me." But he insisted on him, so he went out angry at the king. As for the statement of whoever said that *mughāḍiban* means angry at his Lord, and reported various forms of anger toward his Lord, it must be rejected, since none of these forms befits the station of prophethood. Those scholars who said this, such as al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Jubayr, and others among the Successors (al-Tabi'un), and Ibn Mas'ud among the Companions, should be interpreted so that the meaning of their statement "angry at his Lord" is "for the sake of his Lord and his religion." The *lām* here is the *lām* of cause (*lām al-'illa*), not the *lām* that conveys the object. Abu Sharaf read *mughḍiban* as a passive participle (*ism maf'ūl*).

*Fa-ẓanna an lan naqdira 'alayh* ("and thought that We would not decide upon him"): that is, that We would not constrict upon him, from *qadar* (decree), not from *qudra* (power). It was also said that it means from *qudra* (power), in the sense of: "that We would not have power over him" with the trial. The majority read *naqdira* with the "We" of majesty (*nūn al-'aẓama*), lightened. Ibn Abi Layla, Abu Sharaf, al-Kalbi, Humayd ibn Qays, and Ya'qub read it with a ḍammah on the *yā'* and a fatḥah on the *dāl*, lightened. Isa and al-Hasan read it with a *yā'* with a fatḥah and a kasrah on the *dāl*. Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Yamani read it with a ḍammah on the *yā'*, a fatḥah on the *qāf* and *dāl*, doubled. Al-Zuhri read it with a *nūn* with a ḍammah, a fatḥah on the *qāf*, and a kasrah on the *dāl*, doubled.

"There was granted to me, from among my enemies, a warner, by whom I was protected from the spreading evil."

The narrators of reports (al-akhbariyyun, i.e., the historians who relate accounts) have been lengthy regarding the story of Job. Job was a Roman, from the descendants of Isaac son of Jacob. It was also said that it was less than that. One day his wife said to him: "If only you would call upon Allah." He said to her: "How long was the period of ease?" She said: "Eighty years." He said: "I am ashamed before Allah to call upon Him, for the period of my trial has not reached the period of my ease." When Allah removed the harm from him, He brought his children back to life, gave him the like of them, and gave him additional ones from among them. They also mentioned details about the loss of his property and family and about Iblis being given power over him in that matter, but Allah knows best the soundness of these reports.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (ﷺ) *annī* with a fatḥah on the hamzah. Isa ibn Umar read it with a kasrah. This is either by supposing an elided verb of speech, meaning "saying: *annī*," or by treating *nādā* (called out) as if it were *qāla* (said), and then breaking *inna* with a kasrah after it. The second is the view of the Kufans (al-Kufiyyun), and the first is the view of the Basrans (al-Basriyyun). *Al-ḍurr* with a ḍammah means harm in the self, such as from illness or emaciation. *Al-ḍarr* with a fatḥah means harm in everything. The difference between the two forms is due to the difference in meaning. Job was gentle in his request: he mentioned himself in a way that calls for mercy, described his Lord with the utmost mercy, did not state the thing he wanted explicitly, and did not specify the harm that had touched him.

The exegetes differed about this in seventeen opinions. The most sound of them is that he rose to pray, but could not stand up, and so he said: "Harm has touched me," as a report about a state, not a complaint about his trial. It was also mentioned that He gave him the like of them as a multiplied number in the Hereafter. *Raḥmatan* ("as a mercy") is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ūl min ajlih*), meaning: "because of Our mercy towards him." *Dhikrā* ("a reminder") is from Us, through the goodness shown to those who are with Us. It was said its meaning is *ghaḍbān* (angry). It is from the form *mufā'ala*, which does not necessarily imply mutual participation, as in: "I punished the thief (*'āqabtu al-liṣṣ*)" and "I travelled (*sāfartu*)." It was also said that *mughāḍiban* means he was angry at his people, whom he angered by leaving them, since they feared the descent of punishment, and they angered him when he invited them to Allah for a period but they did not respond to him. So he threatened them with punishment. Then he went out from among them in the manner of the prophets when punishment descends, before Allah had permitted him to leave. It was also said that it means from *qudra* (power), in the sense of: "that We would not have power over him" with the trial. The majority read *naqdira* with the "We" of majesty (*nūn al-'aẓama*), lightened. Ibn Abi Layla, Abu Sharaf, al-Kalbi, Humayd ibn Qays, and Ya'qub read it with a ḍammah on the *yā'* and a fatḥah on the *dāl*, lightened. Isa and al-Hasan read it with a *yā'* with a fatḥah and a kasrah on the *dāl*. Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Yamani read it with a ḍammah on the *yā'*, a fatḥah on the *qāf* and *dāl*, doubled. Al-Zuhri read it with a *nūn* with a ḍammah, a fatḥah on the *qāf*, and a kasrah on the *dāl*, doubled.

*Fa-nādā fī al-ẓulumāt* ("then he called out in the darknesses"): in the speech there are elided sentences, which have been clarified in surah al-Saffat, and there we will mention his story, Allah willing. *Al-ẓulumāt* is in the plural because of its intense density, as if it were darkness upon darkness. It was said: the darknesses of the belly of the fish, of the sea, and of the night. It was said: another fish swallowed his fish, so he was in the darkness of the bellies of the two fish and the darkness of the sea. It is reported that Jonah prostrated inside the belly of the fish when he heard the glorification of the fish at the bottom of the sea. The *an* in *an lā ilāha illā anta* ("that there is no god but You") is explanatory (*tafsīriyya*), because *fa-nādā* came before it and has the sense of speech. It is also possible that the estimate is *bi-annahu*, so it would be the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, and the restriction of divinity to Him, may He be exalted, then glorifying Him from attributes of deficiency, then acknowledging what follows.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "No one in distress calls with this supplication except that he is answered." *Al-ghamm* ("distress") is what he suffered when the fish swallowed him, and the duration of his stay in its belly. The majority read *nunjī* as the imperfect of *anjā* (to save). Al-Jahdari read it doubled as the imperfect of *najjā*. Ibn Amir and Abu Bakr read *najjā* with a ḍammah on the *nūn*, a doubled *jīm*, and a quiescent *yā'*. It is the same in the Imam's codex (*muṣḥaf al-imām*) and the codices of the regions, with a single *nūn*. Abu Ubayd preferred it for its agreement with the codices. Al-Zajjaj and al-Farisi said it is a solecism (*laḥn*). It was said: it is an imperfect in which the *nūn* was assimilated into the *jīm*, but this was rejected, since it is not permitted to assimilate the *nūn* into the *jīm* which is the first radical of the verb, because of the meeting of two identical letters, just as it was elided in the reading of whoever read *wa-nazala al-malā'ika*, meaning *wa-nunzilu al-malā'ika*. On this basis Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) derived it. It was also said: it is a past verb in the passive voice, and the *yā'* was made quiescent just as whoever read *wa-dharū mā baqiya min al-ribā* made it quiescent. The place of the subject is occupied by the verbal noun pronoun, meaning *najjā* (He saved): it, that is the rescue, saves the believers, like the reading of Abu Ja'far, *li-yajziya qawman* (Q. 45:14), meaning *wa-li-yajziya huwa*, that is, the recompense itself. Al-Akhfash, the Kufans, and Abu Ubayd permitted placing something other than the object in the position of the subject, such as a verbal noun, an adverb of place, an adverb of time, or a prepositional phrase, even when the object is present. The poetic usage supports placing a prepositional phrase in the position of the subject even when the object is present, as in the saying:

"There was granted to me, from among my enemies, a warner, by whom I was protected from the spreading evil."

Al-Akhfash said, regarding examples: "*ḍaraba al-ḍarba al-shadīda Zaydan*" (he struck the severe blow Zayd), "*ḍaraba al-yawmāni Zaydan*" (the two days struck Zayd), "*ḍaraba makānuka Zaydan*" (your place struck Zayd), and "*u'ṭiya i'ṭā'a ḥasanin akhāka dirhaman*" (a good giving was given to your brother a dirham), and "*maḍrūban 'abduhu Zaydan*" (his slave was struck, Zayd). It was said: the pronoun of the verbal noun was placed in the position of the subject, and *al-mu'minīn* ("the believers") is in the accusative by an elided verb, meaning: "*wa-ka-dhālika nunjī*" (and thus do We save), "it" (the rescue) "*nunjī al-mu'minīn*" (saves the believers). The well-known view among the Basrans is that whenever the object is present, nothing else may be placed in the position of the subject. However, the author of al-Lubab reported the disagreement on this among the Basrans, and that some of them permitted it.

*Lā tadharnī fardan* ("do not leave me alone"): that is, solitary, without an heir. He asked his Lord to grant him a son to inherit him, then he referred his matter to Allah and said: "*wa-anta khayru al-wārithīn*" (and You are the best of inheritors), meaning: if You do not grant me one who inherits me, then You are the best inheritor. The "making fit for him" of his wife refers to her good character. She had a bad character, as said by Ata, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, and Awn ibn Abd Allah. It was said: making her fit refers to her ability to bear children after she had been barren, as said by Qatada. It was said: making her fit means restoring her youth to him. The pronoun in *innahum* refers to the prophets previously mentioned, meaning: their being answered in their requests was because of their hastening to goodness and their supplication to Us.

*Raghaban wa-rahaban* ("in hope and in fear") means at the time of hope and at the time of fear, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: "He fears the Hereafter and hopes for the mercy of his Lord" (Q. 39:9). It was said the pronoun refers to Zachariah, his wife, and their son Yahya. A group read *yad'ūnanā* with the *nūn* of the nominative elided. Talha read it with a doubled *nūn*, assimilating the *nūn* of the nominative into *nā*, the object pronoun. Ibn Thabit, al-A'mash, Wahb ibn Amr, al-Nahwi, Harun, Abu Ma'mar, al-Asma'i, al-Lu'lu'i, Yunus, Abu Zayd, and seven of them from Abu Amr (who are among those who read it this way) read *raghaban wa-rahaban* with a fatḥah and a quiescent *hā'*. The more famous reading from al-A'mash is with two ḍammahs on them. A group read with a ḍammah on the two *rā'*s and a quiescence on the *ghayn* and *hā'*. *Raghaban wa-rahaban* in the accusative, both are verbal nouns in the position of a circumstantial state, or an object of purpose.

*Wa-allatī aḥṣanat farjahā* ("and she who guarded her chastity"): she is Mary, daughter of Imran, mother of Jesus, peace be upon him. The apparent meaning is that *al-farj* here is the modesty of a woman. She guarded it, meaning she prevented it from lawful and unlawful things, as she said: "No man has touched me, and I have not been unchaste" (Q. 19:20). It was said: *al-farj* here is the slit of her shirt, which she prevented Gabriel from reaching when he came near to her to breathe, since he did not realize it. The apparent meaning of His statement *fa-nafakhnā fīhā min rūḥinā* ("so We breathed into her of Our spirit") is a metaphor for the bringing into existence of Jesus alive in her womb, and there was no literal breathing there. He attributed the spirit to Himself in the manner of honour. It was said: there was literal breathing, namely that Gabriel, peace be upon him, breathed into the opening of her garment, and the breathing was attributed to Him, may He be exalted, because it was from Gabriel by His command, as an honour. It was also said: the spirit here is Gabriel, as He said: "So We sent to her Our spirit, and it appeared to her in the form of a man" (Q. 19:17). The meaning is: *fa-nafakhnā fīhā* (so We breathed into her), from the direction of Gabriel, and Gabriel had breathed through the opening of her garment, so the breath reached her inside.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: the breathing of the spirit into the body is an expression for its revival, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: "So when I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My spirit" (Q. 15:29), meaning I gave him life; and if that is established, then His statement *fa-nafakhnā fīhā min rūḥinā* is clearly problematic, because it indicates the revival of Mary. I say: its meaning is that We breathed the spirit into Jesus within her, meaning We gave him life in her womb. Similar to this is when the piper says: "I breathed into the house of so-and-so," meaning I played the pipe in his house. End.

There is no difficulty in this, for it is by omitting a noun (mudaf): i.e., (we breathed) into her son "from Our spirit" (min ruhina). His statement "I said its meaning is: We breathed the spirit into Isa" uses nafakha (to breathe) transitively, whereas the established usage is that it is not transitive, so making it transitive requires a complement (ji'ma', i.e., sexual intercourse). And he used it intransitively in his saying: i.e., "I blew into the flute in his house." Ended. There is no difficulty in this.

He said "a sign" (ayah) in the singular because their condition together constitutes one single sign, namely her giving birth to him without a male (fahl, i.e., a father). Although there are many signs in the case of Maryam and many signs in the case of Isa, here he has focused on the matter of the birth without mentioning anything else, and that is one sign. His saying "for the worlds" (lil-'alamin) means: for those among the people of their time who take heed from it, and those who came after them. The mention of Maryam alongside the prophets in this surah indicates that she was a prophetess, since she is mentioned together with them in the remembrance. As for one who denies that women could be prophetesses, he said: she was mentioned on account of Isa, and the mention of the two of them here is fitting alongside the story of Zakariyya, his wife and Yahya, because of the kinship that is between them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 83–91 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And Job, when he called out to his Lord: "Harm has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ ﴿So We answered him and removed the harm that was upon him, and We gave him his family and the like of them with them, as a mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers.﴾ ﴿And Ishmael, and Idris, and Dhul-Kifl; each was among the patient.﴾ ﴿And We admitted them into Our mercy; indeed, they were among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And Dhul-Nun, when he went off in anger and thought that We would not decide upon him; then he called out in the darknesses: "There is no god but You; glory be to You. Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿So We answered him and saved him from distress, and thus do We save the believers.﴾ ﴿And Zachariah, when he called to his Lord: "My Lord, do not leave me alone (fardan), and You are the best of inheritors."﴾ ﴿So We answered him and gave him Yahya, and We made his wife fit for him. Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds, and they called upon Us in hope and in fear, and they were humble before Us.﴾ ﴿And she who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our spirit and made her and her son a sign for the worlds.﴾
