It was said: *al-farj* here is the slit of her shirt, which she prevented Gabriel from reaching when he came near to her to breathe, since he did not realize it. The apparent meaning of His statement *fa-nafakhnā fīhā min rūḥinā* ("so We breathed into her of Our spirit") is a metaphor for the bringing into existence of Jesus alive in her womb, and there was no literal breathing there. He attributed the spirit to Himself in the manner of honour. It was said: there was literal breathing, namely that Gabriel, peace be upon him, breathed into the opening of her garment, and the breathing was attributed to Him, may He be exalted, because it was from Gabriel by His command, as an honour. It was also said: the spirit here is Gabriel, as He said: "So We sent to her Our spirit, and it appeared to her in the form of a man" (Q. 19:17). The meaning is: *fa-nafakhnā fīhā* (so We breathed into her), from the direction of Gabriel, and Gabriel had breathed through the opening of her garment, so the breath reached her inside.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: the breathing of the spirit into the body is an expression for its revival, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: "So when I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My spirit" (Q. 15:29), meaning I gave him life; and if that is established, then His statement *fa-nafakhnā fīhā min rūḥinā* is clearly problematic, because it indicates the revival of Mary. I say: its meaning is that We breathed the spirit into Jesus within her, meaning We gave him life in her womb. Similar to this is when the piper says: "I breathed into the house of so-and-so," meaning I played the pipe in his house. End.

There is no difficulty in this, for it is by omitting a noun (mudaf): i.e., (we breathed) into her son "from Our spirit" (min ruhina). His statement "I said its meaning is: We breathed the spirit into Isa" uses nafakha (to breathe) transitively, whereas the established usage is that it is not transitive, so making it transitive requires a complement (ji'ma', i.e., sexual intercourse). And he used it intransitively in his saying: i.e., "I blew into the flute in his house." Ended. There is no difficulty in this.

He said "a sign" (ayah) in the singular because their condition together constitutes one single sign, namely her giving birth to him without a male (fahl, i.e., a father). Although there are many signs in the case of Maryam and many signs in the case of Isa, here he has focused on the matter of the birth without mentioning anything else, and that is one sign. His saying "for the worlds" (lil-'alamin) means: for those among the people of their time who take heed from it, and those who came after them. The mention of Maryam alongside the prophets in this surah indicates that she was a prophetess, since she is mentioned together with them in the remembrance. As for one who denies that women could be prophetesses, he said: she was mentioned on account of Isa, and the mention of the two of them here is fitting alongside the story of Zakariyya, his wife and Yahya, because of the kinship that is between them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 83–91 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And Job, when he called out to his Lord: "Harm has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ ﴿So We answered him and removed the harm that was upon him, and We gave him his family and the like of them with them, as a mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers.﴾ ﴿And Ishmael, and Idris, and Dhul-Kifl; each was among the patient.﴾ ﴿And We admitted them into Our mercy; indeed, they were among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And Dhul-Nun, when he went off in anger and thought that We would not decide upon him; then he called out in the darknesses: "There is no god but You; glory be to You. Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿So We answered him and saved him from distress, and thus do We save the believers.﴾ ﴿And Zachariah, when he called to his Lord: "My Lord, do not leave me alone (fardan), and You are the best of inheritors."﴾ ﴿So We answered him and gave him Yahya, and We made his wife fit for him. Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds, and they called upon Us in hope and in fear, and they were humble before Us.﴾ ﴿And she who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our spirit and made her and her son a sign for the worlds.﴾

The narrators of reports (al-akhbariyyun, i.e., the historians who relate accounts) have been lengthy regarding the story of Job. Job was a Roman, from the descendants of Isaac son of Jacob. Allah made him a prophet, spread worldly wealth over him, and multiplied his family and property. He had seven sons and seven daughters, and he owned various kinds of livestock and five hundred plows (faddan), each followed by five hundred servants, and each servant had a wife, a child, and palm trees. Then Allah tested him by the loss of his sons, when the house collapsed upon them and they perished, by the loss of his property, and by illness in his body for eighteen years. It was also said that it was less than that. One day his wife said to him: "If only you would call upon Allah." He said to her: "How long was the period of ease?" She said: "Eighty years." He said: "I am ashamed before Allah to call upon Him, for the period of my trial has not reached the period of my ease." When Allah removed the harm from him, He brought his children back to life, gave him the like of them, and gave him additional ones from among them. It is also reported that his wife afterwards bore him twenty-six sons. They also mentioned details about the loss of his property and family and about Iblis being given power over him in that matter, but Allah knows best the soundness of these reports.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (ﷺ) *annī* with a fatḥah on the hamzah. Isa ibn Umar read it with a kasrah. This is either by supposing an elided verb of speech, meaning "saying: *annī*," or by treating *nādā* (called out) as if it were *qāla* (said), and then breaking *inna* with a kasrah after it. The second is the view of the Kufans (al-Kufiyyun), and the first is the view of the Basrans (al-Basriyyun). *Al-ḍurr* with a ḍammah means harm in the self, such as from illness or emaciation. *Al-ḍarr* with a fatḥah means harm in everything. The difference between the two forms is due to the difference in meaning. Job was gentle in his request: he mentioned himself in a way that calls for mercy, described his Lord with the utmost mercy, did not state the thing he wanted explicitly, and did not specify the harm that had touched him.

The exegetes differed about this in seventeen opinions. The most sound of them is that he rose to pray, but could not stand up, and so he said: "Harm has touched me," as a report about a state, not a complaint about his trial. This was narrated from Anas, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ). The article *al* in *al-ḍurr* is generic, covering harm to the body, the family, and the property. As for the giving of his family, its apparent meaning is that whoever of his family had died, He returned to him and brought them back to life in their same persons, and He gave him the like of his family along with them, of children and followers. It was also mentioned that He gave him the like of them as a multiplied number in the Hereafter. *Raḥmatan* ("as a mercy") is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ūl min ajlih*), meaning: "because of Our mercy towards him." *Dhikrā* ("a reminder") is from Us, through the goodness shown to those who are with Us. Or *raḥmatan* is a mercy from Us to Job, and *dhikrā* means an admonition to others among the worshippers, so that they may be patient as he was patient, until they are rewarded as he was rewarded.

Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Mujahid said: Dhul-Kifl was a righteous servant, but not a prophet. Most of the scholars said: he was a prophet. It was said he was Ilyas (Elijah), and it was said he was Zachariah, and it was said he was Yushu' (Joshua). *Al-kifl* means portion and share, so Dhul-Kifl means the one with a share of Allah, bounded by reality. It was also said that he had double the deeds of the prophets of his time and double their reward. It was said that the explanations of his name Dhul-Kifl are confused and not sound. *Mughāḍiban* ("in anger") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*). It was said its meaning is *ghaḍbān* (angry). It is from the form *mufā'ala*, which does not necessarily imply mutual participation, as in: "I punished the thief (*'āqabtu al-liṣṣ*)" and "I travelled (*sāfartu*)." It was also said that *mughāḍiban* means he was angry at his people, whom he angered by leaving them, since they feared the descent of punishment, and they angered him when he invited them to Allah for a period but they did not respond to him. So he threatened them with punishment. Then he went out from among them in the manner of the prophets when punishment descends, before Allah had permitted him to leave. It was also said that *mughāḍiban* means angry at King Hizqiya when he appointed him to fight a king who had insulted the Children of Israel. Jonah said to him: "Did Allah order you to expel me?" He said: "No." He said: "Did He name me to you?" He said: "No." He said: "Here are other prophets besides me." But he insisted on him, so he went out angry at the king. As for the statement of whoever said that *mughāḍiban* means angry at his Lord, and reported various forms of anger toward his Lord, it must be rejected, since none of these forms befits the station of prophethood. Those scholars who said this, such as al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Jubayr, and others among the Successors (al-Tabi'un), and Ibn Mas'ud among the Companions, should be interpreted so that the meaning of their statement "angry at his Lord" is "for the sake of his Lord and his religion." The *lām* here is the *lām* of cause (*lām al-'illa*), not the *lām* that conveys the object. Abu Sharaf read *mughḍiban* as a passive participle (*ism maf'ūl*).

*Fa-ẓanna an lan naqdira 'alayh* ("and thought that We would not decide upon him"): that is, that We would not constrict upon him, from *qadar* (decree), not from *qudra* (power). It was also said that it means from *qudra* (power), in the sense of: "that We would not have power over him" with the trial. The majority read *naqdira* with the "We" of majesty (*nūn al-'aẓama*), lightened. Ibn Abi Layla, Abu Sharaf, al-Kalbi, Humayd ibn Qays, and Ya'qub read it with a ḍammah on the *yā'* and a fatḥah on the *dāl*, lightened. Isa and al-Hasan read it with a *yā'* with a fatḥah and a kasrah on the *dāl*. Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Yamani read it with a ḍammah on the *yā'*, a fatḥah on the *qāf* and *dāl*, doubled. Al-Zuhri read it with a *nūn* with a ḍammah, a fatḥah on the *qāf*, and a kasrah on the *dāl*, doubled.

*Fa-nādā fī al-ẓulumāt* ("then he called out in the darknesses"): in the speech there are elided sentences, which have been clarified in surah al-Saffat, and there we will mention his story, Allah willing. *Al-ẓulumāt* is in the plural because of its intense density, as if it were darkness upon darkness. It was said: the darknesses of the belly of the fish, of the sea, and of the night. It was said: another fish swallowed his fish, so he was in the darkness of the bellies of the two fish and the darkness of the sea. It is reported that Jonah prostrated inside the belly of the fish when he heard the glorification of the fish at the bottom of the sea. The *an* in *an lā ilāha illā anta* ("that there is no god but You") is explanatory (*tafsīriyya*), because *fa-nādā* came before it and has the sense of speech. It is also possible that the estimate is *bi-annahu*, so it would be the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, and the restriction of divinity to Him, may He be exalted, then glorifying Him from attributes of deficiency, then acknowledging what follows.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "No one in distress calls with this supplication except that he is answered." *Al-ghamm* ("distress") is what he suffered when the fish swallowed him, and the duration of his stay in its belly. The majority read *nunjī* as the imperfect of *anjā* (to save). Al-Jahdari read it doubled as the imperfect of *najjā*. Ibn Amir and Abu Bakr read *najjā* with a ḍammah on the *nūn*, a doubled *jīm*, and a quiescent *yā'*. It is the same in the Imam's codex (*muṣḥaf al-imām*) and the codices of the regions, with a single *nūn*. Abu Ubayd preferred it for its agreement with the codices. Al-Zajjaj and al-Farisi said it is a solecism (*laḥn*). It was said: it is an imperfect in which the *nūn* was assimilated into the *jīm*, but this was rejected, since it is not permitted to assimilate the *nūn* into the *jīm* which is the first radical of the verb, because of the meeting of two identical letters, just as it was elided in the reading of whoever read *wa-nazala al-malā'ika*, meaning *wa-nunzilu al-malā'ika*. On this basis Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) derived it. It was also said: it is a past verb in the passive voice, and the *yā'* was made quiescent just as whoever read *wa-dharū mā baqiya min al-ribā* made it quiescent. The place of the subject is occupied by the verbal noun pronoun, meaning *najjā* (He saved): it, that is the rescue, saves the believers, like the reading of Abu Ja'far, *li-yajziya qawman* (Q. 45:14), meaning *wa-li-yajziya huwa*, that is, the recompense itself. Al-Akhfash, the Kufans, and Abu Ubayd permitted placing something other than the object in the position of the subject, such as a verbal noun, an adverb of place, an adverb of time, or a prepositional phrase, even when the object is present. The poetic usage supports placing a prepositional phrase in the position of the subject even when the object is present, as in the saying:

"There was granted to me, from among my enemies, a warner, by whom I was protected from the spreading evil."

Al-Akhfash said, regarding examples: "*ḍaraba al-ḍarba al-shadīda Zaydan*" (he struck the severe blow Zayd), "*ḍaraba al-yawmāni Zaydan*" (the two days struck Zayd), "*ḍaraba makānuka Zaydan*" (your place struck Zayd), and "*u'ṭiya i'ṭā'a ḥasanin akhāka dirhaman*" (a good giving was given to your brother a dirham), and "*maḍrūban 'abduhu Zaydan*" (his slave was struck, Zayd). It was said: the pronoun of the verbal noun was placed in the position of the subject, and *al-mu'minīn* ("the believers") is in the accusative by an elided verb, meaning: "*wa-ka-dhālika nunjī*" (and thus do We save), "it" (the rescue) "*nunjī al-mu'minīn*" (saves the believers). The well-known view among the Basrans is that whenever the object is present, nothing else may be placed in the position of the subject. However, the author of al-Lubab reported the disagreement on this among the Basrans, and that some of them permitted it.

*Lā tadharnī fardan* ("do not leave me alone"): that is, solitary, without an heir. He asked his Lord to grant him a son to inherit him, then he referred his matter to Allah and said: "*wa-anta khayru al-wārithīn*" (and You are the best of inheritors), meaning: if You do not grant me one who inherits me, then You are the best inheritor. The "making fit for him" of his wife refers to her good character. She had a bad character, as said by Ata, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, and Awn ibn Abd Allah. It was said: making her fit refers to her ability to bear children after she had been barren, as said by Qatada. It was said: making her fit means restoring her youth to him. The pronoun in *innahum* refers to the prophets previously mentioned, meaning: their being answered in their requests was because of their hastening to goodness and their supplication to Us.

*Raghaban wa-rahaban* ("in hope and in fear") means at the time of hope and at the time of fear, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: "He fears the Hereafter and hopes for the mercy of his Lord" (Q. 39:9). It was said the pronoun refers to Zachariah, his wife, and their son Yahya. A group read *yad'ūnanā* with the *nūn* of the nominative elided. Talha read it with a doubled *nūn*, assimilating the *nūn* of the nominative into *nā*, the object pronoun. Ibn Thabit, al-A'mash, Wahb ibn Amr, al-Nahwi, Harun, Abu Ma'mar, al-Asma'i, al-Lu'lu'i, Yunus, Abu Zayd, and seven of them from Abu Amr (who are among those who read it this way) read *raghaban wa-rahaban* with a fatḥah and a quiescent *hā'*. The more famous reading from al-A'mash is with two ḍammahs on them. A group read with a ḍammah on the two *rā'*s and a quiescence on the *ghayn* and *hā'*. *Raghaban wa-rahaban* in the accusative, both are verbal nouns in the position of a circumstantial state, or an object of purpose.

*Wa-allatī aḥṣanat farjahā* ("and she who guarded her chastity"): she is Mary, daughter of Imran, mother of Jesus, peace be upon him. The apparent meaning is that *al-farj* here is the modesty of a woman. She guarded it, meaning she prevented it from lawful and unlawful things, as she said: "No man has touched me, and I have not been unchaste" (Q. 19:20). It was said: *al-farj* here is the slit of her shirt, which she prevented Gabriel from reaching when he came near to her to breathe, since he did not realize it. The apparent meaning of His statement *fa-nafakhnā fīhā min rūḥinā* ("so We breathed into her of Our spirit") is a metaphor for the bringing into existence of Jesus alive in her womb, and there was no literal breathing there. He attributed the spirit to Himself in the manner of honour. It was said: there was literal breathing, namely that Gabriel, peace be upon him, breathed into the opening of her garment, and the breathing was attributed to Him, may He be exalted, because it was from Gabriel by His command, as an honour. It was also said: the spirit here is Gabriel, as He said: "So We sent to her Our spirit, and it appeared to her in the form of a man" (Q. 19:17). The meaning is: *fa-nafakhnā fīhā* (so We breathed into her), from the direction of Gabriel, and Gabriel had breathed through the opening of her garment, so the breath reached her inside.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: the breathing of the spirit into the body is an expression for its revival, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: "So when I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My spirit" (Q. 15:29), meaning I gave him life; and if that is established, then His statement *fa-nafakhnā fīhā min rūḥinā* is clearly problematic, because it indicates the revival of Mary. I say: its meaning is that We breathed the spirit into Jesus within her, meaning We gave him life in her womb. Similar to this is when the piper says: "I breathed into the house of so-and-so," meaning I played the pipe in his house. End.

There is no difficulty in this, for it is by omitting a noun (mudaf): i.e., (we breathed) into her son "from Our spirit" (min ruhina). His statement "I said its meaning is: We breathed the spirit into Isa" uses nafakha (to breathe) transitively, whereas the established usage is that it is not transitive, so making it transitive requires a complement (ji'ma', i.e., sexual intercourse). And he used it intransitively in his saying: i.e., "I blew into the flute in his house." Ended. There is no difficulty in this.

He said "a sign" (ayah) in the singular because their condition together constitutes one single sign, namely her giving birth to him without a male (fahl, i.e., a father). Although there are many signs in the case of Maryam and many signs in the case of Isa, here he has focused on the matter of the birth without mentioning anything else, and that is one sign. His saying "for the worlds" (lil-'alamin) means: for those among the people of their time who take heed from it, and those who came after them. The mention of Maryam alongside the prophets in this surah indicates that she was a prophetess, since she is mentioned together with them in the remembrance. As for one who denies that women could be prophetesses, he said: she was mentioned on account of Isa, and the mention of the two of them here is fitting alongside the story of Zakariyya, his wife and Yahya, because of the kinship that is between them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 21, verses 92–100 (part 1 of 2):

[p. 337] ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so worship Me.﴾ ﴿But they divided their affair among themselves into sects; each of them will return to Us.﴾ ﴿So whoever does good deeds while he is a believer, his effort will not be denied, and indeed We record it for him.﴾ ﴿And it is forbidden for a town which We have destroyed that they should not return.﴾ ﴿Until, when Gog and Magog are released, and they come swarming from every slope.﴾ ﴿And the true promise draws near, and then the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare fixedly: "Woe to us! We were heedless of this; indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell; you will be coming to it.﴾ ﴿If these had been gods, they would not have come to it; but all of them will abide in it forever.﴾ ﴿For them therein is a roaring, and they therein will not hear.﴾

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿this community of yours﴾ is an address to the contemporaries of the Messenger (ﷺ), and ﴿this﴾ refers to the religion of Islam. That is, the religion of Islam is your religion, which you must follow, not deviating from it, one religion without disagreement. It is also possible that ﴿this﴾ refers to the path that the prophets mentioned were upon, namely the monotheism of Allah the Exalted: your path and your religion are one path without disagreement regarding the foundations of belief. Rather, what the prophets brought of that is what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿one community﴾ is "created by Him, owned by Him," so the "community" refers to all people. It has been said that the discourse may be connected to the story of Mary and her son, meaning ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91], in that he was sent to them with a religion and a book, and it was said to them ﴿Indeed this community of yours﴾, that is, he called all of them to belief in Allah and to worshipping Him.

Then the Exalted informed that after that they differed, ﴿and they divided their affair among themselves﴾. The majority read ﴿community of yours﴾ with the nominative (ar-raf') as the predicate of inna, and ﴿one community﴾ in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). It has also been said that it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿this﴾. Al-Hasan read ﴿ummatakum﴾ with the accusative as a substitute for ﴿this﴾. He also read, together with Ibn Ishaq, al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi 'Abla, al-Ju'fi, Harun (on the authority of Abu 'Amr), and al-Za'farani, ﴿ummatukum ummatan wahidatan﴾ with the nominative for all three words, on the basis that ﴿ummatukum﴾ and ﴿ummatan wahidatan﴾ are the predicate of inna; or ﴿ummatan wahidatan﴾ is a substitute for ﴿ummatukum﴾, a substitution of an indefinite noun for a definite one; or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is one community." The pronoun in ﴿wa-taqatta'u﴾ refers back to the pronoun of address by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), meaning "and you divided."

Since this act is among the most abominable of deeds, He shifted away from address to the third person, as if this act did not proceed from those addressed. In reporting about them this way there is a rebuke of them for what they corrupted, and it is as if He were informing others of the ugly deed that had proceeded from them, saying: "Do you not see what these people have committed in the religion of Allah? They made the matter of their religion into pieces, as a group divides a thing: for this one a share, and for this one a share," as a figurative illustration of their disagreement. (p. 338) Then He threatened them with the return of this divided sect to His recompense. It has also been said: each of them, the one who remains steadfast in his true religion and the one who strays from it to another. Al-A'mash read ﴿zubura﴾ with a fatḥa on the bāʾ, the plural of zubra (a piece). Then He mentioned the state of the one who does good and that his effort is not denied. The word al-kufran (denial, ingratitude) is a figurative expression for the deprivation of reward, just as shukr (gratitude) is a figurative expression for giving it. It is said "Allah is Shakur" (the Most Appreciative), but not for negating the genus. So it is more eloquent than His saying ﴿so his effort will not be denied﴾. Recording (al-kitaba) is an expression for affirming his good deed in the register of deeds so that he is rewarded for it, and it will not be lost. Al-kufran is a verbal noun like al-kufr. The poet said:

*I have seen people whose grandfathers do not sleep, and my grandfather, and by Allah's ingratitude, none sleeps.*

In the codex of 'Abd Allah it reads "lā kufra" (without the tanwin). The phrase ﴿li-sa'yihi﴾ is connected to an omitted verb, meaning "we deny his effort." It cannot be connected to al-kufran, because if it were connected to it, it would be a noun not extended by a complement, so it would require tanwin.

The majority read ﴿wa-ḥarāmun﴾. Ḥamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr, Talha, al-A'mash, Abu Hanifa, and Abu 'Amr in one narration read ﴿wa-ḥirmun﴾ with a kasra on the ḥāʾ and a sukūn on the rāʾ. Qatada, Matar al-Warraq, and Mahbub on the authority of Abu 'Amr read it with a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ and a sukūn on the rāʾ. 'Ikrima read ﴿wa-ḥaramun﴾ with a kasra on the rāʾ and tanwin. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima also, Ibn al-Musayyab, and Qatada also, read it with a kasra on the rāʾ and a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ and the mīm, in the past tense, with variation reported from the two of them. Abu al-'Aliya and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with a ḍamma on the rāʾ and a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ and the mīm, in the past tense. Ibn 'Abbas also read it with a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ, the rāʾ, and the mīm, in the past tense. Al-Yamani read ﴿wa-ḥurrima﴾ with a ḍamma on the ḥāʾ, a kasra on the rāʾ with shadda, and a fatḥa on the mīm. The majority read ﴿ahlaknāhā﴾ with the first person plural of majesty (nūn al-'aẓama, "we").

Al-Sulami and Qatada read it with the first person singular tā' (the "I" form). Harām is borrowed for what is impossible to exist, and from it: ﴿Indeed Allah has forbidden them both to the disbelievers﴾ [al-A'raf: 50]. The meaning of ﴿we destroyed it﴾ is "we decreed its destruction in the state in which it was of disbelief," so the destruction here is destruction on account of disbelief. The lā in ﴿they will not return﴾ is an extra particle (ṣila), and this is the view of Abu 'Ubayd, as in your saying: "What prevented you from not prostrating?" meaning "they return to belief." The sense is: it is impossible for the people of a town whose destruction We have decreed because of their disbelief to return in this world to belief until the Resurrection. Then, when it comes, they will return and say ﴿Woe to us! We were heedless of this﴾. And "ghayya" (an intensifying phrase) refers to what is close to the coming of the Hour, which is the opening of ﴿Gog and Magog﴾. It is read ﴿innahum﴾ with a kasra, in which case the sentence is complete at His saying "we destroyed it," and a omitted element is supposed by which ﴿And forbidden upon a town which We have destroyed﴾ becomes a sentence meaning "that is." The reference is to the righteous deed mentioned in the counterpart of these destroyed people. The meaning: ﴿And it is forbidden upon﴾ the people of "a town" whose destruction We decreed because of their disbelief, a righteous deed by which they would be saved from destruction. Then He emphasized that and gave its reason: that they ﴿will not return﴾ from disbelief. So how is that not impossible? In this case the omitted element is the subject, and the predicate is ﴿wa-ḥarām﴾. Some of them supposed it to be preceding, as if he said: "And the cancellation and repentance are forbidden." The reading of the majority with the fatḥa is valid on this meaning, and lā is negating in its original function, the supposition being "because they will not return." It has also been said: "we destroyed them" means the destruction befell them, and their return to the world means they would repent, but rather they are headed to punishment. It has also been said: the destruction is by sealing the hearts, and the return is to repentance and belief.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿And forbidden upon a town which We have destroyed﴾ means We judged by its destruction that We would not accept their deeds, because ﴿they will not return﴾, that is, they will not repent. This meaning is indicated by His earlier saying ﴿so his effort will not be denied﴾, that is, his deed will be accepted. Then He mentioned this after it and showed that the disbeliever's deed is not accepted.

Abu Muslim ibn Bahr said: ﴿ḥarām﴾ means "impossible," and ﴿that they will not return﴾ is the negation of return to the Hereafter. When the negation is impossible, return becomes obligatory. So the meaning is that their return to life in the Hereafter is necessary, and the purpose is to deny the words of one who denies resurrection, and to confirm what preceded: that no one's effort is denied, and that he will be recompensed for it on the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said: ḥarām comes with the meaning of "obligatory," as indicated by ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you: that you not associate anything with Him﴾ [al-An'am: 151], and abandoning association is obligatory. Al-Khansa' said:

*It is forbidden to me (ḥarām ʿalayya) that I should see the age weeping over its grief except that I weep over Sakhr.*

Also, from the usage is the application of a pronoun to its opposite. On this view, Mujahid and al-Hasan said ﴿they will not return﴾ means "from polytheism." Qatada and Muqatil said it means "to this world." Ibn 'Atiyya said: a clear threat is implied in the verse, because He mentioned the one who does righteous deeds while being a believer, then returned to mention the disbelievers who, out of their disbelief and belief, held that they would not be gathered to a Lord and would not return to a Resurrection. So they supposed that no punishment would reach them. The verse therefore came to refute their supposition: "and it is impossible for the destroyed disbelievers that they should not return," but rather they are returning to the punishment of Allah and His painful torment. In this case the lā is in its original function and ḥarām in its original function. The same applies to al-ḥurum, so consider it. End of quotation.

As for ﴿ḥattā﴾ (until), Abu al-Baqa' said it is connected in meaning to ḥarām, meaning that the prohibition continues until this time, and it has no governing effect on ﴿idhā﴾ (when). Al-Hawfi said ﴿ḥattā﴾ is a limit, and what governs it is what the meaning indicates, namely their regret over what they neglected of obedience when the opportunity to make up for it had passed. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "To what is ḥattā connected, being a limit to it, and which of the three is it?" I say: it is connected to ḥarām, and it is a limit to it, because the impossibility of their return does not cease until the Resurrection comes. It is the ḥattā that reports speech, and the reported speech is the conditional and its response, namely idhā and what is within its scope. End of quotation.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is connected to His saying ﴿and they divided﴾. It is possible, according to some of the earlier interpretations, that it be connected to ﴿yarji'ūn﴾ (they return). It is also possible that it is the particle of beginning, and this is more apparent because of idhā, since it requires a response, which is the intended mention. End of quotation. That ḥattā is connected here is far-fetched in terms of the separation involved, but in terms of meaning it is good: they will not cease to disagree, not gathered upon the religion of truth, until the Hour draws near. When the Hour comes, that disagreement ends, and everyone knows that their Master is the Truth, and that the saving religion was the religion of monotheism. The response to idhā is omitted, its supposition being ﴿they will say, "Woe to us!"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 14], as al-Zajjaj and a group said. Or its supposition is "then they will be resurrected," ﴿then suddenly it is staring﴾.

Or it is mentioned, namely ﴿and the promise drew near﴾, with the wāw being extra, as some said. This is the view of the Kufans, who permit extra wāw and fā' in "fa-idhā hiya." This was said by al-Hawfi. Al-Zamakhshari said: idhā here is the sudden-occurrence idhā (idhā al-mufājaʾa), and it occurs with sudden events, taking the place of the fā', as in His saying ﴿when they are despairing﴾ [al-Rum: 36]. When fā' comes with it, they cooperate to join the response to the condition, so it is emphasized. Had it been said ﴿then it is staring﴾, it would have been sound.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: What I say is that the response is in His saying ﴿then it is staring﴾, and this is the meaning intended to be mentioned, because it is their return, which they used to deny, and which He made forbidden for them to avoid. The disagreement over ﴿futtiḥat﴾ (is opened) has been mentioned in al-An'am. Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and Ibn 'Amir agreed in shadding the tā', as did the same in al-An'am and al-Qamar. The majority read them with the light form. ﴿Futtiḥat Yājūj﴾ is with an omitted noun, meaning "the barrier of Gog and Magog." The disagreement over the reading of ﴿Yājūj wa-Mājūj﴾ has been mentioned. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿wa-hum﴾ refers back to ﴿Gog and Magog﴾, meaning they emerge from every elevated place and high ground and overspread the earth. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to humanity, and this is supported by the reading of 'Abd Allah and Ibn 'Abbas, ﴿min kulli jadath﴾ with the letter thāʾ, meaning "grave." It is also read with fā' and thāʾ, where the Hijazis use thāʾ and the Tamim use fā', which replaces thāʾ, just as they replaced thāʾ with it; they say the origin of it is maghfūr.

The majority read ﴿yansilūn﴾ with a kasra on the sīn, while Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu al-Sammal read it with a ḍamma. ﴿And the true promise drew near﴾, that is, the promise of the true resurrection about which there is no doubt. ﴿Drew near﴾ (iqtaraba) is said to be more intensive in nearness than qariba. The pronoun in ﴿hiya﴾ refers to the event, as if it were said: "then suddenly the matter and the occurrence," with ﴿staring﴾ (shākhiṣatan) as the predicate, and ﴿the eyes of those who disbelieved﴾ as the subject. It is not permissible for ﴿abṣār shākhiṣatun﴾ to be nominative, because that would require that after a pronoun of matter or event there be a sentence explaining the pronoun, with both its parts stated explicitly; this is permitted on the view of the Kufans. Al-Zamakhshari said: "hiya" is an ambiguous pronoun which "the eyes" clarifies and explains, just as "those who did wrong and kept secret" explains it. End of quotation. He mentioned no other view than this one, and it is an opinion of al-Farra'. Al-Farra' said: "hiya" is a pronoun for "the eyes," which came earlier because of the indication of the context and the presence of what explains it, and he cited the verse of the poet:

*So, by her father, my beloved does not say anything except that Malik ibn Abi Ka'b is pleasing to me.*

Al-Farra' also mentioned that "hiya" is a dummy pronoun (ʿimād) which can take its place, and he cited:

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 92–100 (part 2 of 2):

*Bi-thawbin wa-dinarin wa-shatin wa-dirhamin* ∗∗∗ *fa-hal huwa marfu'un bi-ma hahuna ra'su*

[Poetry: "With a garment, a dinar, a sheep, and a dirham / Is his head raised by what is here?"]

This does not hold except according to one of the two opinions of al-Kisa'i, who permitted placing the separating pronoun (*fasl*, the pronoun that separates the subject from the predicate) together with the predicate before the subject. He said: *huwa al-qa'imu Zaydun* ("he is the one standing, Zayd"), with Zayd being the subject (*mubtada'*) and *al-qa'imu* its predicate (*khabar*). The separating pronoun here is a *'imad* (a support pronoun, the same as *fasl*). The origin of the matter is *Zaydun huwa al-qa'imu*. He says its origin is *hadhihi*, so when [the verse reads] ﴿the eyes of those who disbelieved﴾ *hiya* (*shakhisatun*), then *shakhisatun* is the predicate of *absaru* and has been placed before the *'imad*. This also fits the view of those who permit the *'imad* to come before an indefinite predicate.

Al-Tha'labi mentioned another interpretation, that the sentence ends at *fa-idha hiya* meaning "present and occurring," referring to the Hour, and then begins: ﴿Fixed open are the eyes of those who disbelieved﴾. This is a forced interpretation with a discordant construction.

Hudhayfah narrated: "If a man were to acquire [a mount] and then let it go, he would not ride it until the Hour arises," meaning that at the coming of the Hour, it will come right after the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj.

﴿Woe to us!﴾ is the object (*ma'mul*) of a deleted verb of saying. Al-Zamakhshari said: its estimate is "they will say," and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from ﴿those who disbelieved﴾. The statement of al-Zajjaj was mentioned earlier, that this saying is the answer to *idha* (the apodosis). *Shukhus* means fixing the gaze without blinking, in heedlessness of this. End of quote. That is, [they will say] regarding what they have now found and realized of the realities. Then they turned away from their saying ﴿We were in heedlessness of this﴾ and informed of what they had deliberately done of disbelief and turning away from faith, and so they said ﴿Rather, we were wrongdoers﴾. The address in ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah﴾ is to the disbelievers contemporary with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), especially the people of Makkah, and their objects of worship are the idols.

The majority read *hasabu* with an unpointed *ha'* and an unpointed *sad*, which is what is thrown (*yuhsabu bihi*), i.e., what is thrown into the fire of Hell. Before it is thrown, it is not called *hasab* except metaphorically. Ibn al-Sumayfi', Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Mahbub, and Abu Hatim from Ibn Kathir read it with a sukun on the *sad*, and it was reported from Ibn 'Abbas. It is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle, i.e., *al-mahsub* (that which is thrown). Ibn 'Abbas read it with an unpointed *dad* (*dad* pronounced as an emphatic letter), vowelled with a fatha, and from him with a sukun. Kuthayyir 'Azzah read it this way too. *Al-Hadb* is what is thrown into the fire, and *al-mihdab* is the stick or iron rod or other thing with which the fire is stirred. The poet said:

*Fa-la taku fi harbina mihdaban* ∗∗∗ *fa-taj'ala qawmaka shatta shu'ubA*

[Poetry: "So do not be among us one who stirs the fire of war, lest you make your people scattered tribes."]

Ubayy, 'Ali, 'A'ishah, Ibn al-Zubayr, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read *hatab* with a *ta'*. The gathering of the disbelievers with their objects of worship in the Fire is to increase their distress and regret, by seeing them with them in it, since they are punished because of them. They used to hope for good from their worship, so evil came to them from them. And because they became enemies to them, and seeing the enemy is something that increases the torment, as the poet said:

*Wa-ihtimalu al-adha wa-ru'yatu janiyihi* ∗∗∗ *ghidha'un tudna bihi al-ajsamu*

[Poetry: "Enduring harm and seeing the one who inflicted it are a nourishment by which bodies waste away."]

﴿You, to it﴾, i.e., to the Fire, ﴿are its bound-for﴾. *Al-wurud* here means entering. ﴿If these had been gods, they would not have entered it﴾, i.e., the idols you worship. That it means entering is indicated by His saying ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾. The majority read *alihatan* in the accusative as the predicate of *kana*. Talhah read it in the nominative, taking *kana* to have the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*). ﴿And all therein﴾, i.e., each of the worshippers and their objects of worship.

﴿For them therein is groaning﴾. *Al-zafir* is the sound of the breath of one who is distressed, coming out from the heart. Apparently, groaning only comes from one who has life, and those [who have life] are the worshippers. As for the objects of worship, [they are of two kinds]: those who claimed divinity, like Pharaoh and the extremists of the Isma'ilis who were the kings of Egypt from the sons of 'Ubayd Allah, their first kings; and it is permissible that Allah grants life to the idols that were worshipped, so that they too have groaning. Al-Zamakhshari said: If they and their idols are in one generation, it is permissible to say that they have groaning therein, even if the groaners are none but those who are in it. ﴿They will not hear﴾ [al-Anbiya: 102]. It was narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that they will be placed in coffins of fire and will not hear. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind and mute and deaf﴾ [al-Isra: 97]. In hearing things there is comfort, so Allah prevented the disbelievers from that in the Fire. It was also said that ﴿They will not hear﴾ [al-Anbiya: 102] means they will not hear what would please them from the speech of the angels of punishment (*al-zabaniyah*).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 21, verses 92–100 (part 1 of 2):

[p. 337] ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so worship Me.﴾ ﴿But they divided their affair among themselves into sects; each of them will return to Us.﴾ ﴿So whoever does good deeds while he is a believer, his effort will not be denied, and indeed We record it for him.﴾ ﴿And it is forbidden for a town which We have destroyed that they should not return.﴾ ﴿Until, when Gog and Magog are released, and they come swarming from every slope.﴾ ﴿And the true promise draws near, and then the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare fixedly: "Woe to us! We were heedless of this; indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell; you will be coming to it.﴾ ﴿If these had been gods, they would not have come to it; but all of them will abide in it forever.﴾ ﴿For them therein is a roaring, and they therein will not hear.﴾

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿this community of yours﴾ is an address to the contemporaries of the Messenger (ﷺ), and ﴿this﴾ refers to the religion of Islam. That is, the religion of Islam is your religion, which you must follow, not deviating from it, one religion without disagreement. It is also possible that ﴿this﴾ refers to the path that the prophets mentioned were upon, namely the monotheism of Allah the Exalted: your path and your religion are one path without disagreement regarding the foundations of belief. Rather, what the prophets brought of that is what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿one community﴾ is "created by Him, owned by Him," so the "community" refers to all people. It has been said that the discourse may be connected to the story of Mary and her son, meaning ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91], in that he was sent to them with a religion and a book, and it was said to them ﴿Indeed this community of yours﴾, that is, he called all of them to belief in Allah and to worshipping Him.

Then the Exalted informed that after that they differed, ﴿and they divided their affair among themselves﴾. The majority read ﴿community of yours﴾ with the nominative (ar-raf') as the predicate of inna, and ﴿one community﴾ in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). It has also been said that it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿this﴾. Al-Hasan read ﴿ummatakum﴾ with the accusative as a substitute for ﴿this﴾. He also read, together with Ibn Ishaq, al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi 'Abla, al-Ju'fi, Harun (on the authority of Abu 'Amr), and al-Za'farani, ﴿ummatukum ummatan wahidatan﴾ with the nominative for all three words, on the basis that ﴿ummatukum﴾ and ﴿ummatan wahidatan﴾ are the predicate of inna; or ﴿ummatan wahidatan﴾ is a substitute for ﴿ummatukum﴾, a substitution of an indefinite noun for a definite one; or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is one community." The pronoun in ﴿wa-taqatta'u﴾ refers back to the pronoun of address by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), meaning "and you divided."

Since this act is among the most abominable of deeds, He shifted away from address to the third person, as if this act did not proceed from those addressed. In reporting about them this way there is a rebuke of them for what they corrupted, and it is as if He were informing others of the ugly deed that had proceeded from them, saying: "Do you not see what these people have committed in the religion of Allah? They made the matter of their religion into pieces, as a group divides a thing: for this one a share, and for this one a share," as a figurative illustration of their disagreement. (p. 338) Then He threatened them with the return of this divided sect to His recompense. It has also been said: each of them, the one who remains steadfast in his true religion and the one who strays from it to another. Al-A'mash read ﴿zubura﴾ with a fatḥa on the bāʾ, the plural of zubra (a piece). Then He mentioned the state of the one who does good and that his effort is not denied. The word al-kufran (denial, ingratitude) is a figurative expression for the deprivation of reward, just as shukr (gratitude) is a figurative expression for giving it. It is said "Allah is Shakur" (the Most Appreciative), but not for negating the genus. So it is more eloquent than His saying ﴿so his effort will not be denied﴾. Recording (al-kitaba) is an expression for affirming his good deed in the register of deeds so that he is rewarded for it, and it will not be lost. Al-kufran is a verbal noun like al-kufr. The poet said:

*I have seen people whose grandfathers do not sleep, and my grandfather, and by Allah's ingratitude, none sleeps.*

In the codex of 'Abd Allah it reads "lā kufra" (without the tanwin). The phrase ﴿li-sa'yihi﴾ is connected to an omitted verb, meaning "we deny his effort." It cannot be connected to al-kufran, because if it were connected to it, it would be a noun not extended by a complement, so it would require tanwin.

The majority read ﴿wa-ḥarāmun﴾. Ḥamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr, Talha, al-A'mash, Abu Hanifa, and Abu 'Amr in one narration read ﴿wa-ḥirmun﴾ with a kasra on the ḥāʾ and a sukūn on the rāʾ. Qatada, Matar al-Warraq, and Mahbub on the authority of Abu 'Amr read it with a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ and a sukūn on the rāʾ. 'Ikrima read ﴿wa-ḥaramun﴾ with a kasra on the rāʾ and tanwin. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima also, Ibn al-Musayyab, and Qatada also, read it with a kasra on the rāʾ and a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ and the mīm, in the past tense, with variation reported from the two of them. Abu al-'Aliya and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with a ḍamma on the rāʾ and a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ and the mīm, in the past tense. Ibn 'Abbas also read it with a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ, the rāʾ, and the mīm, in the past tense. Al-Yamani read ﴿wa-ḥurrima﴾ with a ḍamma on the ḥāʾ, a kasra on the rāʾ with shadda, and a fatḥa on the mīm. The majority read ﴿ahlaknāhā﴾ with the first person plural of majesty (nūn al-'aẓama, "we").

Al-Sulami and Qatada read it with the first person singular tā' (the "I" form). Harām is borrowed for what is impossible to exist, and from it: ﴿Indeed Allah has forbidden them both to the disbelievers﴾ [al-A'raf: 50]. The meaning of ﴿we destroyed it﴾ is "we decreed its destruction in the state in which it was of disbelief," so the destruction here is destruction on account of disbelief. The lā in ﴿they will not return﴾ is an extra particle (ṣila), and this is the view of Abu 'Ubayd, as in your saying: "What prevented you from not prostrating?" meaning "they return to belief." The sense is: it is impossible for the people of a town whose destruction We have decreed because of their disbelief to return in this world to belief until the Resurrection. Then, when it comes, they will return and say ﴿Woe to us! We were heedless of this﴾. And "ghayya" (an intensifying phrase) refers to what is close to the coming of the Hour, which is the opening of ﴿Gog and Magog﴾. It is read ﴿innahum﴾ with a kasra, in which case the sentence is complete at His saying "we destroyed it," and a omitted element is supposed by which ﴿And forbidden upon a town which We have destroyed﴾ becomes a sentence meaning "that is." The reference is to the righteous deed mentioned in the counterpart of these destroyed people. The meaning: ﴿And it is forbidden upon﴾ the people of "a town" whose destruction We decreed because of their disbelief, a righteous deed by which they would be saved from destruction. Then He emphasized that and gave its reason: that they ﴿will not return﴾ from disbelief. So how is that not impossible? In this case the omitted element is the subject, and the predicate is ﴿wa-ḥarām﴾. Some of them supposed it to be preceding, as if he said: "And the cancellation and repentance are forbidden." The reading of the majority with the fatḥa is valid on this meaning, and lā is negating in its original function, the supposition being "because they will not return." It has also been said: "we destroyed them" means the destruction befell them, and their return to the world means they would repent, but rather they are headed to punishment. It has also been said: the destruction is by sealing the hearts, and the return is to repentance and belief.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿And forbidden upon a town which We have destroyed﴾ means We judged by its destruction that We would not accept their deeds, because ﴿they will not return﴾, that is, they will not repent. This meaning is indicated by His earlier saying ﴿so his effort will not be denied﴾, that is, his deed will be accepted. Then He mentioned this after it and showed that the disbeliever's deed is not accepted.

Abu Muslim ibn Bahr said: ﴿ḥarām﴾ means "impossible," and ﴿that they will not return﴾ is the negation of return to the Hereafter. When the negation is impossible, return becomes obligatory. So the meaning is that their return to life in the Hereafter is necessary, and the purpose is to deny the words of one who denies resurrection, and to confirm what preceded: that no one's effort is denied, and that he will be recompensed for it on the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said: ḥarām comes with the meaning of "obligatory," as indicated by ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you: that you not associate anything with Him﴾ [al-An'am: 151], and abandoning association is obligatory. Al-Khansa' said:

*It is forbidden to me (ḥarām ʿalayya) that I should see the age weeping over its grief except that I weep over Sakhr.*

Qatada and Muqatil said it means "to this world." So they supposed that no punishment would reach them. The verse therefore came to refute their supposition: "and it is impossible for the destroyed disbelievers that they should not return," but rather they are returning to the punishment of Allah and His painful torment. In this case the lā is in its original function and ḥarām in its original function. The same applies to al-ḥurum, so consider it. End of quotation.

As for ﴿ḥattā﴾ (until), Abu al-Baqa' said it is connected in meaning to ḥarām, meaning that the prohibition continues until this time, and it has no governing effect on ﴿idhā﴾ (when). Al-Hawfi said ﴿ḥattā﴾ is a limit, and what governs it is what the meaning indicates, namely their regret over what they neglected of obedience when the opportunity to make up for it had passed. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "To what is ḥattā connected, being a limit to it, and which of the three is it?" I say: it is connected to ḥarām, and it is a limit to it, because the impossibility of their return does not cease until the Resurrection comes. It is the ḥattā that reports speech, and the reported speech is the conditional and its response, namely idhā and what is within its scope. End of quotation.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is connected to His saying ﴿and they divided﴾. It is possible, according to some of the earlier interpretations, that it be connected to ﴿yarji'ūn﴾ (they return). It is also possible that it is the particle of beginning, and this is more apparent because of idhā, since it requires a response, which is the intended mention. End of quotation. That ḥattā is connected here is far-fetched in terms of the separation involved, but in terms of meaning it is good: they will not cease to disagree, not gathered upon the religion of truth, until the Hour draws near. When the Hour comes, that disagreement ends, and everyone knows that their Master is the Truth, and that the saving religion was the religion of monotheism. The response to idhā is omitted, its supposition being ﴿they will say, "Woe to us!"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 14], as al-Zajjaj and a group said. Or its supposition is "then they will be resurrected," ﴿then suddenly it is staring﴾.

This was said by al-Hawfi. Ibn 'Atiyya said: What I say is that the response is in His saying ﴿then it is staring﴾, and this is the meaning intended to be mentioned, because it is their return, which they used to deny, and which He made forbidden for them to avoid. The disagreement over ﴿futtiḥat﴾ (is opened) has been mentioned in al-An'am. Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and Ibn 'Amir agreed in shadding the tā', as did the same in al-An'am and al-Qamar. The majority read them with the light form. ﴿Futtiḥat Yājūj﴾ is with an omitted noun, meaning "the barrier of Gog and Magog." The disagreement over the reading of ﴿Yājūj wa-Mājūj﴾ has been mentioned. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿wa-hum﴾ refers back to ﴿Gog and Magog﴾, meaning they emerge from every elevated place and high ground and overspread the earth. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to humanity, and this is supported by the reading of 'Abd Allah and Ibn 'Abbas, ﴿min kulli jadath﴾ with the letter thāʾ, meaning "grave." It is also read with fā' and thāʾ, where the Hijazis use thāʾ and the Tamim use fā', which replaces thāʾ, just as they replaced thāʾ with it; they say the origin of it is maghfūr.

The majority read ﴿yansilūn﴾ with a kasra on the sīn, while Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu al-Sammal read it with a ḍamma. ﴿And the true promise drew near﴾, that is, the promise of the true resurrection about which there is no doubt. ﴿Drew near﴾ (iqtaraba) is said to be more intensive in nearness than qariba. The pronoun in ﴿hiya﴾ refers to the event, as if it were said: "then suddenly the matter and the occurrence," with ﴿staring﴾ (shākhiṣatan) as the predicate, and ﴿the eyes of those who disbelieved﴾ as the subject. It is not permissible for ﴿abṣār shākhiṣatun﴾ to be nominative, because that would require that after a pronoun of matter or event there be a sentence explaining the pronoun, with both its parts stated explicitly; this is permitted on the view of the Kufans. Al-Zamakhshari said: "hiya" is an ambiguous pronoun which "the eyes" clarifies and explains, just as "those who did wrong and kept secret" explains it. End of quotation. He mentioned no other view than this one, and it is an opinion of al-Farra'. Al-Farra' said: "hiya" is a pronoun for "the eyes," which came earlier because of the indication of the context and the presence of what explains it, and he cited the verse of the poet:

*So, by her father, my beloved does not say anything except that Malik ibn Abi Ka'b is pleasing to me.*

Al-Farra' also mentioned that "hiya" is a dummy pronoun (ʿimād) which can take its place, and he cited:

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verses 92–100 (part 2 of 2):

*Bi-thawbin wa-dinarin wa-shatin wa-dirhamin* ∗∗∗ *fa-hal huwa marfu'un bi-ma hahuna ra'su*

[Poetry: "With a garment, a dinar, a sheep, and a dirham / Is his head raised by what is here?"]

This does not hold except according to one of the two opinions of al-Kisa'i, who permitted placing the separating pronoun (*fasl*, the pronoun that separates the subject from the predicate) together with the predicate before the subject. He said: *huwa al-qa'imu Zaydun* ("he is the one standing, Zayd"), with Zayd being the subject (*mubtada'*) and *al-qa'imu* its predicate (*khabar*). The separating pronoun here is a *'imad* (a support pronoun, the same as *fasl*). The origin of the matter is *Zaydun huwa al-qa'imu*. He says its origin is *hadhihi*, so when [the verse reads] ﴿the eyes of those who disbelieved﴾ *hiya* (*shakhisatun*), then *shakhisatun* is the predicate of *absaru* and has been placed before the *'imad*. This also fits the view of those who permit the *'imad* to come before an indefinite predicate.

Al-Tha'labi mentioned another interpretation, that the sentence ends at *fa-idha hiya* meaning "present and occurring," referring to the Hour, and then begins: ﴿Fixed open are the eyes of those who disbelieved﴾. This is a forced interpretation with a discordant construction.

Hudhayfah narrated: "If a man were to acquire [a mount] and then let it go, he would not ride it until the Hour arises," meaning that at the coming of the Hour, it will come right after the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj.

﴿Woe to us!﴾ is the object (*ma'mul*) of a deleted verb of saying. Al-Zamakhshari said: its estimate is "they will say," and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from ﴿those who disbelieved﴾. The statement of al-Zajjaj was mentioned earlier, that this saying is the answer to *idha* (the apodosis). *Shukhus* means fixing the gaze without blinking, in heedlessness of this. End of quote. That is, [they will say] regarding what they have now found and realized of the realities. Then they turned away from their saying ﴿We were in heedlessness of this﴾ and informed of what they had deliberately done of disbelief and turning away from faith, and so they said ﴿Rather, we were wrongdoers﴾. The address in ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah﴾ is to the disbelievers contemporary with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), especially the people of Makkah, and their objects of worship are the idols.

The majority read *hasabu* with an unpointed *ha'* and an unpointed *sad*, which is what is thrown (*yuhsabu bihi*), i.e., what is thrown into the fire of Hell. Before it is thrown, it is not called *hasab* except metaphorically. Ibn al-Sumayfi', Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Mahbub, and Abu Hatim from Ibn Kathir read it with a sukun on the *sad*, and it was reported from Ibn 'Abbas. It is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle, i.e., *al-mahsub* (that which is thrown). Ibn 'Abbas read it with an unpointed *dad* (*dad* pronounced as an emphatic letter), vowelled with a fatha, and from him with a sukun. Kuthayyir 'Azzah read it this way too. *Al-Hadb* is what is thrown into the fire, and *al-mihdab* is the stick or iron rod or other thing with which the fire is stirred. The poet said:

*Fa-la taku fi harbina mihdaban* ∗∗∗ *fa-taj'ala qawmaka shatta shu'ubA*

[Poetry: "So do not be among us one who stirs the fire of war, lest you make your people scattered tribes."]

Ubayy, 'Ali, 'A'ishah, Ibn al-Zubayr, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read *hatab* with a *ta'*. The gathering of the disbelievers with their objects of worship in the Fire is to increase their distress and regret, by seeing them with them in it, since they are punished because of them. They used to hope for good from their worship, so evil came to them from them. And because they became enemies to them, and seeing the enemy is something that increases the torment, as the poet said:

*Wa-ihtimalu al-adha wa-ru'yatu janiyihi* ∗∗∗ *ghidha'un tudna bihi al-ajsamu*

[Poetry: "Enduring harm and seeing the one who inflicted it are a nourishment by which bodies waste away."]

﴿You, to it﴾, i.e., to the Fire, ﴿are its bound-for﴾. *Al-wurud* here means entering. ﴿If these had been gods, they would not have entered it﴾, i.e., the idols you worship. That it means entering is indicated by His saying ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾. The majority read *alihatan* in the accusative as the predicate of *kana*. Talhah read it in the nominative, taking *kana* to have the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*). ﴿And all therein﴾, i.e., each of the worshippers and their objects of worship.

﴿For them therein is groaning﴾. *Al-zafir* is the sound of the breath of one who is distressed, coming out from the heart. Apparently, groaning only comes from one who has life, and those [who have life] are the worshippers. As for the objects of worship, [they are of two kinds]: those who claimed divinity, like Pharaoh and the extremists of the Isma'ilis who were the kings of Egypt from the sons of 'Ubayd Allah, their first kings; and it is permissible that Allah grants life to the idols that were worshipped, so that they too have groaning. Al-Zamakhshari said: If they and their idols are in one generation, it is permissible to say that they have groaning therein, even if the groaners are none but those who are in it. ﴿They will not hear﴾ [al-Anbiya: 102]. It was narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that they will be placed in coffins of fire and will not hear. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind and mute and deaf﴾ [al-Isra: 97]. In hearing things there is comfort, so Allah prevented the disbelievers from that in the Fire. It was also said that ﴿They will not hear﴾ [al-Anbiya: 102] means they will not hear what would please them from the speech of the angels of punishment (*al-zabaniyah*).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 21, verses 92–100 (part 1 of 2):

[p. 337] ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so worship Me.﴾ ﴿But they divided their affair among themselves into sects; each of them will return to Us.﴾ ﴿So whoever does good deeds while he is a believer, his effort will not be denied, and indeed We record it for him.﴾ ﴿And it is forbidden for a town which We have destroyed that they should not return.﴾ ﴿Until, when Gog and Magog are released, and they come swarming from every slope.﴾ ﴿And the true promise draws near, and then the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare fixedly: "Woe to us! We were heedless of this; indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell; you will be coming to it.﴾ ﴿If these had been gods, they would not have come to it; but all of them will abide in it forever.﴾ ﴿For them therein is a roaring, and they therein will not hear.﴾

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿this community of yours﴾ is an address to the contemporaries of the Messenger (ﷺ), and ﴿this﴾ refers to the religion of Islam. That is, the religion of Islam is your religion, which you must follow, not deviating from it, one religion without disagreement. It is also possible that ﴿this﴾ refers to the path that the prophets mentioned were upon, namely the monotheism of Allah the Exalted: your path and your religion are one path without disagreement regarding the foundations of belief. Rather, what the prophets brought of that is what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿one community﴾ is "created by Him, owned by Him," so the "community" refers to all people. It has been said that the discourse may be connected to the story of Mary and her son, meaning ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91], in that he was sent to them with a religion and a book, and it was said to them ﴿Indeed this community of yours﴾, that is, he called all of them to belief in Allah and to worshipping Him.

Then the Exalted informed that after that they differed, ﴿and they divided their affair among themselves﴾. The majority read ﴿community of yours﴾ with the nominative (ar-raf') as the predicate of inna, and ﴿one community﴾ in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). It has also been said that it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿this﴾. Al-Hasan read ﴿ummatakum﴾ with the accusative as a substitute for ﴿this﴾. He also read, together with Ibn Ishaq, al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi 'Abla, al-Ju'fi, Harun (on the authority of Abu 'Amr), and al-Za'farani, ﴿ummatukum ummatan wahidatan﴾ with the nominative for all three words, on the basis that ﴿ummatukum﴾ and ﴿ummatan wahidatan﴾ are the predicate of inna; or ﴿ummatan wahidatan﴾ is a substitute for ﴿ummatukum﴾, a substitution of an indefinite noun for a definite one; or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is one community." The pronoun in ﴿wa-taqatta'u﴾ refers back to the pronoun of address by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), meaning "and you divided."

Since this act is among the most abominable of deeds, He shifted away from address to the third person, as if this act did not proceed from those addressed. In reporting about them this way there is a rebuke of them for what they corrupted, and it is as if He were informing others of the ugly deed that had proceeded from them, saying: "Do you not see what these people have committed in the religion of Allah? They made the matter of their religion into pieces, as a group divides a thing: for this one a share, and for this one a share," as a figurative illustration of their disagreement. (p. 338) Then He threatened them with the return of this divided sect to His recompense. It has also been said: each of them, the one who remains steadfast in his true religion and the one who strays from it to another. Al-A'mash read ﴿zubura﴾ with a fatḥa on the bāʾ, the plural of zubra (a piece). Then He mentioned the state of the one who does good and that his effort is not denied. The word al-kufran (denial, ingratitude) is a figurative expression for the deprivation of reward, just as shukr (gratitude) is a figurative expression for giving it. It is said "Allah is Shakur" (the Most Appreciative), but not for negating the genus. So it is more eloquent than His saying ﴿so his effort will not be denied﴾. Recording (al-kitaba) is an expression for affirming his good deed in the register of deeds so that he is rewarded for it, and it will not be lost. Al-kufran is a verbal noun like al-kufr. The poet said:

*I have seen people whose grandfathers do not sleep, and my grandfather, and by Allah's ingratitude, none sleeps.*

In the codex of 'Abd Allah it reads "lā kufra" (without the tanwin). The phrase ﴿li-sa'yihi﴾ is connected to an omitted verb, meaning "we deny his effort." It cannot be connected to al-kufran, because if it were connected to it, it would be a noun not extended by a complement, so it would require tanwin.

The majority read ﴿wa-ḥarāmun﴾. Ḥamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr, Talha, al-A'mash, Abu Hanifa, and Abu 'Amr in one narration read ﴿wa-ḥirmun﴾ with a kasra on the ḥāʾ and a sukūn on the rāʾ. Qatada, Matar al-Warraq, and Mahbub on the authority of Abu 'Amr read it with a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ and a sukūn on the rāʾ. 'Ikrima read ﴿wa-ḥaramun﴾ with a kasra on the rāʾ and tanwin. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima also, Ibn al-Musayyab, and Qatada also, read it with a kasra on the rāʾ and a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ and the mīm, in the past tense, with variation reported from the two of them. Abu al-'Aliya and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with a ḍamma on the rāʾ and a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ and the mīm, in the past tense. Ibn 'Abbas also read it with a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ, the rāʾ, and the mīm, in the past tense. Al-Yamani read ﴿wa-ḥurrima﴾ with a ḍamma on the ḥāʾ, a kasra on the rāʾ with shadda, and a fatḥa on the mīm. The majority read ﴿ahlaknāhā﴾ with the first person plural of majesty (nūn al-'aẓama, "we").

Al-Sulami and Qatada read it with the first person singular tā' (the "I" form). Harām is borrowed for what is impossible to exist, and from it: ﴿Indeed Allah has forbidden them both to the disbelievers﴾ [al-A'raf: 50]. The meaning of ﴿we destroyed it﴾ is "we decreed its destruction in the state in which it was of disbelief," so the destruction here is destruction on account of disbelief. The lā in ﴿they will not return﴾ is an extra particle (ṣila), and this is the view of Abu 'Ubayd, as in your saying: "What prevented you from not prostrating?" meaning "they return to belief." The sense is: it is impossible for the people of a town whose destruction We have decreed because of their disbelief to return in this world to belief until the Resurrection. Then, when it comes, they will return and say ﴿Woe to us! We were heedless of this﴾. And "ghayya" (an intensifying phrase) refers to what is close to the coming of the Hour, which is the opening of ﴿Gog and Magog﴾. It is read ﴿innahum﴾ with a kasra, in which case the sentence is complete at His saying "we destroyed it," and a omitted element is supposed by which ﴿And forbidden upon a town which We have destroyed﴾ becomes a sentence meaning "that is." The reference is to the righteous deed mentioned in the counterpart of these destroyed people. The meaning: ﴿And it is forbidden upon﴾ the people of "a town" whose destruction We decreed because of their disbelief, a righteous deed by which they would be saved from destruction. Then He emphasized that and gave its reason: that they ﴿will not return﴾ from disbelief. So how is that not impossible? In this case the omitted element is the subject, and the predicate is ﴿wa-ḥarām﴾. Some of them supposed it to be preceding, as if he said: "And the cancellation and repentance are forbidden." The reading of the majority with the fatḥa is valid on this meaning, and lā is negating in its original function, the supposition being "because they will not return." It has also been said: "we destroyed them" means the destruction befell them, and their return to the world means they would repent, but rather they are headed to punishment. It has also been said: the destruction is by sealing the hearts, and the return is to repentance and belief.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿And forbidden upon a town which We have destroyed﴾ means We judged by its destruction that We would not accept their deeds, because ﴿they will not return﴾, that is, they will not repent. This meaning is indicated by His earlier saying ﴿so his effort will not be denied﴾, that is, his deed will be accepted. Then He mentioned this after it and showed that the disbeliever's deed is not accepted.

Abu Muslim ibn Bahr said: ﴿ḥarām﴾ means "impossible," and ﴿that they will not return﴾ is the negation of return to the Hereafter. When the negation is impossible, return becomes obligatory. So the meaning is that their return to life in the Hereafter is necessary, and the purpose is to deny the words of one who denies resurrection, and to confirm what preceded: that no one's effort is denied, and that he will be recompensed for it on the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said: ḥarām comes with the meaning of "obligatory," as indicated by ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you: that you not associate anything with Him﴾ [al-An'am: 151], and abandoning association is obligatory. Al-Khansa' said:

*It is forbidden to me (ḥarām ʿalayya) that I should see the age weeping over its grief except that I weep over Sakhr.*

Also, from the usage is the application of a pronoun to its opposite. On this view, Mujahid and al-Hasan said ﴿they will not return﴾ means "from polytheism." Qatada and Muqatil said it means "to this world." Ibn 'Atiyya said: a clear threat is implied in the verse, because He mentioned the one who does righteous deeds while being a believer, then returned to mention the disbelievers who, out of their disbelief and belief, held that they would not be gathered to a Lord and would not return to a Resurrection. So they supposed that no punishment would reach them. The verse therefore came to refute their supposition: "and it is impossible for the destroyed disbelievers that they should not return," but rather they are returning to the punishment of Allah and His painful torment. In this case the lā is in its original function and ḥarām in its original function. The same applies to al-ḥurum, so consider it. End of quotation.

As for ﴿ḥattā﴾ (until), Abu al-Baqa' said it is connected in meaning to ḥarām, meaning that the prohibition continues until this time, and it has no governing effect on ﴿idhā﴾ (when). Al-Hawfi said ﴿ḥattā﴾ is a limit, and what governs it is what the meaning indicates, namely their regret over what they neglected of obedience when the opportunity to make up for it had passed. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "To what is ḥattā connected, being a limit to it, and which of the three is it?" I say: it is connected to ḥarām, and it is a limit to it, because the impossibility of their return does not cease until the Resurrection comes. It is the ḥattā that reports speech, and the reported speech is the conditional and its response, namely idhā and what is within its scope. End of quotation.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is connected to His saying ﴿and they divided﴾. It is possible, according to some of the earlier interpretations, that it be connected to ﴿yarji'ūn﴾ (they return). It is also possible that it is the particle of beginning, and this is more apparent because of idhā, since it requires a response, which is the intended mention. End of quotation. That ḥattā is connected here is far-fetched in terms of the separation involved, but in terms of meaning it is good: they will not cease to disagree, not gathered upon the religion of truth, until the Hour draws near. When the Hour comes, that disagreement ends, and everyone knows that their Master is the Truth, and that the saving religion was the religion of monotheism. The response to idhā is omitted, its supposition being ﴿they will say, "Woe to us!"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 14], as al-Zajjaj and a group said. Or its supposition is "then they will be resurrected," ﴿then suddenly it is staring﴾.

Or it is mentioned, namely ﴿and the promise drew near﴾, with the wāw being extra, as some said. This is the view of the Kufans, who permit extra wāw and fā' in "fa-idhā hiya." This was said by al-Hawfi. Al-Zamakhshari said: idhā here is the sudden-occurrence idhā (idhā al-mufājaʾa), and it occurs with sudden events, taking the place of the fā', as in His saying ﴿when they are despairing﴾ [al-Rum: 36]. When fā' comes with it, they cooperate to join the response to the condition, so it is emphasized. Had it been said ﴿then it is staring﴾, it would have been sound.
