This is not the vocative of an indefinite noun addressed directly; rather, this is among the permitted dialects in (ya ghulami), where you build it on the damma while intending the possessive pronoun, when you have cut it off from the possessive, while you intend its form. So the meaning of (Rabbu) is "O my Lord." The majority read (uhkum) as an imperative from hakama. Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, al-Jahdari and Ibn Muhaysin read (Rabbi) with the yaa sukun, making it the superlative (af'al al-tafdil): "My Lord is most just," as a subject and predicate. A group read (ahkama) as a past-tense verb. The majority read (tasifun) with the taa of address. It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited to Ubayy (ʿalā mā yasifūn) with the yaa of the third person, and this was also narrated from Ibn Amir and Asim.

(p-342)﴿Surely those for whom the Best (reward) has already gone forth from Us, they will be kept far from it.﴾ ﴿They will not hear its faintest sound, and they will abide forever in what their souls desire.﴾ ﴿The Greatest Terror will not grieve them, and the angels will receive them: "This is your Day, which you were promised."﴾ ﴿On the Day We roll up the heaven like the rolling of the scroll for writings, just as We began the first creation, We shall bring it back. It is a promise binding upon Us; surely We are ever the Doers.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly written in the Psalms, after the Reminder, that the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants.﴾ ﴿Surely in this there is a message for a people who worship.﴾ ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds.﴾ ﴿Say: "It is only revealed to me that your God is one God. Will you then submit?"﴾ ﴿But if they turn away, say: "I have announced to you on equal terms, and I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far."﴾ ﴿Surely He knows what is spoken aloud and He knows what you conceal.﴾ ﴿And I do not know: perhaps it is a trial for you, and an enjoyment for a time.﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, judge with truth. And our Lord is the Most Merciful, whose help is sought against what you describe."﴾.

**Occasion of revelation of ﴿Surely those for whom the Best has already gone forth from Us﴾:** It is the statement of Ibn al-Zibaʿrā (Ibn al-Zibaʿrā) when he heard ﴿Surely you and what you worship besides God are the fuel of Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98]. He said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I have defeated you, by the Lord of the Ka'ba! Did not the Jews worship ʿUzayr, the Christians worship the Messiah, and the Banu Mulayh worship the angels?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "They worshipped the devils, who commanded them to do so." Then God revealed: ﴿Surely those for whom the Best has already gone forth from Us﴾. It is also said: when Ibn al-Zibaʿrā raised his objection, it was said to them: "Are you not an Arab people? Do you not know that *man* is for those who reason and *ma* is for what does not reason?" According to the first view, Ibn al-Zibaʿrā understood a generality from ﴿what you worship﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98], so God revealed ﴿Surely those for whom the Best has already gone forth﴾ as a specification of that generality. According to this second view, Ibn al-Zibaʿrā intended a sophistry, and he was answered that *man* is for those who reason and *ma* is for what does not reason, so his objection collapsed.

(al-Husna) is the most preferred quality in goodness; it is the feminine form of *al-aḥsan* (the best). It is either happiness, or the glad tidings of reward, or the granting of success in obedience. The apparent meaning of ﴿they will be kept far﴾ and what follows is that the one for whom the Best has gone forth will not enter the Fire. It is narrated that ʿAlī, may God honor his face, recited this verse and then said: "I am among them, and Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, Saʿd, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf." Then the prayer was called, and he got up dragging his garment, saying ﴿They will not hear its faintest sound﴾. The *ḥasīs* (faintest sound) is the sound perceived from the movement of bodies. This keeping far and the absence of hearing its sound is said to be before entering Paradise. It is also said: after their entry and settling in it. The *shahwa* (desire) is the soul's seeking of pleasure.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This is a description of them after their entry into Paradise, because the hadith implies that at the place of standing (on the Day of Judgment), Hell will give out a roar such that no prophet or king will remain except that he falls on his knees." The ﴿Greatest Terror﴾ is general to every dread that occurs on the Day of Resurrection, so the Day of Resurrection as a whole is ﴿the Greatest Terror﴾; and if it is specified by something, it must be intended as the greatest that it is for him. End of quotation.

It is also said: ﴿the Greatest Terror﴾ is the closing of the layer of Hell over its people; this was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk. It is said: it is the final blast (of the trumpet). It is said: it is the command concerning the people of the Fire to enter the Fire; this is narrated from Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Jurayj, and al-Ḥasan. It is said: it is the slaughter of Death. It is said: it is when it is called out: ﴿Be silent therein, and do not speak to Me﴾ [al-Muminun: 108]. It is said: ﴿On the Day We roll up the heaven﴾; this was mentioned by Makkī.

﴿And the angels will receive them﴾ with greetings of peace upon them. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās: the angels will receive them with mercy at their coming out of the graves, saying to them: ﴿This is your Day, which you were promised﴾, with honor, reward, and bliss.

Abu Jaʿfar read ﴿will not grieve them﴾ as the imperfect of *aḥzana* (a fourth-form verb), which is the dialect of Tamim; *ḥazina* is the dialect of Quraysh. The governing element of (the Day, when they will not be grieved) and (they will be received) is... Abu al-Baqāʾ permitted that it be a substitute for the omitted returning pronoun in (you were promised), so the governing element there would be ﴿you were promised﴾, meaning "is it promised to them?" Or it is an object of *udhkur* (mention), or an accusative by *aʿnī* (I mean). Al-Zamakhsharī permitted that the governing element be (the Terror), but this is not permissible, because (the Terror) is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and it has been described before taking its complement, so what was mentioned is not allowed. (p-343)

The majority read *nanṭawī* (We roll up) with the plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓama). A group among them, Shayba ibn Nisāḥ, read *yaṭwī* with a *yāʾ*, meaning God. Abu Jaʿfar and a group read with *tāʾ* vowelled with a *ḍamma* and the *wāw* with a *fatḥa*, with *al-samāʾ* in the nominative. The majority read *al-Sijill* on the pattern of *al-Ṭimirr*. Abu Hurayra and his companion, and Abu Zurʿa ibn ʿAmr ibn Jarīr, read it with two *ḍammas* and a doubled *lām*. Al-Aʿmash, Ṭalḥa, and Abu al-Simāk read *al-Sajl* with a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*. Al-Ḥasan and ʿĪsā read it with a *kasra* on both. In these two readings the *jīm* is quiescent and the *lām* is light. Abu ʿAmr said: the reading of the people of Mecca is like the reading of al-Ḥasan.

Mujāhid said: *al-Sijill* is the scroll (ṣaḥīfa). It is also said: it is a specific kind of scroll, the scroll of the covenant. The meaning is: a folding like the folding of the *sijill*. The *ṭayy* (folding) is a verbal noun annexed to its object, meaning: so that writing may be placed on it, or because of the many meanings written on it. The original is *kaṭayy* (like the folding of) the one who folds the *sijill*, and the agent was deleted; its deletion is permissible with a verbal noun that is equivalent to a verb plus a letter of the verbal-noun type. Al-Zamakhsharī took it as passive, meaning: as the *sijill* is folded. Ibn ʿAbbās and a group said: *al-Sijill* is an angel who folds the books of the children of Adam when they are lifted up to him. Another group said: he is a scribe who was for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). According to these two views, the verbal noun is annexed to its agent. Abu al-Faḍl al-Rāzī said: the most correct view is that it is Persian, Arabicized.

It is also said: its origin is from *musājala* (the contest of drawing water), which derives from *sijil*, a bucket full of water. Al-Zajjāj said: it is a man's name in the Abyssinian language.

The majority read *lil-kitāb* (for the Book) in the singular, while Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Ḥafṣ read *lil-kutub* (for the books) in the plural. Al-Aʿmash read the *tāʾ* quiescent.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: ﴿awwal khalq﴾ (first creation) is the object of *nuʿīd* (We bring back), which is explained by *nuʿīduh* (We bring it back). The *kāf* (like) is disconnected by *mā* (the particle that disconnects it). The meaning is: We bring back the first creation as We began it, making the return like the beginning in the power's dealing with both equally. If you say: what is the "first creation," so that He would bring it back as He began it? I say: its first is its bringing into existence from non-existence; just as He brought it into existence first from non-existence, He brings it back a second time from non-existence. If you say: why is *khalq* indefinite? I say: it is like your saying: "He is the first man who came to me," meaning the first of men; but you made it singular and indefinite intending to detail them man by man. Likewise, the meaning of *awwal khalq* is the first of the creatures, because *khalq* is a verbal noun which is not pluralized. Another way: that the *kāf* be in the accusative by a hidden verb explained by *nuʿīduh*, and *mā* is relative, meaning: We bring back the like of that which We began (nuʿīduh). And ﴿awwal khalq﴾ is an adverb of time for *badaʾnā* (We began), meaning: at the first time He created, or a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun of the relative clause which is dropped from the wording but retained in meaning. End of quotation.

The apparent reading is that the *kāf* is not disconnected as he mentioned; rather it is a preposition (governing a noun), and what follows it is a verbal (maṣdarī) clause, from which with the verb a verbal noun is formed that is in the genitive position after the *kāf*. ﴿Awwal khalq﴾ is the object of *badaʾnā*, and the meaning is: We bring back the first creation with a bringing back like Our beginning of it, that is, as We brought it out from non-existence into existence, We bring it back from non-existence into existence. In what al-Zamakhsharī proposed, he prepared *badaʾnā* to govern ﴿awwal khalq﴾ as an object, and separating it from that without necessity that calls for it, plus an omitted element that refers back explained by *nuʿīduh*, is a foreignism in the Book of God. As for his saying "another way: that the *kāf* be in the accusative by a hidden verb explained by *nuʿīduh*," it is very weak, because it is based on the *kāf* being a noun rather than a particle. This is not the view of the majority; this view was taken by al-Akhfash, and the *kāf* being a noun is the view of the Basrans, but it is not restricted to poetry.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it allows two meanings. One: that it is a report about the resurrection, meaning: just as We originated creation at first without a model, so We bring them into being again at another time, and We raise them from the graves. The second: that it is a report that every person will be raised on the Day of Resurrection in the state in which he came out into the world, and this is supported by the hadith: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised," and God's words ﴿as We began the first creation, We shall bring it back﴾. The *kāf* in ﴿as We began﴾ is connected to *nuʿīduh*. End of quotation.

*Waʿdan* (as a promise) is in the accusative as an object of a verbal noun emphasizing the content of the preceding declarative sentence. ﴿Surely We are ever the Doers﴾ is an emphasis on the certainty of the report, meaning: We are able to do it.

Regarding *al-Zabūr* (the Psalms): the apparent meaning is that it is the Psalms of David; this is said by al-Shaʿbī, and the meaning of this verse is present in the Psalms of David, and We read it in it. *Al-Dhikr* (the Reminder) is the Torah; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbās. It is also said: *al-Zabūr* is what came after the Torah of books, and *al-Dhikr* is the Torah. It is also said: *al-Zabūr* includes all the revealed books, and *al-Dhikr* is the Preserved Tablet. (*Al-Arḍ*) (the earth): Ibn ʿAbbās said: the land of Paradise. It is also said: the holy land. (*Yarithuhā*) (will inherit it): the community of Muḥammad (ﷺ).

The reference in ﴿Surely in this﴾ is to what is mentioned in this surah of reports, promises, threats, and most eloquent admonitions; a message, meaning a sufficiency by which one reaches good. It is also said: the reference is to the Qur'an as a whole. His being a mercy (peace be upon him) is because he came to them with what makes them happy. (*Lil-ʿālamīn*) (for the worlds): it is said to be specific to those who believed in him. It is also said: it is general, and his being a mercy to the unbeliever is in that He delayed their punishment and did not uproot the disbelievers with the chastisement. Ibn ʿAbbās said this is its meaning, and said: he was spared what befell other nations of transformation, sinking, drowning, and a shower of stones, and his affair was deferred to the Hereafter. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it may be that its meaning is ﴿We have not sent you﴾ to the worlds ﴿except as a mercy﴾, meaning: he is a mercy in himself, and a clear guidance; whoever takes it takes it, and whoever turns away from it turns away. End of quotation.

It is not permissible, according to the well-known view, for the preposition phrase after *illā* (except) to be governed by the verb before it, unless the governing verb is left without a complement, as in: "I have not passed except by Zayd." Al-Zamakhsharī said: you restrict a judgment to something, or you restrict something to a judgment, as in your saying: "Only Zayd is standing" and "Only Zayd stands." The two patterns have come together in this verse, because ﴿It is only revealed to me﴾ with its agent is like "Only Zayd stands," and ﴿that your God is one God﴾ is like "Only Zayd is standing." The benefit of their combination is the indication that the revelation to the Messenger (ﷺ) is restricted to God's singling out of oneness. End of quotation. As for what he mentioned about *innamā* (only), that it is for restricting what he mentioned, this is based on *innamā* being for exclusive restriction, and we have already established that it is not exclusive. *Innamā* together with *anna* is like *inna* with *kāna* and with *laʿalla*. Just as it does not confer exclusivity in comparison or in hoping, so it does not confer it with *anna*. As for his making *anna* (with an opened hamza) like its kasra-form, which indicates restriction, we know of no disagreement except regarding *innamā* with a kasra. With a fatḥa, *anna* is a verbal particle that with what follows forms a verbal noun; the clause after it is not an independent sentence. If *innamā* indicated exclusivity, it would follow that nothing was revealed to him except monotheism, and that is not correct, because other things were revealed to him besides monotheism. The verse is evidence that transmitted knowledge concurs with rational knowledge, and that transmission is one of the two paths to monotheism. It is permissible in *mā* in *innamā* that it be relative.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verse 101–112 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Do you then submit?﴾ This is an interrogative that carries the command to devote sincere monotheism (tawhid) and submission to Allah, the Exalted. (Ādhantukum) "I have informed you," and it carries the meaning of warning and admonition. ﴿On equal terms﴾: I did not single out one person over another. This notification (iidhan) is an announcement of the punishment that will befall those who turn away, and the triumph of Islam. But I do not know when that will be. (In) is negating, (adri) is suspended, and the interrogative clause is in the place of a accusative object of (adri). The interrogated element is placed later because it serves as the verse-ending (fasila); if the construction were (aqarib) ﴿what you are promised﴾ ﴿or is it far?﴾, it would not be a verse-ending. Often a ruling is given preference over something because of its being the verse-ending of a verse. In a narration from Ibn Amir, ﴿wa in adri﴾ is read with a fatha on the yaa in both verses, likening it to the yaa of possession in pronunciation, although it is the lam of the verb and is not vowelled with a fatha except by a governing element. Ibn Mujahid denied the fathah on this yaa. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, did not inform me of His knowledge and did not make me aware of it, and Allah is the All-Knowing, from whom nothing is hidden.

﴿And I do not know, perhaps it is a trial﴾: that is, perhaps the delay of this promised time is a test for you, to see how you act; or it is a postponement for you until a term, so that this is an argument against you, and so that the promise occurs at a time that is wisdom. (La'alla) here is also suspended, and the clause of hope is the object of the verb. The Kufans treat (la'alla) like (hal), so just as suspension occurs after (hal), it also occurs after (la'alla). I know of no one who held that (la'alla) is among the particles of suspension, although that is evident in it, as in His saying ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Shura: 17], and ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾ [Abasa: 3]. It was said: ﴿until a time﴾ means until the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: until the Day of Badr.

The majority read (Qul Rabbi), with the ba' in the kasra form as an imperative. Hafs read (qala), and Abu Ja'far read (Rabbu) with a damma. The majority read *lil-kitāb* (for the Book) in the singular, while Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Ḥafṣ read *lil-kutub* (for the books) in the plural. Al-Aʿmash read the *tāʾ* quiescent.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: ﴿awwal khalq﴾ (first creation) is the object of *nuʿīd* (We bring back), which is explained by *nuʿīduh* (We bring it back). The *kāf* (like) is disconnected by *mā* (the particle that disconnects it). The meaning is: We bring back the first creation as We began it, making the return like the beginning in the power's dealing with both equally. If you say: what is the "first creation," so that He would bring it back as He began it? I say: its first is its bringing into existence from non-existence; just as He brought it into existence first from non-existence, He brings it back a second time from non-existence. If you say: why is *khalq* indefinite? I say: it is like your saying: "He is the first man who came to me," meaning the first of men; but you made it singular and indefinite intending to detail them man by man. Likewise, the meaning of *awwal khalq* is the first of the creatures, because *khalq* is a verbal noun which is not pluralized. Another way: that the *kāf* be in the accusative by a hidden verb explained by *nuʿīduh*, and *mā* is relative, meaning: We bring back the like of that which We began (nuʿīduh). And ﴿awwal khalq﴾ is an adverb of time for *badaʾnā* (We began), meaning: at the first time He created, or a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun of the relative clause which is dropped from the wording but retained in meaning. End of quotation.

The apparent reading is that the *kāf* is not disconnected as he mentioned; rather it is a preposition (governing a noun), and what follows it is a verbal (maṣdarī) clause, from which with the verb a verbal noun is formed that is in the genitive position after the *kāf*. ﴿Awwal khalq﴾ is the object of *badaʾnā*, and the meaning is: We bring back the first creation with a bringing back like Our beginning of it, that is, as We brought it out from non-existence into existence, We bring it back from non-existence into existence. In what al-Zamakhsharī proposed, he prepared *badaʾnā* to govern ﴿awwal khalq﴾ as an object, and separating it from that without necessity that calls for it, plus an omitted element that refers back explained by *nuʿīduh*, is a foreignism in the Book of God. As for his saying "another way: that the *kāf* be in the accusative by a hidden verb explained by *nuʿīduh*," it is very weak, because it is based on the *kāf* being a noun rather than a particle. This is not the view of the majority; this view was taken by al-Akhfash, and the *kāf* being a noun is the view of the Basrans, but it is not restricted to poetry.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it allows two meanings. One: that it is a report about the resurrection, meaning: just as We originated creation at first without a model, so We bring them into being again at another time, and We raise them from the graves. The second: that it is a report that every person will be raised on the Day of Resurrection in the state in which he came out into the world, and this is supported by the hadith: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised," and God's words ﴿as We began the first creation, We shall bring it back﴾. The *kāf* in ﴿as We began﴾ is connected to *nuʿīduh*. End of quotation.

*Waʿdan* (as a promise) is in the accusative as an object of a verbal noun emphasizing the content of the preceding declarative sentence. ﴿Surely We are ever the Doers﴾ is an emphasis on the certainty of the report, meaning: We are able to do it.

Regarding *al-Zabūr* (the Psalms): the apparent meaning is that it is the Psalms of David; this is said by al-Shaʿbī, and the meaning of this verse is present in the Psalms of David, and We read it in it. *Al-Dhikr* (the Reminder) is the Torah; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbās. It is also said: *al-Zabūr* is what came after the Torah of books, and *al-Dhikr* is the Torah. It is also said: *al-Zabūr* includes all the revealed books, and *al-Dhikr* is the Preserved Tablet. (*Al-Arḍ*) (the earth): Ibn ʿAbbās said: the land of Paradise. It is also said: the holy land. (*Yarithuhā*) (will inherit it): the community of Muḥammad (ﷺ).

The reference in ﴿Surely in this﴾ is to what is mentioned in this surah of reports, promises, threats, and most eloquent admonitions; a message, meaning a sufficiency by which one reaches good. It is also said: the reference is to the Qur'an as a whole. His being a mercy (peace be upon him) is because he came to them with what makes them happy. (*Lil-ʿālamīn*) (for the worlds): it is said to be specific to those who believed in him. It is also said: it is general, and his being a mercy to the unbeliever is in that He delayed their punishment and did not uproot the disbelievers with the chastisement. Ibn ʿAbbās said this is its meaning, and said: he was spared what befell other nations of transformation, sinking, drowning, and a shower of stones, and his affair was deferred to the Hereafter. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it may be that its meaning is ﴿We have not sent you﴾ to the worlds ﴿except as a mercy﴾, meaning: he is a mercy in himself, and a clear guidance; whoever takes it takes it, and whoever turns away from it turns away. End of quotation.

It is not permissible, according to the well-known view, for the preposition phrase after *illā* (except) to be governed by the verb before it, unless the governing verb is left without a complement, as in: "I have not passed except by Zayd." Al-Zamakhsharī said: you restrict a judgment to something, or you restrict something to a judgment, as in your saying: "Only Zayd is standing" and "Only Zayd stands." The two patterns have come together in this verse, because ﴿It is only revealed to me﴾ with its agent is like "Only Zayd stands," and ﴿that your God is one God﴾ is like "Only Zayd is standing." The benefit of their combination is the indication that the revelation to the Messenger (ﷺ) is restricted to God's singling out of oneness. End of quotation. As for what he mentioned about *innamā* (only), that it is for restricting what he mentioned, this is based on *innamā* being for exclusive restriction, and we have already established that it is not exclusive. *Innamā* together with *anna* is like *inna* with *kāna* and with *laʿalla*. Just as it does not confer exclusivity in comparison or in hoping, so it does not confer it with *anna*. As for his making *anna* (with an opened hamza) like its kasra-form, which indicates restriction, we know of no disagreement except regarding *innamā* with a kasra. With a fatḥa, *anna* is a verbal particle that with what follows forms a verbal noun; the clause after it is not an independent sentence. If *innamā* indicated exclusivity, it would follow that nothing was revealed to him except monotheism, and that is not correct, because other things were revealed to him besides monotheism. The verse is evidence that transmitted knowledge concurs with rational knowledge, and that transmission is one of the two paths to monotheism. It is permissible in *mā* in *innamā* that it be relative.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verse 101–112 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Do you then submit?﴾ This is an interrogative that carries the command to devote sincere monotheism (tawhid) and submission to Allah, the Exalted. (Ādhantukum) "I have informed you," and it carries the meaning of warning and admonition. ﴿On equal terms﴾: I did not single out one person over another. This notification (iidhan) is an announcement of the punishment that will befall those who turn away, and the triumph of Islam. But I do not know when that will be. (In) is negating, (adri) is suspended, and the interrogative clause is in the place of a accusative object of (adri). The interrogated element is placed later because it serves as the verse-ending (fasila); if the construction were (aqarib) ﴿what you are promised﴾ ﴿or is it far?﴾, it would not be a verse-ending. Often a ruling is given preference over something because of its being the verse-ending of a verse. In a narration from Ibn Amir, ﴿wa in adri﴾ is read with a fatha on the yaa in both verses, likening it to the yaa of possession in pronunciation, although it is the lam of the verb and is not vowelled with a fatha except by a governing element. Ibn Mujahid denied the fathah on this yaa. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, did not inform me of His knowledge and did not make me aware of it, and Allah is the All-Knowing, from whom nothing is hidden.

﴿And I do not know, perhaps it is a trial﴾: that is, perhaps the delay of this promised time is a test for you, to see how you act; or it is a postponement for you until a term, so that this is an argument against you, and so that the promise occurs at a time that is wisdom. (La'alla) here is also suspended, and the clause of hope is the object of the verb. The Kufans treat (la'alla) like (hal), so just as suspension occurs after (hal), it also occurs after (la'alla). I know of no one who held that (la'alla) is among the particles of suspension, although that is evident in it, as in His saying ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Shura: 17], and ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾ [Abasa: 3]. It was said: ﴿until a time﴾ means until the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: until the Day of Badr.

The majority read (Qul Rabbi), with the ba' in the kasra form as an imperative. Hafs read (qala), and Abu Ja'far read (Rabbu) with a damma. The author of al-Lawami said: this is on the basis that it is a singular vocative, and the particle of address has been omitted in what may be an attribute of any distant (noun), its domain being poetry. End of quote.

This is not the vocative of an indefinite noun addressed directly; rather, this is among the permitted dialects in (ya ghulami), where you build it on the damma while intending the possessive pronoun, when you have cut it off from the possessive, while you intend its form. So the meaning of (Rabbu) is "O my Lord." The majority read (uhkum) as an imperative from hakama. Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, al-Jahdari and Ibn Muhaysin read (Rabbi) with the yaa sukun, making it the superlative (af'al al-tafdil): "My Lord is most just," as a subject and predicate. A group read (ahkama) as a past-tense verb. The majority read (tasifun) with the taa of address. It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited to Ubayy (ʿalā mā yasifūn) with the yaa of the third person, and this was also narrated from Ibn Amir and Asim.

(p-342)﴿Surely those for whom the Best (reward) has already gone forth from Us, they will be kept far from it.﴾ ﴿They will not hear its faintest sound, and they will abide forever in what their souls desire.﴾ ﴿The Greatest Terror will not grieve them, and the angels will receive them: "This is your Day, which you were promised."﴾ ﴿On the Day We roll up the heaven like the rolling of the scroll for writings, just as We began the first creation, We shall bring it back. It is a promise binding upon Us; surely We are ever the Doers.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly written in the Psalms, after the Reminder, that the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants.﴾ ﴿Surely in this there is a message for a people who worship.﴾ ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds.﴾ ﴿Say: "It is only revealed to me that your God is one God. Will you then submit?"﴾ ﴿But if they turn away, say: "I have announced to you on equal terms, and I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far."﴾ ﴿Surely He knows what is spoken aloud and He knows what you conceal.﴾ ﴿And I do not know: perhaps it is a trial for you, and an enjoyment for a time.﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, judge with truth. And our Lord is the Most Merciful, whose help is sought against what you describe."﴾.

**Occasion of revelation of ﴿Surely those for whom the Best has already gone forth from Us﴾:** It is the statement of Ibn al-Zibaʿrā (Ibn al-Zibaʿrā) when he heard ﴿Surely you and what you worship besides God are the fuel of Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98]. He said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I have defeated you, by the Lord of the Ka'ba! Did not the Jews worship ʿUzayr, the Christians worship the Messiah, and the Banu Mulayh worship the angels?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "They worshipped the devils, who commanded them to do so." Then God revealed: ﴿Surely those for whom the Best has already gone forth from Us﴾. It is also said: when Ibn al-Zibaʿrā raised his objection, it was said to them: "Are you not an Arab people? Do you not know that *man* is for those who reason and *ma* is for what does not reason?" According to the first view, Ibn al-Zibaʿrā understood a generality from ﴿what you worship﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98], so God revealed ﴿Surely those for whom the Best has already gone forth﴾ as a specification of that generality. According to this second view, Ibn al-Zibaʿrā intended a sophistry, and he was answered that *man* is for those who reason and *ma* is for what does not reason, so his objection collapsed.

(al-Husna) is the most preferred quality in goodness; it is the feminine form of *al-aḥsan* (the best). It is either happiness, or the glad tidings of reward, or the granting of success in obedience. The apparent meaning of ﴿they will be kept far﴾ and what follows is that the one for whom the Best has gone forth will not enter the Fire. It is narrated that ʿAlī, may God honor his face, recited this verse and then said: "I am among them, and Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, Saʿd, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf." Then the prayer was called, and he got up dragging his garment, saying ﴿They will not hear its faintest sound﴾. The *ḥasīs* (faintest sound) is the sound perceived from the movement of bodies. This keeping far and the absence of hearing its sound is said to be before entering Paradise. It is also said: after their entry and settling in it. The *shahwa* (desire) is the soul's seeking of pleasure.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This is a description of them after their entry into Paradise, because the hadith implies that at the place of standing (on the Day of Judgment), Hell will give out a roar such that no prophet or king will remain except that he falls on his knees." The ﴿Greatest Terror﴾ is general to every dread that occurs on the Day of Resurrection, so the Day of Resurrection as a whole is ﴿the Greatest Terror﴾; and if it is specified by something, it must be intended as the greatest that it is for him. End of quotation.

It is also said: ﴿the Greatest Terror﴾ is the closing of the layer of Hell over its people; this was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk. It is said: it is the final blast (of the trumpet). It is said: it is the command concerning the people of the Fire to enter the Fire; this is narrated from Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Jurayj, and al-Ḥasan. It is said: it is the slaughter of Death. It is said: it is when it is called out: ﴿Be silent therein, and do not speak to Me﴾ [al-Muminun: 108]. It is said: ﴿On the Day We roll up the heaven﴾; this was mentioned by Makkī.

﴿And the angels will receive them﴾ with greetings of peace upon them. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās: the angels will receive them with mercy at their coming out of the graves, saying to them: ﴿This is your Day, which you were promised﴾, with honor, reward, and bliss.

Abu Jaʿfar read ﴿will not grieve them﴾ as the imperfect of *aḥzana* (a fourth-form verb), which is the dialect of Tamim; *ḥazina* is the dialect of Quraysh. The governing element of (the Day, when they will not be grieved) and (they will be received) is... Abu al-Baqāʾ permitted that it be a substitute for the omitted returning pronoun in (you were promised), so the governing element there would be ﴿you were promised﴾, meaning "is it promised to them?" Or it is an object of *udhkur* (mention), or an accusative by *aʿnī* (I mean). Al-Zamakhsharī permitted that the governing element be (the Terror), but this is not permissible, because (the Terror) is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and it has been described before taking its complement, so what was mentioned is not allowed. (p-343)

The majority read *nanṭawī* (We roll up) with the plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓama). A group among them, Shayba ibn Nisāḥ, read *yaṭwī* with a *yāʾ*, meaning God. Abu Jaʿfar and a group read with *tāʾ* vowelled with a *ḍamma* and the *wāw* with a *fatḥa*, with *al-samāʾ* in the nominative. The majority read *al-Sijill* on the pattern of *al-Ṭimirr*. Abu Hurayra and his companion, and Abu Zurʿa ibn ʿAmr ibn Jarīr, read it with two *ḍammas* and a doubled *lām*. Al-Aʿmash, Ṭalḥa, and Abu al-Simāk read *al-Sajl* with a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*. Al-Ḥasan and ʿĪsā read it with a *kasra* on both. In these two readings the *jīm* is quiescent and the *lām* is light. Abu ʿAmr said: the reading of the people of Mecca is like the reading of al-Ḥasan.

Mujāhid said: *al-Sijill* is the scroll (ṣaḥīfa). It is also said: it is a specific kind of scroll, the scroll of the covenant. The meaning is: a folding like the folding of the *sijill*. The *ṭayy* (folding) is a verbal noun annexed to its object, meaning: so that writing may be placed on it, or because of the many meanings written on it. The original is *kaṭayy* (like the folding of) the one who folds the *sijill*, and the agent was deleted; its deletion is permissible with a verbal noun that is equivalent to a verb plus a letter of the verbal-noun type. Al-Zamakhsharī took it as passive, meaning: as the *sijill* is folded. Ibn ʿAbbās and a group said: *al-Sijill* is an angel who folds the books of the children of Adam when they are lifted up to him. Another group said: he is a scribe who was for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). According to these two views, the verbal noun is annexed to its agent. Abu al-Faḍl al-Rāzī said: the most correct view is that it is Persian, Arabicized.

The meaning is: We bring back the first creation as We began it, making the return like the beginning in the power's dealing with both equally. If you say: what is the "first creation," so that He would bring it back as He began it? I say: its first is its bringing into existence from non-existence; just as He brought it into existence first from non-existence, He brings it back a second time from non-existence. If you say: why is *khalq* indefinite? I say: it is like your saying: "He is the first man who came to me," meaning the first of men; but you made it singular and indefinite intending to detail them man by man. Likewise, the meaning of *awwal khalq* is the first of the creatures, because *khalq* is a verbal noun which is not pluralized. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, did not inform me of His knowledge and did not make me aware of it, and Allah is the All-Knowing, from whom nothing is hidden.

﴿And I do not know, perhaps it is a trial﴾: that is, perhaps the delay of this promised time is a test for you, to see how you act; or it is a postponement for you until a term, so that this is an argument against you, and so that the promise occurs at a time that is wisdom. (La'alla) here is also suspended, and the clause of hope is the object of the verb. The Kufans treat (la'alla) like (hal), so just as suspension occurs after (hal), it also occurs after (la'alla). I know of no one who held that (la'alla) is among the particles of suspension, although that is evident in it, as in His saying ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Shura: 17], and ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾ [Abasa: 3]. It was said: ﴿until a time﴾ means until the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: until the Day of Badr.

The majority read (Qul Rabbi), with the ba' in the kasra form as an imperative. Hafs read (qala), and Abu Ja'far read (Rabbu) with a damma. The author of al-Lawami said: this is on the basis that it is a singular vocative, and the particle of address has been omitted in what may be an attribute of any distant (noun), its domain being poetry. End of quote.

This is not the vocative of an indefinite noun addressed directly; rather, this is among the permitted dialects in (ya ghulami), where you build it on the damma while intending the possessive pronoun, when you have cut it off from the possessive, while you intend its form. So the meaning of (Rabbu) is "O my Lord." The majority read (uhkum) as an imperative from hakama. Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, al-Jahdari and Ibn Muhaysin read (Rabbi) with the yaa sukun, making it the superlative (af'al al-tafdil): "My Lord is most just," as a subject and predicate. A group read (ahkama) as a past-tense verb. The majority read (tasifun) with the taa of address. It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited to Ubayy (ʿalā mā yasifūn) with the yaa of the third person, and this was also narrated from Ibn Amir and Asim.

(p-342)﴿Surely those for whom the Best (reward) has already gone forth from Us, they will be kept far from it.﴾ ﴿They will not hear its faintest sound, and they will abide forever in what their souls desire.﴾ ﴿The Greatest Terror will not grieve them, and the angels will receive them: "This is your Day, which you were promised."﴾ ﴿On the Day We roll up the heaven like the rolling of the scroll for writings, just as We began the first creation, We shall bring it back. It is a promise binding upon Us; surely We are ever the Doers.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly written in the Psalms, after the Reminder, that the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants.﴾ ﴿Surely in this there is a message for a people who worship.﴾ ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds.﴾ ﴿Say: "It is only revealed to me that your God is one God. Will you then submit?"﴾ ﴿But if they turn away, say: "I have announced to you on equal terms, and I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far."﴾ ﴿Surely He knows what is spoken aloud and He knows what you conceal.﴾ ﴿And I do not know: perhaps it is a trial for you, and an enjoyment for a time.﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, judge with truth. And our Lord is the Most Merciful, whose help is sought against what you describe."﴾.

**Occasion of revelation of ﴿Surely those for whom the Best has already gone forth from Us﴾:** It is the statement of Ibn al-Zibaʿrā (Ibn al-Zibaʿrā) when he heard ﴿Surely you and what you worship besides God are the fuel of Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98]. He said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I have defeated you, by the Lord of the Ka'ba! Did not the Jews worship ʿUzayr, the Christians worship the Messiah, and the Banu Mulayh worship the angels?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "They worshipped the devils, who commanded them to do so." Then God revealed: ﴿Surely those for whom the Best has already gone forth from Us﴾. It is also said: when Ibn al-Zibaʿrā raised his objection, it was said to them: "Are you not an Arab people? Do you not know that *man* is for those who reason and *ma* is for what does not reason?" According to the first view, Ibn al-Zibaʿrā understood a generality from ﴿what you worship﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98], so God revealed ﴿Surely those for whom the Best has already gone forth﴾ as a specification of that generality. According to this second view, Ibn al-Zibaʿrā intended a sophistry, and he was answered that *man* is for those who reason and *ma* is for what does not reason, so his objection collapsed.

(al-Husna) is the most preferred quality in goodness; it is the feminine form of *al-aḥsan* (the best). It is either happiness, or the glad tidings of reward, or the granting of success in obedience. The apparent meaning of ﴿they will be kept far﴾ and what follows is that the one for whom the Best has gone forth will not enter the Fire. It is narrated that ʿAlī, may God honor his face, recited this verse and then said: "I am among them, and Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, Saʿd, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf." Then the prayer was called, and he got up dragging his garment, saying ﴿They will not hear its faintest sound﴾. The *ḥasīs* (faintest sound) is the sound perceived from the movement of bodies. This keeping far and the absence of hearing its sound is said to be before entering Paradise. It is also said: after their entry and settling in it. The *shahwa* (desire) is the soul's seeking of pleasure.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This is a description of them after their entry into Paradise, because the hadith implies that at the place of standing (on the Day of Judgment), Hell will give out a roar such that no prophet or king will remain except that he falls on his knees." The ﴿Greatest Terror﴾ is general to every dread that occurs on the Day of Resurrection, so the Day of Resurrection as a whole is ﴿the Greatest Terror﴾; and if it is specified by something, it must be intended as the greatest that it is for him. End of quotation.

It is also said: ﴿the Greatest Terror﴾ is the closing of the layer of Hell over its people; this was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk. It is said: it is the final blast (of the trumpet). It is said: it is the command concerning the people of the Fire to enter the Fire; this is narrated from Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Jurayj, and al-Ḥasan. It is said: it is the slaughter of Death. It is said: it is when it is called out: ﴿Be silent therein, and do not speak to Me﴾ [al-Muminun: 108]. It is said: ﴿On the Day We roll up the heaven﴾; this was mentioned by Makkī.

﴿And the angels will receive them﴾ with greetings of peace upon them. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās: the angels will receive them with mercy at their coming out of the graves, saying to them: ﴿This is your Day, which you were promised﴾, with honor, reward, and bliss.

Abu Jaʿfar read ﴿will not grieve them﴾ as the imperfect of *aḥzana* (a fourth-form verb), which is the dialect of Tamim; *ḥazina* is the dialect of Quraysh. The governing element of (the Day, when they will not be grieved) and (they will be received) is... Abu al-Baqāʾ permitted that it be a substitute for the omitted returning pronoun in (you were promised), so the governing element there would be ﴿you were promised﴾, meaning "is it promised to them?" Or it is an object of *udhkur* (mention), or an accusative by *aʿnī* (I mean). Al-Zamakhsharī permitted that the governing element be (the Terror), but this is not permissible, because (the Terror) is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and it has been described before taking its complement, so what was mentioned is not allowed. (p-343)

The majority read *nanṭawī* (We roll up) with the plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓama). A group among them, Shayba ibn Nisāḥ, read *yaṭwī* with a *yāʾ*, meaning God. Abu Jaʿfar and a group read with *tāʾ* vowelled with a *ḍamma* and the *wāw* with a *fatḥa*, with *al-samāʾ* in the nominative. The majority read *al-Sijill* on the pattern of *al-Ṭimirr*. Abu Hurayra and his companion, and Abu Zurʿa ibn ʿAmr ibn Jarīr, read it with two *ḍammas* and a doubled *lām*. Al-Aʿmash, Ṭalḥa, and Abu al-Simāk read *al-Sajl* with a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*. Al-Ḥasan and ʿĪsā read it with a *kasra* on both. In these two readings the *jīm* is quiescent and the *lām* is light. Abu ʿAmr said: the reading of the people of Mecca is like the reading of al-Ḥasan.

Mujāhid said: *al-Sijill* is the scroll (ṣaḥīfa). It is also said: it is a specific kind of scroll, the scroll of the covenant. The meaning is: a folding like the folding of the *sijill*. The *ṭayy* (folding) is a verbal noun annexed to its object, meaning: so that writing may be placed on it, or because of the many meanings written on it. The original is *kaṭayy* (like the folding of) the one who folds the *sijill*, and the agent was deleted; its deletion is permissible with a verbal noun that is equivalent to a verb plus a letter of the verbal-noun type. Al-Zamakhsharī took it as passive, meaning: as the *sijill* is folded. Ibn ʿAbbās and a group said: *al-Sijill* is an angel who folds the books of the children of Adam when they are lifted up to him. Another group said: he is a scribe who was for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). According to these two views, the verbal noun is annexed to its agent. Abu al-Faḍl al-Rāzī said: the most correct view is that it is Persian, Arabicized.

It is also said: its origin is from *musājala* (the contest of drawing water), which derives from *sijil*, a bucket full of water. Al-Zajjāj said: it is a man's name in the Abyssinian language.

The majority read *lil-kitāb* (for the Book) in the singular, while Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Ḥafṣ read *lil-kutub* (for the books) in the plural. Al-Aʿmash read the *tāʾ* quiescent.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: ﴿awwal khalq﴾ (first creation) is the object of *nuʿīd* (We bring back), which is explained by *nuʿīduh* (We bring it back). The *kāf* (like) is disconnected by *mā* (the particle that disconnects it). The meaning is: We bring back the first creation as We began it, making the return like the beginning in the power's dealing with both equally. If you say: what is the "first creation," so that He would bring it back as He began it? I say: its first is its bringing into existence from non-existence; just as He brought it into existence first from non-existence, He brings it back a second time from non-existence. If you say: why is *khalq* indefinite? I say: it is like your saying: "He is the first man who came to me," meaning the first of men; but you made it singular and indefinite intending to detail them man by man. Likewise, the meaning of *awwal khalq* is the first of the creatures, because *khalq* is a verbal noun which is not pluralized. Another way: that the *kāf* be in the accusative by a hidden verb explained by *nuʿīduh*, and *mā* is relative, meaning: We bring back the like of that which We began (nuʿīduh). And ﴿awwal khalq﴾ is an adverb of time for *badaʾnā* (We began), meaning: at the first time He created, or a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun of the relative clause which is dropped from the wording but retained in meaning. End of quotation.

The apparent reading is that the *kāf* is not disconnected as he mentioned; rather it is a preposition (governing a noun), and what follows it is a verbal (maṣdarī) clause, from which with the verb a verbal noun is formed that is in the genitive position after the *kāf*. ﴿Awwal khalq﴾ is the object of *badaʾnā*, and the meaning is: We bring back the first creation with a bringing back like Our beginning of it, that is, as We brought it out from non-existence into existence, We bring it back from non-existence into existence. In what al-Zamakhsharī proposed, he prepared *badaʾnā* to govern ﴿awwal khalq﴾ as an object, and separating it from that without necessity that calls for it, plus an omitted element that refers back explained by *nuʿīduh*, is a foreignism in the Book of God. As for his saying "another way: that the *kāf* be in the accusative by a hidden verb explained by *nuʿīduh*," it is very weak, because it is based on the *kāf* being a noun rather than a particle. This is not the view of the majority; this view was taken by al-Akhfash, and the *kāf* being a noun is the view of the Basrans, but it is not restricted to poetry.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it allows two meanings. One: that it is a report about the resurrection, meaning: just as We originated creation at first without a model, so We bring them into being again at another time, and We raise them from the graves. The second: that it is a report that every person will be raised on the Day of Resurrection in the state in which he came out into the world, and this is supported by the hadith: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised," and God's words ﴿as We began the first creation, We shall bring it back﴾. The *kāf* in ﴿as We began﴾ is connected to *nuʿīduh*. End of quotation.

*Waʿdan* (as a promise) is in the accusative as an object of a verbal noun emphasizing the content of the preceding declarative sentence. ﴿Surely We are ever the Doers﴾ is an emphasis on the certainty of the report, meaning: We are able to do it.

Regarding *al-Zabūr* (the Psalms): the apparent meaning is that it is the Psalms of David; this is said by al-Shaʿbī, and the meaning of this verse is present in the Psalms of David, and We read it in it. *Al-Dhikr* (the Reminder) is the Torah; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbās. It is also said: *al-Zabūr* is what came after the Torah of books, and *al-Dhikr* is the Torah. It is also said: *al-Zabūr* includes all the revealed books, and *al-Dhikr* is the Preserved Tablet. (*Al-Arḍ*) (the earth): Ibn ʿAbbās said: the land of Paradise. It is also said: the holy land. (*Yarithuhā*) (will inherit it): the community of Muḥammad (ﷺ).

The reference in ﴿Surely in this﴾ is to what is mentioned in this surah of reports, promises, threats, and most eloquent admonitions; a message, meaning a sufficiency by which one reaches good. It is also said: the reference is to the Qur'an as a whole. His being a mercy (peace be upon him) is because he came to them with what makes them happy. (*Lil-ʿālamīn*) (for the worlds): it is said to be specific to those who believed in him. It is also said: it is general, and his being a mercy to the unbeliever is in that He delayed their punishment and did not uproot the disbelievers with the chastisement. Ibn ʿAbbās said this is its meaning, and said: he was spared what befell other nations of transformation, sinking, drowning, and a shower of stones, and his affair was deferred to the Hereafter. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it may be that its meaning is ﴿We have not sent you﴾ to the worlds ﴿except as a mercy﴾, meaning: he is a mercy in himself, and a clear guidance; whoever takes it takes it, and whoever turns away from it turns away. End of quotation.

It is not permissible, according to the well-known view, for the preposition phrase after *illā* (except) to be governed by the verb before it, unless the governing verb is left without a complement, as in: "I have not passed except by Zayd." Al-Zamakhsharī said: you restrict a judgment to something, or you restrict something to a judgment, as in your saying: "Only Zayd is standing" and "Only Zayd stands." The two patterns have come together in this verse, because ﴿It is only revealed to me﴾ with its agent is like "Only Zayd stands," and ﴿that your God is one God﴾ is like "Only Zayd is standing." The benefit of their combination is the indication that the revelation to the Messenger (ﷺ) is restricted to God's singling out of oneness. End of quotation. As for what he mentioned about *innamā* (only), that it is for restricting what he mentioned, this is based on *innamā* being for exclusive restriction, and we have already established that it is not exclusive. *Innamā* together with *anna* is like *inna* with *kāna* and with *laʿalla*. Just as it does not confer exclusivity in comparison or in hoping, so it does not confer it with *anna*. As for his making *anna* (with an opened hamza) like its kasra-form, which indicates restriction, we know of no disagreement except regarding *innamā* with a kasra. With a fatḥa, *anna* is a verbal particle that with what follows forms a verbal noun; the clause after it is not an independent sentence. If *innamā* indicated exclusivity, it would follow that nothing was revealed to him except monotheism, and that is not correct, because other things were revealed to him besides monotheism. The verse is evidence that transmitted knowledge concurs with rational knowledge, and that transmission is one of the two paths to monotheism. It is permissible in *mā* in *innamā* that it be relative.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verse 101–112 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Do you then submit?﴾ This is an interrogative that carries the command to devote sincere monotheism (tawhid) and submission to Allah, the Exalted. (Ādhantukum) "I have informed you," and it carries the meaning of warning and admonition. ﴿On equal terms﴾: I did not single out one person over another. This notification (iidhan) is an announcement of the punishment that will befall those who turn away, and the triumph of Islam. But I do not know when that will be. (In) is negating, (adri) is suspended, and the interrogative clause is in the place of a accusative object of (adri). The interrogated element is placed later because it serves as the verse-ending (fasila); if the construction were (aqarib) ﴿what you are promised﴾ ﴿or is it far?﴾, it would not be a verse-ending. Often a ruling is given preference over something because of its being the verse-ending of a verse. In a narration from Ibn Amir, ﴿wa in adri﴾ is read with a fatha on the yaa in both verses, likening it to the yaa of possession in pronunciation, although it is the lam of the verb and is not vowelled with a fatha except by a governing element. Ibn Mujahid denied the fathah on this yaa. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, did not inform me of His knowledge and did not make me aware of it, and Allah is the All-Knowing, from whom nothing is hidden.

Mujāhid said: *al-Sijill* is the scroll (ṣaḥīfa). It is also said: it is a specific kind of scroll, the scroll of the covenant. The meaning is: a folding like the folding of the *sijill*. The *ṭayy* (folding) is a verbal noun annexed to its object, meaning: so that writing may be placed on it, or because of the many meanings written on it. The original is *kaṭayy* (like the folding of) the one who folds the *sijill*, and the agent was deleted; its deletion is permissible with a verbal noun that is equivalent to a verb plus a letter of the verbal-noun type. Al-Zamakhsharī took it as passive, meaning: as the *sijill* is folded. Ibn ʿAbbās and a group said: *al-Sijill* is an angel who folds the books of the children of Adam when they are lifted up to him. Another group said: he is a scribe who was for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). According to these two views, the verbal noun is annexed to its agent. Abu al-Faḍl al-Rāzī said: the most correct view is that it is Persian, Arabicized.

It is also said: its origin is from *musājala* (the contest of drawing water), which derives from *sijil*, a bucket full of water. Al-Zajjāj said: it is a man's name in the Abyssinian language.

The majority read *lil-kitāb* (for the Book) in the singular, while Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Ḥafṣ read *lil-kutub* (for the books) in the plural. Al-Aʿmash read the *tāʾ* quiescent.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: ﴿awwal khalq﴾ (first creation) is the object of *nuʿīd* (We bring back), which is explained by *nuʿīduh* (We bring it back). The *kāf* (like) is disconnected by *mā* (the particle that disconnects it). The meaning is: We bring back the first creation as We began it, making the return like the beginning in the power's dealing with both equally. If you say: what is the "first creation," so that He would bring it back as He began it? I say: its first is its bringing into existence from non-existence; just as He brought it into existence first from non-existence, He brings it back a second time from non-existence. If you say: why is *khalq* indefinite? I say: it is like your saying: "He is the first man who came to me," meaning the first of men; but you made it singular and indefinite intending to detail them man by man. Likewise, the meaning of *awwal khalq* is the first of the creatures, because *khalq* is a verbal noun which is not pluralized. Another way: that the *kāf* be in the accusative by a hidden verb explained by *nuʿīduh*, and *mā* is relative, meaning: We bring back the like of that which We began (nuʿīduh). And ﴿awwal khalq﴾ is an adverb of time for *badaʾnā* (We began), meaning: at the first time He created, or a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun of the relative clause which is dropped from the wording but retained in meaning. End of quotation.

The apparent reading is that the *kāf* is not disconnected as he mentioned; rather it is a preposition (governing a noun), and what follows it is a verbal (maṣdarī) clause, from which with the verb a verbal noun is formed that is in the genitive position after the *kāf*. ﴿Awwal khalq﴾ is the object of *badaʾnā*, and the meaning is: We bring back the first creation with a bringing back like Our beginning of it, that is, as We brought it out from non-existence into existence, We bring it back from non-existence into existence. In what al-Zamakhsharī proposed, he prepared *badaʾnā* to govern ﴿awwal khalq﴾ as an object, and separating it from that without necessity that calls for it, plus an omitted element that refers back explained by *nuʿīduh*, is a foreignism in the Book of God. As for his saying "another way: that the *kāf* be in the accusative by a hidden verb explained by *nuʿīduh*," it is very weak, because it is based on the *kāf* being a noun rather than a particle. This is not the view of the majority; this view was taken by al-Akhfash, and the *kāf* being a noun is the view of the Basrans, but it is not restricted to poetry.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it allows two meanings. One: that it is a report about the resurrection, meaning: just as We originated creation at first without a model, so We bring them into being again at another time, and We raise them from the graves. The second: that it is a report that every person will be raised on the Day of Resurrection in the state in which he came out into the world, and this is supported by the hadith: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised," and God's words ﴿as We began the first creation, We shall bring it back﴾. The *kāf* in ﴿as We began﴾ is connected to *nuʿīduh*. End of quotation.

*Waʿdan* (as a promise) is in the accusative as an object of a verbal noun emphasizing the content of the preceding declarative sentence. ﴿Surely We are ever the Doers﴾ is an emphasis on the certainty of the report, meaning: We are able to do it.

Regarding *al-Zabūr* (the Psalms): the apparent meaning is that it is the Psalms of David; this is said by al-Shaʿbī, and the meaning of this verse is present in the Psalms of David, and We read it in it. *Al-Dhikr* (the Reminder) is the Torah; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbās. It is also said: *al-Zabūr* is what came after the Torah of books, and *al-Dhikr* is the Torah. It is also said: *al-Zabūr* includes all the revealed books, and *al-Dhikr* is the Preserved Tablet. (*Al-Arḍ*) (the earth): Ibn ʿAbbās said: the land of Paradise. It is also said: the holy land. (*Yarithuhā*) (will inherit it): the community of Muḥammad (ﷺ).

The reference in ﴿Surely in this﴾ is to what is mentioned in this surah of reports, promises, threats, and most eloquent admonitions; a message, meaning a sufficiency by which one reaches good. It is also said: the reference is to the Qur'an as a whole. His being a mercy (peace be upon him) is because he came to them with what makes them happy. (*Lil-ʿālamīn*) (for the worlds): it is said to be specific to those who believed in him. It is also said: it is general, and his being a mercy to the unbeliever is in that He delayed their punishment and did not uproot the disbelievers with the chastisement. Ibn ʿAbbās said this is its meaning, and said: he was spared what befell other nations of transformation, sinking, drowning, and a shower of stones, and his affair was deferred to the Hereafter. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it may be that its meaning is ﴿We have not sent you﴾ to the worlds ﴿except as a mercy﴾, meaning: he is a mercy in himself, and a clear guidance; whoever takes it takes it, and whoever turns away from it turns away. End of quotation.

It is not permissible, according to the well-known view, for the preposition phrase after *illā* (except) to be governed by the verb before it, unless the governing verb is left without a complement, as in: "I have not passed except by Zayd." Al-Zamakhsharī said: you restrict a judgment to something, or you restrict something to a judgment, as in your saying: "Only Zayd is standing" and "Only Zayd stands." The two patterns have come together in this verse, because ﴿It is only revealed to me﴾ with its agent is like "Only Zayd stands," and ﴿that your God is one God﴾ is like "Only Zayd is standing." The benefit of their combination is the indication that the revelation to the Messenger (ﷺ) is restricted to God's singling out of oneness. End of quotation. As for what he mentioned about *innamā* (only), that it is for restricting what he mentioned, this is based on *innamā* being for exclusive restriction, and we have already established that it is not exclusive. *Innamā* together with *anna* is like *inna* with *kāna* and with *laʿalla*. Just as it does not confer exclusivity in comparison or in hoping, so it does not confer it with *anna*. As for his making *anna* (with an opened hamza) like its kasra-form, which indicates restriction, we know of no disagreement except regarding *innamā* with a kasra. With a fatḥa, *anna* is a verbal particle that with what follows forms a verbal noun; the clause after it is not an independent sentence. If *innamā* indicated exclusivity, it would follow that nothing was revealed to him except monotheism, and that is not correct, because other things were revealed to him besides monotheism. The verse is evidence that transmitted knowledge concurs with rational knowledge, and that transmission is one of the two paths to monotheism. It is permissible in *mā* in *innamā* that it be relative.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verse 101–112 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Do you then submit?﴾ This is an interrogative that carries the command to devote sincere monotheism (tawhid) and submission to Allah, the Exalted. (Ādhantukum) "I have informed you," and it carries the meaning of warning and admonition. ﴿On equal terms﴾: I did not single out one person over another. This notification (iidhan) is an announcement of the punishment that will befall those who turn away, and the triumph of Islam. But I do not know when that will be. (In) is negating, (adri) is suspended, and the interrogative clause is in the place of a accusative object of (adri). The interrogated element is placed later because it serves as the verse-ending (fasila); if the construction were (aqarib) ﴿what you are promised﴾ ﴿or is it far?﴾, it would not be a verse-ending. Often a ruling is given preference over something because of its being the verse-ending of a verse. In a narration from Ibn Amir, ﴿wa in adri﴾ is read with a fatha on the yaa in both verses, likening it to the yaa of possession in pronunciation, although it is the lam of the verb and is not vowelled with a fatha except by a governing element. Ibn Mujahid denied the fathah on this yaa. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, did not inform me of His knowledge and did not make me aware of it, and Allah is the All-Knowing, from whom nothing is hidden.

﴿And I do not know, perhaps it is a trial﴾: that is, perhaps the delay of this promised time is a test for you, to see how you act; or it is a postponement for you until a term, so that this is an argument against you, and so that the promise occurs at a time that is wisdom. (La'alla) here is also suspended, and the clause of hope is the object of the verb. The Kufans treat (la'alla) like (hal), so just as suspension occurs after (hal), it also occurs after (la'alla). I know of no one who held that (la'alla) is among the particles of suspension, although that is evident in it, as in His saying ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Shura: 17], and ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾ [Abasa: 3]. It was said: ﴿until a time﴾ means until the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: until the Day of Badr.

The majority read (Qul Rabbi), with the ba' in the kasra form as an imperative. Hafs read (qala), and Abu Ja'far read (Rabbu) with a damma. The author of al-Lawami said: this is on the basis that it is a singular vocative, and the particle of address has been omitted in what may be an attribute of any distant (noun), its domain being poetry. End of quote.

This is not the vocative of an indefinite noun addressed directly; rather, this is among the permitted dialects in (ya ghulami), where you build it on the damma while intending the possessive pronoun, when you have cut it off from the possessive, while you intend its form. So the meaning of (Rabbu) is "O my Lord." The majority read (uhkum) as an imperative from hakama. Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, al-Jahdari and Ibn Muhaysin read (Rabbi) with the yaa sukun, making it the superlative (af'al al-tafdil): "My Lord is most just," as a subject and predicate. A group read (ahkama) as a past-tense verb. The majority read (tasifun) with the taa of address. It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited to Ubayy (ʿalā mā yasifūn) with the yaa of the third person, and this was also narrated from Ibn Amir and Asim.

(p-342)﴿Surely those for whom the Best (reward) has already gone forth from Us, they will be kept far from it.﴾ ﴿They will not hear its faintest sound, and they will abide forever in what their souls desire.﴾ ﴿The Greatest Terror will not grieve them, and the angels will receive them: "This is your Day, which you were promised."﴾ ﴿On the Day We roll up the heaven like the rolling of the scroll for writings, just as We began the first creation, We shall bring it back. It is a promise binding upon Us; surely We are ever the Doers.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly written in the Psalms, after the Reminder, that the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants.﴾ ﴿Surely in this there is a message for a people who worship.﴾ ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds.﴾ ﴿Say: "It is only revealed to me that your God is one God. Will you then submit?"﴾ ﴿But if they turn away, say: "I have announced to you on equal terms, and I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far."﴾ ﴿Surely He knows what is spoken aloud and He knows what you conceal.﴾ ﴿And I do not know: perhaps it is a trial for you, and an enjoyment for a time.﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, judge with truth. And our Lord is the Most Merciful, whose help is sought against what you describe."﴾.

**Occasion of revelation of ﴿Surely those for whom the Best has already gone forth from Us﴾:** It is the statement of Ibn al-Zibaʿrā (Ibn al-Zibaʿrā) when he heard ﴿Surely you and what you worship besides God are the fuel of Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98]. He said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I have defeated you, by the Lord of the Ka'ba! Did not the Jews worship ʿUzayr, the Christians worship the Messiah, and the Banu Mulayh worship the angels?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "They worshipped the devils, who commanded them to do so." Then God revealed: ﴿Surely those for whom the Best has already gone forth from Us﴾. It is also said: when Ibn al-Zibaʿrā raised his objection, it was said to them: "Are you not an Arab people? Do you not know that *man* is for those who reason and *ma* is for what does not reason?" According to the first view, Ibn al-Zibaʿrā understood a generality from ﴿what you worship﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98], so God revealed ﴿Surely those for whom the Best has already gone forth﴾ as a specification of that generality. According to this second view, Ibn al-Zibaʿrā intended a sophistry, and he was answered that *man* is for those who reason and *ma* is for what does not reason, so his objection collapsed.

(al-Husna) is the most preferred quality in goodness; it is the feminine form of *al-aḥsan* (the best). It is either happiness, or the glad tidings of reward, or the granting of success in obedience. The apparent meaning of ﴿they will be kept far﴾ and what follows is that the one for whom the Best has gone forth will not enter the Fire. It is narrated that ʿAlī, may God honor his face, recited this verse and then said: "I am among them, and Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, Saʿd, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf." Then the prayer was called, and he got up dragging his garment, saying ﴿They will not hear its faintest sound﴾. The *ḥasīs* (faintest sound) is the sound perceived from the movement of bodies. This keeping far and the absence of hearing its sound is said to be before entering Paradise. It is also said: after their entry and settling in it. The *shahwa* (desire) is the soul's seeking of pleasure.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This is a description of them after their entry into Paradise, because the hadith implies that at the place of standing (on the Day of Judgment), Hell will give out a roar such that no prophet or king will remain except that he falls on his knees." The ﴿Greatest Terror﴾ is general to every dread that occurs on the Day of Resurrection, so the Day of Resurrection as a whole is ﴿the Greatest Terror﴾; and if it is specified by something, it must be intended as the greatest that it is for him. End of quotation.

It is also said: ﴿the Greatest Terror﴾ is the closing of the layer of Hell over its people; this was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk. It is said: it is the final blast (of the trumpet). It is said: it is the command concerning the people of the Fire to enter the Fire; this is narrated from Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Jurayj, and al-Ḥasan. It is said: it is the slaughter of Death. It is said: it is when it is called out: ﴿Be silent therein, and do not speak to Me﴾ [al-Muminun: 108]. It is said: ﴿On the Day We roll up the heaven﴾; this was mentioned by Makkī.

﴿And the angels will receive them﴾ with greetings of peace upon them. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās: the angels will receive them with mercy at their coming out of the graves, saying to them: ﴿This is your Day, which you were promised﴾, with honor, reward, and bliss.

Abu Jaʿfar read ﴿will not grieve them﴾ as the imperfect of *aḥzana* (a fourth-form verb), which is the dialect of Tamim; *ḥazina* is the dialect of Quraysh. The governing element of (the Day, when they will not be grieved) and (they will be received) is... Abu al-Baqāʾ permitted that it be a substitute for the omitted returning pronoun in (you were promised), so the governing element there would be ﴿you were promised﴾, meaning "is it promised to them?" Or it is an object of *udhkur* (mention), or an accusative by *aʿnī* (I mean). Al-Zamakhsharī permitted that the governing element be (the Terror), but this is not permissible, because (the Terror) is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and it has been described before taking its complement, so what was mentioned is not allowed. (p-343)

The majority read *nanṭawī* (We roll up) with the plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓama). A group among them, Shayba ibn Nisāḥ, read *yaṭwī* with a *yāʾ*, meaning God. Abu Hurayra and his companion, and Abu Zurʿa ibn ʿAmr ibn Jarīr, read it with two *ḍammas* and a doubled *lām*. Al-Aʿmash, Ṭalḥa, and Abu al-Simāk read *al-Sajl* with a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*. The meaning is: We bring back the first creation as We began it, making the return like the beginning in the power's dealing with both equally. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 21, verse 101–112 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Do you then submit?﴾ This is an interrogative that carries the command to devote sincere monotheism (tawhid) and submission to Allah, the Exalted. (Ādhantukum) "I have informed you," and it carries the meaning of warning and admonition. ﴿On equal terms﴾: I did not single out one person over another. This notification (iidhan) is an announcement of the punishment that will befall those who turn away, and the triumph of Islam. But I do not know when that will be. (In) is negating, (adri) is suspended, and the interrogative clause is in the place of a accusative object of (adri). The interrogated element is placed later because it serves as the verse-ending (fasila); if the construction were (aqarib) ﴿what you are promised﴾ ﴿or is it far?﴾, it would not be a verse-ending. Often a ruling is given preference over something because of its being the verse-ending of a verse. In a narration from Ibn Amir, ﴿wa in adri﴾ is read with a fatha on the yaa in both verses, likening it to the yaa of possession in pronunciation, although it is the lam of the verb and is not vowelled with a fatha except by a governing element. Ibn Mujahid denied the fathah on this yaa. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, did not inform me of His knowledge and did not make me aware of it, and Allah is the All-Knowing, from whom nothing is hidden.

﴿And I do not know, perhaps it is a trial﴾: that is, perhaps the delay of this promised time is a test for you, to see how you act; or it is a postponement for you until a term, so that this is an argument against you, and so that the promise occurs at a time that is wisdom. (La'alla) here is also suspended, and the clause of hope is the object of the verb. The Kufans treat (la'alla) like (hal), so just as suspension occurs after (hal), it also occurs after (la'alla). I know of no one who held that (la'alla) is among the particles of suspension, although that is evident in it, as in His saying ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Shura: 17], and ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾ [Abasa: 3]. It was said: ﴿until a time﴾ means until the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: until the Day of Badr.

The majority read (Qul Rabbi), with the ba' in the kasra form as an imperative. Hafs read (qala), and Abu Ja'far read (Rabbu) with a damma. The author of al-Lawami said: this is on the basis that it is a singular vocative, and the particle of address has been omitted in what may be an attribute of any distant (noun), its domain being poetry. End of quote.

This is not the vocative of an indefinite noun addressed directly; rather, this is among the permitted dialects in (ya ghulami), where you build it on the damma while intending the possessive pronoun, when you have cut it off from the possessive, while you intend its form. So the meaning of (Rabbu) is "O my Lord." The majority read (uhkum) as an imperative from hakama. Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, al-Jahdari and Ibn Muhaysin read (Rabbi) with the yaa sukun, making it the superlative (af'al al-tafdil): "My Lord is most just," as a subject and predicate. A group read (ahkama) as a past-tense verb. The majority read (tasifun) with the taa of address. It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited to Ubayy (ʿalā mā yasifūn) with the yaa of the third person, and this was also narrated from Ibn Amir and Asim.
